Requirement for Attestation by All Persons Arriving in the United States From Any Foreign Country via Transportation by Aircraft and Controlled Free Pratique for Airlines and Other Aircraft Operators Confirming That Such Persons Have Not Been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the Past 21 Days
Summary
Pursuant to
42 CFR 71.20
,
71.31(b)
, and
71.32(b)
, and as set forth in greater detail below, this Notice and Order prohibit the boarding of any person who is not otherwise subject to an exemption on any aircraft destined to the United States from a foreign country unless the person presents:
A signed attestation in paper or digital format confirming that the person has not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States.
This includes any flight arriving in the United States, regardless of whether the United States is its final destination or the flight is connecting through the United States en route to another country. This Order does not apply to overflights that do not land at any airport in the United States.
Further, pursuant to
42 CFR 71.31(b)
and as set forth in greater detail below, this Notice and Order operates as a controlled free pratique requiring an airline or other aircraft operator with an aircraft arriving into the United States to confirm to the U.S. Government that every person onboard the aircraft has completed and signed an attestation confirming that the person has not been in the DRC during the 21 days prior to boarding the flight to the United States as a condition of the airline or aircraft operator being granted permission to enter a U.S. port of entry, disembark persons, and begin operations with respect to arriving at a U.S. airport.
A parent or other authorized representative may complete and sign the required attestation on behalf of a person under 18 years of age. An authorized representative may also act on behalf of any person who is in their traveling party or any person who is unable to act on their own behalf (
e.g.,
by reason of age, or physical or mental impairment). An airline or aircraft operator employee or agent may assist with data entry or submission at the direction of the person or authorized representative.
The person must provide the airline or aircraft operator with a paper or digital copy of the completed attestation reflecting that the person has not been present in the DRC in the past 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States. The airline or aircraft operator must retain the paper or digital copy of each person's completed and signed attestation for at least 42 days after the person's flight departs for the United States from a foreign country and provide the attestation to the U.S. Government upon request.
CDC encourages airlines and aircraft operators to incorporate the attestation into paperless check-in processes. An airline or aircraft operator may use a third party (including a third-party digital application) to provide translations. However, an airline or aircraft operator has sole legal responsibility to ensure the accuracy of any translation and to comply with all other obligations under this Order. An airline or aircraft operator is responsible for any failure to comply with its responsibilities as set forth in this Order, including for actions of a third party used to help effectuate its compliance with this Order. As between the airline or aircraft operator and the U.S. Government, the airline or aircraft operator remains responsible for compliance with this Order regardless of the involvement of any third party.
Pursuant to
42 U.S.C. 268
, customs officers and U.S. Coast Guard officers will assist in the implementation of this Order. Other federal departments and agencies, including the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Department of Transportation, may also cooperate and assist with implementation of this Order consistent with their own legal authorities.
The U.S. Department of Justice may seek to prosecute individuals who knowingly and willfully submit false attestations in violation of
18 U.S.C. 1001
.
Relationship to Other Orders
This Order operates in addition to, and does not supersede, modify, or replace, other CDC orders currently in effect concerning Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, including the Order Suspending the Right to Introduce Certain Persons from Countries Where a Quarantinable Communicable Disease Exists issued pursuant to
42 U.S.C. 265
,
268
and
42 CFR 71.40
, as most recently continued. Nothing in this Order limits the authority of CDC, the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Transportation, or any other federal department or agency to take additional measures under their own separate legal authority.
Statement of Intent
This Order shall be interpreted and implemented to achieve the following paramount objectives:
Preservation of human life;
Preventing the introduction, transmission, and spread of the Ebola virus into the United States; and
Preserving the health and safety of crew members, passengers, airport personnel, and communities.
Definitions
21 days
for purposes of the individual attestation means a 21-day waiting period based on calendar days. Day 0 is the day the individual departed the DRC. Day 1 is the first full calendar day the individual is outside the DRC. A person who was present in the DRC may board a flight to the United States on day 22.
Aircraft
shall have the same definition as under
49 U.S.C. 40102(a)(6)
. “Aircraft” includes, but is not limited to, commercial, general aviation, cargo, and private aircraft destined for the United States from a foreign country.
Aircraft Operator
means an individual or organization causing or authorizing the operation of an aircraft.
Airline
shall have the same definition as under
42 CFR 71.1(b)
.
Attest/Attestation
means completion and signature of the attestation in Attachment A. Such attestation may be completed and signed in paper or digital form, including through electronic signature. The attestation is a statement, writing, entry, or other representation made under
18 U.S.C. 1001
.
Authorized representative
means a parent, guardian, travel companion, adult member of a person in the same traveling party or person authorized by the person required to complete and submit an attestation on the person's behalf. An airline or aircraft operator employee or agent who assists with data entry or submission at the direction of the person or authorized representative does not, solely by providing such assistance, become the authorized representative or provide the attestation on the person's behalf.
Foreign country
means anywhere that is not a state, territory, or possession of the United States.
(
printed page 68520)
Person(s)
means any of the persons (including passengers, air crew, or conveyance operators) on any aircraft destined for the United States from a foreign country. This includes crewmembers on official duty assigned by the airline or aircraft operator, including for activities that involve operation of aircraft or the positioning of crew not operating the aircraft (
e.g.,
on “deadhead” status)
Present/Presence
in the DRC means any physical presence, including entering or traveling through the country by air (excluding overflights), land, or sea. Presence also includes connecting through an airport in the DRC, even if the person did not disembark the plane or leave the airport.
United States
has the same definition as “United States” in
42 CFR 71.1(b)
, meaning “the 50 States, District of Columbia, and the territories (also known as possessions) of the United States, including American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.”
Exemptions
The following are exempt from the requirements of this Order:
Aircraft operators transporting passengers with Ebola disease pursuant to U.S. Government authorization and in accordance with CDC guidance.
Individuals for whom the CDC has issued an exemption based on humanitarian or other important government considerations,
e.g.,
emergency medical evacuations. Additional conditions may be placed on individuals granted such exemptions, including but not limited to, observing precautions during travel, providing consent to post-arrival monitoring, and/or self-quarantine after arrival in the United States, as may be directed by federal, state, territorial, tribal or local public health authorities to reduce the risk of disease transmission.
Background
A. Ebola Disease
Viral hemorrhagic fever refers to a group of severe illnesses caused by certain viruses that damage the body's blood vessels and affect the ability of the blood to clot properly. Viral hemorrhagic fevers include diseases such as Ebola, Marburg, and Lassa fever.
Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe and often fatal illness caused by one of the viruses in the Ebola family. Ebola disease outbreaks occur mainly in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and can spread rapidly in communities with limited healthcare resources. Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus is a rare form of Ebola first identified during an outbreak in Bundibugyo District, Uganda, in 2007. BVD is one of several species within the orthoebolavirus family and causes symptoms similar to other forms of Ebola, including fever, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and, in severe cases, hemorrhagic complications and organ failure. The disease spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated materials.
The incubation period for BVD is typically between 2 and 21 days, with most people developing symptoms within 4 to 10 days after exposure. During this incubation period, infected individuals do not spread BVD until symptoms begin.
Screening for BVD focuses on identifying symptoms and possible exposure history, such as recent travel to affected areas or contact with infected individuals. Patients with suspected BVD are evaluated for symptoms including fever, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding, and laboratory confirmation is performed using specialized tests such as PCR (polymerase chain reaction) to detect the virus in blood and other body fluid samples. Health authorities also use temperature checks and contact tracing to identify suspected cases, and quarantine and isolation procedures, as applicable, to prevent transmission.
There are currently no widely approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for BVD. Treatment mainly consists of supportive care, including intravenous fluids, electrolyte replacement, oxygen support, pain and fever management, and treatment of secondary infections. Early medical care significantly improves survival chances. Robust public health measures such as early detection, rapid isolation, strong infection prevention measures (
i.e.,
use of personal protective equipment [PPE]), and monitoring of contacts are critical to controlling outbreaks and reducing deaths. Clinical trials of monoclonal antibodies and of an existing vaccine approved for use to prevent disease caused by the Ebola Zaire virus are presently underway in the DRC.
[
1 2
]
However, experts expect it will be several months before these therapeutics are potentially available for wider use.
B. Ongoing Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak
The confirmed ongoing outbreak of BVD in the DRC continues to escalate in intensity. The outbreak remains centered in eastern DRC's Ituri Province, although cases have been identified in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé, Tshopo, North Ubangi, and South Ubangi provinces. This geographic expansion is concerning, particularly given that response efforts are still not at the scale required for outbreak containment. As of October 18, 2026, the DRC reports 9,455 confirmed cases and 4,561 deaths in 66 health zones across eight provinces.
The World Health Organization has reported substantial under-ascertainment of cases and persistent challenges with contact tracing. As of its most recent assessment, only approximately 20 percent of BVD cases were identified through follow-up of listed contacts, and approximately 40 percent were ultimately linked to a known chain of transmission, indicating substantial undetected transmission.
[
3
]
Surveillance challenges persist in the most heavily affected areas, with conflict and insecurity, weak health infrastructure, and relatively porous borders in the region complicating containment efforts. Although contact tracing efforts are underway, they remain insufficient and the daily follow-up necessary to rapidly detect symptomatic individuals and ensure their prompt isolation has not been achieved.
Persons who have unknowingly been infected with BVD may travel before becoming symptomatic. Such travelers may spread the virus beyond DRC and ultimately reach the United States. The DRC is connected to the global aviation network through a series of regional and international transit hubs that provide pathways into the United States. These international transportation corridors support continuous movement of travelers between Central and East Africa and major U.S. metropolitan centers, increasing the likelihood that persons exposed to Ebola disease could enter the United States before symptoms become apparent. Complex multi-leg
(
printed page 68521)
itineraries and the rapid pace of international travel create substantial challenges for identifying potentially infected persons before arrival.
The risk of BVD introduction into the United States is heightened by the virus's incubation period, which can extend up to 21 days, allowing infected persons to travel internationally while asymptomatic and therefore unlikely to be detected through routine symptom-based screening measures. The current outbreak has demonstrated this risk: for example, a physician infected while providing patient care in the DRC traveled internationally before becoming ill and was diagnosed only after arriving in France.
[
4
]
That case required extensive public health coordination, including federal, state, and local government efforts to identify, notify, and monitor potentially exposed U.S. citizens, demonstrating that a single infected traveler can impose significant cross-border public health response demands even without onward transmission occurring within the United States. Additionally, on October 6, 2026, the Kenya Ministry of Health announced the country's first BVD case and death in an individual who had traveled from DRC to Uganda, flown from Kampala to Nairobi on October 2, and was hospitalized before dying on October 5, 2026.
[
5
]
By October 19, 2026, Kenya had announced another seven cases had been confirmed in previously identified close contacts, reaching a total of eight BVD cases in Kenya, including the initial case that resulted in a death.
[
6
]
The interconnected nature of global air travel presents a credible pathway for BVD importation into the United States, underscoring the importance of aggressive surveillance, traveler monitoring, airport public health screening, healthcare preparedness, and rapid containment capabilities.
The ongoing outbreak has also demonstrated that substantial U.S. public health resources may be required to respond to an Ebola exposure or infection in any U.S. citizen. On July 10, 2026, CDC announced that an additional U.S. citizen working for a humanitarian organization in the DRC had tested positive for BVD.
[
7
]
The individual, who was not involved in direct patient care,
[
8
]
prompted an extensive U.S. public health response. CDC, in coordination with the humanitarian organization, initiated contact tracing, exposure risk assessments, and monitoring activities to identify high-risk contacts and evaluate potential exposures among humanitarian personnel who had recently returned to, or are planning to return to, the United States. The Department of State arranged medical evacuation outside of the DRC for treatment. This incident demonstrates that even when an infected U.S. citizen remains overseas, the outbreak can require substantial U.S. public health resources to identify, assess, and monitor potentially exposed individuals associated with international humanitarian operations.
Persons utilizing air transit pathways originating in the DRC include U.S. and non-U.S. citizens, regional migrants, foreign contract workers, humanitarian personnel, business travelers, crew members students, refugees, and third-country nationals moving through international aviation hubs in Africa, the Middle East, and Europe. Many travelers entering U.S.-bound itineraries from these pathways may do so under temporary visas, refugee or asylum processing mechanisms, international organizational travel, or multi-country itineraries that obscure their original point of departure. As a result, public health screening and border security systems face heightened operational complexity in identifying travelers with recent exposure histories linked to Ebola-affected regions, particularly when travelers transit through multiple jurisdictions prior to arrival at major U.S. metropolitan airports.
CDC has issued Travel Health Notices (THN) for affected countries and regions. Currently, there is a Level 4 THN for Ituri and Nord-Kivu Provinces of DRC (avoid all travel); a Level 3 THN for Haut-Uélé and Tshopo Provinces of DRC (reconsider nonessential travel); a Level 2 THN (practice enhanced precautions) for the remainder of the DRC and Uganda; and a Level 1 THN (practice usual precautions) for Nairobi, Kenya.
[
9
]
CDC modeling indicates that, absent rapid and sustained public health interventions, the outbreak could become one of the largest Ebola epidemics ever recorded.
[
10
]
The analysis further demonstrates that early identification of cases, contact tracing, isolation, and treatment of symptomatic persons, community engagement, and safe burial practices are critical to reducing transmission and mitigating outbreak growth.
[
11
]
CDC has concluded that the current outbreak is already the largest known outbreak of BVD and that large-scale, temporary public health measures are necessary to prevent further international spread of the disease and to reduce the risk of introduction of infected persons into the United States.
[
12
]
Commensurate with the deterioration of the epidemiological situation in the DRC, CDC escalated its response to the outbreak to a Level 1, the highest level within the agency's Graduated Response Framework.
[
13
]
CDC has determined that the risk profile presented by the DRC is materially distinct from that of other affected countries. The DRC remains the epicenter of the outbreak, with an estimated 80 percent of newly confirmed cases in Ituri Province not linked to known contacts, indicating substantial undetected community transmission. Contact tracing, surveillance, and containment capacity in the DRC are impaired by conflict, insecurity, weak health infrastructure, and porous borders. CDC has therefore determined that a categorical temporary measure directed at travelers with recent presence in the DRC is appropriately tailored to the elevated importation risk presented by that country. CDC will continue to monitor conditions in the DRC and other affected countries and may modify the scope of this Order accordingly.
Statement of Good Cause Under the Administrative Procedure Act
This Order is not a rule within the meaning of the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”) but rather is an action taken under the existing authority of
42 U.S.C. 264(a)
and
42 CFR 71.20
,
71.31(b)
, and
71.32(b)
, which were promulgated in accordance with
(
printed page 68522)
the APA after full notice and comment rulemaking and a delayed effective date. If this Order qualifies as a new rule under the APA, notice and comment and a delayed effective date are not required because there is good cause to dispense with prior public notice and comment and a delay in effective date.
See
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, (d)(3).
Based on the foregoing, I have determined that Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a highly transmissible quarantinable communicable disease designated as such by
Executive Order 13295
, as amended, is confirmed present in the DRC. I have also determined that Ebola disease if introduced into the United States would constitute a public health emergency. I have considered other alternatives, including reliance on airport-based public health screening, voluntary questioning, and expansion of the existing federal public health travel restrictions process, and have determined that these alternatives, standing alone or in combination, would not adequately address the identified risk given the disease's incubation period of up to 21 days, the substantial proportion of asymptomatic transmission-window travel, and the demonstrated capacity of a single infected person to consume substantial U.S. public health resources. Finally, I determine that requiring persons arriving in the United States via transportation by aircraft to submit an attestation confirming that they have not been present in the DRC during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States, combined with a conditioning of controlled free pratique on airline or aircraft operator confirmation of such attestations, is a necessary public health measure to protect the public health and prevent the introduction, transmission, and spread of Ebola disease into the United States. In making these determinations I have considered the prevalence of Ebola disease in the DRC, that country's limited ability to screen for the disease and engage in other mitigation measures, and the potential for spread in the United States. Accordingly, I find that any delay in issuing this Order beyond the minimum necessary for operationally feasible implementation would be contrary to the public's health in the United States and therefore the public's interest.
Any delay in the effective date, would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest for the additional reason that the outbreak in the DRC continues to expand, the 21-day incubation period of Ebola disease means that each additional day of pre-effective delay materially increases the risk that infected persons will board flights bound for the United States while asymptomatic, and public notice of a forthcoming attestation requirement could prompt individuals presently in the DRC to accelerate their travel to the United States before the requirement takes effect, defeating the purpose of this Order.
If any provision of this Order, or the application of any provision to any carriers, persons, or circumstances, shall be held invalid, the remainder of the provisions, or the application of such provisions to any carriers, persons, or circumstances other than those to which it is held invalid, shall remain valid and in effect.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, and for the reasons stated above, I hereby conclude that notice-and-comment rulemaking would defeat the purpose of the Order and endanger the public health, and is, therefore, impracticable and contrary to the public interest. For the same reasons, I have determined, consistent with
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, that there is good cause to make this Order effective immediately following the minimum delay necessary for the Order's implementation to be operationally feasible.
Action
For the reasons outlined above, I hereby determine that persons covered by this Order are at risk of transmitting Ebola disease and requiring persons to attest that they have not been present in the DRC during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States is needed as a public health measure to protect the health of other travelers and U.S. communities.
This Order shall remain in effect until rescinded or modified based on specific public health or other considerations, or until December 18, 2026, whichever occurs first. Any amendment or extension of this Order will be based on a review of then-current outbreak metrics, including case counts, geographic spread, community-transmission indicators, and containment capacity in affected countries.
1. Requirements for Airlines & Other Aircraft Operators
This Order conditions the grant of controlled free pratique on the airline and aircraft operator compliance measures specified below. This Order does not regulate landing rights, airspace access, or aircraft certification, which remain within the jurisdiction of the Department of Transportation, the Federal Aviation Administration, and other agencies exercising their respective legal authorities.
Any airline or other aircraft operator with persons who are not otherwise exempt from the requirements of this Order boarding a flight to the United States from a foreign country, shall:
A. Confirm to the U.S. Government, at or before the time of boarding, that all persons boarding or onboard the aircraft have completed and signed an attestation in paper or digital format confirming that they have not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days preceding their boarding a flight to the United States. For purposes of this requirement, “confirm” means that the airline or aircraft operator has reviewed the completed attestation from each covered person prior to boarding and has determined, based on the face of the attestation, that the attestation is complete and signed; and
B. Not board any person who has failed to complete and present such an attestation.
C. Retain a paper or digital copy each person's completed and signed attestation for at least 42 days after the person's flight departs for the United States from a foreign country and provide the attestation to the U.S. Government on request.
Any airline or other aircraft operator that fails to comply with section 1, “Requirements for Airlines & Other Aircraft Operators,” may be subject to criminal penalties under,
inter alia,
42 U.S.C. 270
and
271
and
42 CFR 71.2
, in conjunction with
18 U.S.C. 3559
and
3571
(providing for fines of up to $100,000 for individuals and $200,000 for organizations, and/or imprisonment of up to one year). CDC anticipates that separate compliance mechanisms may be established by the Transportation Security Administration pursuant to its own statutory authorities.
Any airline or other aircraft operator that fails to provide the U.S. Government the confirmation of completed attestations of all persons as outlined above will not receive controlled free pratique to enter a U.S. port of entry, disembark passengers, and begin operation with respect to arriving at an airport in the United States.
2. Requirements for Persons Traveling Via Transportation by Aircraft Who Are Not Otherwise Exempt
A. Complete and sign the attestation under penalty of law as provided by
18 U.S.C. 1001
which provides criminal penalties for knowingly and willfully submitting false statements to the U.S. government; and
(
printed page 68523)
B. Provide for confirmation the completed and signed attestation to the airline or other aircraft operator confirming that they have not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days preceding their boarding a flight to the United States.
The required attestation text is attached to this Order as Attachment A. Unless otherwise permitted by law, a parent or other authorized representative may present the required documentation on behalf of a person required to submit such an attestation.
Any person who fails to provide this attestation, or submits false or misleading information, may face a delay of travel, denial of boarding, or denial of boarding on future travel.
Any person who fails to comply with the requirements of section 2, “Requirements for Persons Traveling via Transportation by Aircraft,” may be subject to criminal penalties under,
inter alia,
42 U.S.C. 271
and
42 CFR 71.2
, in conjunction with
18 U.S.C. 3559
and
3571
. Willfully giving false or misleading information to the government may result in criminal penalties under,
inter alia,
18 U.S.C. 1001
. This Order shall be enforceable through the provisions of
18 U.S.C. 3559
,
3571
;
42 U.S.C. 243
,
268
,
270
,
271
; and
42 CFR 71.2
. The U.S. Department of Justice in its discretion may prosecute any individual who knowingly and willfully submits a false statement in violation of
18 U.S.C. 1001
.
Effective Date
This Order takes effect at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 3, 2026. For individuals intending to travel to the United States by air, the Order will apply to flights departing at or after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 3, 2026.
In testimony whereof, the Assistant Secretary for Health, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, has hereunto set his hand at _____, this October 28, 2026.
Dated:
Brian Christine,
Assistant Secretary for Health (ASH) and Head of the United States Public Health Service (USPHS) Commissioned Corps, Department of Health and Human Services
.
Authority
The authority for this order is Sections 361, 365, 368, and 369 of the Public Health Service Act (
42 U.S.C. 264
,
268
,
270
, and
271
), as amended.
Brian Christine,
Assistant Secretary for Health (ASH) and Head of the United States Public Health Service (USPHS) Commissioned Corps, Department of Health and Human Services.

Department of Commerce

(

The Department of Commerce will submit the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and clearance in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, on or after the date of publication of this notice. We invite the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. Public comments were previously requested via the
Federal Register
on January 27, 2026, during a 60-day comment period. This notice allows for an additional 30 days for public comments.
Agency:
Office of the Secretary, Department of Commerce.
Title:
Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments.
OMB Control Number:
0690-0037.
Form Number(s):
CD-350.
Type of Request:
Regular submission, Extension of approved information collection.
Number of Respondents:
20.
Average Hours per Response:
1 hour (30 minutes claimant/30 minutes physician).
Burden Hours:
20.
Needs and Uses:
An individual wishing to make a claim under the HAVANA Act IFR will fill out the “Patient Demographics” portion of the Eligibility Questionnaire (CD-350) and provide it to a physician currently certified with the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN), the American Osteopathic Board of Neurology and Psychiatry (AOBNP), the American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) or the American Osteopathic Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (AOBPMR). The board-certified physician will complete the form after examining the individual and reviewing their records and will fax or email the completed form to the Department. The physician's findings will be instrumental in determining the individual's eligibility for payment under the HAVANA Act.
As noted in the IFR, the Department believes that many respondents to this information are already known to the Department due to prior reporting. Nevertheless, the Department notes that this form, which will be available on
www.commerce.gov/​havana-act
, can be completed by any Department covered employee, covered individual, or covered dependent as a way of beginning an application for a HAVANA Act payment.
Respondents to this information collection are individuals who believe they are eligible for payment under the HAVANA Act (Section I of the form) and physicians responsible for evaluating their symptoms and impairment (Section II of the form).
Affected Public:
Individuals or Federal Government personnel.
Frequency:
One-time payment.
Respondent's Obligation:
Voluntary.
Legal Authority:
HAVANA Act of 2021 (
Pub. L. 117-46
).
This information collection request may be viewed at
www.reginfo.gov
. Follow the instructions to view the Department of Commerce collections currently under review by OMB.
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be submitted within 30 days of the publication of this notice on the following website
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
. Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function and entering either the title of the collection or the OMB Control Number 0690-0037.

Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary of Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is planning to submit an information collection request (ICR), “Motor Vehicle and Engine Compliance Program Fees (Renewal)” (EPA ICR No. 2080.09, OMB Control No. 2060-0545) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act Before doing so, EPA is soliciting public comments on specific aspects of the proposed information collection as described below. This is a proposed extension of the ICR, which is currently approved through July 31, 2027. An Agency may not conduct or sponsor and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 29, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments, referencing Docket ID Number EPA-HQ-OAR-2013-0119, to EPA online using
www.regulations.gov
(our preferred method), or by mail to: EPA Docket Center, Environmental Protection Agency, Mail Code 28221T, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460. EPA's policy is that all comments received will be included in the public docket without change including any personal information provided, unless the comment includes profanity, threats, information claimed to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Noah Goldberg, Implementation, Analysis, and Compliance Division, Diesel Engine Compliance Branch, Environmental Protection Agency, 2000 Traverwood, Ann Arbor, MI 48105; telephone number: (734) 214-4772; email address:
goldberg.noah@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This is a proposed extension of the ICR, which is currently approved through July 31,
(
printed page 68516)
2027. An agency may not conduct or sponsor and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
This notice allows 60 days for public comments. Supporting documents, which explain in detail the information that the EPA will be collecting, are available in the public docket for this ICR. The docket can be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
or in person at the EPA Docket Center, WJC West, Room 3334, 1301 Constitution Ave. NW, Washington, DC. The telephone number for the Docket Center is 202-566-1744. For additional information about EPA's public docket, visit
http://www.epa.gov/​dockets
.
Pursuant to section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA, EPA is soliciting comments and information to enable it to: (i) evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (ii) evaluate the accuracy of the Agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (iii) enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (iv) minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate forms of information technology. EPA will consider the comments received and amend the ICR as appropriate. The final ICR package will then be submitted to OMB for review and approval. At that time, EPA will issue another
Federal Register
notice to announce the submission of the ICR to OMB and the opportunity to submit additional comments to OMB.
Abstract:
As required by the Clean Air Act, EPA has regulations establishing emission standards and other requirements for various classes of vehicles, engines, and evaporative emission components. These regulations require that compliance be demonstrated prior to EPA granting a “Certificate of Conformity”. EPA charges fees for administering this certification program. In 2004, then in 2008 the fees program was expanded to include nonroad categories of vehicles and engines, such as several categories of marine engines, locomotives, non-road recreational vehicles, many nonroad compression-ignition and spark-ignition engines and evaporative emission components. Manufacturers and importers of covered vehicles, engines and components are required to pay the applicable certification fees prior to their certification applications being reviewed by the Agency. Under section 208 of the Clean Air Act (
42 U.S.C. 7542(c)
) all information, other than trade secret processes or methods, must be publicly available. Information about fee payments is treated as confidential information prior to certification.
Form Numbers:
3520-29.
Respondents/affected entities:
Manufacturers or importers of passenger cars, motorcycles, light trucks, heavy duty truck engines, nonroad vehicles or engines, and evaporative emissions components are required to receive a certificate of conformity from EPA prior to selling or introducing these products into commerce in the U.S.
Respondent's obligation to respond:
Required to obtain or retain a benefit (
40 CFR part 1027
).
Estimated number of respondents:
633 (total).
Frequency of response:
An average of approximately eight responses per respondent per year.
Total estimated burden:
1058 hours (per year). Burden is defined at
5 CFR 1320.03(b)
.
Total estimated cost:
$96,118 (per year), includes $15,179 annualized capital or operation and maintenance costs.
Changes in Estimates:
There is an increase of 36 hours in the total estimated respondent burden compared with the ICR currently approved by OMB. This increase is due to the greater number of responses in the number of certificates and, therefore, the number of fees paid from year to year. The estimate of the costs associated with the fees program have increased from $77,444 to $96,118 due to wage estimate increases, as well as an average higher pay grade for cert reps. The average increased due to employee progression, as well as attrition.
Byron Bunker,
Director,  Implementation, Analysis and Compliance Division.

AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Interim final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
On July 24, 2026, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new drug application for Simtriyo (centanafadine) for the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older, weighing at least 20 kg. The Department of Health and Human Services provided the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) with a scheduling recommendation to place centanafadine, chemically known as (1R,5S)-1-(naphthalen-2-yl)-3-azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane, in schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). In accordance with the CSA, as amended by the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act, DEA is hereby issuing an interim final rule placing centanafadine, including its salts, isomers (whether optical, positional, or geometric), and salts of such isomers whenever the existence of such salts, isomers, and salts of isomers is possible in schedule III of the CSA.
DATES:
This rule is effective October 30, 2026. Comments must be submitted electronically or postmarked on or before November 30, 2026. The electronic Federal Docket Management System will not accept comments after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the last day of the comment period.
Requests for hearing and waivers of an opportunity for a hearing or to participate in a hearing, together with a written statement of position on the matters of fact and law asserted in the hearing, must be received on or before November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Interested persons may file written comments on this rulemaking in accordance with
21 U.S.C. 811(j)(3)
and
21 CFR 1308.43(g)
. To ensure proper handling of comments, please reference “Docket No. DEA-1743” on all correspondence, including any attachments.
Electronic comments:

If you have received a Comment Tracking Number, your comment has been successfully submitted and there is no need to resubmit the same comment. Commenters should be aware that the electronic Federal Docket Management System will not accept comments after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the last day of the comment period.

Such requests must be sent to: Drug Enforcement Administration, Attn: Administrator, 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, Virginia 22152. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In this Interim Final Rule (IFR), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is adding centanafadine, including its salts, to schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA).
Posting of Public Comments
All comments received in response to this docket are considered part of the public record. DEA will make comments available for public inspection online at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
unless reasonable cause is given. Such information includes personal or business identifying information (such as name, address, State or Federal identifiers, etc.) voluntarily submitted by the commenter.
Commenters submitting comments which include personal identifying information (PII), confidential, or proprietary business information that the commenter does not want made publicly available should submit two copies of the comment. One copy must be marked “CONTAINS CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION” and should clearly identify all PII or business information the commenter does not want to be made publicly available, including any supplemental materials. DEA will review this copy, including the claimed PII and confidential business information, in its consideration of comments. The second copy should be marked “TO BE PUBLICLY POSTED” and must have all claimed confidential PII and business information already redacted. DEA will post only the redacted comment on
https://www.regulations.gov
for public inspection. DEA generally will not redact additional information contained in the comment marked “TO BE PUBLICLY POSTED.” The Freedom of Information Act applies to all comments received.
For easy reference, an electronic copy of this document and supplemental information to this IFR are available at
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Request for Hearing or Appearance; Waiver
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 811(j)(3)
, an interested person may “request a hearing.” Such proceedings are conducted pursuant to the provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),
5 U.S.C. 551-559
.
[
1
]
Interested persons, as defined in
21 CFR 1300.01(b)
, may file requests for a hearing in conformity with the requirements of
21 CFR 1308.44(a)
and
1316.47(a)
, and such requests must:
(1) state with particularity the interest of the person in the proceeding;
(2) state with particularity the objections or issues concerning which the person desires to be heard; and
(3) state briefly the position of the person with regard to the objections or issues. Any interested person may file a waiver of an opportunity for a hearing or to participate in a hearing in conformity with the requirements of
21 CFR 1308.44(c)
, together with a written statement of position on the matters of fact and law involved in any hearing.
[
2
]
All requests for hearings and waivers of participation, together with a written statement of position on the matters of fact and law involved in such hearing, must be sent to DEA using the address information provided above. The decision whether a hearing will be needed to address such matters of fact and law in the rulemaking will be made by the Administrator. If a hearing is needed, DEA will publish a notice of hearing on the IFR in the
Federal Register
.
[
3
]
Further, once the Administrator determines a hearing is needed to address such matters of fact and law in rulemaking, he will then designate an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) to preside over the hearing. The ALJ's functions shall commence upon designation, as provided in
21 CFR 1316.52
.
In accordance with
21 U.S.C. 811
and
812
, the purpose of a hearing would be to determine whether centanafadine meets the statutory criteria for placement in schedule III.
Legal Authority
Under the CSA, as amended in 2015 by the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act (section 2(b) of
Pub. L. 114-89
), DEA is required to commence an expedited scheduling action with respect to certain new drugs approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). As provided in
21 U.S.C. 811(j)
, this expedited scheduling is required where both of the following conditions apply: (1) The Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has advised DEA that a New Drug Application (NDA) has been submitted for a drug that has a stimulant, depressant, or hallucinogenic effect on the central nervous system (CNS), and that it appears that such drug has an abuse potential; and (2) the Secretary of HHS recommends that DEA control the drug in schedule II, III, IV, or V pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 811(a)
and
(b)
. In these circumstances, DEA is required to issue an IFR controlling the drug within 90 days.
Subsection 811(j)(2) states that the 90-day timeframe starts the later of (1) the date DEA receives HHS's scientific and medical evaluation and scheduling recommendation, or (2) the date DEA receives notice of the NDA approval by HHS. Subsection 811(j)(3) specifies that the rulemaking shall become immediately effective as an IFR without requiring DEA to demonstrate good cause therefore. Thus, the purpose of subsection 811(j) is to speed the process by which DEA schedules newly approved drugs that are currently either in schedule I or not controlled (but which have sufficient abuse potential to warrant control) so that such drugs may be marketed without undue delay following FDA approval.
[
4
]
Subsection 811(j)(3) further provides that the IFR shall give interested persons the opportunity to comment and to request a hearing. After the conclusion of such proceedings, DEA must issue a final rule in accordance with the scheduling criteria of
21 U.S.C. 811(b)
through
(d)
, and
812(b)
.
Background
Centanafadine is a new molecular entity with CNS activity, acting as a novel triple reuptake inhibitor that targets norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin. Its mechanism of action has some similarities to schedule II stimulants like cocaine.
On November 24, 2025, Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development and Commercialization, Inc. (Sponsor) submitted an NDA for centanafadine to FDA. On July 24, 2026, FDA approved the NDA for centanafadine for the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older, weighing at least 20 kg. Centanafadine will be formulated as extended-release capsules for once-daily oral administration.
Determination To Schedule Centanafadine
On July 18, 2026, DEA received from HHS a scientific and medical evaluation entitled “Basis for the Recommendation to Control Centanafadine and Its Salts in Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act” and a scheduling recommendation. Pursuant to 21 U.S.C.
(
printed page 68472)
811(b) and (c), this document contained an eight-factor analysis of the abuse potential, legitimate medical use, and dependence liability of centanafadine, along with HHS's recommendation to control centanafadine under schedule III of the CSA.
In response, DEA reviewed the scientific and medical evaluation and scheduling recommendation provided by HHS, along with all other relevant data, and completed its own eight-factor review pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 811(c)
. DEA concluded that centanafadine meets the
21 U.S.C. 812(b)(3)
criteria for placement in schedule III of the CSA.
Pursuant to subsection 811(j), and based on HHS's scheduling recommendation, the approval of the NDA by HHS/FDA, and DEA's determination, DEA is issuing this IFR to schedule centanafadine as a schedule III controlled substance under the CSA.
Included below is a brief summary of each factor as analyzed by HHS and DEA, and as considered by DEA in its scheduling action. Please note that both DEA and HHS analyses are available in their entirety under “Supporting Documents” in the public docket for this IFR at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
under Docket Number “DEA-1743.” Full analysis of, and citations to, the information referenced in the summary may also be found in the supporting and related material.
1. Its Actual or Relative Potential for Abuse
According to HHS, because centanafadine has not been legally marketed in the United States or any other country, the legitimate drug channels for centanafadine are limited to the research conducted with the drug, and to manufacturing facilities and the supply chain to produce centanafadine for legitimate drug research. HHS further notes that, because centanafadine has not been legally marketed in the United States or any other country, abuse of centanafadine would be limited to incidents during the conduct of clinical studies or following diversion of supplies from research or manufacturing activities of centanafadine. According to HHS, suspected diversion of centanafadine occurred in one of the thirty-seven clinical studies conducted during the development of centanafadine. Three subjects in the study were suspected of abusing or diverting centanafadine based on medication handling irregularities. DEA's National Forensic Laboratory Information System (NFLIS)-Drug
[
5
]
data show that there is no report of law enforcement encounters of centanafadine in the United States. Centanafadine is a triple reuptake inhibitor that targets the specific transporters of norepinephrine (NET), dopamine (DAT), and serotonin (SERT), and it is a CNS stimulant. HHS states that centanafadine produces self-administration in rats and full generalization to amphetamine in a rat drug discrimination study (
see
Factor 2). In two human abuse potential studies, centanafadine produced subjective responses that indicate the drug has rewarding properties (see Factor 2). Accordingly, its mechanism of action and reinforcing properties share similarities with schedule II stimulants, like cocaine and methylphenidate, with known abuse potential. Both FDA and DEA concluded that centanafadine has an abuse potential lower than those of schedule II stimulants.
2. Scientific Evidence of Its Pharmacological Effects, if Known In Vitro Studies
Based on
in vitro
binding and functional reports, HHS noted that centanafadine acts as a triple reuptake inhibitor that targets norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin to achieve its CNS stimulant effects.
Binding Affinity and Functional Study:
Centanafadine binds with high affinity to NET, SERT, and DAT, and inhibits the reuptake of these neurotransmitters. Conversely, its major metabolite, EB-10601, showed weak-to-no affinity for these three transporters, suggesting that it likely does not contribute to centanafadine's therapeutic efficacy. Neither compound showed significant activity at other CNS receptors measured.
[
6
]
Intracerebral Microdialysis Study:
Oral administration of centanafadine (3-30 mg/kg) in rats dose-dependently increased extracellular norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin in the prefrontal cortex, as well as dopamine and serotonin in the ventral striatum. These microdialysis findings support the mechanism of action for centanafadine as a triple reuptake inhibitor at NET, DAT, and SERT.
Preclinical Behavioral Studies
Drug Discrimination:
An HHS-reviewed drug discrimination study demonstrated that oral centanafadine fully generalizes to an amphetamine cue, indicating substantial potential for human abuse. In female rats trained to distinguish schedule II stimulant, amphetamine (0.3 mg/kg, intraperitoneal) from saline under a fixed-ratio (FR) 5 schedule, centanafadine achieved full generalization (76 percent) at the 10 mg/kg oral dose, producing a mean plasma concentration of 718 ng/mL, which is roughly half the human highest concentration (C
max
) (1460 ng/mL) achieved at a dose of 200 mg twice daily. Similar to schedule II stimulant methylphenidate (83 percent generalization at 5 mg/kg oral dose) and schedule IV stimulant phentermine (93 percent generalization at 3 mg/kg oral dose), centanafadine mimics the interoceptive stimulus effects of amphetamine, strongly indicating an inherent abuse liability.
[
7
]
Self-Administration:
An HHS-reviewed intravenous self-administration study demonstrated that centanafadine possesses rewarding properties that sustain reinforcement, signaling an inherent risk of human abuse. In rats trained on a FR5 schedule to self-administer cocaine (0.36 mg/kg/injection, maintained at 19 injections per session) or undergo saline extinction (not greater than 5 injections per session), centanafadine sustained self-administration above saline levels across all doses tested. The two highest doses produced a degree of self-administration of 13 injections per session at the 0.03 mg/kg/injection dose and 15 injections/session from the 0.10 mg/kg/injection dose (p < 0.001 for both compared to saline). Schedule II methylphenidate and unscheduled bupropion similarly sustained cocaine-like self-administration at their highest doses, though bupropion data was excluded from the final assessment due to its uncontrolled regulatory status. While the rate of centanafadine self-administration remained statistically lower than cocaine (maintained at 19 injections per session) across all doses (p < 0.001), centanafadine's capacity to
(
printed page 68473)
maintain active reinforcement mimics the profiles of schedule II stimulants, confirming its potential for abuse.
[
8
]
Pharmacological and Behavioral Studies in Human
Human Abuse Potential (HAP) studies assess a drug's abuse liability by comparing a test drug to active controls and placebos. As described in HHS's scientific and medical evaluation, two HAP studies were conducted by the drug sponsor to assess the abuse potential of centanafadine in participants who were non-dependent, recreational drug users.
The first HAP study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled, crossover trial that evaluated the oral abuse potential of immediate-release centanafadine (400 mg and 800 mg, representing 2 and 4 times the therapeutic levels) against placebo and active positive controls: immediate-release amphetamine (40 mg) and lisdexamfetamine (150 mg) in 36 healthy male, nondependent recreational stimulant users. Data from the study demonstrated that supratherapeutic doses of centanafadine produced positive subjective effects that were significantly greater than those by placebo and comparable to those by schedule II stimulants (amphetamine and lisdexamfetamine).
The second HAP study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled, single-dose crossover trial evaluating the oral abuse potential of immediate-release centanafadine (200, 400, and 800 mg) against a schedule II positive control (15 and 30 mg immediate-release amphetamine) and placebo in 61 healthy, nondependent recreational stimulant users. Unlike the first study, which focused exclusively on supratherapeutic doses, this second trial evaluated both therapeutic and supratherapeutic ranges by testing doses roughly equivalent to the final marketing therapeutic strengths (210 and 280 mg) alongside doses that were approximately 2 and 4 times higher than the therapeutic doses. Throughout each session, subjective responses were tracked using Visual Analogue Scales (VAS) and the Addiction Research Center Inventory (ARCI) scales, which measured stimulant-specific effects on the Amphetamine subscale (0-11 range) and the Benzedrine subscale (0-13 range).
Subjective Visual Analog Scale Outcomes
Primary Liking and Reinforcement:
Centanafadine produced responses just outside the placebo range that were statistically significantly lower than amphetamine, except when comparing 800 mg centanafadine to 15 mg amphetamine. For Overall Drug Liking, amphetamine demonstrated high scores that differed significantly from all centanafadine doses; meanwhile, centanafadine produced a dose-dependent shift toward drug disliking, with the 400-mg and 800-mg doses differing significantly from placebo. Similarly, on the “Take Drug Again” scale, amphetamine elicited a strong desire to take the drug again that was statistically significantly different than all centanafadine treatments.
Stimulant Profiles and Identification
ARCI-Amphetamine and ARCI-Benzedrine scales:
Centanafadine and amphetamine generated stimulant-like responses above placebo, with 30 mg amphetamine producing the highest scores across both measures. ARCI-Amphetamine scores reached 5.9 and 7.7 for the 15 and 30-mg doses of amphetamine, respectively, compared to scores of 5.1, 4.8, and 4.9 from the 200-, 400-, and 800-mg doses of centanafadine, respectively, and score of 2.8 from placebo. On the ARCI-Benzedrine scale, the 15- and 30- mg doses of amphetamine produced scores of 8.3 and 9.6, respectively, which were slightly higher than the scores of 7.3, 6.8, and 6.5 from the 200-, 400-, and 800-mg doses of centanafadine, respectively, and score of 5.6 from placebo.
Drug Similarity:
On the drug similarity question, centanafadine was categorized as a stimulant generally (either as amphetamine or cocaine), but it was more frequently identified as amphetamine than as cocaine; placebo was identified as any of the stimulants less than 10% of the time.
Adverse Events (AEs)
Euphoria and Stimulant Signs:
As described in detail in HHS's review,
[
9
]
oral administration of centanafadine exhibited classic stimulant-associated AEs. Both centanafadine and amphetamine produced comparable rates of euphoric mood, decreased appetite, anxiety, agitation, and bruxism (
i.e.,
teeth grinding or jaw clenching). However, amphetamine produced higher rates of hypervigilance, whereas centanafadine was uniquely associated with disorientation at higher doses, dose-dependent tremor, and somnolence (
i.e.,
drowsiness), as well as certain other negative AEs, including nausea and vomiting.
Centanafadine demonstrated a clinical abuse potential profile distinct from schedule II stimulants (amphetamine and lisdexamfetamine), as its detectable stimulant-like activity at supratherapeutic doses (2 and 4 times the therapeutic dose) produced drug liking that was statistically greater than placebo but less than the positive control drug, amphetamine. Furthermore, centanafadine elicited a clear lack of willingness to take the drug again, contrasting sharply with the robust liking and desire for repeat self-administration of amphetamine. Ultimately, the reinforcing properties of centanafadine at high exposure levels are effectively restricted by negative user experiences, limiting its relative abuse liability. Overall data from the two HAP studies demonstrated that supratherapeutic doses of centanafadine produced negative subjective responses and AEs, which are likely to limit the abuse potential of the drug relative to the schedule II drugs, amphetamine and lisdexamfetamine.
Adverse Events in Clinical Safety and Efficacy Studies With Centanafadine
Combined safety data from 19 Phase 1 studies (872 centanafadine-treated and 66 placebo-treated healthy subjects) revealed a very low incidence of abuse-related and psychiatric AEs, with most incidents occurring in under 2 percent of participants across all formulation groups. Stimulant-associated AEs exceeding a 2 percent incidence were concentrated primarily in the highest-exposure group (>400 mg sustained release [SR]) or with specific formulations.
Psychiatric and Mood Effects:
Euphoric mood occurred in only one subject (2.0 percent) receiving >400 mg SR (0.2-0.9 percent in lower doses; 0 percent in placebo). Altered mood appeared exclusively with other formulations (2.1 percent). Insomnia (4.1 percent) and hypervigilance (2.0 percent) were also highest in the >400 mg SR group.
Cardiovascular Effects:
Tachycardia occurred in 4.1 percent of subjects receiving >400 mg SR (0-1.3 percent in lower doses; 0 percent in placebo).
Gastrointestinal and Appetite Effects:
Decreased appetite was most prevalent in the >400 mg SR cohort (10.2 percent), followed by other formulations (2.1
(
printed page 68474)
percent) and <329 mg extended-release (2.0 percent). Gastrointestinal symptoms peaked in the >400 mg SR group, led by nausea (14.3 percent), abdominal discomfort (8.2 percent), and diarrhea (10.2 percent).
Human Accidental Overdose and Diversion
Across 37 clinical trials evaluating centanafadine, HHS reported zero instances of drug overdose and suspected cases of drug diversion from one clinical site. In a multicenter, 52-week, open-label Phase 3 trial evaluating the long-term safety of centanafadine SR (400 mg total dose daily) in 662 adults with ADHD, three participants exhibited medication handling irregularities involving suspected or documented abuse or diversion, leading to their removal. Specifically, one participant was disqualified at Week 8 for suspected diversion after a second occurrence of lost or stolen medication, a second participant was removed after accelerating their intake to consume an entire 30-tablet supply within 9 days, and a third participant was discharged after failing a urine drug screen and subsequently claiming to have lost 10 tablets down a drain upon learning of their termination.
In summary, centanafadine is a new molecular entity that exhibits a pharmacological profile similar to that of cocaine (schedule II), functioning as a triple reuptake inhibitor of NET, DAT, and SERT. Preclinical drug discrimination studies in rats demonstrate that centanafadine produces interoceptive effects similarly to amphetamine (schedule II), matching the profiles of established stimulants like methylphenidate (schedule II) and phentermine (schedule IV). HAP studies indicate that centanafadine's subjective stimulant effects are generally less intense than those of amphetamine or lisdexamfetamine, leading to an overall clinical assessment of low misuse potential; however, the drug's administration remains associated with classic stimulant-type AEs. Consequently, based on a comprehensive review of
in vitro
testing, animal self-administration, drug discrimination, HAP studies, and clinical safety profiles, both HHS and DEA concluded that centanafadine possesses abuse potential and requires control under the CSA.
3. The State of Current Scientific Knowledge Regarding the Drug or Other Substance
Centanafadine, chemically known as (1R,5S)-1-(naphthalen-2-yl)-3-azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane, is a new molecular entity. Centanafadine drug products are formulated as proportionally similar, extended-release capsules in 140 mg, 210 mg, and 280 mg free base strengths (equivalent to 164.4 mg, 246.6 mg, and 328.8 mg hydrochloride salt, respectively). Each capsule utilizes a multi-bead delivery system distributed as 12.2 percent immediate-release, 43.9 percent delayed-release, and 43.9 percent sustained-release beads. According to HHS, chronic once-daily administration of centanafadine (140 mg to 280 mg) results in a slightly greater than dose-proportional increase in C
max
and Area Under the Curve, with peak plasma concentrations occurring approximately 5 hours post-dose. Steady state is achieved by day 2 with minimal drug accumulation and a mean elimination half-life of 5.2 hours. The drug is primarily metabolized by monoamine oxidase A into an inactive primary lactam metabolite, with excretion occurring via urine (88 percent) and feces (7 percent). Notably,
in vitro
dissolution testing demonstrates a risk of alcohol-induced dose-dumping.
As discussed in the background section, centanafadine has a currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States because it has been approved by FDA.
4. Its History and Current Pattern of Abuse
Centanafadine has no history of legal or illegal marketing globally, and current data do not reflect an actual real-world pattern of abuse. While distributed for clinical trials and research, evidence of diversion from legitimate channels remains minimal. For instance, a Phase 3 study evaluating centanafadine SR (400 mg daily) in 662 adults with ADHD reported only three subjects with medication handling irregularities involving suspected or known abuse or diversion (
see
Factor 2). Consequently, the assessment of abuse liability of centanafadine relies entirely on nonclinical and clinical studies, which collectively indicate a lower potential for abuse than schedule II stimulants, such as amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, and methylphenidate. Consistent with the status of centanafadine as a new molecular entity, DEA's parallel search of NFLIS-Drug yielded zero records of law enforcement encounters.
In summary, pharmacological data on centanafadine show that it produces abuse-related effects and has an abuse potential lower than those of schedule II stimulants.
5. The Scope, Duration, and Significance of Abuse
Centanafadine has been not marketed in any country and remains unavailable in the United States, resulting in limited abuse data. Because nonclinical and clinical evaluations indicate that centanafadine possesses an abuse liability profile that overlaps with known schedule II stimulants, there is a risk of post-marketing diversion and abuse. DEA's comprehensive search of law enforcement data yielded zero domestic law enforcement encounters involving centanafadine. However, based on cumulative pharmacology data, centanafadine is anticipated to possess a post-marketing abuse potential that is less than those of schedule II stimulants, such as amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, and methylphenidate.
6. What, if Any, Risk There Is to the Public Health
A drug's abuse potential is a key indicator of its overall risk to public health risk. HHS stated that, while centanafadine possesses an abuse potential comparable to those of schedule II stimulants (
e.g.,
cocaine, amphetamine, and methylphenidate), it is likely that centanafadine will exhibit a lesser abuse profile and present fewer public health risks than those of schedule II stimulants based on dependency data and negative AEs reported in studies. To evaluate public health risk associated with centanafadine, HHS analyzed clinical trial AEs, overdose data, and abuse potential studies and confirmed moderate signals that centanafadine poses some public health risks but to a lesser degree than those posed by schedule II stimulants.
In summary, data from nonclinical and clinical studies indicate that centanafadine's abuse potential and public health risks are comparable, but to a lesser degree, than to those of schedule II stimulants.
7. Its Psychic or Physiological Dependence Liability
Psychic (or psychological) dependence is a state similar to addiction and can be informed by animal self-administration studies, HAP studies and AE reports.
HHS cited investigations that demonstrate that while centanafadine generates clear rewarding properties in both preclinical and clinical studies, centanafadine concurrently elicits dose-dependent negative subjective effects in humans. Collectively, these findings show that it is likely that centanafadine
(
printed page 68475)
can produce psychological dependence, but likely to a lesser degree than with schedule II stimulants, such as amphetamine and cocaine.
Physical dependence develops from physiological adaptation to repeated drug use and manifests as withdrawal symptoms after abrupt drug discontinuation or reduction of a drug. According to HHS, experimental animal data evaluating chronic administration profiles for centanafadine are currently limited. Although the NDA applicant submitted two physical dependence studies in rats, HHS concluded that these evaluations were invalid for characterizing withdrawal potential, because the utilized dosing regimens failed to achieve systemic plasma concentrations matching therapeutic exposures in humans.
HHS reviewed withdrawal data from two Phase 3 clinical trials in adults with ADHD. Following abrupt discontinuation of centanafadine SR (200 mg or 400 mg daily), patients were monitored for 10 days using the Study Medication Withdrawal Questionnaire (SMWQ). SMWQ scores were indistinguishable between the active treatment and placebo groups at all time points. Based on these data, HHS concluded that centanafadine does not induce a withdrawal syndrome, indicating that chronic therapeutic administration followed by abrupt cessation does not produce physical dependence.
8. Whether the Substance Is an Immediate Precursor of a Substance Already Controlled Under the CSA
Centanafadine is not an immediate precursor of any controlled substance, as defined by
21 U.S.C. 802(23)
.
Conclusion:
After considering the scientific and medical evaluation and scheduling recommendation provided by HHS, as well as DEA's own eight-factor analysis, DEA has determined that these facts and all relevant data constitute substantial evidence of potential for abuse of centanafadine. As such, DEA hereby schedules centanafadine as a controlled substance under the CSA.
Determination of Appropriate Schedule
The CSA lists the findings required to place a drug or other substance in any particular schedule (I, II, III, IV, or V).
[
10
]
After consideration of the analysis and recommendation of the Assistant Secretary for Health of HHS and review of all available data, the Administrator of DEA, pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 812(b)
(3-), finds that:
(1) Centanafadine has a potential for abuse less than the drugs or other substances in schedules I and II.
Centanafadine is a novel triple reuptake inhibitor that targets NET, DAT, and SERT and is a CNS stimulant. While its mechanism of action shares similarities with those of schedule II stimulants, preclinical and clinical data demonstrate that centanafadine possesses an abuse potential lower than those of substances in schedules I and II. In animal self-administration and drug discrimination models, centanafadine produced reinforcing and interoceptive effects similar to known schedule II stimulants, including cocaine, amphetamine, and methylphenidate. Similarly, in two HAP studies, centanafadine elicited positive subjective responses that were significantly greater than those of placebo, closely approximating or falling slightly below those of amphetamine and lisdexamfetamine. However, centanafadine produced a dose-dependent increase in negative subjective responses and a higher prevalence of AEs like nausea from supratherapeutic doses. Overall, the evidence from nonclinical and clinical evaluations indicates that centanafadine possesses an abuse liability lower than those of schedule II controlled substances.
(2) Centanafadine has a currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States.
Centanafadine was approved by FDA for the treatment of ADHD in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older weighing at least 20 kg. Thus, centanafadine has a currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States.
(3) Abuse of centanafadine may lead to moderate or low physical dependence or high psychological dependence.
According to HHS, therapeutic use of centanafadine did not produce a withdrawal syndrome in patients who were abruptly discontinued from the drug following chronic use. However, the ability of centanafadine to produce positive subjective responses at supratherapeutic doses suggests that centanafadine can produce psychic dependence, although this may be mediated by concurrent negative subjective responses and AEs. In contrast, schedule II drugs amphetamine and lisdexamfetamine produced positive responses without comparable negative responses. Overall, these data suggest that centanafadine has a dependence potential less than that of certain schedule II stimulants and may lead to moderate or low physical dependence or high psychological dependence.
Based on these findings, the Administrator concludes that centanafadine and its salts warrant control in schedule III of the CSA.
[
11
]

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Request for information.
SUMMARY:
HUD is issuing this Request for Information (RFI) to solicit feedback from stakeholders on the Melania Trump Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) initiative. HUD will use the information gathered through this RFI to make recommendations to Congress (1) to improve program operations; (2) to assist youth in navigating the housing search process and preventing returns to homelessness after the subsidized rental assistance sunsets; and (3) on how Federal, State, and local stakeholders can best support participants as they transition from foster care to successful adulthood.
DATES:
Comments are requested on or before December 14, 2026. Late-filed comments will be considered to the extent practicable.

https://www.regulations.gov
.
To receive consideration as public comments, comments must be submitted through one of the two methods specified below. All submissions must refer to the docket number and title above.

Electronic Submission of Comments.

.
