SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The Melania Trump Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) was established in 2019 in response to the advocacy of foster youth and alumni regarding the need for housing assistance for young people upon their exit from foster care. According to the Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System, on average 15,000 young people age-out of foster care each year, and nearly 25 percent of youth responding to the National Youth in Transition Database report experiencing homelessness after leaving foster care. Yet, there were no Federal housing resources solely dedicated to serving this population.
Prior to the establishment of FYI, the primary Federal housing resource for young people transitioning out of foster care was the Family Unification Program (FUP). Through public housing agencies (PHAs), FUP provides housing choice vouchers (HCVs) that can be issued to either child welfare-involved families or youth transitioning out of foster care.
[
1
]
FUP participants use their HCVs to rent housing in the private market and generally pay 30 percent of their adjusted monthly income towards rent while the voucher pays the remaining portion of the rent. However, FUP vouchers are only available in a small number of communities
[
2
]
and have been primarily used to assist child welfare-involved families, rather than youth transitioning out of foster care. When FYI was established in 2019, 95 percent of FUP vouchers were being used to serve child welfare-involved families, and the remaining 5 percent were being used to serve youth transitioning out of foster care.
FYI provides a dedicated source of vouchers for youth transitioning out of foster care. Since fiscal year (FY) 2020, Congress has appropriated a total of $165 million for new incremental FYI vouchers. Further, in FY 2021, Congress codified an on-demand distribution mechanism for FYI vouchers, meaning that any of the more than 2,000 PHAs administering the HCV program can establish an FYI program and request FYI vouchers on a rolling basis to serve youth as they are identified.
[
3
]
This enables HUD to provide young people with FYI vouchers that are timed with their emancipation from foster care so that they do not experience homelessness when they leave care.
To establish an FYI program, a PHA must enter into a partnership agreement with a public child welfare agency (PCWA). Under the partnership agreement, the PHA provides the youth with FYI voucher assistance for 36 months, which may be extended for up to an additional 24 months if the youth is working toward economic self-sufficiency or meets one of the statutory exceptions to this requirement.
[
4
]
The
(
printed page 68535)
PCWA provides or secures the provision of supportive services for the youth for 36 months. The combination of time-limited rental assistance and supportive services is intended to provide youth with a platform to move toward economic self-sufficiency.
Since the rollout of FYI, HUD has allocated more than 9,000 FYI vouchers to assist individual youth. Yet, HUD recognizes that many more youth can benefit from the program. While FYI has experienced steady growth with the program being administered by 373 PHAs in 48 states and the U.S. Virgin Islands as of June 2026 Voucher Management System (VMS) data, there are still many communities where youth cannot access FYI. Further, as of June 2026 VMS data, eligible youth are utilizing only 64 percent of the more than 8,000 available FYI vouchers to lease a unit.
HUD has heard anecdotally that the uptake of FYI vouchers has been limited due to various administrative barriers that communities and young people face when trying to access FYI. Through this RFI, HUD is interested in learning what statutory, regulatory, and policy requirements are preventing communities from participating in FYI; what barriers young people face in accessing and utilizing an FYI voucher; and what changes can be made to reduce these barriers. Since FY 2024, Congress has provided HUD with the authority to establish waivers and alternative requirements related to the administration of waiting lists, local preferences, the initial term and extensions of tenant-based vouchers, and the timing of referral of youth leaving foster care, in order to reduce barriers to accessing and utilizing an FYI voucher. HUD implemented this waiver authority through Notice PIH 2025-08. HUD is interested in learning whether statutory or regulatory barriers remain and, if so, what statutory changes and/or waiver authority for the HCV program or FYI program beyond that which has already been provided would help increase utilization of FYI. HUD is also interested in learning how PHAs are taking advantage of the changes that were recently made through Notice PIH 2026-19 to help expand access to FYI, specifically the elimination of the utilization threshold and the removal of the cap on the number of FYI vouchers that can be requested.
HUD has also heard that the lack of dedicated Federal resources for supportive services can pose a barrier to establishing an FYI program, particularly in smaller, rural communities where there are few or no local resources for supportive services. HUD welcomes comments on how Federal resources can be better targeted or coordinated to reduce these barriers and support youth as they transition from foster care to successful adulthood. Additionally, HUD is interested in feedback on what changes can be made to the program to ensure that it provides a platform for youth to achieve economic self-sufficiency consistent with the goals of the Fostering the Future initiative established under
Executive Order 14359
,
Fostering the Future for American Children and Families.
II. Purpose of This Request for Information
HUD is interested in promoting and strengthening FYI and supporting the goals of the Fostering the Future initiative established under
Executive Order 14359
,
Fostering the Future for American Children and Families.
HUD will share the information received through this RFI with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and separately consult with HHS on these topics. In accordance with Senate Report 119-47, HUD will use the information gathered through this RFI and its consultation with HHS to issue a report to Congress with its recommendations: (1) to improve program operations; (2) to assist youth in navigating the housing search process and preventing returns to homelessness after the subsidized rental assistance sunsets; and (3) on how Federal, State, and local stakeholders can best support participants as they transition from foster care to successful adulthood.
III. Request for Information
Senate Report 119-47 requests that HUD consult with stakeholders on FUP, which includes FYI. While FUP serves two eligible populations—families and youth—HUD interprets the Senate Report language as being specific to the youth population served under FUP. For example, the Senate Report suggests that HUD consult with stakeholders on statutory time limits, which only apply to the youth population served under FUP. Further, the Senate Report asks HUD to use the information gathered through the stakeholder consultations to make recommendations to Congress on areas that are specific to youth (
i.e.,
assisting youth in navigating the housing search process, preventing returns to homelessness after the subsidized rental assistance ends, and supporting participants as they transition from foster care to successful adulthood). Therefore, HUD is issuing this RFI to solicit feedback on FYI specifically from current and former foster youth, PHAs, PCWAs, experts on child welfare, and other stakeholders regarding any potential program challenges due to statutory time limits, statutory criteria, policy definitions, or other operational aspects of FYI. While this RFI focuses on FYI, HUD also welcomes comments from PHAs that do not participate in FYI but administer FUP vouchers issued to youth, particularly those administering the FUP-FSS demonstration established under Notice PIH 2016-01 (
https://www.hud.gov/​sites/​documents/​16-01pihn.pdf
). HUD also welcomes comments from PHAs that do not currently participate in FYI regarding barriers to implementing an FYI program.
Consistent with Senate Report 119-47, HUD is requesting information on the topics below but welcomes comments on all aspects of FYI.
Statutory time limits.
By statute, a youth may receive FYI assistance for 36 months, which may be extended for up to an additional 24 months if the youth meets one of the following criteria:
1. The youth is participating in an FSS program under section 23 of the U.S. Housing Act of 1937;
2. If the youth is unable to enroll in an FSS program, the youth engaged in education, workforce development, or employment activities for at least 9 months of the 12-month period preceding the extension; or
3. The youth meets one of the following exceptions: the youth is a parent or other household member responsible for the care of a dependent child under the age of 6 or for the care of an incapacitated person; the youth is a person who is regularly and actively participating in a drug addiction or alcohol treatment and rehabilitation program; or the youth is a person who is incapable of complying with the requirement to participate in an FSS program or engage in education, workforce development, or employment activities, as applicable, due to a documented medical condition.
Questions for consideration:
Is 36 months, with an opportunity for a 24-month extension, the appropriate amount of time for youth to achieve self-sufficiency? If not, what would be the appropriate amount of time?
Have youth been able to take advantage of the 24-month extension? If not, why not?
Are there other types of self-sufficiency activities that should qualify youth for the 24-month extension in addition to those already recognized under the law?
(
printed page 68536)
Are there unique challenges for PHAs to administer a time-limited voucher in comparison to regular vouchers?
Statutory criteria.
By statute, a youth must meet the following criteria to be eligible for FYI:
1. Is at least 18 years of age and not more than 24 years of age;
2. Has left foster care, or will leave foster care within 180 days,
[
5
]
in accordance with a transition plan described in section 475(5)(H) of the Social Security Act; and
3. Is homeless or at risk of becoming homeless at age 16 or older.
Questions for consideration:
Does the age eligibility requirement pose a barrier to otherwise eligible youth accessing FYI?
HUD recently extended the referral timeframe from 90 days to 180 days prior to when a youth will transition out of foster care in order to allow more time for the youth to find housing with an FYI voucher prior to leaving foster care. Is 180 days enough time or would another timeframe be more appropriate?
While not required by statute, HUD has historically defined “homeless” and “at risk of becoming homeless” in the FYI program using the definitions for “homeless” and “at risk of homelessness” in the Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG) program and the Continuum of Care (CoC) program. In the most recent FYI notice,
[
6
]
HUD no longer uses the ESG and CoC definition of “at risk of homelessness” verbatim but has made several changes to the definition to expand who is considered “at risk of becoming homeless” for FYI vouchers awarded through the non-competitive process. Specifically, HUD revised the definition to change the income eligibility requirement from 30 percent of area median income to 50 percent of area median income, removed the requirement to not have sufficient resources or support networks immediately available to prevent moving to an emergency shelter or another place described in the ESG and CoC definition of “homeless,” and revised several items on the list of additional conditions. Are these the appropriate definitions to apply or should HUD use different definitions of “homeless” and “at risk of becoming homeless” in the FYI program?
Policy definitions.
The policy definitions applicable to FYI can be found in the various funding notices for the program.
[
7
]
Most significantly, the funding notices establish policies in the following areas: partnership agreements, supportive services, and youth prioritization.
Questions for consideration:
What are changes that HUD can make in these policy areas to help facilitate the provision of FYI and better support youth?
Operational aspects:
HUD requests information on any other operational aspects of FYI that could be improved.
Questions for consideration:
What changes can be made to FYI to better assist youth in navigating the housing search process?
What changes can be made to FYI to better prevent youth from returning to homelessness after the subsidized rental assistance sunsets?
How can Federal, State, and local stakeholders best support FYI youth?
What barriers do communities face when trying to establish an FYI program?
What barriers do youth face in accessing and utilizing an FYI voucher?
Does the lack of dedicated Federal resources for supportive services pose a barrier to establishing an FYI program, and how can Federal resources be better targeted or coordinated to support youth as they transition from foster care to successful adulthood?
Since FY 2024, Congress has provided HUD with the authority to establish waivers and alternative requirements related to the administration of waiting lists, local preferences, the initial term and extensions of tenant-based vouchers, and the timing of referral of youth leaving foster care, in order to reduce barriers to accessing and utilizing an FYI voucher. HUD implemented this waiver authority through Notice PIH 2025-08. Are there statutory changes and/or waiver authority for the HCV program or FYI program beyond that which has already been provided that would help increase utilization of FYI? If yes, please explain.
How are PHAs taking advantage of the changes that were recently made through Notice PIH 2026-19 to help expand access to FYI, specifically the elimination of the utilization threshold and the removal of the cap on the number of FYI vouchers that can be requested?
What are other aspects of FYI that could be improved?
HUD is also interested in feedback on what changes can be made to the program to ensure that it provides a platform for youth to achieve economic self-sufficiency consistent with the goals of the Fostering the Future initiative established under
Executive Order 14359
,
Fostering the Future for American Children and Families.
Benjamin Hobbs,
Assistant Secretary for Public and Indian Housing.

title: Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended To Deliver Drugs and Biological Products; Revised Draft Guidance for Industry; Availability
abstract: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or Agency) is announcing the availability of a revised draft guidance for industry entitled "Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products." This revised draft guidance revises and replaces the draft guidance entitled "Essential Drug Delivery Outputs Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products" announced in the Federal Register on July 1, 2024 (89 FR 54470). In accordance with its mission of protecting, promoting, and advancing public health, this guidance addresses key aspects of drug delivery performance information for devices, and combination products that include device constituent parts, intended for delivery of a human drug, including a biological product (herein referred to as drug delivery devices). This guidance provides recommendations for development and organization of device drug-delivery performance information and data to improve the consistency of this information in applications and to facilitate transparency and predictability in development and regulatory review. The guidance is intended to facilitate and streamline development and lifecycle management of drug delivery devices.
dates: Submit either electronic or written comments on the revised draft guidance by January 28, 2027 to ensure that the Agency considers your comment on this revised draft guidance before it begins work on the final version of the guidance.

AGENCY:
Food and Drug Administration, HHS.
ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or Agency) is announcing the availability of a revised draft guidance for industry entitled “Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products.” This revised draft guidance revises and replaces the draft guidance entitled “Essential Drug Delivery Outputs Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products” announced in the
Federal Register
on July 1, 2024 (
89 FR 54470
). In accordance with its mission of protecting, promoting, and advancing public health, this guidance addresses key aspects of drug delivery performance information for devices, and combination products that include device constituent parts, intended for delivery of a human drug, including a biological product (herein referred to as
drug delivery devices
). This guidance provides recommendations for development and organization of device drug-delivery performance information and data to improve the consistency of this information in applications and to facilitate transparency and predictability in development and regulatory review. The guidance is intended to facilitate and streamline development and lifecycle management of drug delivery devices.
DATES:
Submit either electronic or written comments on the revised draft guidance by January 28, 2027 to ensure that the Agency considers your comment on this revised draft guidance before it begins work on the final version of the guidance.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments on any guidance at any time as follows:
Electronic Submissions
Submit electronic comments in the following way:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments. Comments submitted electronically, including attachments, to
https://www.regulations.gov
will be posted to the docket unchanged. Because your comment will be made public, you are solely responsible for ensuring that your comment does not include any confidential information that you or a third party may not wish to be posted, such as medical information, your or anyone else's Social Security number, or confidential business information, such as a manufacturing process. Please note that if you include your name, contact information, or other information that identifies you in the body of your comments, that information will be posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
If you want to submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made available to the public, submit the comment as a written/paper submission and in the manner detailed (see “Written/Paper Submissions” and “Instructions”).
Written/Paper Submissions
Submit written/paper submissions as follows:
Mail/Hand delivery/Courier (for written/paper submissions):
Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852.
For written/paper comments submitted to the Dockets Management Staff, FDA will post your comment, as well as any attachments, except for information submitted, marked and identified, as confidential, if submitted as detailed in “Instructions.”
Instructions:
All submissions received must include the Docket No. FDA-2024-D-2560 for “Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products.” Received comments will be placed in the docket and, except for those submitted as “Confidential Submissions,” publicly viewable at
https://www.regulations.gov
or at the Dockets Management Staff between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, 240-402-7500.
Confidential Submissions—To submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made publicly available, submit your comments only as a written/paper submission. You should submit two
(
printed page 68524)
copies total. One copy will include the information you claim to be confidential with a heading or cover note that states “THIS DOCUMENT CONTAINS CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION.” The Agency will review this copy, including the claimed confidential information, in its consideration of comments. The second copy, which will have the claimed confidential information redacted/blacked out, will be available for public viewing and posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Submit both copies to the Dockets Management Staff. If you do not wish your name and contact information to be made publicly available, you can provide this information on the cover sheet and not in the body of your comments and you must identify this information as “confidential.” Any information marked as “confidential” will not be disclosed except in accordance with
21 CFR 10.20
and other applicable disclosure law. For more information about FDA's posting of comments to public dockets, see
80 FR 56469
, September 18, 2015, or access the information at:
https://www.govinfo.gov/​content/​pkg/​FR-2015-09-18/​pdf/​2015-23389.pdf
.
Docket:
For access to the docket to read background documents or the electronic and written/paper comments received, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and insert the docket number, found in brackets in the heading of this document, into the “Search” box and follow the prompts and/or go to the Dockets Management Staff, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852, 240-402-7500.
You may submit comments on any guidance at any time (see
21 CFR 10.115(g)(5)
).
Submit written requests for single copies of the revised draft guidance to the Office of Combination Products, Food and Drug Administration, 10903 New Hampshire Ave., Bldg. 32, Rm. 5129, Silver Spring, MD 20993-0002. Send one self-addressed adhesive label to assist that office in processing your requests. See the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for electronic access to the revised draft guidance document.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Patricia Love, Office of Combination Products, Food and Drug Administration, 10903 New Hampshire Ave., Bldg. 32, Rm. 5129, Silver Spring, MD 20993, 301-796-8930,
patricia.love@fda.hhs.gov
or
combination@fda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
FDA is announcing the availability of a revised draft guidance for industry entitled “Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products.” This revised draft guidance revises and replaces the draft guidance entitled “Essential Drug Delivery Outputs Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products” announced on July 1, 2024 (
89 FR 54470
). This guidance provides updates to clarify content on testing and controlling device drug-delivery performance and to align with the revised Quality Management System Regulation,
21 CFR part 820
.
The guidance describes FDA's recommendations related to information that is essential for establishing and assessing drug delivery performance for drug delivery devices. Device drug-delivery performance information is intended to demonstrate that the device drug-delivery function consistently performs as intended. The guidance focuses on recommendations for the information and data to submit in investigational, marketing, and post-market change applications.
This revised draft guidance is being issued consistent with FDA's good guidance practices regulation (
21 CFR 10.115
). The revised draft guidance, when finalized, will represent the current thinking of FDA on “Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products.” It does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on FDA or the public. You can use an alternative approach if it satisfies the requirements of the applicable statutes and regulations.
As we develop final guidance on this topic, FDA will consider comments on costs or cost savings the guidance may generate, relevant for
Executive Order 14192
.
II. Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995
While this guidance contains no collection of information, it does refer to previously approved FDA collections of information. Therefore, clearance by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
) is not required for this guidance. The previously approved collections of information are subject to review by OMB under the PRA. The collections of information in
21 CFR part 312
for investigational new drug applications have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0014 and the collections of information in
21 CFR part 812
for investigational device exemptions have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0078. The collections of information in
21 CFR part 314
for new drug applications and abbreviated new drug applications, including the collections of information contained in the guidance for industry entitled “Formal Meetings Between the FDA and Sponsors or Applicants of PDUFA Products” have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0001. The collections of information in
21 CFR parts 601
and
610
for biologics license applications have been approved under 0910-0338. The collections of information in section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act (
42 U.S.C. 262(k)
) have been approved under 0910-0718. The collections of information in
21 CFR part 814
for premarket approval applications have been approved under 0910-0231. The collections of information in section 510(k) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (
21 U.S.C. 360(k)
),
21 CFR part 807, subpart E
for premarket notifications, have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0120. The collections of information in
21 CFR 860, subpart D
for De Novo classifications have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0844. The collections of information in
21 CFR part 211
for current good manufacturing practice for finished pharmaceuticals have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0139. The collections of information in
21 CFR part 820

full_text:

Department of Energy
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
[Docket No. CP27-3-000]
The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) will prepare an environmental document that will discuss the environmental impacts of the Texas Mainline Compressor Station Project involving construction and operation of facilities by Double E Pipeline, LLC (Double E) in Loving County, Texas. The Commission will use this environmental document in its decision-making process to determine whether the project is in the public convenience and necessity.
This notice announces the opening of the scoping process the Commission will use to gather input from the public and interested agencies regarding the project. As part of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process, the Commission takes into account concerns the public may have about proposals and the environmental impacts that could result from its action whenever it considers the issuance of a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. This gathering of public input is referred to as “scoping.” The main goal of the scoping process is to focus the analysis in the environmental document on the important environmental issues. Additional information about the Commission's NEPA process is described below in the
NEPA Process and Environmental Document
section of this notice.
By this notice, the Commission requests public comments on the scope of issues to address in the environmental document. To ensure that your comments are timely and properly recorded, please submit your comments so that the Commission receives them in Washington, DC on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 27, 2026. Comments may be submitted in written form. Further details on how to submit comments are provided in the
Public Participation
section of this notice.
Your comments should focus on the potential environmental effects, reasonable alternatives, and measures to avoid or lessen environmental impacts. Your input will help the Commission staff determine what issues they need to evaluate in the environmental document. Commission staff will consider all written comments during the preparation of the environmental document.
If you submitted comments on this project to the Commission before the opening of this docket on October 2, 2026, you will need to file those comments in Docket No. CP27-3-000 to ensure they are considered as part of this proceeding.
This notice is being sent to the Commission's current environmental mailing list for this project. State and local government representatives should notify their constituents of this proposed project and encourage them to comment on their areas of concern.
If you are a landowner receiving this notice, a pipeline company representative may contact you about the acquisition of an easement to construct, operate, and maintain the proposed facilities. The company would seek to negotiate a mutually acceptable easement agreement. You are not required to enter into an agreement. However, if the Commission approves the project, the Natural Gas Act conveys the right of eminent domain to the company. Therefore, if you and the company do not reach an easement agreement, the pipeline company could initiate condemnation proceedings in court. In such instances, compensation would be determined by a judge in accordance with state law. The Commission does not subsequently grant, exercise, or oversee the exercise of that eminent domain authority. The courts have exclusive authority to handle eminent domain cases; the Commission has no jurisdiction over these matters.
Double E provided landowners with a fact sheet prepared by the FERC entitled “An Interstate Natural Gas Facility On My Land? What Do I Need To Know?” which addresses typically asked questions, including the use of eminent domain and how to participate in the Commission's proceedings. This fact sheet along with other landowner topics of interest are available for viewing on the FERC website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the Natural Gas, Landowner Topics link.
Public Participation
There are three methods you can use to submit your comments to the Commission. Please carefully follow these instructions so that your comments are properly recorded. The Commission encourages electronic filing of comments and has staff available to assist you at (866) 208-3676 or
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
.
(1) You can file your comments electronically using the eComment feature, which is located on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the link to FERC Online. Using eComment is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments on a project;
(2) You can file your comments electronically by using the eFiling feature, which is located on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” You will be asked to select the type of filing you are making; a comment on a particular project is considered a “Comment on a Filing”; or
(
printed page 68501)
(3) You can file a paper copy of your comments by mailing them to the Commission. Be sure to reference the project docket number (CP27-3-000) on your letter. Submissions sent via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, MD 20852.
Additionally, the Commission offers a free service called eSubscription which makes it easy to stay informed of all issuances and submittals regarding the dockets/projects to which you subscribe. These instant email notifications are the fastest way to receive notification and provide a link to the document files which can reduce the amount of time you spend researching proceedings. Go to
https://www.ferc.gov/​ferc-online/​overview
to register for eSubscription.
For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions, comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202) 502-6595 or
OPP@ferc.gov
.
Summary of the Proposed Project
Double E proposes to construct and operate a natural gas compressor station (“Mainline Compressor Station”) including two centrifugal compressor units driven by two natural gas-fired turbines totaling approximately 54,000 horsepower, associated piping, valves, controls, coolers, conditioning equipment, and other appurtenant facilities; two approximately 250-foot-long, 42-inch-diameter pipelines connecting the station to Double E's existing Double E Pipeline; and an associated permanent access road. The Texas Mainline Compressor Station Project would create approximately 800,000 dekatherms per day of firm transportation capacity on Double E's existing pipeline system from receipt points to gas processing complexes in the Permian and Delaware Basins and the Waha Market Hub.
The general location of the project facilities is shown in appendix 1.
[
1
]
Land Requirements for Construction
Construction of the proposed facilities would disturb about 17.87 acres of land for the aboveground facilities and the pipeline. Following construction, Double E would maintain about 15.80 acres for permanent operation of the project's facilities, and the remaining acreage would be restored and revert to former uses.
NEPA Process and the Environmental Document
Any environmental document issued by the Commission will discuss impacts that could occur as a result of the construction and operation of the proposed project under the relevant general resource areas:
geology and soils;
vegetation and wildlife;
threatened and endangered species;
cultural resources;
socioeconomics;
land use;
air quality and noise; and
reliability and safety.
Commission staff will also evaluate reasonable alternatives to the proposed project or portions of the project and make recommendations on how to lessen or avoid impacts on the various resource areas. Your comments will help Commission staff identify and focus on the issues that might have an effect on the human environment and potentially eliminate others from further study and discussion in the environmental document.
Following this scoping period, Commission staff will determine whether to prepare an Environmental Assessment (EA) or an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). The EA or the EIS will present Commission staff's independent analysis of the issues. If Commission staff prepares an EA, a
Notice of Schedule for the Preparation of an Environmental Assessment
will be issued. The EA may be issued for an allotted public comment period. The Commission would consider timely comments on the EA before making its decision regarding the proposed project. If Commission staff prepares an EIS, a
Notice of Intent to Prepare an EIS/Notice of Schedule
will be issued, which will open up an additional comment period. Staff will then prepare a draft EIS which will be issued for public comment. Commission staff will consider all timely comments received during the comment period on the draft EIS and revise the document, as necessary, before issuing a final EIS. Any EA or draft and final EIS will be available in electronic format in the public record through eLibrary
[
2
]
and the Commission's natural gas environmental documents web page (
https://www.ferc.gov/​industries-data/​natural-gas/​environment/​environmental-documents
). If eSubscribed, you will receive instant email notification when the environmental document is issued.
With this notice, the Commission is asking agencies with jurisdiction by law and/or special expertise with respect to the environmental issues of this project to formally cooperate in the preparation of the environmental document.
[
3
]
Agencies that would like to request cooperating agency status should follow the instructions for filing comments provided under the
Public Participation
section of this notice.
Consultation Under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act
In accordance with the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation's implementing regulations for section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, the Commission is using this notice to initiate consultation with the applicable State Historic Preservation Office(s), and to solicit their views and those of other government agencies, interested Indian tribes, and the public on the project's potential effects on historic properties.
[
4
]
The environmental document for this project will document findings on the impacts on historic properties and summarize the status of consultations under section 106.
Environmental Mailing List
The environmental mailing list includes federal, state, and local government representatives and agencies; elected officials; Native American Tribes; environmental and public interest groups; other interested parties; and regional libraries, newspapers, and media outlets. This list also includes all affected landowners (as defined in the Commission's regulations) who are potential right-of-way grantors, whose property may be used temporarily for project purposes, or who own homes within certain distances of aboveground facilities, and anyone who submits comments on the
(
printed page 68502)
project and includes a mailing address with their comments. Commission staff will update the environmental mailing list as the analysis proceeds to ensure that Commission notices related to this environmental review are sent to all individuals, organizations, and government entities interested in and/or potentially affected by the proposed project.
If you need to make changes to your name/address, or if you would like to remove your name from the mailing list, please complete one of the following steps:
(1) Send an email to
GasProjectAddressChange@ferc.gov
stating your request. You must include the docket number CP27-3-000 in your request. If you are requesting a change to your address, please be sure to include your name and the correct address. If you are requesting to delete your address from the mailing list, please include your name and address as it appeared on this notice. This email address is unable to accept comments.
OR
(2) Return the attached “Mailing List Update Form” (appendix 2).
Additional Information
Additional information about the project is available from the FERC website at
www.ferc.gov
using the eLibrary link. Click on the eLibrary link, click on “General Search” and enter the docket number in the “Docket Number” field. Be sure you have selected an appropriate date range. For assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
or (866) 208-3676, or for TTY, contact (202) 502-8659. The eLibrary link also provides access to the texts of all formal documents issued by the Commission, such as orders, notices, and rulemakings.
Public sessions or site visits will be posted on the Commission's calendar located at
https://www.ferc.gov/​news-events/​events
along with other related information.
(Authority:
18 CFR 2.1
)

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action amends the Class D airspace and establishes Class E airspace at Chandler and Phoenix, AZ. This action is the result of biennial airspace reviews pursuant to FAA Order JO 7400.2R, Procedures for Handling Airspace Matters. The name and geographic coordinates of the Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ, are also being updated to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database. This action brings the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and supports instrument flight rule (IFR) procedures and operations.
DATES:
Effective 0901 UTC, February 18, 2027. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under
1 CFR part 51
, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), all comments received, this final rule, and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from
www.federalregister.gov
.
FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, and subsequent amendments can be viewed online at
www.faa.gov/​air_​traffic/​publications/​
. You may also contact the Rules and Regulations Group, Office of Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jeffrey Claypool, Federal Aviation Administration, Operations Support Group, Central Service Center, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177; telephone (817) 222-5711.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it amends the Class D airspace and establishes Class E airspace at the affected airports to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2025-5571 in the
Federal Register
(
90 FR 59081
; December 18, 2025) proposing to amend the Class D airspace and establish Class E airspace at Chandler and Phoenix, AZ. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. The FAA appreciates the public's participation in the rulemaking process. Ninety-six comments were received and all comments have been reviewed and considered. The following responses are provided.
The airspace requirements for airports with public instrument procedures and air traffic control towers (ATCT) are outlined in FAA Order JO 7400.2R and
14 CFR part 71
, Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Air Traffic Service Routes; and Reporting Points. The FAA only designates controlled airspace required under FAA orders and
14 CFR part 71
and makes every effort to respect and protect the public's right of transit.
A majority of the airports within the Phoenix area have not received a complete airspace review in 25 years or longer. During that timeframe, instrument procedures and FAA orders and regulations governing airspace requirements have changed, thus requiring the airspace modification to bring the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and regulations and to support IFR operations. The changes to FAA orders and regulations require the modification and expansion of the controlled airspace at Chandler Municipal Airport and Mesa Gateway Airport.
Two comments expressed general dissatisfaction with the proposal without identifying any specific aspects to which they object or making any recommendations on how to revise the proposal. Due to the lack of specificity, the FAA is unable to provide a detailed response but acknowledges the general objections.
Fifty-nine comments raised concerns regarding the impact the proposed airspace modifications would have on VFR operations within the Phoenix area. The majority of these comments did not provide recommendations for how to revise the proposal or recommended either leaving the current airspace in place or reducing the current controlled airspace. All of these 59 comments expressed dissatisfaction with raising the vertical limits of the Chandler, AZ Class D airspace from 3,000 feet MSL to 3,700 feet MSL and the possible safety implications of leaving only 300 feet between the top of the Chandler, AZ, Class D airspace and the bottom of the Phoenix, AZ, Class B airspace. A comment from the Arizona Pilots Association objects to the lateral increase in the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace, which “would close the distance” between that Class D airspace and the Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport Class B airspace, further constraining and concentrating VFR traffic.
The proposed modification to the vertical limit was derived from FAA Order JO 7400.2R, paragraph 17-2-8 which states that “Class D areas should normally extend upward from the surface up to and including 2,500 feet AGL.” As such, reducing the vertical limit from what was proposed is not consistent with the referenced FAA order. In response to the safety concern expressed in the comments, the vertical limit of the Class D airspace at Chandler, AZ, is being raised from 3,000 feet MSL to up to but excluding 4,000 feet MSL rather than 3,700 feet MSL as initially proposed. This change eliminates the possibility of VFR traffic attempting to transit through the 300-foot area between the Chandler, AZ, Class D and the Phoenix, AZ, Class B airspace. Aircraft will still be able to transit the same area but will need to contact Chandler FAA Contract Tower (FCT) for clearance. The FAA believes that positive control of aircraft transiting this area is in the best interest of safety and will eliminate the risk of midair collisions expressed in the comments.
Twenty-five comments stated concerns regarding the impact of the proposed airspace changes on Pegasus Airpark. The following is the categorization of the comments: 6
(
printed page 68450)
expressed dissatisfaction without providing recommendations for modifying the proposal; 18 recommended increasing the exclusion area from the proposed 1.2-mile radius to a 1.5-mile radius; 5 recommended an exclusion area that matches or is smaller than the one proposed; 1 suggested increasing the exclusion area from a 1.2-mile radius to a 1.8-mile radius; 1 suggested increasing the exclusion area from a 1.2-mile radius to a 2-mile radius; and 2 suggested increasing the exclusion area from a 1.2-mile radius to a 3-mile radius.
The FAA acknowledges the comments expressing general dissatisfaction but is unable to respond further to comments lacking specificity or a recommendation for modifying the proposal. The suggestions to increase the exclusion area cited an increase in high-performance aircraft operating at Pegasus Airpark that need more uninhibited airspace to remain clear of the Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ, Class D airspace. The proposed exclusion area is equal to the airspace area currently outside of the Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ Class D airspace. Therefore, it does not shrink the airspace available for these operations.
Pursuant to Advisory Circular (AC) 90-66C, Non-Towered Airport Flight Operations, it is the responsibility of the airport owners and operators to coordinate the establishment of nonstandard traffic patterns with the FAA. The airport owner is then responsible for publishing the traffic pattern information in the Chart Supplement. The operator of the Pegasus Airpark has not accomplished this, so a standard traffic pattern is assumed and the appropriate Class G airspace provided. The air traffic manager (ATM) at Mesa Gateway Airport was asked to consider an increase in the exclusion area. However, as there have not been any incursions into the Class D airspace in the area of Pegasus Airpark; Pegasus Airpark has not made any coordination request to accommodate a larger air traffic pattern; and the proposed exclusion area is equal to the area currently outside of the Mesa Gateway Airport Class D airspace, the ATM does not believe that an increase in the exclusion area is needed at this time. If the situation changes and the proper coordination is complete, the issue of expanding the exclusion area may be revisited.
Twenty-eight comments objected to the potential impact of the proposed airspace changes on Stellar Airpark. The following is the categorization of the comments: 19 expressed dissatisfaction without providing recommendations for how to modify the proposal; 5 recommended an exclusion area that matched the proposal; and 1 comment stated the Stellar Airpark is not a VFR airport. The FAA is unable to respond to the comments expressing general dissatisfaction without details or providing any recommendations as it is impossible to address them without specifics.
Many comments cited an increase in high-performance aircraft operating at Stellar Airpark that needed more Class G airspace to remain clear of the Chandler Municipal Airport, Chandler, AZ Class D airspace. One comment objected to the airspace changes because they would allegedly frustrate the ability of VFR pilots to continue using the same visual landmarks for navigation. And one comment expressed concern with the impact on a privately funded instrument approach procedure at Stellar Airpark. The proposed exclusion area provides for a standard cutout for VFR airports and accommodates the public instrument procedures into Stellar Airpark.
As previously stated, pursuant to AC 90-66C, it is the responsibility of the airport owners and operators to coordinate the establishment of nonstandard traffic patterns with the FAA. The airport owner is then responsible for publishing the traffic pattern information in the Chart Supplement. The Stellar Airpark operator has not accomplished this, and there is no information regarding traffic patterns in the Stellar Airpark Chart Supplement entry, so a standard traffic pattern is assumed and the appropriate Class G airspace provided. If the situation changes and the proper coordination is complete, the issue of expanding the exclusion area may be revisited.
The FAA also confirms Stellar Airpark's status as a VFR airport. While Stellar Airpark does have instrument procedures—which were considered in the development of Chandler, AZ Class D exclusion area—that does not make Stellar Airpark an IFR or controlled airport. Stellar Airpark is an uncontrolled airport, and operators are required to take off and land following visual flight rules, thus Stellar Airpark is an uncontrolled, VFR airport.
Seventeen comments stated that the proposed airspace changes would increase the workload of pilots and would increase air traffic controller workloads beyond the capabilities of the affected air traffic facilities [
i.e.
, Chandler Municipal Airport FCT, Mesa Gateway Airport FCT, and Phoenix TRACON (P50)]. The ATMs from Chandler Municipal Airport FCT and Mesa Gateway Airport FCT, and management from P50 and the Albuquerque Air Traffic Services District participated in the planning of the airspace changes. These ATMs understand the added responsibilities the airspace changes will have on the air traffic controllers and have complete confidence that these facilities are capable of handling the responsibilities. Regarding the increased workload on the pilots, the airspace changes are required by and consistent with FAA orders and regulations.
Six comments alleged that there was no coordination with airspace stakeholders, including the ATMs at Chandler Municipal Airport FCT, Mesa Gateway Airport FCT, Falcon Field Air Traffic Control Tower (ATCT), P50, or the airport managers at Pegasus Airpark and Stellar Airpark, and that the assigned airspace specialist was not familiar enough with the Phoenix airspace to understand the impacts of the proposed changes. The ATMs from Chandler Municipal Airport FCT and Mesa Gateway Airport FCT requested the biennial airspace reviews of their respective airspaces. These ATMs and the P50 Airspace Manager participated in numerous meetings regarding these amendments and the proposal to ensure that the local conditions were taken into consideration and adjustments were made in accordance with their recommendations and consistent with FAA orders and regulations. The ATM from Falcon Field was not included in these efforts as the airspace is outside of that ATM's geographic area of responsibility. Coordination for Class D and Class E airspace involves the air traffic facility providing control to the affected area. The FAA obtains input from other stakeholders through the rulemaking comment period, which occurred. The personnel assigned to this effort have the requisite training and experience with the FAA orders and regulations regarding airspace and applicable requirements.
One comment questioned whether a safety risk management assessment was completed for this proposal. The standards codified in FAA Order JO 7400.2R, including all amendments, receive a safety risk management assessment. Accordingly, compliance with FAA Order JO 7400.2R when making changes to the National Airspace System satisfies the FAA and ICAO requirements for safety risk management. All changes comply with FAA Order JO 7400.2R.
One comment from Hughes Aerospace Corporation opined that the proposed Class E airspace extending upward from
(
printed page 68451)
700 feet above the surface at Stellar Airpark is insufficient and requested a review of the proposed Class E airspace. All data submitted by the commenter was reviewed; however, the official data from the FAA databases showed higher values than those submitted by the commenter. Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface must be designated to accommodate arriving IFR operations below 1,500 feet above the surface and departing IFR operations from 700 feet above the surface until they reach 1,200 feet above the surface. The data used for these computations are contained within FAA Form 8260-9, Part D, Airspace.
The commenter's concern is that the initial approach fix, JEWLZ, and holding pattern for the RNAV (GPS) RWY 35 would not be contained in the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface. The altitude requirement for JEWLZ is no lower than 3,000 MSL (mean sea level), equivalent to 1,821 feet AGL (above ground level), which places JEWLZ in the existing Class E airspace extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface. The holding pattern for RNAV (GPS) RWY 35 is restricted to an altitude no higher than 4,000 feet MSL (2,821 AGL) and no lower than 3,000 feet MSL (1,821 AGL), so the entire holding pattern is within the existing Class E airspace extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface.
The FAA reviewed the RNAV (GPS) RWY 35 into Stellar Airpark, as requested, and determined that the instrument approach procedure is contained in the appropriate airspace pursuant to FAA Order JO 7400.2R, and the proposed Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface for Stellar Airpark is sufficient and correct.
One comment questioned the need to increase the Class D airspace associated with Mesa Gateway Airport. FAA Order JO 7400.2R requires that Class D airspace is of adequate dimensions to: (a) allow an aircraft departing the airport at a standard rate of climb to reach the adjoining airspace while maintaining a 700 feet AGL clearance from the terrain in the area; and (b) protect the instrument approach procedures below 1,000 feet AGL and any departure procedure until the aircraft reaches the next adjoining airspace. In this case, the adjoining airspace for both (a) and (b) is the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface. The Class D airspace at 5.4 miles meets all requirements outlined in FAA Order JO 7400.2R.
One comment stated, “Now normally, a busy Class B area one would request Flight Following—however the FAA policy of the PHX Tracon has been to not grant these VFR FF requests.” The commenter did not provide or cite evidentiary support for this claim. It is FAA policy that flight following services are provided upon request as allowed by the air traffic controller workload. The P50 ATM and the General Manager for the Albuquerque Air Traffic Services District were contacted regarding this comment, and their response is, “flight following is and will continue to be granted to all pilots, upon request and workload.”
One comment stated that the proposed airspace change would create an overlap between the current Falcon Field, Mesa, AZ, Class D airspace and the proposed Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ, Class D airspace. The FAA reviewed the airspace and confirmed there is no overlap. Other comments objected to the elimination of the existing corridor of Class G airspace between the Class D airspace associated with Falcon Field and Mesa Gateway Airport. However, as described earlier, the expansion of the Mesa Gateway Airport Class D airspace is required for compliance with FAA Order JO 7400.2R.
One comment stated that it would be helpful to have a graphical depiction of the proposed airspace. Pursuant to FAA Order JO 7400.2R, graphical depictions are only required for Class B and Class C airspace proposals. Moreover, providing graphical depictions of every Class D airspace proposal is not feasible considering the high volume of Class D airspace amendments throughout the National Airspace System.
One comment from Brandon Esquer, a member of the P50 National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA), stated that the expansion of the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace is unnecessary and not in compliance with FAA orders. This commenter asserted that the existing IFR transitional airspace is adequate. The commenter's interpretation of the FAA orders and requirements is correct but incomplete. The commenter cited a requirement to protect departures to the lateral limits of the Class D airspace and into the transitional Class E airspace, which is correct. More specifically, the complete requirement for Class D airspace contained in FAA Order JO 7400.2R is that the airspace is sufficiently sized to: (a) allow an aircraft departing the airport at a standard rate of climb to reach the adjoining airspace while maintaining a 700 feet AGL clearance from the terrain in the area; and (b) protect the instrument approach procedures below 1,000 feet AGL and any departure procedures until the aircraft reaches the next adjoining airspace. In this case, the adjoining airspace for both (a) and (b) is the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface.
In the case of Chandler Municipal Airport, aircraft are unable to maintain a 700 feet AGL clearance above terrain in the Class D surface area within the current 4-mile radius and reach the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface. Additionally, the departure procedure for runways 04L and 04R at Chandler Municipal Airport is a climbing left hand turn to heading 220° to intercept the Stanfield VORTAC 350° radial, then southbound to the Stanfield VORTAC. Prior to this final rule, in the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace aircraft would exit the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace, enter the Mesa Gateway Airport Class D airspace, and re-enter the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace before finally exiting the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace at 3,000 feet MSL directly into a VFR flyway. With the airspace modified by this final rule, aircraft can maintain the required 700 feet AGL terrain clearance within the Class D surface area, and an aircraft on the departure procedure for runways 04L 04R can turn back into the Class D airspace upon reaching the 4.8-mile Class D airspace boundary and exiting the Class D airspace when reaching 4,000 feet MSL.
Furthermore, FAA Order JO 7400.2R requires that departure procedures within the Class D airspace maintain 700 feet AGL clearance of terrain and include airspace 1.8 NM either side of the track to be flown. The requirement within Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface is to provide airspace 1.8 NM either side of the track to be flown. For Class E airspace extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface, the requirement is to provide airspace 4 NM either side of the track to be flown. The expansion of the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace to 4.8 miles meets all the requirements for Class D airspace contained in FAA Order JO 7400.2R, using the Mesa Gateway Airport Class D airspace to protect the eastern area of the departure procedure without requiring additional airspace.
Additionally, raising the vertical limit of the Class D airspace up to but excluding 4,000 feet MSL further protects the IFR aircraft on the departure procedure and reduces the risk of a midair collision with aircraft
(
printed page 68452)
operating VFR. The FAA appreciates the comment from this NATCA member; however, his interpretation of FAA orders is incomplete. The expansion of the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace is needed to bring the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and regulations and will enhance safety of aircraft operating IFR from Chandler Municipal Airport by reducing the possibility of midair collisions.
Lastly, a comment from the Mesa Gateway Airport Authority (MGAA) cited five concerns: (1) the proposal does not take into account the volume of training and general aviation operations in the area; (2) the proposed airspace changes for the Mesa Gateway Airport Class D airspace will reduce the arrival and departure capacity and create bottlenecks, forcing complex procedures that will increase taxiing, runway crossings, and create delays; (3) the proposed airspace changes will adversely impact the VFR flyway and VFR traffic; (4) the proposal constitutes an isolated rulemaking that is not harmonized with the Phoenix Area Modernization Plan (PAMP); and (5) the proposal will have an adverse economic impact on Mesa Gateway Airport. The FAA provides the following responses.
The FAA acknowledges MGAA's concerns about impacts to other operations in the area, including the VFR flyway. The FAA only designates controlled airspace as required under FAA orders and
14 CFR part 71
and makes every effort to respect and protect the public's right of transit. However, the changes are required to bring the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and regulations and to support IFR operations in the Phoenix area.
The FAA also acknowledges MGAA's concerns that the proposed airspace changes will reduce the arrival and departure capacity at the Mesa Gateway Airport. The FAA designed the airspace for Mesa Gateway Airport based on the current instrument procedures, bringing the airspace into compliance with current FAA orders and regulations. There are no new instrument procedures in development, and the airspace change does not require new, complex procedures to be developed or implemented at Mesa Gateway Airport. The expansion of the airspace allows aircraft to maintain 700 feet AGL clearance from the terrain required by FAA Order JO 7400.2R. Additionally, the FAA does not agree that expanding the Class D airspace will create ground delays predicted by MGAA (
e.g.
, air traffic bottleneck, increased taxi times, increased runway crossing requirements, air traffic delays, etc.) as the airspace change accommodates existing procedures and operations at the airport and does not change or impact taxi procedures.
The FAA also acknowledges the ongoing work of the PAMP. The review and amendment of the Mesa Gateway Airport Class D airspace was requested by Mesa Gateway Airport FCT ATM. The Director of Operations for the Central Service Area Air Traffic Services was aware of the pending airspace amendment and has monitored the progress and possible impact of the PAMP. Additionally, the FAA is not bypassing any environmental process. Modification of Class D airspace requires an independent environmental review, which has been completed and is summarized in the Environmental Review section of this action.
Lastly, the FAA declines to alter the proposal based on the claim that the airspace changes will have an adverse economic impact on Mesa Gateway Airport. The FAA does not have statutory authority to consider economic factors as part of its airspace designations. Further, the comment from MGAA did not explain how the expansion of the Class D airspace at Mesa Gateway Airport would result in adverse economic impacts, instead providing only a general explanation of how Mesa Gateway Airport contributes to the economy of the area. The airspace change expands the Class D airspace to support the existing instrument procedures. It does not add or change any instrument procedures or otherwise directly impact operations at Mesa Gateway Airport.
Differences From the NPRM
Subsequent to publication of the NPRM, a typographical error was discovered in the NPRM. In the Chandler, AZ, Class D airspace legal description, “latitude” was used instead of “longitude.” Correction of this typographic error does not change the boundaries of the airspace as they currently exist or as proposed or impose any additional requirements on users of the airspace. Accordingly, the FAA finds good cause that recirculating this action for public comment is unnecessary.
In response to the comments received on the NPRM and in the interest of safety, the vertical limit of the Chandler, AZ, Class D airspace is being raised from the current limit of 3,000 feet MSL up to but excluding 4,000 feet MSL rather than 3,700 feet MSL as proposed in the NPRM. This will close the gap between the expanded Class D airspace and the overlying Class B airspace, reducing hazards to Class B operations and preventing VFR pilots from attempting to navigate through the narrow gap without communicating with air traffic control. The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) authorizes agencies to dispense with ordinary notice and comment requirements for rules when the agency for “good cause” finds that those procedures are “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.”
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
. This change is made in response to a valid safety concern raised by the numerous comments received on the NPRM. The FAA finds good cause that recirculating this action for public comment is unnecessary, as the change directly responds to dozens of comments already received.
Incorporation by Reference
Class D and E airspace designations are published in paragraphs 5000 and 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in
14 CFR 71.1
on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11K, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action amends
14 CFR part 71
by modifying the Class D airspace and establishing Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Chandler, Arizona, and Phoenix, Arizona, due to biennial airspace reviews conducted pursuant to FAA Order JO 7400.2R.
For the Chandler Municipal Airport, Chandler, AZ, Class D airspace this action: (1) increases the radius from 4 miles to 4.8 miles; (2) increases the vertical limit from 3,000 feet MSL to up to but excluding 4,000 feet MSL; (3) removes Williams Gateway Airport and the associated exclusion area as they are no longer required; (4) adds an exclusion area west of longitude 111°53′41″ W; (5) updates the airspace legal description header from “Chandler Municipal Airport, AZ” to “Chandler, AZ” to comply with changes to FAA Order JO 7400.2R; and (6) updates the outdated term of “Airport/Facility Directory” to “Chart Supplement.”
For the Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ, this action: (1) increases the radius from 5 miles to 5.4 miles; (2) adds an exclusion area for the Chandler
(
printed page 68453)
Municipal Airport Class D airspace; (3) adds an exclusion area within a 1.2-mile radius of Pegasus Airpark, Queen Creek, AZ; (4) updates the name of the airport from Williams Gateway Airport to Mesa Gateway Airport and updates the geographic coordinates of the airport to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database; (5) updates the airspace legal description header from “Chandler, AZ” to “Phoenix, AZ” to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database; and (6) updates the outdated term of “Airport/Facility Directory” to “Chart Supplement.”
This action establishes Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Stellar Airpark, Chandler, AZ, within a 13.9-mile radius of the airport.
This action establishes Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ: (1) within a 7.9-mile radius of the airport; (2) within 4 miles northeast and 8 miles southwest of the 136° bearing for the Mesa Gateway: RWY 30C-LOC extending from the 7.9-mile radius of the airport to 17.7 miles southeast of the Mesa Gateway: RWY 30C-LOC; and (3) within 7.9 miles northeast and 4 miles southwest of the 136° bearing from the airport extending from the 7.9-mile radius of the airport to 12.6 miles southeast of the airport.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Policies and Procedures for Rulemakings” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” Paragraph B-2.5(a). This airspace action is not expected to cause any potentially significant environmental impacts, and no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of an environmental assessment.

as follows:

Pursuant to section 1009 of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended, notice is hereby given of a meeting of the National Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases Advisory Council.
The meeting will be open to the public as indicated below, with attendance limited to space available. Individuals who plan to attend and need special assistance, such as sign language interpretation or other reasonable accommodations, should notify the Contact Person listed below in advance of the meeting.
The meeting will be closed to the public in accordance with the provisions set forth in sections 552b(c)(4) and 552b(c)(6), Title 5 U.S.C., as amended. The grant applications and the discussions could disclose confidential trade secrets or commercial property such as patentable material, and personal information concerning individuals associated with the grant applications, the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.
