d. CY 2027 ESRD Market Basket Update
Under section 1881(b)(14)(F)(i) of the Act, beginning in CY 2012, the ESRD PPS payment amounts are required to be annually increased by an ESRD market basket percentage increase factor and reduced by the productivity adjustment described in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act. We proposed to use the 2024-based ESRDB market basket as described in section II.B.1.b. of the proposed rule to compute the CY 2027 ESRDB market basket percentage increase based on the best available data. Consistent with historical practice, we proposed to estimate the ESRDB market basket percentage increase based on IHS Global Inc.'s (IGI) forecast using the most recently available data at the time of rulemaking. IGI is a nationally recognized economic and financial forecasting firm with which CMS contracts to forecast the components of the market baskets. As outlined in section II.B.1.d.(3) of the proposed rule, we calculated the proposed ESRDB market basket update for CY 2027 based on the 2024-based ESRDB market basket percentage increase and the proposed productivity adjustment, following our longstanding methodology.
(1) CY 2027 ESRDB Market Basket Percentage Increase
Using this methodology and IGI's first quarter of 2026 forecast of the 2024-based ESRDB market basket (with historical data through the fourth quarter of 2025), and consistent with our historical practice of estimating market basket increases based on the best available data, the proposed CY 2027 ESRDB market basket increase factor was projected to be 2.6 percent. We also proposed that if more recent data became available after the publication of the proposed rule and before the publication of the final rule (for example, a more recent estimate of the market basket percentage increase), we would use such data to determine the CY 2027 ESRDB market basket percentage increase in the final rule, provided such data is appropriate (meaning methodologically consistent with the proposed approach, sufficiently complete, and available in time to be reasonably evaluated for the final rule). Based on the more recent data available for this CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule (that is, IGI's third quarter 2026 forecast of the 2024-based ESRDB market basket with historical data through the second quarter of 2026), the CY 2027 ESRDB market basket percentage increase is 2.9 percent.
We invited public comment on the proposed CY 2027 ESRDB market basket percentage increase. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses. Several comments discussing the ESRDB market basket percentage increase also discussed the overall ESRD PPS payment level, the ESRD PPS base rate, budget neutrality adjustments, or payment adequacy under the ESRD PPS. These comments are summarized and responded to in section II.B.4. of this final rule.
Comment:
Several commenters acknowledged the proposed ESRDB productivity-adjusted market basket increase of 1.6 percent; however, most expressed that this update is insufficient to address the current inflationary environment and workforce shortages. A few commenters pointed to their own experience or broader trends in labor costs as an indication that the update is insufficient. Several commenters noted that most of the $17.84 proposed increase to the ESRD PPS base rate (to $299.55) is attributable to the $15.96 added to account for phosphate-binders, leaving an effective increase of only about $1.88, or roughly 0.7 to 1.1 percent, once the phosphate binder amount is excluded. Some commenters underscored the importance of accurate payments to ensure ESRD facilities can hire and retain essential clinical staff, mitigate high rates of staff turnover to higher-paying settings, which has had a negative impact on patient experience. A commenter claimed that the proposed ESRDB market basket percentage increase is lower than economy-wide measures of inflation like the CPI and PPI. A couple of commenters noted that the ESRD PPS update has consistently been lower than updates under other Medicare facility-based PPS systems.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the CY 2027 productivity-adjusted market basket update. Section 1881(b)(14)(F)(i)(I) of the Act requires that the ESRD PPS payment rate be increased by the ESRD bundled (ESRDB) market basket percentage increase, reduced by the productivity adjustment described in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act. We note that the phosphate binder payment amount is a separate, distinct modification to the base rate and is not part of the ESRDB market basket update itself; we clarified that they do not offset one another. Additionally, we note that the application of several budget neutrality factors is decreasing the CY 2027 ESRD PPS base rate. We discuss these budget neutrality factors in greater detail in section II.B.4. of this final rule, however, we want to emphasize that these factors maintain estimated payment at the same amount and do not offset the overall payment impact of the ESRDB market basket update.
The 2024-based ESRDB market basket percent change is equal to the weighted price change of the individual price proxies and their respective cost weights. The cost weights are primarily derived using the freestanding ESRD Medicare cost reports and reflect relative shares of input costs needed to provide medical services to ESRD beneficiaries. Similarly, the other CMS PPS market baskets, such as the 2022-based SNF market basket and 2023-based IPPS market basket, reflect the relative share of input costs needed to provide skilled nursing and hospital care to Medicare beneficiaries based on the data reported on the respective provider cost reports.
While we understand that commenters may compare the annual updates in the ESRDB market basket to other Medicare market baskets, the ESRDB market basket is developed in accordance with section 1881(b)(14)(F)(i) of the Act requiring that the index reflect the composition of costs associated with providing renal dialysis services. These costs (and the subsequent cost distributions) are reported by ESRD facilities on the Medicare cost reports and may differ (appropriately) from the relative distribution of costs of other medical care providers such as inpatient hospitals or skilled nursing facilities. Additionally, the price proxies used in the ESRD market basket are intended to reflect the price pressures faced by ESRD facilities. While some price proxies may be similar to those used across other CMS market baskets, in most cases they are appropriately different because they reflect the price pressures faced by ESRD facilities. For example, the rate of increase in the ESRD market basket compensation category reflects the weighted average of the price increase for occupations employed by ESRD facilities.
At the time of the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, based on the IHS Global Inc. first quarter 2026 forecast with historical data through the fourth quarter of 2025, the 2024-based ESRDB

market basket update was forecasted to be 2.6 percent for CY 2027, reflecting forecasted compensation price growth of 3.2 percent. In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed that if more recent data became available, we would use such data, if appropriate, to derive the final CY 2027 ESRDB market basket update for the final rule. For this final rule, we now have an updated forecast of the price proxies underlying the market basket that includes more recent historical data and reflects a revised outlook regarding the U.S. economy and expected price inflation for CY 2027. Based on IHS Global Inc.'s third quarter 2026 forecast with historical data through the second quarter of 2026, we are projecting a CY 2027 ESRDB market basket update of 2.9 percent and a final ESRDB productivity-adjusted market basket update of 1.9 percent (2.9 percent reduced by the 1.0 percentage point productivity adjustment) will be applicable, compared to the 1.6 percent productivity-adjusted market basket update that was proposed.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that the ESRDB market basket has been consistently under-forecast relative to actual realized inflation, estimating a cumulative error ranging from 6.0 to 7.7 percent that a commenter did not believe were random. Many commenters continued to request that CMS adopt a forecast-error correction policy for the ESRD PPS similar to that used in the SNF PPS, including both a one-time retrospective adjustment to correct the accumulated error and a forward-looking policy triggered when the forecast error exceeds a threshold (most commenters proposed ±0.5 percentage point). Several commenters requested greater transparency into IHS Global Inc.'s (IGI) forecasting methodology of the price proxies used in the market basket.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' continued concerns regarding market basket forecast error; however, the ESRDB market basket updates are set prospectively, which means that the update relies on a mix of both historical data for part of the period for which the update is calculated and forecasted data for the remainder. For instance, the CY 2027 market basket update in this final rule reflects historical data through the second quarter of CY 2026 and forecasted data through the fourth quarter of CY 2027. While there is no precedent to adjust for market basket forecast error in the ESRD PPS payment update, a forecast error can be calculated by comparing the actual market basket increase for a given year less the forecasted market basket increase. Due to the uncertainty regarding future price trends, forecast errors can be both positive and negative, as has occurred since the implementation of the ESRD PPS in CY 2011. Over most of this history the forecast errors were smaller in magnitude, with the largest error (in absolute terms) prior to 2021 being an over forecast (the actual market basket increase is less than the forecasted market basket increase) of 0.8 percentage point in 2017. More recently the ESRDB market basket has been under forecast, as noted by the commenters, with larger errors occurring for 2021 through 2024. The cumulative forecast error since ESRD PPS inception (CY 2012 to CY 2025) is 5.5 percent. These recent forecast errors were largely a function of uncertainty in the overall economy and the health sector specifically due to the nature of the Public Health Emergency for COVID-19 and the unforeseen rapidly accelerating inflationary environment.
We understand the request for greater transparency into IGI's forecasting methodology of the price proxies used in the CMS market baskets; however, we continue to reiterate that CMS purchases independent forecasts of the price proxies used in the CMS market baskets from IGI, a nationally recognized economic and financial forecasting firm. The rationale for using an independent forecaster is to ensure neutrality in the update while reflecting comprehensive economic and health sector forecasting model capabilities that extend beyond CMS' expertise. As the forecasting models are proprietary in nature, we are not licensed to share information related to the detailed models. More information on the IGI economic forecasts can be found at the following website or by contacting the company directly
https://www.spglobal.com/​market-intelligence/​en/​solutions/​products/​us-economic-modeling-forecasting-services
.
We recognize that forecast error under the ESRD PPS has been an important concern of commenters in recent years. We did not propose a policy to modify the ESRDB market basket update or ESRD PPS base rate for CY 2027 to address forecast error and are not finalizing any such policy in this final rule.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing the CY 2027 ESRDB market basket percentage increase of 2.9 percent, based on the more recent data available for this CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule (that is, IGI's third quarter 2026 forecast of the 2024-based ESRDB market basket with historical data through the second quarter of 2026).
(2) CY 2027 Productivity Adjustment
Under section 1881(b)(14)(F)(i) of the Act, as amended by section 3401(h) of the Affordable Care Act, for CY 2012 and each subsequent year, the ESRDB market basket percentage increase shall be reduced by the productivity adjustment described in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act. The statute defines the productivity adjustment to be equal to the 10-year moving average of changes in annual economy-wide, private nonfarm business multifactor productivity (as projected by the Secretary for the 10-year period ending with the applicable fiscal year (FY), year, cost reporting period, or other annual period), hereafter referred to as the “productivity adjustment”.
BLS publishes the official measures of productivity for the United States economy. The productivity measure referenced in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act is published by BLS as private nonfarm business total factor productivity (TFP) (previously referred to as multifactor productivity).

Comment:
Several commenters had concerns regarding the application and magnitude of the productivity adjustment. Some commenters requested that CMS use its “special exceptions and adjustments” authority
(

to eliminate or reduce the 1.0 percentage point productivity cut for CY 2027. A commenter stated that the 1.0 percentage point productivity adjustment would be the largest applied in ESRD PPS history and stated that it does not reflect verifiable productivity gains specific to the dialysis sector.
Response:
Section 1881(b)(14)(F)(i)(II) of the Act requires the application of the productivity adjustment, described in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II), to the ESRD PPS market basket increase factor. The CY 2027 productivity adjustment is derived based on the 10-year moving average growth in economy-wide, private nonfarm business total factor productivity for the period ending CY 2027. We recognize the concerns of the commenters regarding the appropriateness of the productivity adjustment; however, as we explained in response to similar comments in prior ESRD PPS final rules (
90 FR 53076
), we are required under section 1881(b)(14)(F)(i)(II) of the Act to apply the specific productivity adjustment described here.
Since 2015, we have provided information on the general method for calculating the productivity adjustment. This information includes providing a link (
http://www.bls.gov/​productivity/​
) to the most recent BLS historical TFP data, which currently allows interested parties to obtain historical TFP annual index levels for 1987 through 2025. We also provide the IGI projection model (
https://www.cms.gov/​research-statistics-data-and-systems/​statistics-trends-and-reports/​medicareprogramratesstats/​downloads/​tfp_​methodology.pdf
), which for this CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule is used to derive annual TFP growth rates for 2026 and 2027. The annual index level derived from this method is then interpolated to quarterly levels, and the CY 2027 productivity adjustment is equal to the percent change in the 40-quarter moving average projected level for the period ending December 31, 2027, relative to the 40-quarter moving average projected level for the period ending December 31, 2026. We believe our methodology for the productivity adjustment is consistent with section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act, which states that the productivity adjustment is equal to the 10-year moving average of changes in annual economy-wide private nonfarm business multi-factor productivity (as projected by the Secretary for the 10-year period ending with the applicable fiscal year, year, cost reporting period, or other annual period).
At the time of this final rule, the 2027 productivity adjustment reflects BLS historical TFP data through 2025 (released on March 19, 2026) and IGI's forecasted TFP growth for 2026 and 2027. The average annual growth rate of historical TFP published by BLS for 2018 through 2025 is currently 1.0 percent and IGI is projecting average TFP growth of about 0.9 percent for 2026 and 2027 based on IGI's third-quarter 2026 forecast. Combining the historical and projected TFP data over the entire 10-year time period and interpolating into quarterly index levels results in a 10-year moving average growth rate of TFP of 1.0 percent for CY 2027 (unchanged from the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule). Interpolation of annual to quarterly data distributes the annual data across quarters by estimating the values between two known annual observations.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing the CY 2027 productivity adjustment of 1.0 percent based on the IGI third quarter 2026 forecast.

We proposed that if more recent data became available after the analysis performed for the publication of the proposed rule and before the publication of this final rule (for example, an update to the May 2025 BLS OEWS mean hourly wage data or more complete CY 2024 cost report data), we would use such data, if appropriate, to determine the CY 2027 ESRD PPS wage index in the final rule. For this final rule, we used the most recently available CY 2024 cost report data. No update to the May 2025 BLS OEWS was published at the time of the development of this final rule.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns about the current ESRD wage index methodology and stated that the legacy ESRD PPS wage index was more appropriate. A commenter expressed support for the wage index floor policy, but urged CMS to increase the floor from 0.6000 to 0.7000. Another commenter urged CMS to use its authority under section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iv) of the Act, which permits CMS to adopt such other payment adjustments as the Secretary determines appropriate, to establish a non-budget neutral wage index floor or supplemental payment adjustment for ESRD facilities in low-wage-index areas.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns raised by the commenters regarding the ESRD PPS wage index methodology. We continue to believe that the ESRD facility-specific methodology is most appropriate for the ESRD PPS. We did not propose any changes to the ESRD PPS wage index methodology for CY 2027, such as a return to the legacy ESRD PPS wage index methodology, and we are not finalizing any such changes in this final rule. We will continue to evaluate the ESRD PPS wage index methodology and consider whether changes may be appropriate through notice-and-comment rulemaking in future years.
Regarding the wage index floor, as we discussed in the CY 2023 ESRD PPS final rule, the 0.6000 wage index floor was based on a statistical analysis (
87 FR 67161
). We did not propose to change the wage index floor or establish any other supplemental policies to increase payments to ESRD facilities in low-wage-index areas, for CY 2027 and are not finalizing any such changes in this final rule. We will continue to monitor the appropriateness of the current wage index floor and consider whether further changes are warranted through notice-and-comment rulemaking in future years.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern about the combined impact of the wage index and the increase to the LRS. A commenter urged CMS to consider changes to the wage index, LRS, and other adjustors together as one connected system rather than in silos.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns that commenters raised about the impact of the updates to the wage index and the LRS on ESRD facilities in low-wage areas. As we discuss in section II.B.1.c. of this final rule, the increase to the LRS reflects the latest available estimates of the labor-related costs in the ESRDB market basket. We do not believe a delay to the implementation of the increase to the LRS is appropriate as the updated LRS will more accurately reflect labor costs as a percentage of the ESRD PPS bundled payment amount. Overall payment impacts, which take into account all payment changes in this final rule, are discussed in section VII.C.5.a. of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS to revisit the ESRD-specific wage index methodology to incorporate wage data drawn specifically from the healthcare sector, or from ESRD facilities directly, rather than an all-industry BLS average, to evaluate whether the current occupational-mix weighting adequately compensates for that underlying data limitation.
Response:
As we have previously noted, we recognize the limitations of the data source upon which the ESRD PPS wage index methodology is built. We discussed these limitations in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS proposed rule (
89 FR 55769
) and, in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule (
89 FR 89099
,
89116
), concluded that, even with these limitations, the methodology represents a significant improvement over the IPPS wage index for use in ESRD facilities. We wish to reiterate that the purpose of the wage index is to estimate the geographic variation in wages, and we believe that this wage index methodology does so appropriately. We note that although we use all-industry wages, the job codes are either for healthcare occupations, such as RNs, or are healthcare-specific occupations, such as Medical Secretaries and Administrative Assistants. Thus, we believe the ESRD PPS wage index is appropriately based on the specific occupations involved in furnishing renal dialysis services. We intend to continue to monitor the ESRD PPS wage index, including the wage data and occupational mix, and may consider future changes through notice and comment rulemaking, if appropriate.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to update the ESRD PPS wage index following our established methodology. For CY 2027, the final wage index is based on wage estimates from the May 2025 BLS OEWS, which represents data from six semiannual surveys spanning November 2022 through May 2025, and the most recently available CY 2024 cost report data. 3. CY 2027 Update to the Outlier Policy
a. Background
Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act requires that the ESRD PPS include a payment adjustment for high-cost outliers due to unusual variations in the type or amount of medically necessary care, including variability in the amount of ESAs necessary for anemia management. Some examples of the patient conditions that may be reflective of higher facility costs when furnishing dialysis care are frailty and obesity. A patient's specific medical condition, such as secondary hyperparathyroidism, may result in higher per treatment costs. The ESRD PPS recognizes that some
(
printed page 68762)
patients require high-cost care, and we have codified the outlier policy and our methodology for calculating outlier payments at § 413.237.
Section 413.237(a)(1) enumerates the following items and services that are eligible for outlier payments as ESRD outlier services:
Renal dialysis drugs and biological products that were or would have been, prior to January 1, 2011, separately billable under Medicare Part B.
Renal dialysis laboratory tests that were or would have been, prior to January 1, 2011, separately billable under Medicare Part B.
Renal dialysis medical/surgical supplies, including syringes, used to administer renal dialysis drugs and biological products that were or would have been, prior to January 1, 2011, separately billable under Medicare Part B.
Renal dialysis drugs and biological products that were or would have been, prior to January 1, 2011, covered under Medicare Part D, including renal dialysis oral-only drugs effective January 1, 2025.
Renal dialysis equipment and supplies, except for capital-related assets that are home dialysis machines (as defined in § 413.236(a)(2)), that receive the transitional add-on payment adjustment as specified in § 413.236 after the payment period has ended.
[
13
]
Renal dialysis drugs and biological products that are Composite Rate Services as defined in § 413.171.
In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49142
), CMS stated that for purposes of determining whether an ESRD facility would be eligible for an outlier payment, it would be necessary for the ESRD facility to identify the actual ESRD outlier services furnished to the patient by line item (that is, date of service) on the monthly claim. Renal dialysis drugs, laboratory tests, and medical/surgical supplies that are recognized as ESRD outlier services were specified in Transmittal 2134, dated January 14, 2011.
[

We use administrative issuances and guidance to continually update the renal dialysis service items available for outlier payment via our quarterly update CMS Change Requests (CRs), when applicable. For example, we use these issuances to identify renal dialysis oral drugs that were or would have been covered under Part D prior to 2011 to provide unit prices for determining the imputed MAP amounts. In addition, we use these issuances to update the list of ESRD outlier services by adding or removing items and services that we determined, based on our monitoring efforts, are either incorrectly included or missing from the list.
Under § 413.237, an ESRD facility is eligible for an outlier payment if its imputed (that is, calculated) MAP amount per treatment for ESRD outlier services exceeds a threshold. In past years, the MAP amount has reflected the average estimated expenditure per treatment for services that were or would have been considered separately billable services prior to January 1, 2011. The threshold is equal to the ESRD facility's predicted MAP per treatment plus the fixed dollar loss (FDL) amount. As described in the following paragraphs, the ESRD facility's predicted MAP amount is the national adjusted average ESRD outlier services MAP amount per treatment, further adjusted for case-mix and facility characteristics applicable to the claim. We use the term “national adjusted average” in this section of this final rule to more clearly distinguish the calculation of the average ESRD outlier services MAP amount per treatment from the calculation of the predicted MAP amount for a claim. The average ESRD outlier services MAP amount per treatment is based on utilization from all ESRD facilities, whereas the calculation of the predicted MAP amount for a claim is based on the individual ESRD facility and patient characteristics of the monthly claim. In accordance with § 413.237(c), ESRD facilities are paid 80 percent of the per treatment amount by which the imputed MAP amount for ESRD outlier services (that is, the actual incurred amount) exceeds this threshold. ESRD facilities are eligible to receive outlier payments for treating both adult and pediatric dialysis patients.
In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule and codified in § 413.220(b)(4), using 2007 data, we established the outlier percentage—which is used to reduce the per treatment ESRD PPS base rate to account for the proportion of the estimated total Medicare payments under the ESRD PPS that are outlier payments—at 1.0 percent of total payments (

We proposed to update the ESRD outlier services FDL amount for pediatric patients using the latest available CY 2025 claims data, and to update the ESRD outlier services FDL amount for adult patients using the latest available claims data from CY 2023, CY 2024, and CY 2025, in accordance with the methodology finalized in the CY 2023 ESRD PPS final rule (

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns about the proposed increases to the FDL and MAP amounts for CY 2027. Some commenters recommended that CMS use more current 2026 utilization data instead of relying on 2025 projections. Other commenters recommended that CMS phase-in MAP and FDL amount increases more gradually rather than a single large jump.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns raised by commenters regarding the projected increase in outlier payments in CY 2026 and corresponding increases in the FDL and MAP amounts for CY 2027. As we noted in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, these increases are primarily attributable to the projected utilization of drugs currently paid for through the TDAPA in CY 2025, which will be ESRD outlier services in CYs 2026 and 2027. Specifically, we projected that payments under the outlier adjustment would be approximately 3.0 percent of total ESRD PPS payments in CY 2026 based on utilization from the latest available CY 2025 claims. As a result, we proposed to increase the MAP and FDL amounts to better achieve the 1.0 percent outlier target in CY 2027. Although the proposed CY 2027 adult FDL amount was higher than the CY 2026 adult FDL amount, we noted that the retrospective FDL methodology that we finalized in the CY 2023 ESRD PPS final rule accounts for the introduction of these new ESRD outlier services by calculating a retrospective trend line based on prior years' TDAPA or TPNIES utilization (
87 FR 67174
).
Regarding the recommendation to use more recent 2026 utilization data, we note that the latest available full CY of claims data is CY 2025, which is the source of the estimates used in the proposed rule. At the time of final rulemaking, CY 2026 utilization is only available through the end of the second quarter and does not incorporate any information about utilization or pricing patterns in the second half of CY 2026. We will take these comments into consideration to potentially inform future changes to the outlier methodology through notice and comment rulemaking.
We do not agree with the recommendation to phase-in the increases to the FDL and MAP amounts over time. As we have previously noted, we update the outlier FDL and MAP amounts each year to target outlier payments at 1.0 percent of total ESRD PPS payments. If we applied a lower FDL or MAP amount in CY 2027, we estimate that outlier payments would exceed 1.0 percent.
Comment:
Several commenters urged CMS to change certain aspects of the ESRD PPS outlier policy. Some commenters stated that a lower target percentage, for example 0.5 percent of total payments, would be more appropriate. These commenters stated that section 1881(b)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act does not require the ESRD PPS outlier percentage to be 1.0 percent. Several commenters also stated that CMS should not include TDAPA and TPNIES payment amounts when calculating total ESRD PPS payments, of which outlier payments are targeted at 1.0 percent.
Response:
We appreciate these comments, but we do not agree that either of the suggested revisions to the outlier methodology would be more appropriate than the current outlier policy. As we have previously stated, while we agree that section 1881(b)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act provides the Secretary with discretion to set an appropriate outlier percentage under the ESRD PPS, we continue to believe the 1.0 percent target is more appropriate than a lower outlier percentage. As discussed in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49134
), we established the 1.0 percent outlier percentage because it struck an appropriate balance between our objective of paying an adequate amount for the costliest, most resource-intensive patients and providing an appropriate level of payment for those patients who do not qualify for outlier payments. We continue to believe the 1.0 percent target strikes the appropriate balance, and as we further noted in the CY 2023 ESRD PPS final rule (
87 FR 67171
), a reduced outlier percentage may not provide the appropriate level of payment for outlier cases and may not protect access for beneficiaries whose care is unusually costly. This is because if we were to decrease the target outlier percentage, we would need to significantly increase the FDL amounts, which would make it more difficult for ESRD facilities to receive outlier payments based on their claims. We did not propose to reduce the outlier percentage for CY 2027, and we are not finalizing any such reduction in this final rule.
Likewise, we do not agree with the suggestion to exclude TDAPA and TPNIES payments from total ESRD PPS payments for the purposes of setting the FDL and MAP amounts for CY 2027. We believe that commenters incorrectly assume that excluding TDAPA and TPNIES payment amounts from this calculation would result in an increase to non-outlier payments (that is, total ESRD PPS payments other than those made as part of the outlier adjustment under the ESRD PPS). To the contrary, this suggested change to our calculations would only reduce the total amount of outlier payments, which would be 1.0 percent of a lower total ESRD PPS payment figure, without increasing other (non-outlier) payments under the ESRD PPS, since the base rate would continue to be reduced by 1.0 percent. This change would require us to increase the FDL amounts, which would make it more difficult for ESRD facilities to receive outlier payments based on their claims.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concerns about the interaction between outlier payments and new drugs. A commenter urged
(
printed page 68764)
CMS to develop a predictable, long-term approach for paying for new drugs after they transition out of a TDAPA period, particularly drugs within an existing ESRD PPS functional category. Another commenter encouraged CMS to reserve outlier payments for unusual clinical variation, not as a payment mechanism for new drugs, stating that new drugs are the primary driver for outlier payments in direct contrast to the purpose of the policy. This commenter stated that patients who require unusually higher-cost services are less likely to qualify for outlier payments under the current system.
Response:
We agree with commenters that the outlier adjustment is intended to recognize unusual variations in cost due to the use of ESRD outlier services and is not intended as a payment mechanism for new renal dialysis drugs. Rather, the drug designation process under
42 CFR 413.234
, which includes the TDAPA and post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, is the ESRD PPS mechanism for incorporating new renal dialysis drugs and biological products. As discussed in section II.B.6. of this final rule, we are finalizing our proposal to calculate the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts more frequently to reflect updated information beginning in CY 2027.

4. Impacts to the CY 2027 ESRD PPS Base Rate
a. Background
In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49071
through
49083
), CMS established the methodology for calculating the ESRD PPS per-treatment base rate, that is, the ESRD PPS base rate, and calculating the per-treatment payment amount, which are codified at §§ 413.220 and 413.230. The CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule also included a detailed discussion of the methodology used to calculate the ESRD PPS base rate and the computation of factors used to adjust the ESRD PPS base rate for projected outlier payments and budget neutrality in accordance with sections 1881(b)(14)(D)(ii) and 1881(b)(14)(A)(ii) of the Act, respectively. Specifically, the ESRD PPS base rate was developed from CY 2007 claims (that is, the lowest per patient utilization year as required by section 1881(b)(14)(A)(ii) of the Act), updated to CY 2011, and represented the average per treatment MAP for composite rate and separately billable services. In accordance with section 1881(b)(14)(D) of the Act and our regulation at § 413.230, the per-treatment payment amount is the sum of the ESRD PPS base rate, adjusted for the patient specific case-mix adjustments, applicable facility-level adjustments, geographic differences in area wage levels using an area wage index, and any applicable outlier payment, home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment, the TDAPA, the TPNIES, the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, and the TPEAPA for CYs 2024, 2025 and 2026.
b. Annual Payment Rate Update for CY 2027
We proposed an ESRD PPS base rate for CY 2027 of $299.55. As discussed in section II.B.1.d. of this final rule, we proposed that if more recent data became available after the publication of the proposed rule and before the publication of the final rule (for example, a more recent estimate of the market basket percentage increase or productivity adjustment), we would use such data, if appropriate, to determine the CY 2027 ESRDB market basket update in the final rule. We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Most commenters who discussed ESRD PPS payment policy supported increasing the overall ESRD PPS payment rate. Many commenters, however, expressed an opinion that the proposed ESRD PPS base rate of $299.55 was insufficient, which added to many commenters' concerns about current payment adequacy under the ESRD PPS. Some commenters noted that this represented an increase of $17.84 over the CY 2026 base rate, $15.96 of which is attributable to the increase to the base rate to account for phosphate binders, resulting in an increase to the base rate of only $1.88 outside of the phosphate binder increase. As discussed in section II.B.7. of this final rule, many commenters supported the base rate increase for phosphate binders. Many commenters acknowledged that the reason why the proposed increase outside of the phosphate binder increase was low was due to the application of various budget neutrality factors. Many commenters expressed support for implementing certain proposed policy changes non-budget neutrally.
Several comments discussed payment adequacy under the ESRD PPS. Multiple commenters listed figures published by MedPAC listing Original Medicare margins for ESRD facilities, noting that MedPAC has found low and occasionally negative margins in past reports.
Many commenters included current or potential future impacts of lower than appropriate ESRD PPS payments. These impacts included difficulty hiring and maintaining skilled staff, ESRD facility closures, difficulty providing certain expensive drugs and biological products, or other cost reductions. Some commenters provided data on ESRD facility closures, predominantly in rural areas, and attributed this trend to concerns about payment adequacy under the ESRD PPS. Several commenters attributed perceived lower than appropriate payment to historical under-forecasts of the ESRDB market basket, which they stated has resulted in a lower base rate than if forecasts had been accurate.
A few commenters indicated a belief that payment rates under the ESRD PPS were generally adequate. A few commenters raised concerns related to cost sharing under the ESRD PPS and noted that higher payment rates result in increased beneficiary cost sharing. A commenter requested CMS assess and publicly report the beneficiary level impact of ESRD PPS payment changes on cost sharing.
Response:
We appreciate support for increasing the ESRD PPS base rate and recognize the concerns over the payment amounts set under the ESRD PPS. The final ESRDB market basket update is 1.9 percent, higher than the proposed value of 1.6 percent, which we believe addresses some of the commenters' concerns about payment adequacy. However, we want to clarify a few points about the proposed CY 2027 ESRD PPS base rate. The proposed ESRD PPS base rate of $299.55 was derived from the CY 2026 ESRD PPS base rate of $281.71, the proposed ESRDB market basket update of 1.6 percent, the proposed increase to incorporate phosphate binders of $15.96, the proposed wage index budget neutrality factor of 1.00267, and the proposed budget neutrality factor of 0.98783 for the proposed policy changes to the LVPA, pediatric payment adjustments and training add-on adjustments. As highlighted by some commenters, the reason why the CY
(
printed page 68766)
2027 ESRD PPS base rate is not, excluding the increase of phosphate binders, 1.6 percent higher (or, 1.9 percent higher using the final ESRDB market basket update) than the CY 2026 ESRD PPS base rate is due to the budget neutrality factors applied. We discuss why we believe applying these budget neutrality factors is appropriate in the following comment and response.
We strongly caution commenters against using the ESRD PPS base rate as an estimate of payment adequacy or as a proxy for payment levels under the ESRD PPS. The proposed budget neutrality factor of 0.98783 reduced the proposed ESRD PPS base rate because the proposed policy changes to the LVPA, training add-on, and pediatric payment modifiers result in increases to the payment adjustment factors. If we did not apply this budget neutrality factor, then these policy changes would increase the overall payment rate. The ESRD PPS base rate is not intended to be an average payment amount for ESRD beneficiaries; it is a base unit of payment that is then adjusted by several adjustment factors, almost all of which increase payment. In practice, the ESRD PPS base rate represents the payment provided for an adult patient aged 70-79, with the average BSA of 1.9, has none of the applicable comorbidities, is not in the onset period, and is being treated in an ESRD facility that is neither rural nor low volume and that has a wage index value of 1.000. We acknowledge that the base rate, adjusted by the wage index and other adjustment factors (on a budget neutral basis), represents the payment for beneficiaries with AKI, as required by section 1834(r)(1) of the Act.
We acknowledge the quality concerns that commenters have raised and the data points cited by commenters. We note that in its March 2026 MedPAC Report to Congress
[
15
]
, MedPAC concluded that payment adequacy indicators for ESRD facilities were generally favorable and recommended that the Congress should eliminate the payment rate update for CY 2027. We agree with MedPAC that payment under the ESRD PPS is appropriate. We share the concerns of commenters regarding ESRD facility closures, especially in rural areas, and note that this was a significant motivator for our changes to the LVPA, which are finalizing, as discussed in section II.B.8. of this final rule.
We agree with the commenters who stated that payments under the ESRD PPS were generally adequate and recognize their concerns related to beneficiary cost sharing. We note that the increase to beneficiary cost sharing associated with the ESRDB market basket update is the result of a statutorily required payment rate update, but we will continue to be mindful of the impact of our payment policies on beneficiary out-of-pocket costs.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should reconsider our longstanding philosophy on applying budget neutrality factors. The commenter acknowledged that budget neutrality was appropriate for certain changes, like case mix adjustment factors, but believed it would not be appropriate for others. The commenter highlighted the new ESRD PPS wage index methodology implemented in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule (
89 FR 89198
through
89107
) as an example of a policy which they believe should not be implemented budget neutrally.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's perspective regarding the application of budget neutrality under the ESRD PPS. Section 1881(b)(14) of the Act establishes the statutory framework for the ESRD PPS. Section 1881(b)(14)(A)(ii) of the Act established the aggregate payment level when the ESRD PPS was implemented in CY 2011, while section 1881(b)(14)(D) of the Act requires or authorizes various adjustments to payments under the ESRD PPS, including adjustments based on case mix, for high-cost outliers, for low-volume facilities, and such other payment adjustments as the Secretary determines appropriate.
Consistent with this statutory framework and our longstanding implementation of the ESRD PPS, we generally believe that it is appropriate to implement changes to payment adjustments in a budget-neutral manner when those changes are intended to redistribute payments to better account for differences in relative resource use for costs that are already reflected in the ESRD PPS base rate. In these circumstances, the purpose of modifying the adjustment is to improve the distribution of payments under the ESRD PPS rather than to increase or decrease the aggregate level of payment for renal dialysis services. This approach is consistent with how we have historically applied budget neutrality to payment adjustments under the ESRD PPS, including case-mix adjustments.
For example, we applied a budget neutrality factor when implementing the new ESRD PPS wage index methodology in CY 2025 because labor costs are already reflected in the ESRD PPS base rate and the purpose of the wage index is to account for geographic differences in those labor costs (
89 FR 89097
through
89116
). The new ESRD PPS wage index methodology changed how the labor-related portion of the existing ESRD PPS payment is distributed among ESRD facilities based on geographic differences in wages; it did not add a new category of renal dialysis services or costs to the ESRD PPS bundle. Accordingly, we believe it was appropriate to implement that methodology in a budget-neutral manner so that the change in methodology itself would not increase or decrease aggregate ESRD PPS payments (
89 FR 89109
).
We believe it is appropriate to implement the modifications to the LVPA in this rule in a budget neutral manner. Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act requires the ESRD PPS to include a payment adjustment that reflects the extent to which costs incurred by low-volume facilities exceed the costs incurred by other facilities. The costs of furnishing renal dialysis services at low-volume facilities were represented in the data used to establish the ESRD PPS bundled payment (
75 FR 49117
through
49125
). The purpose of modifying the LVPA therefore is to better align relative payments with relative resource use among ESRD facilities, rather than to recognize a new category of costs or services that is not already reflected in the ESRD PPS base rate. Implementing such modifications without a corresponding budget neutrality adjustment would increase aggregate ESRD PPS payments solely as a result of a policy intended to recalibrate how payments for existing bundled costs are distributed. Our intention in proposing modifications to payment adjustments like the LVPA is generally to make payments that align relative payments with relative resource use, not to increase the ESRD PPS base rate.
By contrast, where a policy accounts for costs that are not already reflected in the ESRD PPS base rate, an increase in aggregate ESRD PPS payments may be appropriate. As discussed elsewhere in this final rule, phosphate binders were not included in the ESRD PPS base rate when the ESRD PPS was established in CY 2011 and were not subsequently incorporated into the base rate. Accordingly, we are increasing the ESRD PPS base rate to account for the costs of phosphate binders rather than offsetting that increase through a budget neutrality adjustment.
(
printed page 68767)
We therefore do not believe that all changes to the ESRD PPS necessarily should be treated identically for purposes of budget neutrality. Rather, in determining whether budget neutrality is appropriate for a particular policy, we consider the applicable statutory authority and the nature and purpose of the payment change. In general, where a change to an existing payment adjustment is intended to improve the allocation of payments for costs already reflected in the ESRD PPS base rate, we believe that implementing the change in a budget-neutral manner appropriately preserves the distinction between redistributing payments under the ESRD PPS and increasing the payment amount to account for additional costs or services. Where a policy instead incorporates costs or services that are not already reflected in the ESRD PPS base rate, an increase in aggregate ESRD PPS payments may be appropriate, subject to the applicable statutory authority.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concerns over the estimated 1.1 percent increase to overall ESRD PPS payments. Commenters noted that this is lower than the proposed 1.6 percent ESRDB market basket update. Many commenters stated a belief that this 1.1 percent payment increase was insufficient, comparing it to a wide array of estimates for inflation.
Response:
We want to clarify why the estimated year-over-year payment increase is less than the proposed 1.6 percent ESRDB market basket update. In our impact analysis, both for the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule and for this final rule, we simulate claims for CY 2026 and CY 2027 using available CY 2025 claims data. As part of this simulation, we applied the 1.6 percent ESRDB market basket update, as well as simulated the impact of other changes to ESRD PPS payment, including those resulting from policies proposed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule. There are several factors which contribute to the year-over-year estimated increase in payments being lower than the proposed ESRDB market basket update; however, the primary cause driving the lower year over year payment impact for CY 2027 presented in the CY 2027 proposed rule was the impact of the routine changes to the outlier policy as shown in Table 26 in the ESRD PPS CY 2027 proposed rule (
91 FR 38860
). We estimated and are currently estimating outliers being larger than 1 percent for 2026 and we proposed MAP and FDL amounts to better achieve the 1.0 percent outlier target for CY 2027 (
91 FR 38808
). So, it is not surprising that the proposed change to the MAP and FDL amounts are expected to result in a year-over-year decrease in estimated outlier payments.
While we believe that the estimated year-over-year payment increase is an important metric that interested parties may consider when evaluating the impact of the rule, we caution interested parties to interpret it carefully. We include detailed impacts on each of the new policies and many of the routine and established policies in Table 30 in section VII.C.5.a. of this final rule. We note that table indicates that the year-over-year increase in ESRD PPS payments is 2.4 percent, which is higher than the 1.9 percent ESRDB market basket update. These figures are different for the same underlying reasons as the difference the commenters noted.
Comment:
A commenter stated CMS should conduct and publish a comprehensive ESRD PPS base rate adequacy analysis using the most current available and representative facility cost-report data.
Response:
We continually monitor the adequacy of payment rates under the ESRD PPS, which we have used to inform payment policies. We reiterate that we caution interested parties against using the base rate as a proxy for overall payment amount, as budget neutral increases to payment adjustments reduce the base rate while maintaining the overall payment amount. We note that in proposing the modifications to the LVPA, we published an analysis of payment-to-cost ratios using CY 2024 cost report data and CY 2025 claims data (
91 FR 38822
). However, in discussing that analysis, we also discussed the limitations of such an analysis in terms of evaluating payment adequacy. We will take into consideration the commenter's suggestion that we publish further analysis on payment rate adequacy.
Comment:
A commenter stated that a market basket update cannot fully address payment adequacy since it is designed to measure changes in prices for a fixed mix of inputs. The commenter stated that even a perfectly calibrated market basket update would only preserve the purchasing power of the existing base rate but would not determine whether that original rate was adequate to start with.
Response:
We agree with the commenter that the ESRDB market basket update, as required by section 1881(b)(14)(F) of the Act, represents the change in prices of the same mix of goods and services purchased in the base period. It is not intended to capture changes in the types of renal dialysis services purchased by ESRD facilities. We recognize the extent to which this can create perceived payment adequacy concerns, especially as it pertains to new renal dialysis technologies that may be higher cost than those which were utilized when the base rate was established. Additionally, we recognize that it is not a measure of payment adequacy for the initial CY 2011 ESRD PPS base rate. The CY 2011 ESRD PPS base rate was established in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule based on statutory requirements, which required that overall payments be equal to 98 percent of what they would have been under the composite rate system (
75 FR 49071
through
49083
). We believe that payments under the ESRD PPS are sufficient for ESRD facilities to furnish renal dialysis services to Medicare beneficiaries. Although the original payment rate from 2011 and the ESRDB market basket increases are based on that fixed bundle of goods and services; by providing a single bundled payment we allow ESRD facilities to provide whichever services are most appropriate for a patient. This gives ESRD facilities the flexibility to provide new technologies to patients when appropriate.

Wage Index Budget Neutrality Adjustment Factor:
We compute a wage index budget neutrality adjustment factor that is applied to the ESRD PPS base rate. For CY 2027, we did not propose and are not finalizing any changes to the methodology used to calculate this factor, which is described in detail in the CY 2014 ESRD PPS final rule (

Next, we computed the estimated dollar amount that would have been paid for the same ESRD facilities using the CY 2027 ESRD PPS wage index and LRS for CY 2027. The total of these payments becomes the new CY 2027 amount of wage-adjusted expenditures for all ESRD facilities. The wage index budget neutrality factor is calculated as the target amount divided
(

When we multiplied the wage index budget neutrality factor by the applicable CY 2027 estimated payments, aggregate Medicare payments to ESRD facilities would remain budget neutral when compared to the target amount of expenditures. Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern about our post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment policy. Commenters expressed concern that lagged ASP data may not be reflective of current prices. Numerous commenters requested we modify our methodology for calculating the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment to be based on per-claim utilization and only apply to claims that include the drug or biological product in question and not be time limited. Commenters generally expressed the opinion that such a payment adjustment would better support innovation within the ESRD PPS. A commenter stated the belief that the current post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology has harmed patients by failing to provide a sustainable pathway for payment for new drugs and biological products and their suggested methodology would better support innovation.
Response:
As we discussed in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule (
88 FR 76388
through
76396
) we do not agree that a methodology based on per-claim utilization would be appropriate for the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, because it would directly
(
printed page 68770)
incentivize utilization of a particular drug or biological product, which we noted can result in overutilization. While the TDAPA and post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustments share the goal of supporting access to new renal dialysis drugs or biological products used to treat or manage a condition in an ESRD PPS functional category, the TDAPA's short-term objectives are more consistent with a methodology that is based on per-claim utilization. As we discussed in the CY 2019 and CY 2020 ESRD PPS final rules (
83 FR 56935
;
84 FR 60654
), for new renal dialysis drugs and biological products that fall into an existing ESRD PPS functional category, the TDAPA helps ESRD facilities to incorporate the new drugs and biological products and make appropriate changes in their business operations to adopt such products. We also explained that the TDAPA provides additional payments for such associated costs and promotes competition among the products within the ESRD PPS functional categories, while focusing Medicare resources on products that are innovative. The TDAPA for renal dialysis drugs and biological products in existing ESRD PPS functional categories is inherently transitional in nature and therefore not permanent. We later finalized a post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment beginning in CY 2024 that provides a glidepath for inclusion of such new renal dialysis drugs and biological products into the ESRD PPS. In the CY 2024 ESRD PPS proposed rule (
88 FR 42460
), we stated that a 3-year period for the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment would be consistent with the transition period that was finalized at the beginning of the ESRD PPS, when ESRD facilities were transitioned from receiving payments under the composite rate payment system to receiving payments under the ESRD PPS (
75 FR 49162
).
We believe that the current post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology provides the most appropriate incentives for ESRD facilities to be efficient with resources, while providing an appropriate level of payment that supports access to new renal dialysis drugs and biological products. We recognize that the policy would not permanently maintain increased payments for new renal dialysis drugs and biological products that receive the TDAPA, and we do not believe that such a permanent increase in payments would be appropriate. We did not propose any changes to the methodology used to calculate the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, the 3-year timeframe of the adjustment or the application of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment to all ESRD PPS claims for CY 2027 and are not finalizing any such changes in this final rule.

89 FR 89135
through
89136
). However, in that final rule, we did not finalize other circumstances where we would update the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount for a drug or biological product. Specifically, we stated that we did not intend to routinely update the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount quarterly, as we believed this would make it more difficult for ESRD facilities to estimate payments (
89 FR 89136

In response to the proposed post-TDAPA add-on payment amount published in the CY 2026 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we received a comment requesting we finalize a policy to publish the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment for DefenCath® after the publication of the final rule (
90 FR 53091
). This commenter stated that publishing the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount for that drug later, such that data from the third and fourth quarter of 2025 could be included in the calculation, would be more appropriate as it would reflect more recent data that shows increased utilization compared to the third and fourth quarter of 2024. Specifically, they noted that they believed 2024 utilization for DefenCath® was depressed by several factors, which they stated would result in an undervaluing of the drug for the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment. The commenter highlighted that the 2024 data would be two years old by the time the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment would begin in quarter 3 2026. While we did not finalize any such changes in the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule, we noted that we would evaluate whether additional flexibilities may be warranted in the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment calculation.
Since the publication of the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule, interested parties have repeated their concerns with our established post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology and stated a belief that it undervalued new drugs and biological products. We understand the concerns raised by interested parties regarding the time delay of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment calculation inherent in calculating the adjustment once per year during rulemaking and we have reevaluated our policy. Although it is important for ESRD facilities to be able to accurately plan for payments, we recognize that rapid changes in price or utilization might not be fully captured by the current methodology.
In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed to modify the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology to routinely calculate the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts each quarter. The proposed modification would not change the steps for the calculation of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, insofar as we would still be using the most recent quarter of ASP data and the most recently available full year of utilization data. We only proposed to perform the calculation more frequently and publish the amounts in CRs quarterly. We acknowledged that, in the past, we have stated that setting the post-TDAPA add-on payment amount once annually would improve ESRD facilities' ability
(
printed page 68771)
to estimate payments. However, after further consideration, we stated that we believe that setting the post-TDAPA add-on payment amount more frequently would better align the post-TDAPA add-on payment amounts with the actual utilizations and prices of the renal dialysis drugs and biological products. This would allow for the payment amount to consistently be based on the most recently available data, which we believe would address concerns which interested parties have raised that the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount was often based on outdated data. Under this proposal, we explained that we would still publish the first quarter post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts annually in the rule. We stated that we expect that generally the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts would not change drastically throughout the year, which would allow ESRD facilities to reasonably estimate payments in advance.
As we proposed calculating the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment quarterly, we also proposed modifying the conditional ASP policy such that the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment would stop the next quarter after a non-submission of ASP data. We explained in the proposed rule that this is a change from current policy, in which we would wait until the next rulemaking year to discontinue the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment for a drug which failed to report ASP. We noted that the amount of time for processing a CR can vary and there are occasionally other factors which create additional lag in the use of claims data, so the time periods utilized in a given quarter could change from year to year. However, we stated that we intend to generally aim to include data from two quarters prior. For example, for the third quarter post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, which begins July 1 of a year, we would generally include data through December of the prior year, but depending on the year December data may not be available at the time of processing. We proposed that, if an update to the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount for a given quarter is not operationally feasible for some currently unforeseen reason, the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount for the prior quarter would continue until such a time when updating it is operationally feasible. We stated that we intend to include the months from which the post-TDAPA adjustment was calculated, as well as the quarter of ASP we used for the calculation in the CR. We stated that we would also note any discontinuations of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment due to failure to submit ASP data.
We proposed changes to § 413.234(c)(3) to state that the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment would be calculated quarterly and that if we stopped receiving ASP data, we would not calculate the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment for any subsequent quarter (rather than any subsequent year, as it currently reads). We also proposed changes to § 413.234(g) to state that we would calculate the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment quarterly.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that quarterly recalculation of post-TDAPA add-on payment amounts would negatively impact payment stability that facilities rely on for long-term planning. One LDO noted that CMS previously recognized, in prior rulemaking, that setting the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount annually supports ESRD facilities' long-term planning and budgeting for such drugs after the TDAPA period, and that facilities have operated under the expectation that a payment amount established for a calendar year remains fixed for that year. This commenter stated this predictability is crucial to ESRD facilities' pharmaceutical operations, which fundamentally rely on the ability to plan and budget over the longer term and expressed concern about the continued post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment policy.
Some commenters stated that whereas annual updates to post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment have provided sufficient information to establish payment amounts and support accurate payment, quarterly recalculations add complexity and uncertainty without a commensurate benefit.
Response:
While we agree with commenters that quarterly updates to the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount may result in more frequent changes to this adjustment; and therefore, would provide less certainty regarding the amount that will apply throughout an entire calendar year, we do not agree that more frequent recalculation necessarily results in greater payment instability. Rather, quarterly recalculation allows changes in price and utilization to be reflected incrementally as more recent data become available, instead of allowing those changes to accumulate until the next annual recalculation. As a result, quarterly calculation may produce smaller, more gradual changes in the post-TDAPA amount from one quarter to the next and reduce the potential for a larger change when the amount is recalculated for a new calendar year.
As we explained in the proposed rule, we proposed to change our policy to calculate the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount quarterly because rapid changes in price or utilization might not be fully captured by the current annual methodology. Table 11 demonstrates this distinction by comparing the actual post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts for the second, third, and fourth quarters of 2026 with what the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts would have been if they were calculated on a quarterly basis based on the latest available data, as we proposed to do for CY 2027. As shown in this table, if the methodology that we proposed for CY 2027 were applied to CY 2026, it would have resulted in more gradual change in post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts from one quarter to the next than having a larger change between Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. This results in greater stability and directly addresses the key concerns that commenters raised in response to the CY 2026 post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts.
(
printed page 68772)
We do not believe that the proposed quarterly calculation adds complexity with no commensurate benefit. As we demonstrate in Table 11, the proposed methodology has a clear benefit of capturing ongoing changes in price and utilization resulting in more appropriately adjusted payment. Furthermore, as we explained in the proposed rule, the proposed modification would not change the steps for the calculation of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, insofar as we would still be using the most recent quarter of ASP data and the most recently available full year of utilization data. We only proposed to perform the calculation more frequently and publish the amounts in CRs quarterly. Therefore, we do not believe that the proposed methodology increases the complexity of the calculation. Rather, we believe this more responsive approach appropriately balances ESRD facilities' interest in payment predictability with the need for the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts to reflect more current price and utilization data.
CMS appreciates commenters' concerns about payment predictability and the administrative burden of more frequent updates. As we discussed in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule establishing the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, this policy was designed to balance two goals: supporting ESRD facilities' long-term planning and budgeting for new renal dialysis drugs and biological products and ensuring the payment adjustment accurately reflects the actual prices and utilization of those products (
88 FR 76393
). We first adopted a policy of calculating post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts annually, because we believed this would sufficiently address changes in price and utilization over time. However, our experience implementing the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology since CY 2024 has shown that annual calculation, on its own, may not adequately serve the accuracy side of that balance. Specifically, as we noted in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, in response to the CY 2026 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we received a comment requesting that CMS delay publication of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amount for DefenCath® until later-quarter 2025 data could be incorporated, because the calculation otherwise relied on 2024 utilization data that would have been two years old by the time the adjustment took effect in the third quarter of CY 2026. While we did not finalize a change in response to that comment, we stated in the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule that we would evaluate whether additional flexibilities were warranted in the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment calculation (
90 FR 53091
). Since that rule was published, interested parties have continued to raise similar concerns, stating a belief that the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment policy's core purpose of supporting continued access to these products could be better supported by using more recent data to establish the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts. The proposed approach of recalculating post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment amounts quarterly aligns with payment for Part B drugs more broadly, which is more dynamic and responsive to such changes. We believe the proposed post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology appropriately balances the twin goals of the policy, while allowing the payment amount to track actual drug pricing and utilization more closely than the annual approach has allowed.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern about the proposed conditional ASP policy. Commenters stated that abruptly ending the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment due to a manufacturer's non-submission of ASP data could create uncertainty around continued coverage and availability of these therapies.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns that commenters have raised. As we discussed in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule (
88 FR 76393
through
76394
), if drug manufacturers were to stop submitting ASP data for products that are included in the calculation of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, and we had to revert to basing calculation of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment on WAC or invoice pricing, we believe we would be overpaying for the add-on payment adjustment. Therefore, we established a policy to make payment of the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment conditional on receiving ASP data. We continue to believe that our longstanding conditional ASP policy appropriately balances access to new renal dialysis drugs with responsible spending from the Medicare Trust Fund.

a. Background
(1) Background on Oral-Only Renal Dialysis Drugs
Section 1881(b)(14)(A)(i) of the Act requires the Secretary to implement a payment system under which a single payment is made to a provider of services or a renal dialysis facility for renal dialysis services in lieu of any other payment. Section 1881(b)(14)(B) of the Act defines renal dialysis services, and clause (iii) of such section states that these services include other drugs and biologicals that are furnished to individuals for the treatment of ESRD and for which payment was made separately under this title, and any oral equivalent form of such drug or biological.
As we explained in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49044
), we interpret this provision as including not only injectable drugs and biological products used for the treatment of ESRD (other than ESAs) and any oral form of ESAs, which are included under clause (ii) of section 1881(b)(14)(B) of the Act, but also all oral drugs and biological products used for the treatment of ESRD and furnished under Title XVIII of the Act. We also concluded that, to the extent oral-only drugs or biological products used for the treatment of ESRD do not fall within clause (iii) of section 1881(b)(14)(B) of the Act, such drugs or biological products would fall under clause (iv) of such section, and constitute other items and services used for the treatment of ESRD that are not described in clause (i) of section 1881(b)(14)(B) of the Act.
We finalized and issued the payment policies for oral-only renal dialysis service drugs and biological products in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49038
through
49053
), where we defined renal dialysis services at § 413.171 to include other drugs and biological products furnished to individuals for the treatment of ESRD and for which payment was made separately prior to January 1, 2011, under Title XVIII of the Act, including oral-only drugs (
75 FR 49044
). We further described oral-only drugs as those that have no injectable equivalent or other form of administration (

through
49039

We stated that there were certain advantages to delaying the implementation of payment for oral-only drugs and biological products, including allowing ESRD facilities additional time to make operational changes and logistical arrangements to furnish oral-only renal dialysis drugs and biological products to their patients. Accordingly, we codified the delay in payment for oral-only renal dialysis drugs and biological products at § 413.174(f)(6) and specified that payment to an ESRD facility for renal dialysis drugs and biological products with only an oral form will be incorporated into the ESRD PPS payment rate on January 1, 2014. (3) Transitional Drug Add-On Payment Adjustment (TDAPA) Framework
The TDAPA is a payment adjustment under the ESRD PPS for certain new renal dialysis drugs and biological products, as codified at § 413.234(c). As discussed in the CY 2019 and CY 2020 ESRD PPS final rules, for new renal dialysis drugs and biological products that fall into an existing ESRD PPS functional category, the TDAPA helps ESRD facilities to incorporate new drugs and biological products and make appropriate changes in their businesses to adopt such products. Furthermore, the TDAPA provides additional payments for such associated costs and promotes competition among the products within the ESRD PPS functional categories, while also focusing Medicare resources on products that are innovative (
