b. Proposed Methodology for Incorporating Phosphate Binders Into the ESRD PPS Base Rate
(1) General Discussion of Claims Data and Intention
As we discussed previously, oral phosphate binders have been paid under the ESRD PPS through the TDAPA since January 1, 2025. In the CY 2016 ESRD PPS final rule, CMS discussed that phosphate binders fall
(
printed page 68776)
into the bone and mineral metabolism ESRD PPS functional category but are not accounted for in the base rate. We stated that we will utilize the TDAPA to collect utilization data before incorporating these drugs into the ESRD PPS base rate (
80 FR 69025
). We explained that this would allow CMS to collect data reflecting current utilization of oral phosphate binders, as well as payment patterns and beneficiary co-insurance, and after a period of at least 2 years, we would adopt the methodology for including these drugs in the ESRD PPS bundled payment through notice-and-comment rulemaking. This would be consistent with section 217(a)(2) of PAMA, which requires the Secretary to use data from the most recent year available when establishing payment for oral-only drugs under the ESRD PPS.
As discussed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we have collected sufficient claims data to conduct a rate-setting analysis for phosphate binders (
91 FR 38815
). Specifically, we have collected robust claims data since January 1, 2025, and analyzed the utilization of various oral phosphate binders, including sevelamer carbonate, sevelamer hydrochloride, sucroferric oxyhydroxide, lanthanum carbonate, ferric citrate, and calcium acetate. We monitored the ASP data available during the specific utilization periods. Our overall analysis of ESRD claims data for CYs 2025 and 2026 indicated utilization patterns across the various phosphate binder formulations, with variations in ASP reflecting the different product types and market dynamics within this therapeutic class.
Therefore, we stated in the proposed rule that we believe we are at the step of the ESRD PPS drug designation process (outlined at § 413.234) where we propose the methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate to account for phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS bundled payment for CY 2027. We noted that we believe that a base rate increase is warranted in the case of phosphate binders because, as discussed in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule, oral-only drugs, which included phosphate binders, were not included in the ESRD PPS at the inception of the bundled payment system (
75 FR 49043
through
49044
) and currently remain unaccounted for within the ESRD PPS base rate. We proposed to add a per-treatment amount to the ESRD PPS base rate to include phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS bundled payment amount for dates of service on or after January 1, 2027.
In developing the proposed methodology for including phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate, we considered the methodology that we used when we incorporated calcimimetics into the ESRD PPS base rate beginning for CY 2021, as well as the methodology we used when we included Part B drugs and biological products in the ESRD PPS base rate as part of our initial implementation of the ESRD PPS. In the CY 2021 ESRD PPS final rule (
85 FR 71404
through
71410
), we discussed how we established the methodology for incorporating calcimimetics into the ESRD PPS base rate using utilization data from Medicare claims and applying ASP to establish the price for each drug form.
In addition, as discussed in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49064
), we established a dialysis treatment as the unit of payment. Consistent with the approach we used to include calcimimetics in the ESRD PPS base rate and the ESRD PPS unit of payment, we proposed a similar methodology in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule to calculate a one-time modification to the ESRD PPS base rate on a per-treatment basis to account for phosphate binders. The proposed methodology is similar to the calcimimetics approach because we would determine utilization of the drugs, in this case, phosphate binders, along with the payment amounts associated with each phosphate binder product based on ASP, consistent with our established TDAPA pricing policy.
The following sections review each element of our proposed methodology in detail. As an overview, we proposed to calculate a per-treatment amount for phosphate binders that would be added to the ESRD PPS base rate. We proposed to apply 100 percent of the ASP value from the most recent calendar quarter ASP calculations to the utilization data for phosphate binders between April 1, 2025, and December 31, 2025, based on Medicare ESRD claims data, for the proposed rule. For the calculations in this final rule, utilization data is based on ESRD claims from between April 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. This would provide the phosphate binder expenditure amount. We proposed to then multiply the phosphate binder expenditure amount by 1.06, consistent with the methodology that we used to calculate the flat rate add-on per-monthly claim amount of $36.41 during the TDAPA period, to yield the adjusted phosphate binder expenditure amount. Next, we proposed to divide the adjusted phosphate binder expenditure amount by the total number of hemodialysis-equivalent dialysis treatments paid between April 1, 2025, and December 31, 2025, under the ESRD PPS (April 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026, for this final rule). We proposed to reduce this average per-treatment amount by one percent to account for the outlier policy, since phosphate binders would be ESRD outlier services eligible for outlier payments beginning January 1, 2027, under the proposal. We proposed to add the resulting amount to the ESRD PPS base rate, as outlined in section II.B.4. of the proposed rule. We noted that this amount would stay in the base rate and be subject to the annual updates (ESRDB market basket update and application of wage index budget neutrality adjustment factor). Under the proposal, CMS would stop paying for these drugs through the TDAPA for dates of service on or after January 1, 2027.
We stated that, if finalized, this proposal would complete the implementation of § 413.174(f)(6), which provides that oral-only renal dialysis drugs are paid under the ESRD PPS beginning January 1, 2025, and that separate payment for oral-only phosphate binders is no longer provided beginning January 1, 2025. We described that the proposal, if finalized, would establish the methodology for incorporating phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate following the TDAPA period. We proposed revising our drug designation regulation at § 413.234 by adding paragraph (h) to set forth the methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate to account for the costs of phosphate binders. The proposed paragraph (h) would include the data sources and the steps we would take to calculate a per-treatment amount. We proposed that, for dates of service on or after January 1, 2027, oral phosphate binders would no longer be paid for under the ESRD PPS through the TDAPA (§ 413.234(c)) and would be paid for through the ESRD PPS base rate and be eligible for outlier payments as ESRD outlier services under § 413.237.
We noted that the methodology proposed in the proposed rule is only for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate to include phosphate binder drugs. This is consistent with our established policy for renal dialysis drugs and biological products that are not considered to be included in the ESRD PPS base rate, and as outlined at § 413.234(c) and (d). This policy states that we would propose and adopt the methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate, if appropriate, to account for the products through notice-and-comment rulemaking after sufficient claims data collection through the TDAPA process.

(3) Methodology for Determining the Price of Phosphate Binders
For use in the proposed calculation, we would set the price for phosphate binders using values from the most recent calendar quarter of ASP calculations available to the public, at 100 percent of ASP. This would be consistent with § 413.234(c)(1), which provides that TDAPA payment is based on 100 percent of ASP. The ASP-based value is a CMS-derived weighted average of all National Drug Code (NDC) sales prices submitted by drug manufacturers and assigned by CMS to the existing HCPCS codes for phosphate binders. For each billing code, CMS calculates a weighted ASP using data submitted by manufacturers, which includes the following: ASP data at the 11-digit NDC level, the number of units of the 11-digit NDC sold, and the ASP for those units. This calculation methodology is consistent with the approach described in the CY 2009 Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule (
73 FR 69752
) and authorized in section 1847A of the Act.
Consistent with the TDAPA basis of payment established for oral phosphate binders in CY 2025, we proposed to use 100 percent of the weighted ASP value. As we explained in the CY 2020 ESRD PPS final rule, the ESRD PPS accounts for storage and administration costs and ESRD facilities do not have acquisition price variation issues when compared to physicians (
83 FR 56946
). We noted in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule that we believe ASP is reasonable for phosphate binders because it reflects manufacturer sales prices net of applicable price concessions specified under section 1847A and provides a standardized measure for valuing phosphate-binder utilization. As we discussed previously, the ESRD PPS base rate has dollars built in for administrative complexities and overhead costs for renal dialysis drugs and biological products. We proposed an increase to the base rate to account for the newfound responsibility and substantial pill volume associated with ESRD facility dispensing of phosphate binders, which we discussed in detail in the proposed rule.
We stated that we believe using a value based on the most recent calendar quarter ASP calculations available to the public for phosphate binders would provide an accurate representation of the price of these drugs for ESRD facilities because it uses manufacturer sales information that includes discounts (that is, rebates, volume discounts, prompt payment, and cash payment specified in section 1847A of the Act).
For the proposed rule, the values from the most recent calendar quarter of ASP calculations available to the public were from the second quarter of 2026, and due to a two-quarter data lag, these ASP calculations reflected manufacturer sales data submitted to CMS for the fourth quarter of 2025. For this CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule, the most recent calendar quarter of ASP calculations available to the public is the fourth quarter of 2026, which reflects manufacturer sales data submitted into CMS for the second quarter of 2026, and we proposed to use that value for purposes of our final calculation.
We proposed to add § 413.234(h)(2)(ii), under which CMS would use 100 percent of the values from the most recent calendar quarter ASP calculations available to the public for phosphate binders to calculate a price for each product. We solicited comments on the proposed use of the values from the most recent calendar quarter ASP calculations available to the public for phosphate binders for setting the price and the proposed language at § 413.234(h).

(5) Accounting for Operational Costs
In addition to including direct drug costs, we proposed to incorporate an additional amount in the base rate to reflect the operational costs associated with supplying phosphate binders to ESRD facilities. During the TDAPA period, we provided a flat rate increase of $36.41 for monthly ESRD PPS claims to cover these operational costs, which include storage, distribution, staffing, and administrative expenses unique to the high-volume, multi-product nature of phosphate binder therapy. We stated that we expect the ongoing provision of phosphate binders will continue to result in additional operational costs for ESRD facilities. Incorporating these operational costs into the base rate is consistent with our authority under section 1881(b)(14) of the Act to establish a bundled payment that reflects the costs of furnishing renal dialysis services, as CMS considers phosphate binders to be a renal dialysis service as described at § 413.171.
As discussed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, the ESRD PPS base rate includes general overhead and administrative costs that apply broadly across renal dialysis services. Because of this, CMS did not establish a separate operational cost component for calcimimetics during the TDAPA period for calcimimetics or when calcimimetics were incorporated into the ESRD PPS base rate. However, as discussed in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule, oral phosphate binders present unique, high-volume dispensing and logistical demands that are distinct from and not captured by the general overhead and administrative costs discussed previously (
89 FR 89152
). For example, in response to the CY 2025 ESRD PPS proposed rule, one interested party commented that phosphate binders represent an exponential increase in the volume of pills that dialysis providers need to acquire, distribute, store, and manage, and that the relative difference between managing 360 pills per year per patient for cinacalcet as compared with 3,240 pills per year per patient for calcium carbonate is 800 percent (
89 FR 89141
). CMS addressed this comment, among many others, in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule, where we established a flat-rate TDAPA add-on of $36.41 per monthly claim to address the circumstances

Therefore, we stated in the proposed rule, CMS believes proposing to incorporate an equivalent operational cost component into the base rate is not duplicative of existing base rate funds and is necessary to ensure that the base rate accurately reflects the cost of furnishing these renal dialysis services.

We proposed to add a new paragraph § 413.234(h) regarding the data sources and methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate to account for the costs of phosphate binders and the operational expenses associated with providing phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS bundled payment. This new paragraph would state that, for dates of service on or after January 1, 2027, CMS would determine the utilization of phosphate binders by aggregating total units from Medicare ESRD facility claims (837-institutional form with bill type 072X) for the second, third, and fourth quarters of calendar year 2025 and the first two quarters of calendar year 2026. CMS would price each phosphate binder at 100 percent of the most recent calendar quarter ASP calculations available to the public. CMS would then multiply the utilization of each phosphate binder by its respective price and sum the expenditure amounts across all phosphate binder products to calculate the total oral phosphate binder expenditure amount. CMS would then calculate an adjusted phosphate binder expenditure amount by multiplying the phosphate binder expenditure amount by 1.06 to account for operational expenses. CMS would divide the adjusted total expenditure amount by the total number of paid hemodialysis-equivalent dialysis treatments from Medicare ESRD facility claims during the same claims data period to calculate the average per-treatment payment amount. Finally, CMS would reduce the average per-treatment payment amount by 1 percent to account for the outlier policy under § 413.237 to determine the amount added to the ESRD PPS base rate.
Beginning January 1, 2027, phosphate binders would also be eligible ESRD outlier services under § 413.237. The fundamental principle of the ESRD PPS is that the costs of renal dialysis services, including drugs, are incorporated into the base rate and spread across all dialysis treatments rather than assigned only to those treatments for which a particular item or service is furnished (
75 FR 49030
). We stated that, in keeping with this principle, we believe the cost of phosphate binders should be spread across all dialysis treatments rather than be directed only to the treatments for patients who are receiving phosphate binders.
We solicited comment on the proposed revisions to add paragraph (h) to § 413.234 to establish the data sources and methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate to account for phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS bundled payment.
We received public comments on numerous aspects of these proposals to include phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS base rate. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several individual commenters, including registered dietitians, nurses, and other clinical staff, expressed strong support for including phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS bundled payment, citing reduced administrative burden, elimination of prior authorization requirements, and fewer delays related to insurance and pharmacy access. Commenters noted that direct access through the ESRD PPS bundled payment allows for faster response to elevated phosphorus levels, improved medication adherence, and the elimination of out-of-pocket costs that previously led some beneficiaries to ration their medication. Several commenters also noted that home delivery of phosphate binders through the ESRD PPS bundled payment addressed transportation barriers that had previously limited access for some beneficiaries.
Response:
We thank the commenters for sharing their experiences with the TDAPA period for oral phosphate binders. We agree that incorporating these drugs into the ESRD PPS base rate should reduce administrative burden for ESRD facilities and improve timely access to phosphate binders for beneficiaries. We continue to believe that incorporating phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate, consistent with the treatment of other oral-only drugs, appropriately reflects the goals of the ESRD PPS bundled payment methodology.
Comment:
An interested party representing skilled nursing facility and nursing facility (SNF/NF) interests raised operational and clinical concerns regarding care fragmentation for beneficiaries in congregate care settings. The commenter identified timing gaps during weekend and evening discharges when ESRD facility staff are unavailable, a conflict between SNF federal medication timing requirements and the SNF's lack of direct purchasing authority for bundled phosphate binders, and administrative delays resulting from shifting billing pathways between Part D, Part A, and ESRD facilities. The commenter recommended that CMS establish a 14- to 30-day “Transitional Care Access” exemption following a hospital discharge to a congregate care setting, during which the SNF or NF could bill directly under Part D or Part A rather than coordinate through the ESRD facility.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter identifying these operational challenges for beneficiaries transitioning into SNFs and NFs. We recognize that care coordination between ESRD facilities and congregate care settings presents unique logistical considerations that differ from beneficiaries residing in the community. However, we do not believe it would be appropriate to establish a facility-type-specific exemption from the ESRD PPS bundled payment methodology, as doing so would create a parallel payment pathway that could complicate billing and undermine the consistency of the bundled payment across care settings. We encourage ESRD facilities and SNFs/NFs to work together, along with their contracted pharmacies, to establish protocols that support the timely delivery of phosphate binders around the time of discharge and other transitions of care. We will continue to monitor concerns related to care fragmentation in congregate care settings and will consider whether additional guidance or policy refinements are warranted in future rulemaking.
Comment:
One LDO generally supported incorporating phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS bundled payment but emphasized that binder selection should continue to be driven by clinical effectiveness and adherence rather than cost alone. The commenter noted that one sucroferric oxyhydroxide product has a substantial body of real-world evidence demonstrating improved phosphorus control with a lower pill burden compared to alternatives such as sevelamer and calcium acetate. However, the commenter expressed concern that interested parties assuming widespread switching to generic products may be overestimating the ability of providers to achieve equivalent clinical outcomes using lower-cost alternatives. The commenter recommended that CMS finalize the proposed methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate and confirm the policy's applicability to beneficiaries with AKI.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's perspective on the clinical considerations that inform phosphate binder selection. We agree that clinical effectiveness and beneficiary adherence
(
printed page 68782)
should remain the primary drivers of treatment decisions and note that our proposal was not intended to restrict a clinician's ability to prescribe the phosphate binder that best meets a beneficiary's clinical needs. We note that phosphate binders would be an eligible ESRD outlier service, which will help support access for unusual variations in the type or amount of medically necessary care. With respect to AKI beneficiaries receiving outpatient dialysis, we address this issue further in our next response to comments.
Comment:
Several commenters including an LDO and a non-profit dialysis association requested that CMS clarify the responsibility for furnishing phosphate binders to beneficiaries with AKI who receive outpatient dialysis, noting that once phosphate binders are incorporated into the ESRD PPS base rate, this change will also affect AKI beneficiaries prescribed phosphate binders. The commenter requested that CMS clarify these issues in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule or through subsequent guidance and asked that CMS ensure timely communication reaches MACs, ESRD facilities, nephrologists, Part D plans, Medicare Advantage plans, and beneficiaries prior to implementation.
Response:
We thank the commenters for raising this issue and agree that clarity regarding the furnishing of phosphate binders for beneficiaries with AKI receiving outpatient dialysis is important to the implementation of this policy. As discussed in section III.B. of this final rule, the AKI dialysis payment rate applies to all renal dialysis services, and ESRD facilities are responsible for furnishing all medically necessary renal dialysis services to beneficiaries with AKI who are receiving dialysis as specified at § 413.374(a). While oral-only renal dialysis drugs and biological products have always met the definition of renal dialysis services, the statutory delays implemented in our regulations at § 413.174(f)(6) postponed their inclusion in the ESRD PPS bundled payment until January 1, 2025. During the TDAPA payment period for phosphate binders, the TDAPA did not apply to renal dialysis services furnished to beneficiaries with AKI, and ESRD facilities were not yet responsible for furnishing phosphate binders to beneficiaries with AKI (
89 FR 89172
). This is because phosphate binders were not originally included in the ESRD PPS base rate, and therefore were not reflected in the AKI dialysis payment rate that is based on the ESRD PPS base rate. As a result, during the TDAPA period, the AKI dialysis payment rate did not include any amount for phosphate binders, so ESRD facilities had no payment mechanism through which to furnish them to beneficiaries with AKI.
Now that payment for phosphate binders is being incorporated directly into the ESRD PPS base rate, that payment is included in the AKI dialysis payment rate as well, because the AKI dialysis payment rate is based on the ESRD PPS base rate. As a result, ESRD facilities will be expected to furnish medically necessary phosphate binders to beneficiaries with AKI and receive payment under the AKI dialysis payment rate.
We recognize that the payment rate for renal dialysis services furnished to beneficiaries with AKI is based on the ESRD PPS base rate and that, beginning January 1, 2027, the ESRD PPS base rate will include an amount to account for phosphate binders. We intend to issue subregulatory guidance addressing the implications of this policy for the furnishing of phosphate binders for beneficiaries with AKI receiving outpatient dialysis. We will work to ensure that this guidance, along with other operational instructions related to this policy, is disseminated to MACs, ESRD facilities, treating clinicians, Part D plans, MA plans, and beneficiaries in advance of the January 1, 2027, implementation date. For further discussion of CMS policy pertaining to beneficiaries with AKI, please refer to section III.B.1. of this final rule.
Comment:
MedPAC supported bundling phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS in principle but raised several methodological concerns. MedPAC recommended that CMS use a more conservative utilization methodology consistent with the approach taken under the MIPPA, specifically recommending that CMS use the lowest per-patient utilization year rather than utilization data from the TDAPA period to minimize the risk of overpayment. MedPAC also questioned whether the entry of generic alternatives, including an authorized generic in March 2025 and a generic version in March 2026, would affect the cost estimates underlying the proposed base rate increase, and noted that one LDO's product, without a generic alternative, accounts for approximately 73 percent of the proposed rate increase. Additionally, MedPAC recommended that CMS remove the proposed 6 percent operational cost multiplier, noting that operational costs associated with furnishing phosphate binders are already partially reflected in the existing ESRD PPS base rate and that including a separate add-on would be duplicative.
Response:
We thank MedPAC for its continued support of incorporating phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate and for the commission's detailed methodological feedback. Regarding the utilization methodology, CMS considered the approach used under MIPPA, but we continue to believe that using TDAPA-period utilization data provides the most accurate reflection of current phosphate binder use, as it captures a more recent and complete time period than using the single lowest-utilization year. We note that any claims that include the previously mentioned authorized generic in March 2025 and the generic version in March 2026 would be included in the 2026 fourth quarter ASP data and thus included in the final rule calculations for the base rate increase. We will, however, continue to monitor utilization trends, including the effect of generic alternatives on costs and utilization patterns, and will consider adjustments in future rulemaking if actual experience meaningfully diverges from our projections.
With respect to the proposed operational cost multiplier, we disagree that this adjustment is duplicative of costs already embedded in the base rate. As we discussed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule and previously in this final rule, we believe the additional operational costs associated with ordering, dispensing, and coordinating phosphate binders under the ESRD PPS bundled payment are distinct from the general administrative costs reflected in the existing base rate calculation and warrant additional payment. We note that CMS did not incorporate an equivalent operational cost component when calcimimetics were added to the ESRD PPS base rate, because calcimimetics do not present the same high-volume, multi-product dispensing and logistical demands as phosphate binders, which are typically administered several times daily across six or more distinct products with differing storage and handling requirements. This distinction is consistent with the rationale CMS articulated in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule when establishing the $36.41 flat-rate TDAPA add-on for phosphate binders, which recognized that dispensing fees and other operational costs were not included in the ESRD PPS base rate for phosphate binders and that every ESRD facility would incur distribution, storage, and staffing expenses not accounted for in ASP data alone (

through

based expenditures embedded in the base rate rather than as a separate flat-rate add-on reflects the same average, empirically observed costs that underlie the ESRD PPS more broadly, and ensures the base rate accurately captures the full cost of furnishing phosphate binders. Several commenters, including a regional dialysis organization, an ESRD facility, a coalition of dialysis organizations, and a drug manufacturer, expressed concern regarding CMS's proposal to recalculate the operational cost add-on amount for phosphate binders when converting it from a TDAPA-period flat fee into a permanent component of the ESRD PPS base rate. Commenters noted that the costs of storing, managing, and dispensing phosphate binders have not decreased since CMS established the $36.41 monthly operational add-on under the TDAPA methodology, and expressed concern that CMS's proposed recalculation would result in a lower operational cost figure. A few commenters recommended that CMS instead maintain the operational add-on amount calculated during the TDAPA period using the ASP+6 percent methodology, rather than recalculate a new amount for CY 2027. A coalition of dialysis organizations similarly urged CMS to add an amount corresponding to the current TDAPA-period operational add-on. A drug manufacturer recommended that CMS adopt this alternative approach and retain the current operational expense add-on to account for distribution, mailing, and storage costs. A non-profit kidney care alliance more generally urged CMS to continue accounting for both drug and operational costs in future methodology updates.

We thank the commenters for their feedback on our proposed approach to calculating the operational cost component of the phosphate binder base-rate addition. We clarify that the 6 percent adjustment is not an add-on to ASP for purposes of pricing phosphate binders. As described in the proposed rule, we proposed to price phosphate binders using 100 percent of ASP and separately account for the operational costs associated with furnishing phosphate binders in calculating the amount incorporated into the ESRD PPS base rate. We understand commenters' preference for maintaining the TDAPA-period operational add-on amount for consistency and predictability. However, we continue to believe that recalculating the operational cost figure using more recent utilization and cost data provides a more accurate reflection of current operational costs than continuing to rely on the amount established earlier in the TDAPA period. We note that the operational cost add-on, like the drug cost component, is intended to reflect current, rather than static, cost experience, consistent with how we approach other bundled components of the ESRD PPS base rate. We appreciate commenters' support for continuing to account for both drug and operational costs in the base rate and confirm our intention to do so. We recognize the commenters' statement that operational costs associated with ESRD facilities furnishing phosphate binders have not changed since they were first added to the ESRD PPS bundled payment in CY 2025, however we believe that some of the initial costs associated with the transition should decrease over time. For example, we believe that certain costs associated with setting up systems or processes will likely decrease as those processes become standard. We note that the $36.41 monthly operational add-on was based on part D data, and we believe that recalculating the amount based on actual spending and utilization through the TDAPA is more reflective of these costs under the ESRD PPS.
Comment:
A network of dialysis organizations and regional offices and a provider advocacy organization raised concerns regarding whether the operational cost add-on, maintained or recalculated, adequately reflects the real-world costs that ESRD facilities incur in furnishing phosphate binders. The network of dialysis organizations and regional offices supported the proposed $15.96 base-rate increase and associated 6 percent operational adjustment but urged CMS to revise the adjustment if it does not cover real-world dispensing, shipping, counseling, and adherence-support costs. The provider advocacy organization raised a more specific concern, noting that the $36.41 monthly operational add-on was derived from 2023 Part D utilization patterns and does not reflect costs specific to small and independent facilities, including specialty pharmacy arrangements, rural and home delivery logistics, and adherence support. The commenter stated that any inadequacy in the original $36.41 figure has been carried forward, uncorrected, into the proposed permanent base-rate modification.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' detailed feedback on the real-world costs associated with furnishing phosphate binders. We recognize that ESRD facilities, particularly small and independent facilities, may incur costs related to specialty pharmacy arrangements, rural and home delivery logistics, and beneficiary adherence support that can vary based on facility size, location, and patient population. We do not believe it would be operationally feasible to establish a facility-specific or geographically adjusted operational cost add-on at this time, as doing so would introduce complexity inconsistent with the ESRD PPS's per-treatment bundled payment structure. We will, however, continue to monitor the actual operational costs ESRD facilities incur in furnishing phosphate binders under the base rate and will consider whether adjustments to the operational cost methodology are warranted in future rulemaking. We note that the ESRD PPS base rate is adjusted by several factors, including the wage index, several case-mix adjusters, and facility-level adjusters such as the LVPA. The LVPA is a long-standing policy mechanism through which small, low-volume ESRD facilities receive additional payment under the ESRD PPS. Additional payments made through the LVPA reflect the extent to which costs incurred by low-volume facilities in furnishing renal dialysis services exceed the costs incurred by other facilities in furnishing such services, which includes the costs of furnishing phosphate binders.

A pharmacy-related association raised concerns that incorporating phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS bundled payment would threaten beneficiary access to these therapies through community pharmacies. The commenter stated that, once phosphate binders are furnished exclusively through the ESRD facility under the ESRD PPS, community pharmacies that have historically dispensed these medications under Part D would be effectively excluded from this line of business. The commenter further noted that this shift could increase beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs in certain circumstances and reduce the pharmacy touchpoints available to support medication counseling and adherence.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concerns regarding the role of community pharmacies in furnishing phosphate binders to beneficiaries with ESRD. We recognize that incorporating
(
printed page 68784)
phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS on January 1, 2025, shifted the responsibility of furnishing these drugs from Part D pharmacy channels to ESRD facilities, consistent with the treatment of other oral-only renal dialysis drugs under the ESRD PPS. We do not believe that this shift increased beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs, in part because the ASP for phosphate binders has decreased throughout the TDAPA period, and also because the Part D cost-sharing structure (supplemental insurance) no longer applies for these drugs. With respect to medication counseling and adherence support, we expect ESRD facilities, in coordination with their contracted pharmacy arrangements, to continue supporting beneficiaries in managing their phosphate binder regimen. We do not believe that ending the TDAPA period for phosphate binders and incorporating phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate will negatively impact any of the expectations or observations outlined previously, however, we will continue to monitor beneficiary access and adherence outcomes following implementation and will consider whether further guidance is warranted in future rulemaking.

A provider advocacy organization raised concern regarding the data basis for the proposed $15.96 base rate addition, arguing that CMS derived this figure from only nine months of TDAPA claims data (April through December 2025) and that this is a thin basis for a permanent, non-adjustable addition to the base rate.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concern regarding the data period underlying the proposed base rate addition. We confirm that the proposed rule's calculation of $15.96 relied on phosphate binder utilization data from April 1, 2025, through December 31, 2025, representing only nine months of TDAPA claims following our exclusion of first-quarter 2025 data. CMS notes that for this CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule, we have updated our utilization calculations using claims data extending through June 30, 2026, expanding the utilization period to approximately fifteen months and significantly expanding the volume of claims data underlying the calculation compared to the proposed rule. We also updated our price calculations using data from the fourth quarter of 2026, consistent with our proposal to use the most recent calendar quarter of ASP data available. We believe this expanded claims period addresses the commenters' concern regarding the adequacy and timeframe of the data and provides a stronger foundation for this permanent addition to the ESRD PPS base rate. We also note that the one-time amount incorporated into the base rate is not separately repriced each year based on phosphate-binder ASP or utilization, but once incorporated it becomes part of the base rate and is subject to applicable annual ESRD PPS updates.

After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the incorporation of phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate beginning January 1, 2027, with a base rate increase of $12.85 per treatment, using the utilization methodology and operational cost multiplier alongside the most recent available claims (that is, claims from between April 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026) and fourth quarter 2026 ASP data, as proposed. We are also finalizing our proposal to add a new paragraph §  413.234(h) regarding the final data sources and methodology for modifying the ESRD PPS base rate to account for the costs of phosphate binders and the operational expenses associated with providing phosphate binders in the ESRD PPS bundled payment. We are finalizing a slightly modified version of new §  413.234(h)(2)(iv) to more clearly state the proposed methodology for calculating the operational cost component of the base rate increase for phosphate binders. We note that this slight modification is a change in language, not a change in policy. We intend to issue further subregulatory guidance addressing the furnishing of phosphate binders for beneficiaries with AKI receiving outpatient dialysis and will work to ensure timely communication of this guidance to affected interested parties prior to implementation.
8. Changes to the Low-Volume Payment Adjustment (LVPA)
a. Background on the LVPA
Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act provides that the ESRD PPS shall include a payment adjustment that reflects the extent to which costs incurred by low-volume facilities (as defined by the Secretary) in furnishing renal dialysis services exceed the costs incurred by other facilities in furnishing such services, and for payment for renal dialysis services furnished on or after January 1, 2011, and before January 1, 2014, such payment adjustment shall not be less than 10 percent. Therefore, the ESRD PPS provides a facility-level payment adjustment to ESRD facilities that meet the definition of a low-volume facility.
Under § 413.232(b), a low-volume facility is an ESRD facility that, based on the submitted documentation: (1) furnished less than 4,000 treatments in each of the 3 cost reporting years (based on as-filed or final settled 12-consecutive month costs reports, whichever is most recent, except as specified in paragraphs (g)(4) and (5) preceding the payment year; and (2) has not opened, closed, or received a new provider number due to a change in ownership (except where the change in ownership results in a change in facility type or as specified in paragraph (g)(6)) in the 3 cost reporting years (based on as-filed or final settled 12-consecutive month cost reports, whichever is most recent) preceding the payment year.
In addition, under § 413.232(c), for purposes of determining eligibility for the LVPA, the number of treatments considered furnished by the ESRD facility equals the aggregate number of treatments furnished by the ESRD facility and the number of treatments furnished by other ESRD facilities that are both under common ownership with, and 5 road miles or less from, the ESRD facility in question. To receive the LVPA, an ESRD facility must submit a written attestation statement to its MAC confirming that it meets the requirements as specified in § 413.232 and qualifies as a low-volume ESRD facility. For purposes of determining eligibility for the LVPA, “treatments” mean total hemodialysis equivalent treatments (Medicare and non-Medicare). For PD patients, one week of PD is considered equivalent to three HD treatments (
80 FR 68994
). Section 413.232(e) generally imposes a yearly November 1 deadline for attestation submissions, unless extraordinary circumstances justify an exception, and specifies exceptions for certain years where the deadline is in December or January. The November 1 attestation timeframe provides 60 days for a MAC to verify that an ESRD facility meets the LVPA eligibility criteria (
76 FR 70236
). The ESRD facility would then receive the LVPA for all the Medicare-eligible treatments in the payment year. Once an ESRD facility is determined to be eligible for the LVPA, a payment adjustment factor is applied to the ESRD PPS base rate for all applicable treatments furnished by the ESRD facility (
89 FR 89161
).
In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (

While the ESRD PPS is not a cost-based system, analyses of Medicare-allowable ESRD facility costs provide insight into whether payments align with resource use. Additionally, the ESRD PPS has a long history of establishing payment adjustment factors based on cost data (occasionally combined with claims data), including the current 2-tiered LVPA (

We note that directly comparing ESRD PPS payments to ESRD facility costs is not a perfect analysis as it disregards other payors, including Medicare Advantage (MA) and private payors, which could be providing higher payments for specific high-cost services. Nonetheless, this analysis indicates that payments exceed costs for higher volume ESRD facilities, while lower-volume ESRD facilities, particularly those furnishing fewer than 10,000 treatments tend to have costs that exceed payments.
