c. Updated Expanded Tiered Analysis
To estimate cost differences across treatment volumes, CMS conducted a regression analysis using facility-level cost report data from 2022 through 2024. The dependent variable was cost per treatment, and the primary independent variable was facility size. The regression analysis was conducted at the facility level and controlled for the following characteristics: year, ownership, wage index, rurality, region, Medicare percent, home dialysis percent, pediatric share, and average non-LVPA payment adjustment multiplier.
Facility size was specified using the natural logarithm for total treatments and included both linear and quadratic (squared) terms. This specification is intended to estimate cost differences while reducing the influence of extreme values and capturing non-linear effects. Cost estimations associated with size as the natural logarithm makes the scale of comparison smaller, which makes the results less subject to variance of high volume facilities, and including a quadratic term allows us to capture more than just a linear relationship, which is preferable in this instance as we believe the marginal cost-per-treatment difference of an additional treatment is likely different between low and high volume facilities.
CMS then calculated the predicted costs at the upper bound of each tier using the mean values for continuous variables and composite values for categorical variables wherein the value for the categorical variable was the proportion of the overall population of ESRD facilities which belong to that category. For example, if 10 percent of ESRD facilities are in rural areas, the value used for the rural term when determining the proxy would be 0.1. This allowed us to create a proxy facility per-treatment cost value for an ESRD facility based on treatment count. We noted in the proposed rule that, for our purposes of deriving LVPA factors, the values to construct the proxies do not actually impact the final result, so long as the proxies are the same for all calculations; this is because we are using these relative cost values to find the relative difference between proxy values, so the terms cancel in the calculation. As the LVPA is based on the difference in cost between low-volume facilities and other facilities, we then calculated the adjusters by comparing the calculated results to a proxy that represents all non-LVPA facilities, by using the same mean value for continuous control variables and categorical control variables, and the median facility treatment count for non-LVPA facilities. For this non-LVPA proxy, the median facility treatment count was calculated only across non-LVPA facilities and all other values were kept the same. We explained that we are attempting to find the extent to which low-volume facilities faced higher costs than other such facilities; therefore, it is appropriate to have the only difference be the treatment count and it is appropriate for the comparison treatment count to include all non-LVPA facilities. We presented these results in Table 16:
As discussed in the proposed rule, the updated adjustment factors in Table 16 are derived from the regression by taking the ratio of the exponentiated outcome for the tier with the exponentiated outcome of the comparison value. That is, we calculated the proxy value for the tier and the comparison value, applied the exponential function for each, and then divided the proxy value for the tier by the comparison value. For example, the proxy per-treatment cost for a facility with 8,000 treatments in our analysis is $317.77 and the proxy per-treatment cost for a facility with the median non-LVPA treatment count of 10,332 is $302.77. We calculated the adjustment factor for the 7,000-7,999-treatment tier by dividing $317.77 by $302.77 which equals 1.050.
We noted that using these factors in the LVPA would increase payments to current LVPA facilities (those furnishing fewer than 4,000 treatments for each of the past 3 cost reporting years) by approximately $17 million and increase payments to facilities not currently eligible for the LVPA by approximately $67 million. These estimated impacts include the proposed extension of the LVPA to pediatric patients discussed in section II.B.9. of the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule. We stated that these proposed increased adjustment factors, if finalized, would bring relative payments under the ESRD PPS more in line with relative costs, as demonstrated by our cost-to-payment analysis
(
printed page 68789)
discussed in the prior section. We noted that we proposed both policies as budget neutral by reducing the ESRD PPS base rate by a budget neutrality factor, as noted in section II.B.4. of the proposed rule.
d. Proposal for Expanded LVPA
Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act provides that the ESRD PPS shall include a payment adjustment that reflects the extent to which costs incurred by low-volume facilities (as defined by the Secretary) exceed the costs incurred by other facilities. Under this authority, we proposed to revise the definition of a low-volume facility for purposes of § 413.232 to reflect updated empirical findings demonstrating higher costs among facilities furnishing fewer than 8,000 treatments annually, when controlling for various factors including geographic area, wage index, and average case-mix adjustment factor. This proposal is intended to better align ESRD PPS payments with the observed differences in resource use, and support access to care.
As noted in the CY 2016 ESRD PPS final rule (
80 FR 68967
through
69077
), we aim to target the benefit of the LVPA to facilities that serve the access needs of patients in remote locations. CMS analysis indicates higher costs among facilities furnishing between 4,000 and 8,000 treatments per year. Proposing a revised methodology that would increase payment to these ESRD facilities would help protect access to care for ESRD services in areas served by these ESRD facilities. Additionally, we believe that additional tiers would further reduce the incentive for gaming, as the GAO described in its 2013 report.
[
29
]
This may reduce the incentive for some ESRD facilities to limit access to renal dialysis services to keep their treatment volume below the 4,000-treatment threshold. We would expand access through payments that incrementally align resource use with payment to ESRD facilities that furnish different volumes of treatment.
In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, for CY 2027 and subsequent years, CMS proposed to expand LVPA eligibility and implement a tiered structure based on median treatment volume over the prior three years. This expanded eligibility would apply to ESRD facilities that furnish more than 4,000 treatments per year. As discussed in the previous section, we have data which demonstrates higher costs for ESRD facilities which furnish fewer than 8,000 treatments. Building on the tiered LVPA finalized in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule, we proposed 6 tiers with decreasing adjustment factors as treatment volume increases. The proposed adjustment factors are presented in Table 17. Consistent with the current tiered LVPA, the tier determination would be based on the median treatment volume from the past three years. CMS proposed to apply this policy in a budget neutral manner by applying a factor of 0.98898 to the ESRD PPS base rate. We noted that ESRD facilities must attest to being eligible for LVPA to receive the payment adjustment, but our data indicates that not all ESRD facilities which are eligible for the LVPA attest for it. Since these ESRD facilities do not attest for the LVPA, they do not receive it. For the impact analysis from which this budget neutrality factor was derived, we used an attestation proxy to estimate attestation patterns so that our total estimated payments considers that not all eligible ESRD facilities would attest for and receive the LVPA.
We proposed to apply this policy as budget neutral outside of the LVPA, and, if finalized, we would apply the previously mentioned 0.98898 factor to the ESRD PPS base rate. When we established the 2-tiered LVPA methodology in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule (
89 FR 89161
), we did not apply a budget neutrality factor for that methodological change. In the CY 2025 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we stated that we were not proposing to apply a budget neutrality factor because we were making changes only to the LVPA and believed at that time it was most appropriate to keep the impact of the policy change contained to ESRD facilities that were receiving the LVPA (
89 FR 55801
). We stated that the purpose of that change was to better allocate relative payments within the LVPA and it was not our intention at that time to expand the LVPA beyond the facilities currently eligible for the LVPA (
89 FR 55802
). We also discussed that expanding the LVPA beyond 4,000 treatments while scaling the factors to maintain budget neutrality within the LVPA would reduce payments for the lowest volume facilities in a way which was not in alignment with the goals of the LVPA (
89 FR 55801
). In contrast, as discussed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, CMS believes applying budget neutrality to the base rate would be appropriate for this proposal because it would expand LVPA eligibility beyond currently qualifying facilities (that is, to ESRD facilities that furnish more than 4,000 treatments per year). We stated that we believe the proposed tiered structure balances concerns from interested parties regarding payment cliffs while maintaining alignment with statutory requirements.
In constructing this proposal, we carefully considered the responses to
(
printed page 68790)
the CY 2024 RFI on the LVPA.
[
30
]
In this RFI, most respondents supported some sort of tiered system, although most respondents thought there were some issues with the tiered options presented in the RFI. Many of the respondents who supported a tiered system indicated specific support for a structure that included payments up to 6,000 treatments. Many explicitly supported a methodology that incorporated a metric for geographic isolation into the LVPA; however, as we noted in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule our analysis did not find higher costs associated with low-volume facilities in isolated areas (
89 FR 89159
). Further analysis does not reveal higher costs associated with isolated low-volume facilities, although we noted that the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule contained an unrelated payment adjustment for facilities in certain non-contiguous states and territories, the NAPA. We stated in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule that we believe the current NAPA addresses some of the concerns of these commenters (
90 FR 53102
).
In the CY 2024 RFI, we included two potential LVPA structures which both included up to 8,000 treatments per year, but these were 4-tiered and 8-tiered structures. Some respondents opposed the 8-tier LVPA presented in that RFI, with several raising concerns with the budget neutrality factor and others stating that the adjustment factors for the lower-volume tiers were too high and the factors for the higher-volume tiers were miniscule. We considered these comments when designing the 6-tier LVPA proposed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule. By eliminating the 1,000 and 2,000 treatment tiers, we explained, we have mitigated the overall budget neutrality impact of the proposal. Additionally, this reduces concerns related to the high factors associated with these lowest-volume tiers. We disagreed with those commenters that the higher-volume tiers' adjustment factors are miniscule. Our analysis indicates that a 5.0 percent increase is warranted for the 7,000 -treatment count tier, and although the proposed adjustment factor is lower than others, it would still represent a substantial increase in payments to those facilities. Other commenters who supported the tiered approaches in response to that RFI indicated that higher-volume tiers with lower payment adjustments can serve to prevent facilities that are on the border with the more substantial tiers to exceed the treatment volume threshold in one year and still be eligible for the higher payment adjustment tiers in the next year. Several other commenters raised concerns with the tiered system and indicated a belief that it would not eliminate gaming completely.
We noted that we believe that our proposed 6-tier LVPA strikes a balance between appropriately providing higher payment to these higher cost ESRD facilities and addressing the concerns raised by commenters. We believe that the tiered policy finalized in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule (
89 FR 89161
) which uses the median treatment volume from the past three years helps to effectively reduce gaming by eliminating the incentive to lower treatment volume in any single year. We believe that our CY 2027 proposal to have 3,000 treatments be the lowest-volume treatment tier also prevents any concerns related to the high adjustment factors associated with potential lower-volume tiers and reduces budget neutrality concerns. We believe that the higher tiers from 6,000 to 7,999 treatments serve to act as a sort of transition phase allowing facilities to exceed the lower treatment tiers, while still receiving a data-supported payment adjustment. Lastly, these proposed payment tiers are evidence-based as they are derived from the analysis described previously to more fully represent the extent to which these low-volume facilities truly face higher costs.
To effectuate this change, we proposed modifications to our LVPA regulation at § 413.232 to update the current maximum LVPA threshold of 4,000 treatments to the proposed new threshold of 8,000 treatments. Specifically, we proposed modifications to § 413.232(b)(1), which contains the treatment volume threshold for the LVPA, and (g)(5), which notes the exceptions to the treatment volume threshold for disasters and other emergencies finalized in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule, to indicate the new treatment threshold of 8,000. We proposed to update the threshold for the exception to the treatment volume threshold for disasters and other emergencies to ensure consistency with the threshold of § 413.232(b)(1). We noted that these proposed modifications would retain the requirements that an ESRD facility be below the treatment volume threshold in each of the prior three cost reporting years, and that the median treatment volume over the past three cost reporting years would only be used for tier determination for eligible ESRD facilities.
We proposed this policy change be effective January 1, 2027. However, we recognized that the LVPA requires an attestation process with which many ESRD facilities that furnish more than 4,000 treatments per year are likely unfamiliar. We solicited comments on how we can accommodate these facilities to allow them to properly attest for the LVPA for CY 2027, including delaying the effective date of this proposal or allowing attestations after the typical November 1, 2026, deadline. We noted that changes to the attestation deadline would require a modification to § 413.232(e), likely in the form of adding a new paragraph. We stated that we were not proposing any of these changes, but we noted that we may finalize them, or other changes to address any administrative challenges associated with this proposal in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule, depending on comments we receive.
We requested comments on all aspects of the proposal, including the proposed expansion of the LVPA above 4,000 treatments per year, the proposal to extend the LVPA to ESRD facilities which furnish fewer than 8,000 treatments per year, the proposed 6-tiered structure and adjustment factors presented in Table 17, the proposed budget neutrality factor, the proposed effective date of January 1, 2027, and the proposed modifications to § 413.232. Additionally, we requested comments on the potential administrative challenges associated with this proposed change and the potential solutions discussed previously.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Most commenters who opined on the policy expressed support for the expanded LVPA. MedPAC supported the policy change but reiterated past suggestions for methodological improvements which are discussed in further detail later in this section. Some commenters highlighted the particular impact on certain patient populations. Several commenters expressed a belief that this policy would have positive impact on quality of care and access for ESRD patients. Some commenters stated a belief that this expanded policy would help mitigate the “cliff” effect for which interested parties had criticized the LVPA in the past. Additionally, some commenters stated that this expanded policy would recognize the financial pressures that exist for facilities which furnish 4,000 or more treatments per year. A commenter cited a MedPAC figure which stated that the lowest
(
printed page 68791)
quintile of treatment volumes operated at a -11.6 percent margin.
Response:
We appreciate the support for the proposed expansion of the LVPA up to 8,000 treatments and the proposed 6-tier structure. We agree that this policy will have beneficial impacts on many critical populations who are only serviced by a low-volume facility. Likewise, we agree that adding in tiers between 4,000 and 8,000 treatment volume serves both to lower the impact of any “cliff” effect and address the higher costs those facilities face. We acknowledge the citation of MedPAC's margin analysis; although we did not directly consider this analysis in our calculation of the adjustment factors, we believe that the updated LVPA would better align relative payments with resource use for low-volume facilities.
Comment:
Several commenters discussed geographic isolation of ESRD facilities with regard to the LVPA. MedPAC reiterated its support for a low volume and isolated (LVI) methodology which would restrict the LVPA to only facilities in isolated geographic areas and several other commenters expressed support for this LVI methodology. A commenter acknowledged that CMS's past analysis of cost report data did not show differences in cost between low-volume ESRD facilities in isolated and non-isolated areas but stated that there were different costs for ESRD patients in isolated areas, such as increased transportation costs. A commenter supported the fact that the LVPA does not incorporate geographic isolation and noted that specialized facilities can operate at a low volume even if they are in urban areas. Several commenters, including MedPAC, noted the overlap between the rural adjustment and LVPA and some requested that CMS discontinue the rural adjustment and use that money to fund the LVPA in lieu of, or supplementing, budget neutrality.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' array of opinions on whether the LVPA should incorporate geographic isolation. Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act requires the LVPA to reflect the extent to which cost incurred by low-volume facilities in furnishing renal dialysis services exceed the costs incurred by other facilities in furnishing renal dialysis services. As we have noted in the past (
88 FR 76370
,
89 FR 55800
), our analysis has not found a correlation between geographic isolation and higher costs for low-volume facilities. As such we have not proposed to incorporate geographic isolation into our definition of low-volume or our requirements for the LVPA. We continue to acknowledge the suggestion of MedPAC and others, but we believe that if a facility operates at low volume in an urban or otherwise non-geographically isolated area it is appropriate for it to receive the LVPA. We discuss budget neutrality in greater detail later in this section; however, we note that the relatively small rural adjustment factor of 0.8 percent which applies to approximately 14 percent of ESRD PPS treatments is not enough to counteract the budget neutrality of this proposal, which reduces the base rate for all treatments by greater than 1.0 percent. However, removing the rural factor would lessen the impact of the budget neutrality factor. We did not propose to eliminate the rural factor in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, and we do not believe that such a policy would be appropriate at this time. Although there is overlap between what facilities receive the LVPA and the rural adjustment, not all rural facilities receive the LVPA. The rural factor accounts for any higher costs that both LVPA rural and non-LVPA rural facilities face. In calculating the LVPA adjustment factors for the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we controlled for a facility's rural status, as discussed in further detail in the next response.
Comment:
Some commenters questioned whether CMS accounted for other ESRD PPS payment adjustments, such as the rural adjustment or NAPA, in developing the LVPA proposal. These comments often accompanied concerns that the proposed LVPA may overstate the costs associated with low volume. One of these commenters, an LDO, stated a belief that treatment volume may be serving as a proxy for other underlying factors, such as geographic isolation, and expressed concern that continuing to rely on treatment volume alone would not fully address these underlying factors.
Response:
We did control for rurality and being located in a NAPA area in our analysis for the proposed rule. Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act requires the LVPA to reflect the extent to which cost incurred by low volume facilities exceed the costs incurred by other such facilities. We recognize that there are likely other unknown factors which contribute to the LVPA; however, we believe that the analysis upon which the proposed 6-tier LVPA was based is the best available estimate of the extent to which low-volume facilities face higher costs. We acknowledge that it is possible that some other factors are contributing through the LVPA, however, to the extent that those factors result in low-volume facilities facing higher costs than other such facilities, we believe it is reasonable for the LVPA to account for them. While we control for available factors, like rurality and geographic area, it is impossible for our analysis to control for every single potential covariable. We continue to believe our analysis for calculating the LVPA effectively estimates the extent to which low-volume facilities face higher costs than other such facilities. However, we welcome additional information from interested parties on other potential confounders and covariables which we can control for in a future analysis, as appropriate.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS continue to monitor the LVPA and its effectiveness in addressing its goals.
Response:
We thank the commenter for the recommendation. We intend to continue to monitor the LVPA and will make further changes, if appropriate, in potential future rulemaking.
Comment:
A commenter noted that the analysis we included in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule indicated that for the 2022 to 2024 data range most Medicare facilities experienced per-patient costs that exceeded Original Medicare payments for patient care. The commenter emphasized that data point was applicable beyond the context of the LVPA to the broader ESRD PPS.
Response:
We appreciate the insight into the data analysis we included in our proposed rule. We agree that considering Medicare cost data is applicable when considering policies outside the LVPA. However, we note that in the analysis we published, which is included earlier in this section in Table 15, we found that the facilities that tend to have costs exceeding payments are those with less than 8,000 treatments, which helped inform our proposal to expand the LVPA up to 8,000 treatments. Although we did not include this result in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, the analysis from which Table 15 was derived also found that the overall treatment weighted facility level mean payment to cost ratio was 1.01 and the median was 0.98. We reiterate that these figures should not be interpreted directly in terms of payment adequacy for the reasons discussed in the context of Table 15, most notably because they reflect costs for payors other than Original Medicare, which may be different. We believe that the overall payment rate under the ESRD PPS is appropriate and that this LVPA policy will better align payments with resource use.
Comment:
Several commenters specifically discussed the implementation timeline for the proposed 6-tier LVPA. A few of those commenters recommended delaying the attestation deadline for 2026. A
(
printed page 68792)
commenter recommended delaying the implementation of the policy to CY 2028 but also expressed support for delaying the attestation deadline as an alternate recommendation.
Response:
We appreciate the insight and recommendation into the operation timeline for this proposed policy change. In the proposed rule we solicited comments on potential changes to the operational timeline for this policy, including the options recommended by the commenters. We believe that extending the attestation deadline would allow for the ESRD facilities to submit attestations for payment year 2027 and for the MACs to process those attestations in time for CY 2027 payments. After considering these comments and evaluating the potential operational difficulties associated with this change, we are finalizing an extension to the attestation deadline for payment year 2026 to December 31, 2026. This is consistent with past extensions to the attestation deadline in
42 CFR 413.232(e)
which impacted LVPA attestations for payment years 2015, 2016, and 2021. We are finalizing modifications to § 413.232(e) to add a new paragraph to effectuate this delayed attestation deadline.
Comment:
Numerous commenters opined on the proposed budget neutrality of this LVPA proposal. Many commenters requested CMS implement this policy in a non-budget neutral manner. Others requested CMS budget neutralize the policy by removing the rural adjustment factor; some of those requests were combined with requests for an LVI methodology that directly incorporated isolation. A few commenters noted that some high-volume urban facilities treat vulnerable or medically complex patient populations. Many commenters noted the relatively large impact this policy would have on the base rate and stated that such a reduction could have adverse impacts on care. Many commenters highlighted that there is no statutory requirement for budget neutrality for the LVPA.
Response:
We understand the concerns raised by commenters regarding the budget neutrality of this LPVA proposal, as the proposed budget neutrality factor of 0.98898 is relatively large compared to the budget neutrality factors of past changes to adjustment factors. However, budget neutrality is appropriate for this proposal. The LVPA is a longstanding, statutorily required part of the ESRD PPS. When the payment system was implemented in 2011, low-volume facilities were considered in creating the base rate. Thus, the higher costs that low-volume facilities face are included in the ESRD PPS payment rate. The proposed LVPA appropriately recognizes the higher relative costs of low volume facilities, and the application of the budget neutrality factor reduces relative payments to high-volume ESRD facilities.
We considered removing the rural adjustment factor as part of the budget neutrality of this proposal, although we note that it would not be nearly enough to offset the impact of the budget neutrality factor. However, we believe that ensuring access for rural populations is important. While the LVPA addresses some factors which may cause costs to be higher in rural areas, we believe the rural adjustment is still useful in protecting access for higher-volume or otherwise LVPA ineligible ESRD facilities in rural areas.
We likewise recognize that there are some urban facilities with high volume and high costs per treatment. We note that urban areas generally have higher wage index values and receive higher relative payments accordingly. Additionally, the ESRD PPS includes many case-mix adjustment factors which provide higher payment to any ESRD facility which furnishes care to certain medically complex patients as specified at § 413.235. Lastly, for patients whose medical complexity is not addressed by the patient level case-mix adjustment factors, we have an outlier adjustment that can provide increased payment for higher-than-expected use of certain eligible ESRD outlier services as specified at § 413.237. The purpose of the LVPA is to account for the extent to which low-volume facilities face higher costs than other such facilities, and we believe that these other payment adjustments address the concerns of commenters related to high-cost urban ESRD facilities.
The reason this budget neutrality factor is larger than many past budget neutrality factors is because it is reallocating a larger amount of payments. Our analysis indicates that higher volume ESRD facilities have lower costs, and our comparison of Original Medicare payments to costs indicates that payments are notably above costs for these facilities. The purpose of this change is not to increase overall payments, but to better allocate payments within the ESRD PPS. Based on our analysis, this update to the LVPA accomplishes that goal.
We acknowledge and agree with commenters who note that there is no statutory budget neutrality requirement for changes to the LVPA. However, as noted previously, we believe it is most appropriate to implement this policy change in a budget neutral manner.
Comment:
A commenter noted that the payment to cost ratio presented in the proposed rule for facilities with between 8,000 and 10,000 treatments was 0.99 and that a budget neutrality factor would lower payment adequacy for this group of ESRD facilities.
Response:
As discussed previously, the analysis presented in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule was not a comprehensive margin analysis and should not be interpreted in terms of payment adequacy. The average cost per treatment for that analysis was derived from Medicare cost report data, which reflects costs for payers other than Original Medicare. As MA and private plans may pay higher for renal dialysis services, it is reasonable to believe that beneficiaries may be getting different care. As such, we do not believe that the budget neutrality factor would inappropriately lower payment adequacy for the 8,000-10,000 treatment ESRD facility group. As noted previously, budget neutrality is appropriate for this proposal because it is aligning payments under the ESRD PPS with relative resource use. Our analysis has found that those facilities that furnish more treatments have lower costs-per-treatment, on average. As such, a budget neutrality factor that, when combined with the impact of this policy, reallocates money from higher cost to lower cost facilities is appropriate.
Comment:
A commenter stated that it was appropriate for CMS to use an attestation proxy for determining budget neutrality but requested more information and asked if CMS assumed that attestation rates would vary by treatment tier. That commenter noted that higher volume LVPA eligible facilities could be less likely to attest if they determine that the adjustment is not worth the administrative burden. Another commenter recommended that we monitor LVPA participation and make changes in future years if the budget neutrality reduction overestimated LVPA payments.
Response:
We appreciate the thoughtful insight into the attestation proxy. We did not account for varying attestation rates for different tiers, as we have no data for the higher volume tiers upon which to base that attestation proxy. Our attestation proxy was by ownership type. We believe that this is the most appropriate as we observe different attestation rates for certain categories of facility ownership and, while we cannot identify specific reasons for why a seemingly eligible ESRD facility does not attest for the
(
printed page 68793)
LVPA, we can posit two potential reasons which are both related to ownership. The first potential reason is that an ESRD facility lacks the administrative support or resources to attest. We believe that it is reasonable to assume that administrative support would correlate with ownership type. That is, a facility owned by an LDO would likely have more administrative support than an independent facility, and that hospital-based facilities likely also have different levels of administrative support and different administrative hurdles. The second potential reason is that our data may not be identifying all instances of common ownership among ESRD facilities, which is relevant as the determination of treatment volume for the LVPA considers nearby facilities with common ownership. While we can plainly identify some instances of common ownership from our data, there are likely some instances where a seemingly eligible ESRD facility is not attesting for the LVPA because it is not actually eligible due to the common ownership volume aggregation. Using a proxy based on ownership likely catches some of the correlation between an ESRD facility having nearby unidentified commonly owned facilities. The attestation simulation we used for the budget neutrality impacts for this final rule are in Table 18.
We generally do not make retrospective budget neutrality changes as the intention of a budget neutrality factor is to capture the impact attributable to the change itself and not any related or unrelated trends in utilization. For example, if more low-volume ESRD facilities were to open based on this policy, we would not consider that as part of the budget for the proposal, even though overall payment would change. We believe it is appropriate to use the earlier attestation rates observed for currently eligible LVPA facilities for these newly eligible LVPA facilities. However, we recognize that there is no observed data for attestation rates among these mid-sized 4,000 to 8,000 treatment ESRD facilities, which differentiates this proposal from other past proposals where we have historical data. As such, we intend to monitor the actual attestation rates and actual payments under the LVPA. If attestation patterns differ significantly from our observed historical-rate-derived attestation rates, we would consider making changes, if appropriate, in potential future rulemaking.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the 6-tier LVPA as proposed. We are recalculating the budget neutrality factor with our updated impacts simulation. The updated budget neutrality factor is 0.98901. The final LVPA tiers are presented in Table 19.
Additionally, we are finalizing an extension to the attestation deadline to December 31, 2026, for the LVPA for payment year CY 2027. We are finalizing the addition of a new paragraph § 413.232(e)(5) and finalizing conforming edits to paragraphs § 413.232(e)(3) and (e)(4) to effectuate this change. We note that these modifications to the LVPA and attestation deadline for payment year 2027 also apply to payments for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients, as discussed in section II.B.9.d.(3) of this final rule.
9. Payment for Pediatric Patients With ESRD Receiving Renal Dialysis Services
a. Background and History of Pediatric ESRD Payment
Section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iv)(I) of the Act provides that the ESRD PPS may include such payment adjustments as
(
printed page 68794)
the Secretary determines appropriate, including a payment adjustment for pediatric providers of services and renal dialysis facilities. Historically, determining an appropriate payment adjustment for pediatric ESRD patients
[
31
]
has been challenging due to limited data. The Medicare pediatric ESRD patient population receiving dialysis is small compared to the adult ESRD population; the pediatric ESRD patient population represents approximately 0.16 percent of Original Medicare treatments in 2024 from Common Working File data ending June 27, 2025.
In the past, CMS has considered various payment adjustments for pediatric patients with ESRD, including different Medicare payments by sex or comorbidities (
74 FR 49984
through
49986
). However, many of these adjustments were not used as we were unable to get acceptable precision due to the small sample size of pediatric patients with ESRD.
Prior to the establishment of the ESRD PPS, payment for pediatric ESRD renal dialysis services was generally the same rate as adult ESRD renal dialysis services, unless the ESRD facility qualified for an exception to the composite rate. Section 1881(b)(7) of the Act stated that, subject to section 422(a)(2) of the Medicare, Medicaid, and SCHIP Benefits Improvement and Protection Act of 2000 (
Pub. L. 106-554
) (BIPA), the Secretary shall provide for exceptions as may be warranted by unusual circumstances (including the special circumstances of sole facilities located in isolated, rural areas and of pediatric facilities). During this time, CMS received many comments and concerns regarding the payment rate for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric patients with ESRD. Section 623(b) of the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 (
Pub. L. 108-173
) later amended section 422(a)(2) of BIPA to provide that any pediatric ESRD facility would be eligible for an exception to the composite rate, effective October 1, 2002. This statute defined pediatric ESRD facilities as facilities with at least 50 percent patients under the age of 18. These policies enabled pediatric ESRD facilities to receive payments recognizing the higher cost associated with furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients (
69 FR 47530
).
We finalized a basic case-mix adjustment to the composite payment rate in the CY 2005 Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule published on November 15, 2004 (
69 FR 66327
). This included a 62 percent pediatric ESRD payment increase (that is, an adjustment factor of 1.62) applied to the composite payment rate per treatment for any facility when furnishing outpatient renal dialysis services to pediatric patients with ESRD. This factor was derived from the average exception amounts for 20 ESRD facilities that had received exceptions for pediatric patients. This was intended to be a temporary measure, which would be eliminated once we developed the case-mix methodology that would apply for the ESRD PPS bundled payment. The use of this methodology allowed CMS to provide additional payment for the pediatric ESRD population under the composite rate in a data-driven manner to account for the higher costs pediatric ESRD patients faced (
69 FR 66327
).
Section 153(b) of MIPPA added section 1881(b)(14) of the Act, which required CMS to implement an ESRD bundled PPS beginning January 1, 2011, under which a single payment for renal dialysis services is made in lieu of any other payment. Renal dialysis services generally include items and services included in the composite rate for renal dialysis services as of December 31, 2010, and services furnished to individuals for treatment of ESRD, which were formerly separately billable, including drugs and biological products and laboratory tests. In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed a single composite rate factor of 1.199 for all pediatric ESRD patients receiving renal dialysis services (
74 FR 49982
through
49983
). We also proposed an eight-group system for separately billable renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients with two subdivisions for each of the following factors: age (under 13, 13 to 17), modality (HD, PD) and number of comorbidities (none, one or more) (
74 FR 49983
through
49987
).
The CY 2011 ESRD PPS proposed rule then calculated an “expanded bundle” factor, which combined the composite rate factor of 1.199 and the separately billable factors for each of the eight groups (
74 FR 44987
). These expanded bundle factors were the proposed pediatric ESRD patient-specific case-mix adjustment factors that would be applied to the base rate under the ESRD PPS. These factors were based on a regression of costs for all renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients. Comments on this proposed rule indicated that many interested parties believed the expanded bundle factor was insufficient (
75 FR 49128
). In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule, we responded to those comments by implementing the first iteration of the current four-group system for both the expanded bundle and the separately billable services. This methodology was data driven, but unlike the simple regression for composite rate costs, allowed for different Medicare payment amounts based on two sets of two characteristics: age of the patient (under 13 or 13 to 17) and modality of the treatment (HD or PD). Additionally, this methodology used the same groups for the expanded bundle and separately billable factors (
75 FR 49134
). We codified the pediatric ESRD patient payment adjustment in § 413.235(b), which states that CMS adjusts the per treatment base rate for pediatric ESRD patients in accordance with section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iv)(I) of the Act, to account for patient age and treatment modality. These multipliers were updated in the CY 2016 ESRD PPS final rule using the same methodology (
80 FR 69001
through
69002
).
b. Transitional Pediatric ESRD Add-On Payment Adjustment (TPEAPA)
As discussed in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule (
88 FR 76375
), despite these changes intended to improve payment accuracy for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients, CMS continued to receive comments and concerns from interested parties that payment amounts for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients are insufficient. In addition to comments received through the annual ESRD PPS rulemaking, we also solicited comments from interested parties on several occasions. During the Technical Expert Panel (TEP) of December 2020, we queried a panel of experts on how to improve payment for pediatric dialysis care under the ESRD PPS. Panelists generally preferred creating more refined case-mix adjusters over creating an entirely new pediatric ESRD PPS, citing the costs of creating an entirely new system both on CMS and the ESRD facilities and the need for new legislation to be able to increase payment through a separate pediatric ESRD PPS. Panelists also pointed to labor costs as a major reason for higher costs among pediatric dialysis clinics because these patients need more nursing attention and specialized pediatric nutritionists.
[
32
]
In the CY 2023
(
printed page 68795)
ESRD PPS proposed rule (
87 FR 38529
), we issued a request for information regarding equitable access for pediatric patients with ESRD. We noted that interested parties have emphasized the higher labor costs, including the need for increased nursing attention and specialized clinical staff. They noted that Medicare payment for pediatric ESRD patients is too low and that the ESRD PPS bundled payment does not target the unique issues facing ESRD facilities furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients.
We explained that CMS sought to improve payment accuracy for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients by better aligning payments with observed costs. Ensuring Medicare payments are appropriate and align costs for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients would support more ESRD facilities in providing quality care to this vulnerable population. The main barrier to aligning payment has been the lack of sufficient data to determine the relative costs associated with furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients. To improve payment rate accuracy for pediatric ESRD patients, CMS issued changes to the cost reports for hospital-based and freestanding ESRD facilities effective October 1, 2022, and January 1, 2023, respectively (
87 FR 26760
).
[
33 34
]
Nevertheless, accurate payment for pediatric ESRD renal dialysis services under the ESRD PPS remains challenging due to small sample sizes and systematic differences between pediatric and adult renal dialysis services. Pediatric renal dialysis treatments often occur in hospitals which have lower volumes and higher costs. This complicates cost estimation. To address these challenges, we conducted an alternative analysis which used propensity score matching (PSM) to estimate costs accurately. Findings presented in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule indicated facilities that only serve pediatric ESRD patients incur 40 percent higher costs per patient than those not serving pediatric ESRD patients (
88 FR 76376
). Medicare accounted for the current adjustments for higher pediatric costs from established case-mix adjusters, which were about 10 percent higher for pediatric renal dialysis services than adults in 2022.
In the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule, CMS finalized the Transitional Pediatric ESRD Payment Adjustment (TPEAPA) which increased payments for all pediatric ESRD patients under 18 years of age (
88 FR 76344
). CMS finalized the budget neutral 30 percent add-on payment adjustment in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule effective January 1, 2024, for CYs 2024 through 2026 (
88 FR 76380
). CMS finalized the TPEAPA as a time-limited payment adjustment, so we could collect more targeted pediatric data. The time-limited 3-year payment adjustment provided enough time to evaluate data from updates to cost reports specific to pediatric treatments. The TPEAPA is codified at § 413.235(b)(2). Beginning January 1, 2024, the ESRD PPS provided a per-treatment transitional add-on payment adjustment of 30 percent of the per treatment payment amount under § 413.230 for renal dialysis services furnished to Pediatric ESRD Patients, as defined in § 413.171, during calendar years 2024, 2025, and 2026. CMS continued to analyze payment and cost data throughout the implementation of TPEAPA to determine whether to extend the TPEAPA past December 31, 2026, or propose an alternative approach after additional data analysis.
c. Analysis of Additional Pediatric ESRD Cost Data
As noted previously, payment accuracy historically has been difficult for pediatric ESRD renal dialysis services because of the small sample size of pediatric ESRD patients receiving renal dialysis services under the ESRD PPS. Pediatric ESRD renal dialysis treatments differ from adult ESRD renal dialysis treatments in several crucial ways. For example, pediatric ESRD facilities
[
35
]
are more likely to be hospital-based and, on average, have lower treatment volume and are in higher wage index areas. These systematic differences in the treatment site, when combined with the small sample size, make it very difficult to obtain low variance estimates of the differences in costs between pediatric and adult ESRD dialysis patients.
As discussed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule (
91 FR 38827
), to better understand these differences, CMS analyzed cost reports from both freestanding (CMS-265-11) and hospital-based (CMS-2552) facilities for 2023 and 2024 following cost report revisions. We found relatively few freestanding facilities reported unique pediatric staff. Additionally, approximately 30 percent of children's hospitals as defined at
42 CFR 412.23(d)
reported pediatric ESRD nursing staff and 25 percent reported pediatric ESRD staff other than registered nurses on the cost report. For non-children's hospitals these figures were 1 percent and 0.5 percent, respectively.
CMS observed increased reporting of pediatric-specific supply costs in hospital-based ESRD facilities between 2023 and 2024. In 2023, the mean pediatric ESRD patient supply cost per treatment in hospital-based ESRD facilities was $138.23; in 2024, it was $321.22. We noted that this increase in pediatric ESRD patient supply cost per treatment likely reflects increased reporting, rather than increases in pediatric costs of greater than 100 percent. Prior to 2024, the hospital-based (CMS-2552) facilities cost report lacked the specificity to consistently delineate pediatric ESRD patient supply cost from adult ESRD patient supply cost. Additionally, CMS provided interested parties with additional guidance on the completion of cost reports to share with children's hospitals that provide renal dialysis services.
Despite continued limitations in pediatric-specific ESRD reporting, CMS observed statistically significant higher costs associated with the furnishing of renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients. As discussed in the following section, an updated regression analysis of composite rate costs found the incremental cost impact of pediatric ESRD treatment share was approximately 33 percent. Specifically, using data from CYs 2022 and 2023, CMS estimates that the difference in total cost per treatment between facilities with no pediatric ESRD treatments and those furnishing exclusively pediatric ESRD treatments is approximately 33 percent. This does not mean that every pediatric ESRD treatment represents a 33 percent increase in cost.

These findings indicate that facilities furnishing a higher share of renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients incur higher per-treatment costs.
