We received comments from patient and caregiver representatives, patient advocacy organizations, professional associations, dialysis facilities and organizations, and other interested parties regarding the proposed revisions to payment for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric patients. Commenters generally agreed that furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric patients is more resource-intensive than furnishing renal dialysis services to adult patients and supported continued recognition of those additional costs under the ESRD PPS. Commenters differed, however, regarding the appropriate methodology for recognizing those costs, including the proposed pediatric case-mix adjustment factors, the adequacy of the data used to develop the proposed adjustments, continuation of the TPEAPA, and application of budget neutrality. We summarize these comments and provide our responses below.
Comment:
Several commenters supported CMS's recognition that renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients are more resource intensive than renal dialysis services furnished to adult ESRD patients and generally supported establishing a permanent payment methodology following expiration of the TPEAPA. Commenters stated that pediatric dialysis requires specialized pediatric nephrologists, nurses, dietitians, social workers, pharmacists, child life specialists, and other multidisciplinary personnel, as well as pediatric-specific equipment and supplies, specialized clinical protocols, extensive family and caregiver education, psychosocial and nutritional support, care coordination,
(
printed page 68798)
and infrastructure necessary to care for infants, children, and adolescents with complex medical needs. Some commenters noted that pediatric renal dialysis services also must address growth, nutrition, bone health, development, and preparation for kidney transplantation.
Some commenters specifically supported the proposed permanent pediatric case-mix adjustments and application of the LVPA to qualifying pediatric renal dialysis treatments and urged CMS to finalize these policies. Other commenters agreed that a permanent increase in pediatric payment is necessary but disagreed with the proposed methodology for providing that additional payment.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for appropriately recognizing the additional resources associated with furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients. We agree that pediatric renal dialysis patients constitute a small and clinically complex population and that furnishing renal dialysis services to these patients may require specialized staffing, equipment, supplies, clinical expertise, family and caregiver support, and other resources that differ from those required for many adult beneficiaries with ESRD.
The purpose of our pediatric payment policy is to account appropriately for differences in expected resource use within the ESRD PPS while maintaining a methodology that is empirically based, administratively feasible, and consistent with the structure of the ESRD PPS. We appreciate commenters' descriptions of the clinical and operational resources necessary to furnish pediatric renal dialysis services and considered these comments in determining the appropriate payment methodology for CY 2027.
While some commenters disagree with the payment methodology in the CY 2027 proposed rule (
91 FR 38826
through
38830
) for pediatric ESRD patients, we note that the methodology is based on long-standing policy for calculating the case-mix adjusters for the pediatric ESRD PPS payment. We calculated that the average difference in pediatric to adult ESRD costs is 1.3298 (that is, 32.98 percent). This does not mean that every pediatric renal dialysis service should receive an increased payment as has been the case with the TPEAPA while CMS gathered and analyzed data. We proposed to update the SB (outlier) and EB (case-mix) multipliers for pediatric ESRD patients according to the established methodology as presented in Table 21. We noted that these proposed updates would result in functional adjustment factors for pediatric ESRD patients below those established for purposes of the TPEAPA. However, extending the LVPA to pediatric renal dialysis services results in a substantially larger payment increase for hospital-based facilities (8.16 percent) than freestanding facilities (2.06 percent). Additionally, ESRD facilities with greater than 50 percent of pediatric ESRD patients saw a 6.54 percent increase in projected payments across all CY 2027 proposed policy changes. According to data analysis these combined policy changes are targeted at hospital-based ESRD facilities that specialize in providing pediatric renal dialysis services.
We believe the regression methodology remains appropriate for the CY pediatric update. As noted previously, the regression methodology targets PD which the pediatric population uses at a higher rate. The pediatric patients 12 and under PD case-mix factor increased by 32.6 percent, and the PD case-mix adjuster for 13-17 increased by 30.3 percent. Hemodialysis for both age groups is less than the increase resulting from the 30 percent TPEAPA based on the propensity score matching (PSM) analyses presented in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule which indicated facilities that only serve pediatric ESRD patients incur 40 percent higher costs per patient than those not serving pediatric patients (
88 FR 76376
). CMS accounted for the current adjustments for higher pediatric costs from established case-mix adjusters, which were about 10 percent higher for pediatric renal dialysis services than adults in 2022. We continue to believe that it is appropriate to adjust the case-mix for pediatric ESRD patients according to the regression analysis for CY 2027 which is more refined and targeted than the TPEAPA. We note that the decrease in case-mix occurs as the pediatric population moves toward the more traditionally used adult therapy, HD, and as they age. We believe this is a logical progression for payment to follow. While we have not proposed to concurrently update the adult case-mix, we believe this is justified to address the finding that pediatric ESRD patients have higher costs than adult ESRD patients.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern regarding the proposal to replace the TPEAPA with updated pediatric case-mix adjustment factors and to apply the LVPA to treatments furnished to pediatric ESRD patients. Commenters stated that pediatric renal dialysis requires specialized staffing, supplies, and other resources and that these costs are incurred by both low- and high-volume pediatric ESRD facilities. Commenters noted that treatment volume is not an appropriate proxy for the complexity or cost of pediatric renal dialysis care and noted that higher-volume pediatric ESRD facilities may serve as referral centers for more complex pediatric patients while continuing to incur substantial fixed costs associated with specialized pediatric care. Commenters requested that CMS establish a permanent payment adjustment applicable to pediatric ESRD treatments regardless of facility volume or, alternatively, extend the TPEAPA while collecting additional data.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the unique resource needs associated with furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients, including the need for specialized clinical staff and supplies. We agree that pediatric ESRD patients have distinct care needs and that furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric patients is associated with higher costs. Indeed, our updated analysis was specifically intended to quantify those higher costs using more recent cost data and forms the basis for the proposed updates to the permanent pediatric case-mix adjustments.
We clarify, however, that our proposal does not use facility treatment volume as a proxy for the clinical complexity of pediatric ESRD patients or for the additional costs attributable specifically to furnishing pediatric renal dialysis services. Rather, our analysis identifies pediatric ESRD treatment share and facility treatment volume as separate characteristics associated with cost per treatment. As discussed in the proposed rule, after controlling for facility volume and other facility characteristics, we estimated that the difference in total cost per treatment between facilities with no pediatric ESRD treatments and facilities furnishing exclusively pediatric ESRD treatments was approximately 33 percent. This analysis provides the basis for recognizing the additional costs associated with pediatric renal dialysis services through the permanent pediatric case-mix adjustments, independently of the LVPA.
We also conducted additional analysis in response to comments concerning whether the relationship between facility volume and cost observed among ESRD facilities generally is also present among ESRD facilities primarily furnishing pediatric renal dialysis services. For this analysis, we examined facilities with more than 50 percent pediatric ESRD treatment share using cost report and claims data
(
printed page 68799)
from CYs 2022 through 2025. The descriptive results demonstrate a clear inverse relationship between facility treatment volume and median cost per treatment within this pediatric ESRD facility sample.
We additionally estimated regression models using the pediatric ESRD facility sample. These models similarly indicate that, within pediatric ESRD facilities, higher facility treatment volume is associated with lower cost per treatment over the range of treatment volumes represented in the data. We recognize that the relatively small number of pediatric ESRD facilities limits the precision of these estimates. Nevertheless, the regression results are consistent with the strong pattern observed in the descriptive data and with our broader analysis of the relationship between facility volume and cost.
We therefore disagree that extending the LVPA for pediatric renal dialysis service assumes that low volume is a proxy for pediatric complexity. The two adjustments address distinct cost relationships. The updated pediatric case-mix adjustments recognize the higher costs associated with furnishing renal dialysis to pediatric ESRD patients, while the LVPA recognizes the higher per-treatment costs associated with lower facility treatment volume. A pediatric ESRD facility may therefore receive the pediatric adjustment for each qualifying pediatric treatment and, if the facility meets the applicable low-volume criteria, also receive the LVPA.
We also recognize commenters' observation that some higher-volume pediatric ESRD facilities may serve as referral centers for medically complex patients and may incur substantial specialized staffing and supply costs. The additional analysis does not establish that every high-volume pediatric ESRD facility has lower costs than every low-volume pediatric ESRD facility, nor does treatment volume measure patient complexity. Rather, the analysis demonstrates an average relationship between facility treatment volume and per-treatment cost among pediatric ESRD facilities. To the extent that pediatric ESRD facilities generally incur additional costs associated with furnishing pediatric renal dialysis services, including at higher-volume facilities, those costs are reflected in the data used to estimate the pediatric cost differential and are recognized through the permanent pediatric payment adjustments.
Finally, we do not believe it is necessary to extend the TPEAPA to recognize these costs. The TPEAPA was established as a temporary adjustment for CYs 2024 through 2026 while CMS collected and evaluated additional pediatric-specific cost information (
88 FR 76377
). The TPEAPA's 30 percent add-on was developed using an analysis that CMS previously recognized had substantial statistical uncertainty. The additional data now available permit CMS to establish permanent pediatric payment adjustments based on more recent observed costs while separately recognizing the relationship between low facility volume and higher per-treatment costs through the LVPA. We believe this approach better distinguishes and targets these separate cost drivers than continuing the temporary adjustment.
Comment:
Several commenters urged CMS not to replace the TPEAPA with the proposed combination of revised pediatric case-mix adjustment factors and application of the LVPA. These commenters recommended that CMS either make the TPEAPA permanent or extend it while CMS collects additional pediatric-specific cost data and develops and validates a permanent pediatric payment methodology. Some commenters stated that the approximately 30-percent TPEAPA more appropriately reflects CMS's finding that pediatric renal dialysis services costs are approximately 30 to 33 percent higher than adult renal dialysis services costs.
Other commenters recommended using CMS's existing analyses to establish a permanent pediatric adjustment of approximately 30 to 33 percent rather than relying on a combination of case-mix and volume-based adjustments.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for ensuring adequate payment for pediatric renal dialysis services and their recommendations concerning continuation of the TPEAPA. As discussed when the TPEAPA was established, the TPEAPA was intended to be a temporary payment adjustment while CMS obtained and analyzed additional information concerning the relative costs of furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients. In the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule, we noted that it was possible that a future permanent adjustment could result in a lower adjustment factor for pediatric ESRD patients (
88 FR 76377
). However, we note that our proposed adjustment factors based on a 33 percent payment differential and the proposed application of the LVPA to pediatric ESRD patients result in approximately the same overall payment level, with distributional changes. We agree with commenters that a permanent methodology should appropriately reflect the resources associated with pediatric renal dialysis services and should be supported by the best data reasonably available.
We do not believe, however, that an aggregate estimate that pediatric renal dialysis treatment costs are approximately 30 to 33 percent more than adult treatments necessarily demonstrates that every pediatric ESRD treatment or every facility furnishing pediatric renal dialysis services incurs costs that are uniformly 30 to 33 percent higher. A payment methodology must also consider variation in expected resource use among pediatric ESRD patients and facilities.
Comment:
Several commenters questioned whether the available data are sufficiently reliable to establish a permanent pediatric ESRD payment methodology. Commenters stated that pediatric-specific cost reporting remains limited, particularly for hospital-based pediatric ESRD facilities, and noted that the 2022 and 2023 data used in CMS's analysis preceded or did not fully reflect more recent cost-reporting guidance. Commenters explained that children's hospitals may have difficulty allocating the costs of personnel who provide services to both dialysis and non-dialysis patients.
Several commenters recommended that CMS revise the hospital cost report to include pediatric-specific staffing, supplies, and other costs. Commenters stated that more granular pediatric cost reporting would improve CMS's ability to measure the costs of specialized personnel, equipment, supplies, and other resources.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the availability and reporting of pediatric-specific cost information, particularly for hospital-based facilities. We recognize the challenges associated with identifying and allocating costs for personnel and resources that may support both renal dialysis services and other hospital services.
In developing the proposed pediatric payment adjustments, we used the most appropriate cost and claims information available to us and considered the limitations of those data. We agree that continued improvement in pediatric-specific cost information could support future refinements to the ESRD PPS. We will consider commenters' recommendations regarding additional pediatric-specific ESRD cost-reporting fields and other mechanisms for improving the accuracy and consistency of pediatric ESRD cost information in future policy development.
We do not believe that the existence of limitations in pediatric cost reporting
(
printed page 68800)
necessarily requires CMS to continue a temporary payment adjustment indefinitely where the available data permits us to develop an appropriate permanent methodology. Nevertheless, we agree that continued monitoring and data development are important given the small size and clinical heterogeneity of the pediatric renal dialysis population.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that CMS convene a technical expert panel (TEP) before establishing a permanent pediatric ESRD payment methodology, or if CMS determines that additional data are needed. Commenters recommended that a TEP include pediatric nephrology clinicians and other providers and, in some cases, pediatric ESRD patients and families. They suggested that the TEP identify remaining gaps in pediatric cost and utilization data, recommend improved data-collection strategies, evaluate alternative payment methodologies, and ensure that the ESRD PPS reflects the clinical and operational characteristics of pediatric renal dialysis.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recommendation to convene a TEP and agree that input from clinicians, facilities, patients, families, and other interested parties can provide useful information concerning pediatric renal dialysis resource use and payment. While we believe we have accurate and appropriate data to develop these methodological changes, we will consider whether additional technical expert input would be useful in evaluating future refinements to the pediatric ESRD PPS case-mix adjustments and improving pediatric-specific data collection in future rulemakings.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS recalibrate the pediatric and adult ESRD case-mix adjustment factors simultaneously using more recent data. The commenter expressed concern that updating pediatric ESRD adjustment factors using 2022 and 2023 data while retaining adult ESRD adjustment factors based on older data could result in different beneficiary populations being calibrated using different periods of resource use. The commenter also reiterated its recommendation that CMS replace the two-equation regression methodology with a single-equation methodology based on costs for the full ESRD PPS bundled payment.
Other commenters recommended recalibrating the pediatric modifiers using CMS's existing data so that the resulting payment adjustment more directly reflects the approximately 33-percent difference between pediatric and adult renal dialysis services costs.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recommendations regarding the methodology used to develop the pediatric case-mix adjustment factors. The purpose of the CY 2027 pediatric analysis is to update payment for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients in light of the expiration of the TPEAPA and the availability of more recent information concerning pediatric renal dialysis resource use. We disagree with the commenter stating that as we are adjusting the pediatric case-mix adjusters we should also adjust the adult case-mix adjusters. Because pediatric case-mix adjusters are scaled to the average adult case-mix adjuster, the impact to pediatric ESRD PPS payments does not depend on the adult case-mix adjusters. We did not propose to update the adult case-mix adjusters, and we are not finalizing a change to those adjusters in this final rule. We recalibrated the pediatric case-mix adjusters for CY 2027 to address the difference in cost for pediatric ESRD patients. We will continue to monitor the adult and pediatric case-mix adjusters for potential refinement in future rulemaking including a potential one-equation cost model.
Comment:
Several commenters questioned the proposed case-mix adjustment factors for younger pediatric ESRD patients. Commenters stated that younger and smaller children may require more resources than older pediatric ESRD patients, including substantially greater nursing intensity, educational and behavioral support, caregiver involvement, and specialized equipment. A commenter noted that patients under 10 kilograms may require one-to-one nursing. Commenters therefore requested that CMS reexamine whether the proposed adjustment factors adequately account for the resource intensity associated with the youngest and smallest pediatric ESRD patients.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' descriptions of the additional resources that may be required to furnish renal dialysis services to younger and smaller pediatric ESRD patients. We agree that the clinical care of these ESRD patients can involve substantial nursing, caregiver, educational, behavioral, and technical resources.
The proposed pediatric case-mix adjustment factors were derived from the observed relationships in the data using the methodology described in the proposed rule; they were not established based on a policy assumption that older pediatric ESRD patients are inherently more resource intensive than younger pediatric ESRD patients. Therefore, differences among the proposed factors reflect the results of the empirical analysis rather than a judgment concerning the relative clinical complexity of particular age groups.
Our proposed calculations indicate that revisions to the case-mix adjustment will result in an increase for pediatric ESRD patients 12 and under with PD as a modality of 32.6 percent, those 12 and under with HD as a modality will receive a 15.1 percent increase. Pediatric ESRD patients 13-17 with PD as a modality will receive a 30.3 percent case-mix increase and those 13-17 with HD as a modality will receive a 15.7 percent case-mix increase. Additionally, these changes are driven by the separately billable (SB) multipliers which are also used in calculating the outlier adjustment. The SB multiplier increases 12 and under PD 27.6 percent, 13-17 PD increases 29.0 percent, and 13-17 HD increases 2.5 percent. The only SB multiplier which decreases is the factor for 12 and under HD which decreases by 9.7 percent based on empirically observed spending in the data. Essentially, all case-mix adjustments increased appropriately based on our regression analysis for each age group with the exception of the 12 and under HD group.
We will continue to monitor the relationship between pediatric ESRD patient characteristics and resource use, including whether future data demonstrate that the payment methodology should be refined to better account for the costs associated with younger or smaller pediatric ESRD patients. CMS will consider proposing any changes that may be warranted through future rulemaking.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of public comments CMS is finalizing the proposed pediatric case-mix factors without any modifications, because we believe that the case-mix factors are based on the best available data. These updated factors accurately target most fragile pediatric ESRD patients, those 12 and under, by increasing the PD factor by 32.6 percent. We are allowing the TPEAPA to expire as scheduled. We are confident in the regression analysis that targeted increased payment for PD in both age categories. We will continue to collect and refine data for analysis to ensure the most appropriate payment for pediatric ESRD patients. We do not currently plan to convene a TEP as we believe that the available data and notice-and-comment rulemaking process provided adequate information for the basis of the CY 2027 policy, and
(
printed page 68801)
we will continue to listen to the pediatric ESRD community.
(3) Expansion of the LVPA
Historically, the ESRD PPS has not applied the LVPA for treatments furnished to pediatric ESRD patients. Section II.B.8. of this final rule provides background on the LVPA. In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule, we codified the pediatric ESRD patient payment adjustment in § 413.235(b), which states that CMS adjusts the per treatment base rate for pediatric ESRD patients in accordance with section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iv)(I) of the Act, to account for patient age and treatment modality (
75 FR 49134
). Additionally, we finalized the elimination of several exceptions including the pediatric facility exception, which allowed for higher cost pediatric ESRD facilities to receive additional payments when costs exceeded payment amounts under the composite rate payment system. In other words, the pediatric ESRD facility exceptions terminated for ESRD treatment on or after January 1, 2014 (
75 FR 49178
). Finally, the LVPA was only applicable to adult ESRD patients and was not directly used in calculating the payment rate per treatment for pediatric dialysis patients. Facilities qualifying for the LVPA that treat both adult and pediatric ESRD patients have only received the LVPA for adult dialysis patients (
75 FR 49134
). As noted in section II.B.8. of this final rule, small ESRD facilities incur higher costs than larger ESRD facilities, in part because they do not benefit from the same economies of scale as many large ESRD facilities. Due to the low incidents of pediatric ESRD patients most pediatric units are small, which makes accounting for higher costs associated with facility size accurately in payments important; however, the small number of pediatric ESRD patients also makes separate analysis on the costs of treating pediatric ESRD patients difficult. As discussed previously, for the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule we finalized an alternative methodology which was based on the average payments for pediatric treatments under the composite rate system (
75 FR 49132
through
49134
), including those exceptions to the composite rate system for high-cost pediatric facilities. The LVPA was only extended to payments for adult ESRD patients in ESRD facilities because facilities that primarily treat pediatric ESRD patients are typically small, so the higher pediatric payments from which the methodology in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule derived the pediatric case-mix adjusters included any higher costs associated with low volume. As such, we concluded that extending the LVPA to payments for pediatric ESRD patients would be duplicative with the calculation of the pediatric case-mix adjusters under the methodology used for the CY 2011 final rule (
75 FR 49134
). However, for this final rule, we included facility size as a separate characteristic in our regression model. As noted in Table 20, the pediatric ESRD share is an independent indicator of cost from the size of the ESRD facility.
As discussed previously, smaller ESRD facilities experience the greatest financial burden, and our latest analysis finds that this holds for pediatric ESRD facilities and adult ESRD facilities. As shown in Table 20, the natural logarithm of facility size (based on the total volume of treatment counts) is associated with a statistically significant reduction in cost. This means that regardless of a facility's share of pediatric ESRD patients, we observe that cost per treatment decreases as the facility's total number of treatments increases and, conversely, the cost per treatment increases as the facility's total number of treatments decreases. Based on this analysis, we believe that expanding the LVPA to include treatments furnished to pediatric ESRD patients would be appropriate.
Therefore, for CY 2027, we proposed to revise § 413.232(f) to state that the LVPA is applicable for renal dialysis treatments furnished to all ESRD patients. As outlined in section II.B.8. of the proposed rule, we proposed to make budget-neutral changes to the LVPA tier structure and adjustment factors, and we proposed that those changes would be applicable to payments for all ESRD patients beginning in CY 2027. We estimated that this change would appropriately increase payments to ESRD facilities that treat a large share of pediatric ESRD patients, which our data demonstrates face higher costs due to low volume status in addition to the specific costs associated with treating pediatric ESRD patients. Our analysis of the distributional impacts associated with the proposed LVPA changes and the proposed expansion of the LVPA to pediatric ESRD patients can be found in section II.B.8. of the proposed rule.
Additionally, we noted that although the LVPA does not currently apply to pediatric ESRD PPS claims, ESRD facilities that provide renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD beneficiaries are nevertheless permitted to attest to low-volume status and receive the LVPA for any adult ESRD beneficiaries they treat, under current regulation. Among the 32 dedicated children's hospitals furnishing ESRD treatments, two children's hospitals currently receive LVPA payments. Similarly, four of the 52 ESRD facilities that provide most of their treatments to pediatric ESRD patients are also receiving the LVPA for their adult ESRD patients. As discussed in the proposed rule, we believe that the relatively low rates of low-volume attestation among pediatric ESRD facilities is primarily because the LVPA is not applied to most of the treatments furnished to these ESRD facilities' patients. We estimated that approximately 24 pediatric ESRD facilities could be eligible for the LVPA based on the current 4,000 -treatment threshold. We stated that we expect that if we finalize our proposal to expand the LVPA to pediatric ESRD patients beginning for CY 2027, then additional ESRD facilities like these, which are not currently attesting to low-volume status, would begin to attest and would begin receiving the LVPA in CY 2027.
We also considered that small pediatric ESRD facilities within larger institutions could be small, high-cost centers specializing in care for pediatric ESRD patients. We recognized that in some cases, common ownership with other ESRD facilities that are located 5 road miles or less from the pediatric ESRD facility could create barriers to LVPA eligibility for some pediatric ESRD facilities. Under § 413.232(c), for purposes of determining eligibility for the LVPA, the number of treatments considered furnished by the ESRD facility equals the aggregate number of treatments furnished by the ESRD facility and the number of treatments furnished by other ESRD facilities that are both under common ownership with, and 5 road miles or less from, the ESRD facility in question. To receive the LVPA, an ESRD facility must submit a written attestation statement to its MAC confirming that it meets the requirements as specified in § 413.232 and qualifies as a low-volume ESRD facility. For purposes of determining eligibility for the LVPA, “treatments” mean total HD equivalent treatments (Medicare and non-Medicare). For PD patients, one week of PD is considered equivalent to three HD treatments (
80 FR 68994
).
We considered the nature of pediatric ESRD facilities, those ESRD facilities with at least a 50 percent pediatric ESRD patient mix, which are uniquely equipped to meet the specialized needs of a small subset of patients that other nearby adult-focused ESRD facilities may not be able to treat, including ESRD facilities under common ownership. We noted that we believe it would be appropriate to allow pediatric ESRD
(
printed page 68802)
facilities to request an exemption from the aggregation of volume for ESRD facilities under common ownership. While we did not propose a categorical exemption from these regulations, we proposed that a pediatric ESRD facility that is seeking low-volume status could request an exception from the aggregation of treatment volume for ESRD facilities under common ownership at § 413.232(c) through its MAC. To request such an exception, we proposed that an ESRD facility would need to submit documentation to the MAC demonstrating that: (1) the ESRD facility is either owned and operated by a Medicare-certified children's hospital under § 412.23(d) or the ESRD facility provides at least 50 percent of its total treatments (Medicare and non-Medicare) to ESRD patients who are under the age of 18 and (2) the ESRD facility is under common ownership with an ESRD facility that does not provide at least 50 percent of its total treatments (Medicare and non-Medicare) to ESRD patients who are under the age of 18. If approved, the MAC would not consider the treatment volume of the commonly owned ESRD facility when calculating the treatment volume for the excepted ESRD facility. Once approved, the exception would continue for all future years so long as the ESRD facility continues to either be a Medicare-certified children's hospital or provides at least 50 percent of total treatments to ESRD patients who are under the age of 18.
The excepted ESRD facility would still have to meet all other requirements for the LVPA, including the treatment volume threshold described at § 413.232(b)(1). As this exception is only for the purposes of the aggregation of volume of commonly owned ESRD facilities, it is possible for an ESRD facility to receive this exception and not be eligible for the LVPA if it furnished 8,000 treatments or more (or 4,000 had the change in section II.B.8. of this final rule not been finalized) in one of the past three cost reporting years. The aggregation of volume for ESRD facilities under common ownership would still apply for the excepted ESRD facility and any other commonly owned ESRD facilities within 5 road miles for which an exception has not been approved. An ESRD facility could receive exceptions for multiple commonly owned ESRD facilities, should the requirements for the exception be met for each of them. We proposed the addition of paragraph § 413.232(g)(7) to effectuate this proposed exception and detail the process for requesting the exception.
We solicited comments on our proposed expansion to apply the LVPA to payments for pediatric ESRD patients. We also solicited comments on the proposed exception to the aggregation of volume for ESRD facilities under common ownership, the administrative process required to request such an exception, and whether such an exception is needed. We noted that we believe extending the LVPA to these facilities could alleviate financial pressures. The LVPA is designed to offset the disproportionate costs encountered by low-volume ESRD facilities. Expanding its application would help ensure that pediatric ESRD facilities, which typically operate at lower volumes due to the specialized nature of their ESRD patient populations, receive essential financial support not fully addressed by current payment adjustments under the ESRD PPS.
We received comments from ESRD patient and caregiver representatives, patient advocacy organizations, professional associations, ESRDs facilities and organizations, and other interested parties regarding the proposed revisions to payment for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients. Commenters generally agreed that furnishing renal dialysis services to pediatric ESRD patients is more resource intensive than furnishing such services to adult ESRD patients and supported continued recognition of those additional costs under the ESRD PPS. Commenters differed, however, regarding the application of the low-volume payment adjustment (LVPA), use of treatment volume as an indicator of resource use, the adequacy of the data used to develop the proposed adjustments, continuation of TPEAPA, and application of budget neutrality. We summarize these comments and provide our responses in the following section.
Comment:
One pediatric professional organization provided examples of critically ill pediatric ESRD patients with multiple comorbidities from high-volume pediatric nephrology programs to illustrate that treatment volume is not a proxy for the cost of pediatric renal dialysis services.
Response:
We understand the incredible dedication and talent it requires to manage these pediatric ESRD patients. However, the pediatric case-mix does not address comorbidities. The costs for these complicated cases are incorporated into the case-mix that addresses age and modality. We have not removed any money from the case-mix adjustment. The pediatric ESRD case-mix adjustment has increased for every age category. Additionally, these complicated cases would potentially qualify for the ESRD outlier adjustment. The LVPA is in addition to the ESRD case-mix and outlier adjustments.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that the proposed methodology could result in lower payments relative to the TPEAPA for certain higher-volume pediatric ESRD programs. Commenters stated that these ESRD facilities often serve as tertiary referral centers for children with rare genetic or metabolic diseases, cancer, organ transplantation, or other complex conditions and may require broader multidisciplinary teams and subspecialty expertise. Commenters stated that payment reductions could threaten the financial viability of pediatric renal dialysis programs and access to specialized pediatric care.
A commenter reported that its internal comparison suggested that the cost difference between pediatric and adult renal dialysis services was greater than CMS's estimate, although the commenter acknowledged limitations in directly comparing the populations and settings.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding payment adequacy and access to specialized pediatric renal dialysis services. We agree that higher treatment volume does not necessarily indicate lower clinical complexity and recognize the important role that tertiary pediatric centers play in caring for children with complex conditions.
The ESRD PPS methodology is intended to establish payment based on expected resource use across categories of ESRD patients and facilities rather than to reimburse each facility's individually reported costs. Nevertheless, we agree that significant payment changes affecting a small number of highly specialized ESRD facilities warrant careful consideration. We intend to monitor pediatric renal dialysis services utilization, facility participation, and access to care following implementation of the final policy and will consider future refinements through rulemaking if the data indicate unintended effects on access to pediatric renal dialysis services.
Comment:
Numerous commenters opposed using ESRD facility treatment volume as a basis for determining the amount of additional payment for pediatric renal dialysis services. Commenters stated that pediatric renal dialysis programs incur substantial fixed costs for specialized staff, equipment, supplies, multidisciplinary care, and infrastructure regardless of treatment volume. Commenters also stated that higher-volume pediatric
(
printed page 68803)
ESRD centers may serve as regional or national referral centers for the most medically complex children and therefore may have higher, rather than lower, costs.
Commenters expressed concern that the proposed LVPA methodology could reduce payment to larger pediatric ESRD programs, including tertiary children's hospitals, even though those programs furnish highly specialized care. Some commenters also expressed concern about facilities that predominantly treat adults but furnish renal dialysis services to a small number of pediatric ESRD patients, stating that the facility's total treatment volume does not reduce the resources required for its pediatric ESRD patients.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the relationship between treatment volume and pediatric renal dialysis services costs. We agree that treatment volume is not a direct measure of an individual patient's clinical complexity and that high-volume pediatric ESRD programs may treat highly complex patients. We also recognize that pediatric renal dialysis programs may incur certain fixed or semi-fixed costs associated with maintaining specialized staff, equipment, supplies, and infrastructure.
The LVPA, however, is intended to recognize the relationship between ESRD facility treatment volume and per-treatment costs associated with spreading fixed costs across a smaller number of treatments. The proposed application of the LVPA to pediatric renal dialysis treatments was not based on an assumption that low volume captures all differences in pediatric clinical complexity. Rather, the LVPA and the pediatric case-mix adjustment factors address different dimensions of expected resource use. We will continue to monitor whether facility volume appropriately identifies systematic differences in per-treatment costs for pediatric renal dialysis services and whether additional refinements may be warranted as more pediatric-specific data become available.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that, if CMS proceeds with the proposed framework, the agency apply an LVPA to all pediatric renal dialysis services regardless of facility treatment volume. Some commenters recommended applying the LVPA to all pediatric renal dialysis treatments using the adjustment associated with facilities furnishing between 5,000 and 5,999 treatments annually. Commenters stated that pediatric renal dialysis services are inherently a low-volume and highly specialized service and that applying an adjustment to all pediatric renal dialysis treatments would prevent larger pediatric referral centers from being disadvantaged.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recommendations. Applying the LVPA to all pediatric renal dialysis treatments without regard to facility volume would effectively convert the adjustment, in whole or in part, from a low-volume facility adjustment into a broadly applicable pediatric ESRD patient payment adjustment. Such an approach would not target the adjustment based on the relationship between facility volume and per-treatment costs that the LVPA is designed to recognize. While the pediatric ESRD patient population is inherently small, data analysis has shown that there is a cost difference between pediatric ESRD facilities that provide under 8,000 treatments per year, and those pediatric ESRD facilities that provide over 8,000 treatments per year.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that ESRD facilities furnishing a high volume of adult renal dialysis treatments but treating only a small number of pediatric ESRD patients may not receive sufficient additional payment for their pediatric ESRD patients under a facility-volume methodology. The commenter stated that efficiencies associated with treating a large number of adult ESRD patients do not eliminate the specialized resources necessary to furnish care to pediatric ESRD patients and that families should not be disadvantaged for obtaining pediatric renal dialysis from a facility that also treats adults.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concerns. We agree that pediatric ESRD patients may require specialized resources regardless of whether the facility also treats adult patients. This rule increases the case-mix adjusters for all age categories as discussed earlier, which addresses the increased cost of pediatric ESRD patients. At the same time, there are certain facility-level costs and economies of scale may impact costs across treatments, and the ESRD PPS must distinguish between patient-level differences in expected resource use and facility-level differences associated with treatment volume. We will monitor the effects of the policy on ESRD facilities furnishing both adult and pediatric renal dialysis services, including whether the methodology creates unintended access or payment concerns.
Comment:
A commenter supported the proposed exception from the common-ownership treatment-volume aggregation requirement for qualifying pediatric ESRD facilities. The commenter stated that specialized pediatric ESRD programs may be located within larger health systems while continuing to operate as small, high-cost programs serving a clinically distinct population.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support. We agree that application of common-ownership aggregation requirements without consideration of the circumstances of qualifying pediatric ESRD facilities could cause the volume attributed to a pediatric ESRD program to reflect treatments furnished by other ESRD facilities within a larger organization rather than the operating circumstances of the pediatric ESRD facility itself.
Comment:
A commenter supported implementation of the expanded pediatric LVPA beginning in CY 2027 and recommended providing an expanded or later LVPA attestation window rather than delaying implementation until CY 2028. The commenter stated that timely LVPA eligibility would help avoid a payment discontinuity following expiration of the TPEAPA.
Response:
We appreciate the comment. We agree that ESRD facilities should have sufficient time to understand applicable eligibility requirements, submit required attestations, and allow MACs sufficient time to process those attestations. We also recognize the importance of avoiding unnecessary disruption as CMS transitions from the temporary pediatric ESRD payment policy to the permanent methodology. As discussed in section II.B.8.d. of this final rule, we are finalizing an extension of the LVPA attestation deadline for payment year 2027 to December 31, 2026. This extension would equally apply for adult and pediatric ESRD patients.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS monitor whether changes in pediatric renal dialysis services payment affect access to pediatric nephrology expertise, home dialysis training, transplant education, mental health services, nutrition support, and family-centered care. The commenter also recommended monitoring access for children from rural communities, low-income families, racially and ethnically diverse communities, and families whose primary language is not English.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendations regarding access and the range of services needed by pediatric renal dialysis patients and their families. We agree that Medicare payment policy should support continued access to medically necessary renal dialysis
(
printed page 68804)
services and that the effects of payment changes on vulnerable and underserved populations are important considerations.
We will consider available claims, enrollment, facility, quality, and other data in monitoring the effects of the pediatric ESRD payment methodology. We also will consider feedback from interested parties concerning access to pediatric renal dialysis services, including services furnished by specialized pediatric ESRD programs and services needed to support home dialysis and transplantation.
Comment:
A commenter stated that pediatric home dialysis frequently requires extensive parent or caregiver training, competency validation, and ongoing support and requested that CMS consider whether its analysis adequately captures the additional resources associated with caregiver-dependent pediatric home dialysis relative to adult home dialysis.
Response:
We appreciate the comment. We recognize that home dialysis for pediatric ESRD patients may require substantial caregiver involvement and training. The issues raised by the commenter concerning the resources associated with home dialysis training are relevant both to the pediatric payment methodology and to the policies governing payment for home dialysis training. As noted in section II.B.10.e. of this rule, we are adjusting the home and self-dialysis training payment adjustment from $95.60 to $138.00. The case-mix adjustments for PD have increased for both age groups. For the 12 years old and under pediatric ESRD patients the case-mix is 32.6 percent and for those pediatric ESRD patients between 13-17 years of age would have a case-mix increase is 30.3 percent.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS to prioritize simplicity and predictability in the pediatric ESRD payment methodology. The commenter stated that changes in pediatric renal dialysis payment policy and associated administrative requirements can create burdens, particularly for pediatric ESRD programs embedded within facilities that predominantly serve adults.
Response:
We appreciate the comment. We agree that administrative simplicity and payment predictability are important considerations, particularly for a small patient population and the relatively limited number of ESRD facilities furnishing pediatric renal dialysis services. At the same time, payment accuracy may require adjustments that account for meaningful differences in expected resource use.
In developing the proposal and final policy, we sought to balance payment accuracy with administrative feasibility and to rely, to the extent practicable, on existing ESRD PPS mechanisms rather than creating unnecessary new reporting or billing requirements. There are no new reporting requirements for the pediatric case-mix adjusters and only a yearly attestation for low-volume which many adult ESRD programs are familiar with submitting.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS more clearly explain the payment effects of ending the TPEAPA, updating the pediatric case-mix and outlier multipliers, and applying the LVPA to pediatric renal dialysis services. The commenter requested information concerning the effects of these policies individually and in combination and their effects on both pediatric and adult beneficiaries, particularly in light of budget neutrality.
Response:
We appreciate the request for additional transparency concerning the individual impact and interaction of the pediatric ESRD payment policies. We believe the ESRD PPS payment policy for pediatric ESRD patients and extending the LVPA to pediatric ESRD PPS payments has been explained in detail throughout the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule and this final rule. Because the expiration of the TPEAPA, revised pediatric adjustment factors, application of the LVPA, and budget-neutrality calculations affect different components of the ESRD PPS bundled payment, we agree that describing their combined effects is useful for understanding the final policy. We refer the commenter to Table 22 of this section that indicates the impacts on pediatric ESRD facilities collectively. ESRD facilities that provide 50 percent or more of their treatments to pediatric ESRD patients can view the individual effects of the ESRD PPS pediatric ESRD payment changes and extension of the LVPA to pediatric ESRD payments in Appendix B to this final rule. The impact to ESRD facilities providing most treatments to adult beneficiaries with ESRD collectively is provided in the final impacts in Table 30 in section VII.C.5.a. of this final rule. ESRD facilities providing most treatments to adult beneficiaries with ESRD can view the individual effects of the ESRD PPS pediatric ESRD payment changes and extension of the LVPA to pediatric ESRD payments in Appendix B to this final rule. We will monitor and report the effect of payment policy revisions such as ending the TPEAPA, updating the pediatric case-mix and outlier multipliers, and applying the LVPA to pediatric renal dialysis services on pediatric ESRD facilities as warranted in the future.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed implementing the pediatric payment changes on a budget-neutral basis. Commenters stated that the higher costs of pediatric renal dialysis services do not imply that the costs of treating adult dialysis patients have decreased and stated that improving payment for pediatric care should not require reductions in payments for other ESRD patients. A commenter noted that pediatric Medicare beneficiaries constitute a small share of ESRD PPS treatments and noted that the cost of financing pediatric payment improvements without budget neutrality, therefore, would be small relative to total ESRD PPS expenditures.
Other commenters supported the substance of the proposed pediatric case-mix and LVPA policies but specifically requested that CMS implement those policies on a non-budget-neutral basis.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the effects of budget neutrality on payments for other ESRD PPS treatments. We agree that the clinical need for additional resources for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients does not imply that adult dialysis patients require fewer resources.
However, we believe that the application of a budget neutrality factor to the ESRD PPS base rate is appropriate for this payment change as it would ensure that changes in payment adjustments do not result in an unintended change in aggregate ESRD PPS expenditures solely as a result of recalibration. We stated that the TPEAPA applies primarily to costs included in the data used to establish the CY 2011 ESRD PPS bundled payment. Because the methodology attributed pediatric renal dialysis services costs to the general population, the ESRD PPS base rate would be reduced to reflect the reallocation of pediatric renal dialysis services costs. We noted that we believe that future modifications to the pediatric case-mix adjusters must also maintain budget neutrality. We refer the commenter to Table 22 of this section that indicates the impacts on pediatric ESRD facilities. The impact to adult ESRD facilities is provided in the final impacts in Table 30 in section VII.C.5.a. of this final rule. We will continue to monitor the effectives of budget-neutral payment adjustments to the impacts of both pediatric and adult ESRD facilities and will potentially revise payment methodologies as warranted in future rulemaking (
88 FR 76378
). Further
(
printed page 68805)
discussion of budget neutrality is noted in section II.B.4. of this final rule.
Comment:
Several commenters requested continued data collection and monitoring after implementation of any permanent pediatric ESRD payment methodology. Commenters recommended that CMS evaluate payment adequacy, staffing, specialized resource needs, access to pediatric renal dialysis services, the experience of high-volume tertiary centers, and the resource intensity associated with younger and medically complex ESRD patients. Some commenters requested future changes if experience demonstrates that the finalized methodology does not adequately reflect pediatric renal dialysis services costs.
Response:
We agree that continued monitoring is particularly important for pediatric renal dialysis services because the pediatric ESRD population is small and the facilities furnishing these services vary in size, organizational structure, and patient complexity. The relatively small number of pediatric renal dialysis treatments also can make estimates more sensitive to changes in patient mix, facility characteristics, and reporting practices.
We intend to continue evaluating available pediatric cost, claims, utilization, and facility data following implementation of the CY 2027 policy. We will also consider information submitted by pediatric renal dialysis providers, professional organizations, patients, caregivers, and other interested parties. If future data indicate that the pediatric payment methodology does not appropriately reflect resource use or creates unintended access concerns, we may consider additional refinements to cost reports or action through future notice-and-comment rulemaking.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of public comments, available data and additional feedback from interested parties provided directly to CMS, we are finalizing the pediatric payment changes for CY 2027 as proposed, without modification. Our analysis demonstrates a consistent relationship between facility volume and pediatric per-treatment costs, with higher-volume pediatric referral centers and mixed adult/pediatric facilities incurring distinct resource demands. In response to concerns raised by commenters regarding these centers, CMS has evaluated the impact of volume thresholds and the LVPA methodology. We are maintaining the proposed volume thresholds and tiers for pediatric ESRD facilities, as they accurately reflect observed cost differences and ensure payment aligns with pediatric resource use regardless of facility type. Under the finalized LVPA methodology, pediatric renal dialysis treatments and total facility volume are considered, with the aggregation exception for common ownership ensuring qualifying pediatric ESRD facilities are not disadvantaged.
CMS is finalizing the pediatric exception to the common-ownership aggregation requirement as proposed, without modification. The CY 2027 implementation date will be January 1, 2027. As discussed previously, the attestation deadline for payment year CY 2027 is extended to December 31, 2026. That is, ESRD facilities, including those that primarily furnish treatment to pediatric ESRD patients, must submit an attestation by December 31, 2026, to receive the LVPA for payments in CY 2027. The extension to the attestation deadline also allows pediatric ESRD facilities to submit any requests for exceptions to the common ownership aggregation by December 31, 2026. Impact analyses indicate expected payment changes for pediatric ESRD facilities based on volume, facility type, and other characteristics, supporting equitable payment. The finalized pediatric case-mix methodology incorporates modality-specific differences, including the home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment, to further refine payments. Attestation, reporting, and billing requirements under the final policy are specified to ensure transparency and accountability. (4) Conforming Edits to § 413.232(g) To Specify Calendar Days
As discussed in the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed to create an exception process for ESRD facilities that are Medicare-certified children's hospitals or that furnish more than 50 percent of treatments to pediatric ESRD patients. In the proposed new paragraph § 413.232(g)(7), we specify a timeline based on “calendar days,” rather than “days.” We believe that specifying “calendar days” avoids confusion between calendar days, working days, business days, or any other type of day. When we finalized the exceptions for disasters or other emergencies in the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule (
88 FR 76344

We proposed edits to § 413.232(g)(5) and (6) to specify that the timeline for the exceptions is based on calendar days, consistent with the proposed language of § 413.232(g)(7). We also proposed an edit to § 413.232(g)(6)(iv) to add the word “of” to the first sentence following “30 calendar days,” which was omitted in a typographical error. We did not receive any public comments on these proposals. We are finalizing the proposals as proposed.
10. Home and Self-Dialysis Training Add-On Payment Adjustment
a. Background
Under the ESRD PPS, there are three components to payment for home and self-dialysis training: (1) the base rate, (2) a wage-adjusted home and self-dialysis
[
38
]
training add-on payment adjustment, and (3) an allowable number of training treatments. The ESRD PPS includes an add-on payment adjustment for home and self-dialysis training, which is described at § 413.235(c). Hereafter, we refer to the home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment as the training add-on.
CMS makes the same training add-on for both HD and PD. We recognize that the costs for home and self-dialysis training for HD and PD are likely not identical, as supported by our analysis of ESRD facility cost report data discussed later in this section. However, the ESRD PPS is a prospective payment system under section 1881(b)(14)(A)(i) of the Act. As such, payments are not intended to reflect the exact costs incurred by individual facilities, but to provide standardized payments that promote efficiency and access.
When the ESRD PPS was implemented in 2011, we proposed that the cost for all home dialysis services would be included in the bundled payment (
74 FR 49930
), and therefore, the computation of the base rate included home dialysis training add-on payments made to ESRD facilities as well as all composite rate payments, which account for facility costs associated with equipment, supplies, and staffing. In response to public comments, in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule, we noted that although we were continuing to include training payments in computing the ESRD PPS base rate, we agreed with commenters that we should treat training as an adjustment under the ESRD PPS. Accordingly, we finalized the training add-on amount of $33.44 per treatment as an additional payment made under the ESRD PPS when one-on-one home dialysis training is furnished by a nurse for either HD or PD training or retraining (
75 FR 49063
), updated from the previous adjustment amount of $20. This updated amount of $33.44 per treatment was based on the national average hourly wage for Registered Nurses (RN) as published by the Occupational Employment Statistics (OES) data compiled by BLS data updated to 2011 (
75 FR 49063
), and reflected 1 hour of training time by a RN for both HD and PD. This average hourly wage was then inflated to 2011 by the ESRD wages and salaries proxy used in the 2008-based ESRD bundled market basket. In addition, we continued the policy of paying the home dialysis training add-on payment for 15 training treatments for PD and 25 training treatments for HD.
Section 494.100(a)(2) of the Conditions for Coverage for ESRD Facilities stipulates that the RN must conduct the home or self-dialysis training, and CMS has clarified through interpretive guidance (ESRD Program Interpretive Guidance published October 3, 2008 (
http://www.cms.gov/​Medicare/​Provider-Enrollment-and-Certification/​SurveyCertificationGenInfo/​downloads/​SCletter09-01.pdf
) that other members of the clinical dialysis staff may assist in providing the home training. We also elaborated in this guidance that the qualified home training RN is responsible for ensuring that the training is in accordance with the requirements at § 494.100, with oversight from the ESRD facility's interdisciplinary team.
In the CY 2014 ESRD PPS final rule (
78 FR 72185
), CMS increased this amount from $33.44 to $50.16 to reflect 1.5 hours of training time by an RN in response to concerns from interested parties regarding payment adequacy. The $50.16 training add-on amount was consistent with average costs based on an analysis of pre-PPS cost report data. In the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77856
), CMS further updated the home and self-dialysis training add-on to $95.60 based on 2.66 hours of RN time using BLS wage data.
In 2025, Medicare paid approximately $7 million in home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment amounts, which remained relatively stable compared to prior years. This relatively flat trend, in conjunction with feedback from interested parties, may indicate that home dialysis and self-dialysis modalities remain underutilized and that payment adequacy for training may be a contributing factor.
