]
We analyzed CY 2024 ESRD cost report data from freestanding and hospital-based ESRD facilities. The median cost-per-training session was approximately $712 overall, $381 for HD, and $797 for PD. The median labor cost-per-training session was approximately $283 overall, $164 for HD, and $314 for PD. As discussed in the proposed rule, CMS believes that these reported ESRD facility costs include resources associated with routine renal dialysis services in addition to training-specific activities. On average, payment per dialysis treatment was approximately $300 in 2024. As outlined in section II.B.1. of this final rule, the total compensation in the 2024-based ESRDB market basket is 50.9 percent as presented in Table 3. Applying this to the rough per-treatment payment amount of $300 gives us a payment amount of approximately $153. To appropriately determine the extent to which training for home dialysis results in increased labor costs, we can subtract this $153 amount from the median per-training-treatment labor cost of $283. This results in a per-treatment labor net cost of about $130 per training treatment above that which is included in the per-treatment payment.
Because the ESRD PPS is not a cost-based system, and cost report data may not reliably isolate the marginal cost of training, we noted that CMS does not believe it is appropriate to base the training add-on directly on these data. As discussed in further detail in the next section, CMS proposed to continue to rely on a standardized labor-based methodology reflecting RN time, which is more consistent with the design of the ESRD PPS. However, this $130 net labor per-training treatment cost demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology, the results of which we discuss in the following section.
c. Proposed Increase to the Home and Self-Dialysis Training Add-On Payment Adjustment
In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed to increase the training add-on according to the most recently available BLS OEWS, using the same methodology finalized in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77856
), based on 2.66 hours of RN time and updated wage data. CMS proposed to maintain the 2.66-hour basis as cost report data has indicated it is an appropriate basis for the training payment and is administratively simple to calculate. As discussed in the prior section, cost report data shows a net labor cost of approximately $130 per training treatment for 2024. While we did not propose to base the training amount on this cost report data, we note that it lines up with the result from our established methodology closely. Specifically, applying this 2.66-hour basis to the estimate of RN wages from the May 2024 BLS OEWS, $47.32, would give us a training adjustment of $125.87 for 2024, before the application of any wage index. This demonstrates that our longstanding methodology generally accounts for the net labor costs associated with home dialysis training.
[
42
]
We explained that the training add-on is only intended to cover the labor related costs for home and self-dialysis training, as the ESRD PPS base rate includes payment for all other costs associated with furnishing renal dialysis services, as discussed in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49063
).
We stated that this proposed approach would maintain consistency with prior policy while accounting for wage growth over time and aligning with the prospective principles upon which the ESRD PPS was established. Under the ESRD PPS, and in accordance with section 1881(b)(14)(A)(i) of the Act, CMS implemented a single base rate that applies to all dialysis treatment modalities. CMS did not propose to differentiate payment amounts between PD and HD training. Although cost report data suggest differences, maintaining a single rate is consistent with the ESRD PPS structure as HD and PD are paid the same for adult beneficiaries, and avoids creating financial incentives that could influence modality selection.
We calculated the updated payment amount using the mean hourly wage for RNs (SOC 29-1141) from the May 2025 BLS OEWS (
http://www.bls.gov/​oes/​tables.htm
) which was $48.76 in 2025. We then inflated this 2025 mean hourly wage figure to CY 2027 using the growth in the 2024-based ESRDB market basket Wages and Salaries price proxy. We stated that we believe this proposed increase would improve payment adequacy for training while maintaining the integrity of the PPS. This would result in a new RN hourly wage of $51.96. For the hours, we proposed to continue to use the 2.66 hours as the amount of time for home dialysis training by an RN that is accounted for by the training add-on. This results in a proposed training add-on payment of $138.22 (2.66 hours × $51.96 = $138.22). We proposed to update the RN hourly wage estimate in the final rule with more recent data, such as an updated estimate in the growth of the price proxy, if appropriate.
This proposal would provide for an increase of $42.62 per training treatment (that is, $138.22 − $95.60 = $42.62). This approach would provide a significant increase in payment for home and self-dialysis training for CY 2027 while maintaining consistent payment for both PD and HD modalities. After evaluating the cost report data presented previously in the proposed rule, we stated that we believe that this amount is an appropriate proxy for the costs of home dialysis training. We proposed to update this training add-on amount with additional data, for example an update in the growth in the 2024-based ESRDB market basket Wages and Salaries price proxy in the final rule, if appropriate.
CMS proposed to implement this increase for the training add-on in a budget neutral manner through an adjustment to the ESRD PPS base rate. We stated that we believe implementing this budget neutral change, similar to the budget neutral training add-on in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77856
), is appropriate because the ESRD
(
printed page 68808)
PPS base rate includes certain training costs. For more information on the history of training add-on changes, we refer readers to a discussion in response to comments in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77853
through
77854
). We noted that CMS would estimate aggregate impacts for this proposal using claims and cost report data.
d. Payment for Training During Dialysis Onset
In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule we finalized a payment adjustment for ESRD patients in their first 4 months on renal dialysis (
75 FR 49090
through
49094
), which we refer to as the onset adjustment. We stated that as home dialysis training costs represent one-on-one staff time to train a patient for home dialysis, we believed we captured staffing costs for training in the onset adjustment. Since we already accounted for training salary costs in the onset adjustment, we believed that applying the training add-on adjustment in addition to the onset adjustment would have the effect of compounding the composite rate costs and would result in an overpayment of nursing staff costs associated with training renal dialysis patients for home dialysis. Therefore, the rule finalized that ESRD facilities would not receive the training add-on adjustment for ESRD patients who are receiving the onset adjustment. In the CY 2011 final rule we stated that we would continue to study the relationship between costs related to the onset of dialysis and home dialysis training for future refinements of the ESRD PPS (
75 FR 49094
).
At that time, we stated that we believed that the onset adjustment captured additional labor costs for home dialysis training sessions that occur during the onset period, which is the first four months a patient is on renal dialysis (
75 FR 49063
). The CY 2011 onset adjustment factor was finalized at 1.510 (
75 FR 49094
). As the training add-on was $33.44, the onset adjustment factor was generally much larger than the training add-on for any single patient, so it was reasonable to believe that notable additional labor costs associated with home dialysis training were captured by the analysis from which the onset adjustment was derived.
The current onset adjustment factor is 1.327, as finalized in the CY 2016 ESRD PPS final rule (
80 FR 68992
through
68993
). The current CY 2026 ESRD PPS base rate is $281.71 so a 1.327 adjustment factor would be an increase of approximately $92, which is lower than the current training add-on adjustment. As the onset adjustment is intended to account for more than just home dialysis training, the lower multiplicative onset adjustment factor, combined with the relatively low utilization of home dialysis training during the onset period, led us to reevaluate our longstanding policy of not applying the training add-on during the onset period.
In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed to allow ESRD facilities to receive the home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment during the onset period (
91 FR 38833
). We explained that analysis of 2024 claims data indicates that approximately 7.7 percent of onset claims include training. While this is an improvement from the inception of the ESRD PPS, we believe that patient choice would be improved by increased access to home and self-dialysis training during the onset period. Currently, approximately 44 percent of training sessions occurred during the onset period, which demonstrates that most ESRD patients who receive training are not in the onset period. CMS further believes that the training add-on reflects discrete training labor-related resources that are not fully captured by the onset adjustment and therefore would not result in duplicative payment. Home dialysis was included in the data upon which the ESRD PPS base rate was constructed in the 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49084
). However, in that rule, we discussed how the ESRD PPS base payment alone does not address home dialysis training costs, so an additional adjustment was warranted (
75 FR 49062
). In the regression analysis performed for that rule, we stated that we believed the higher costs associated with the onset period were, in part, due to some training labor costs (
75 FR 49063
). However, based on our analysis of the training labor cost and the onset adjustment for the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we stated that we no longer believe this is the case. There are training costs, primarily equipment supply costs, included in the ESRD PPS base rate (
75 FR 49062
) which are likely higher during training which would be captured by the analysis from which the onset adjustment was derived. But, as discussed previously, the ESRD PPS base rate does not contain significant monies for labor related to home dialysis training, so we do not believe that allowing both adjustments would be duplicative now, in large part because the onset adjustment factor has decreased since 2011 (which could have reflected some shifting utilization). Similar to how the training add-on accounts for the extra costs not accounted for by the ESRD PPS base rate, we stated that we believe that most costs associated with home dialysis training are not reflected in the current onset adjustment. Furthermore, our proposal to implement this policy budget neutrally further mitigates the risk of potential duplicative payment. We proposed to base the budget neutrality of this change on the current utilization of home dialysis training during the onset period.
e. Combined Budget Neutrality Implications and Comment Solicitation
The proposed increase to the training add-on and the proposed allowance of the training add-on for ESRD PPS claims during the onset period would result in a budget neutrality adjustment of 0.99884. We solicited comments on these proposed modifications to the home and self-dialysis training adjustment, as well as the proposed budget neutrality of these proposals and the proposed budget neutrality adjustment factor of 0.99884. Additionally, we solicited comments on other ways in which we could improve both home dialysis and self-dialysis utilization. We also solicited comments on the proposal to continue using the calculation established in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77856
), basing the training add-on on 2.66 hours of RN time. As noted previously, we did not propose to base the training add-on on Medicare cost report data, nor did we propose to set different training payment rates for HD and PD but based on comments received in response to the proposed rule, we stated that we may finalize a different policy, if warranted. Such a policy could involve using cost reports to determine the number of hours of nursing time required for home dialysis training or modifying the training add-on for a modality based on the relative cost of that modality reported on cost reports, and we solicited comments on these potential alternative methodologies. We also solicited comments on alternative ways we could budget neutralize this proposal, and specifically whether it would be more appropriate to make the proposal to allow the training add-on during the onset period budget neutral by reducing the onset adjustment factor.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
The majority of commenters, including MedPAC, expressed support for CMS's proposed increase to the training add-on amount. Many commenters noted that labor costs have increased since the last time we
(
printed page 68809)
updated the training add-on. Some commenters expressed the importance of adequate training add-on payment for access to home dialysis. Many commenters emphasized the importance of home dialysis as an option for ESRD patients for whom it is appropriate and similarly emphasized the importance of high-quality home dialysis training.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support. We agree that home dialysis is an important modality option for many ESRD patients.
Comment:
Several commenters requested more frequent updates to the training add-on. A commenter stated that annual updates were not necessary but recommended we update the training add-on routinely when we rebase the ESRDB market basket. MedPAC recommended annual updates using publicly available BLS OEWS data. A commenter highlighted how large the increase is from the $95.60 amount set in CY 2017 to the $138.22 amount proposed for CY 2027.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestions and will consider them for potential future rulemaking. We did not propose a routine methodology to update the training add-on amount and are not finalizing any such methodology in this final rule.
Comment:
Some commenters noted that there were other costs associated with home dialysis that the training add-on did not cover, for example utility costs or storage costs for home dialysis patients. The commenter stated that CMS should not assume that an increase in payment to ESRD facilities will eliminate all barriers to home dialysis and requested we consider other mechanisms to support home dialysis uptake.
Response:
We agree that there are other costs and barriers associated with uptake of home dialysis. In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule we issued an RFI requesting detailed information on such costs and barriers (
91 FR 38848
). We intend to consider the barriers the commenter listed when considering the responses to that RFI for potential future rulemaking.
Comment:
MedPAC generally supported the proposed increase to the home dialysis payment but also offered methodological recommendations. Specifically, MedPAC suggested CMS develop a process to empirically derive the share of treatments that are PD vs home HD and the average length of a training session. MedPAC noted that CMS collects “time on machine” data for hemodialysis treatments which could help this purpose.
Response:
We appreciate MedPAC's methodological suggestions. The 2.66-hour training average that we used for this rule was derived from the following values as described in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77852
): (1) that PD represented 67 percent of all home dialysis training treatments, and (2) that PD training took 2 hours whereas HD training took 4 hours. The values for training time were derived from clinical guidelines on treatment times for both modalities. Analysis of ESRD facility cost report data indicates that the share of PD training treatments has decreased slightly, with PD representing 52 percent of training treatments in 2024. Time on machine data from CY 2025 indicates that the median HD training sessions report approximately 180 minutes, or 3 hours, of time on machine; we note that this is slightly lower than the overall median time on machine for in-center HD treatments, which is approximately 210 minutes, or 3.5 hours. The average time on machine for HD training is 235 minutes, or slightly under 4 hours; we believe the median is probably more representative because there were some implausible outliers for time on machine data, with 5 percent of treatments reporting longer than 7 hours of time on machine. We do not collect time on machine data for PD sessions. Using these updated figures, and maintaining the assumption that PD takes 2 hours, we would get an average training time of 2.48 hours (3 × 0.48 + 2 × 0.52). Basing the calculation instead on the median HD time on machine would yield an average training time of 2.72 hours (3.5 * 0.48 + 2 * 0.52). We reiterate that these figures were based on median values for HD time on machines, rather than average, because implausibly high reported values would likely skew the average in a way that is inappropriate. However, in doing so, these figures also do not consider real outlier treatment lengths, which we believe would be appropriate. Nevertheless, our longstanding assumption of 2.66 hours falls in between these two alternative estimates based on median values. We believe that this is empirical evidence that our longstanding assumption is reasonable as a proxy for the average home dialysis training treatment time. However, we intend to evaluate why the time on machine for training treatments is lower than other HD treatments, and whether that was partially driven by the amount of the training add-on. We did not propose to modify the methodology to use 2.66 hours of nursing time as the basis for the training add-on amount and we are not finalizing any such changes in this final rule.
Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS reevaluate the use of the 2.66-hour figure in the calculation of the training add-on payment. One healthcare organization which operates ESRD facilities stated that their training sessions last anywhere from 3 to 4 hours. Another commenter indicated that training sessions can last 5 to 8 hours. A commenter stated that both HD and PD training sessions can last 5 to 6 hours. A commenter requested we collect actual data on RN time for home dialysis training and use it to determine whether separate payment amounts for PD and HD were appropriate.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' insight on their experience with home dialysis training. We want to note that the 2.66-hour figure used to calculate the training add-on was derived from an assumption of 4 hours of nursing time for HD and 2 hours of nursing time for PD. Those figures were based on Kidney Disease Outcome Quality Initiative (KDOQI) guidelines for HD and PD treatment length (
81 FR 77852
). While a commenter did not indicate which modality training they performed, we note that the 3 to 4 hours they stated is consistent with the assumed training time for HD. We recognize that some training sessions may last longer than the typical length of treatment for PD and HD, and that some patients may require more nursing time in training than others. Likewise, we acknowledge that the training costs for PD and HD are likely different on average. We believe that a single bundled training payment, adjusted by the ESRD facility's wage index, is most consistent with the principles of a bundled payment system. As noted previously, we evaluated data from ESRD facility cost reports and we believe that our assumptions on the average HD and PD training treatment length on which our training add-on is based are reasonable. However, we will continue to evaluate the appropriateness of the training add-on and will consider the commenters' suggestions for potential future rulemaking, if appropriate.
Comment:
A commenter opined that the proposed training add-on amount of $138.22 was still too low. The commenter noted that the analysis CMS included in the proposed rule stated that the median labor cost-per-training session was $283 overall, $164 for HD, and $314 for PD.
Response:
We want to reiterate that the reported figures to which the commenter pointed are not the best comparison alone for the home dialysis training add-on amount as these figures include all labor costs associated with
(
printed page 68810)
furnishing the renal dialysis session. The ESRD PPS base rate includes costs associated with the labor for furnishing renal dialysis services. Dialysis treatments which include home dialysis training, also receive the ESRD PPS base rate which covers the more routine aspects of that dialysis session. Although not every renal dialysis service may be identical between routine maintenance dialysis and dialysis that includes home dialysis training, the nature of a bundled payment allows for ESRD facilities to substitute the specific renal dialysis services as appropriate. In the proposed rule, when we referenced these figures, we then removed a portion of the ESRD PPS payment based on the LRS which resulted in a net increased labor cost-per-training session of approximately $130 for CY 2024 (
91 FR 38831
). This is consistent with our proposed training add-on of $138.22 for CY 2027.
Comment:
One professional association stated that home dialysis training was more resource intensive for pediatric ESRD patients and recommended that CMS recognize the difference.
Response:
We appreciate the insight into home dialysis training costs for pediatric ESRD patients. We are finalizing changes to the case-mix adjustment factors for pediatric ESRD patients and finalizing an extension of the LVPA to payments for pediatric renal dialysis treatments. We note that the cost analysis upon which the updated case-mix adjustments were based included costs associated with home dialysis training. We are confident that the changes to the payment for renal dialysis services furnished for pediatric ESRD patients, including the increase to the training add-on, will continue to support access to home dialysis training for pediatric ESRD patients, including home dialysis performed by a caregiver. Nevertheless, we will consider the commenter's suggestion for potential future rulemaking. We did not propose, and are not finalizing, different training add-on payments for pediatric ESRD patients.
Comment:
Most commenters who opined on the proposal to allow the training add-on during the onset period expressed support for the policy. Many commenters expressed support for this proposal alongside support for the increase to the training add-on and listed the same reasonings for both, including the importance of high-quality home dialysis training. A commenter stated that this would improve patient-centered care. Several commenters highlighted the importance on home dialysis uptake in the initial months of dialysis, with a commenter especially noting the potential impact on those who “crash” into dialysis.
Response:
We appreciate the support of commenters on our proposal to allow the training add-on payment during the onset period. We agree that access to home dialysis training is important to facilitate ESRD beneficiaries' ability to choose the modality best for them. We likewise agree that access to home dialysis training is important for those whose transition to ESRD and dialysis is unexpected.
Comment:
One coalition of kidney organizations raised concerns with the proposal to allow the training add-on to be applied during the onset period. The commenter was uncertain whether it was methodologically reasonable and indicated a belief that it may have been appropriate for CMS to make corresponding decreases to the onset adjustment factor.
Response:
We acknowledge the concerns of commenters regarding the potential overlap between the onset adjustment and training add-on adjustment, should the training add-on be extended during the onset period. When we finalized the training add-on in the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule (
75 FR 49062
) we stated that we believed the onset adjustment accounts for certain higher costs associated with training patients for home dialysis during the first four months of dialysis treatments. In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we stated that we believed that most costs associated with home dialysis training are not reflected in the current onset adjustment and that we were accounting for the potential for duplicative payments by reducing the ESRD PPS base rate (
91 FR 38833
). After consideration of the commenters' concerns, we agree that the onset adjustment captures some of the labor costs associated with home dialysis training and that it would be appropriate to reduce the onset factor to account for the overlap. Additionally, we considered the concerns of several other commenters regarding budget neutrality and recognize that a reduction to the onset factor would mitigate the budget neutrality impact on the ESRD PPS base rate. Thus, after considering all of the comments received, we are finalizing a modification to the onset adjustment to account for the overlap in the payments. Specifically, we are scaling down the onset adjustment factor by the estimated training payments during the onset period. This is an option that we discussed as an alternative in the proposed rule and solicited comments on (
91 FR 38833
). This will ensure that the expansion of the training payment to the onset period is done in a budget neutral manner and prevent duplicative payments between the onset adjustment and the training add-on. By reducing the onset adjustment by the estimated overlap spending and maintaining budget neutrality we are functionally targeting the onset adjustment funds towards ESRD treatments that include home dialysis training. The reduced onset factor is 1.311, which is a modest reduction from the current factor of 1.327, which we believe is reasonable given the expansion of the training add-on during the onset period will maintain total estimated spending during the onset period. We note that the budget neutrality for this calculation was based on CY 2025 claims data on training sessions during the onset period; we expect that this policy would also result in a shift of training sessions which are currently occurring after the onset period.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns with the budget neutrality of the proposal and requested it be implemented in a non-budget neutral manner. Some commenters noted that the original training add-on was established in a non-budget neutral manner and stated a belief that future updates should also be non-budget neutral. A commenter noted that, had the establishment of the training add-on been instead a part of the base rate, it would have been updated by the ESRDB market basket and increased over time. A commenter highlighted that large, infrequent updates to the training add-on concentrate the budget neutrality impact in a single year. MedPAC supported implementing this proposal budget neutrally. Some commenters indicated that they believed lowering the payment rate for budget neutrality would be contrary to the stated goal of supporting home dialysis, as the payment rate for home dialysis would decrease.
Response:
We understand the concerns raised by commenters regarding the decrease to the ESRD PPS base rate associated with budget neutrality. We also acknowledge commenters' observations regarding the history of the training add-on payment adjustment, including that the original training add-on was established on a non-budget neutral basis and that certain subsequent changes have been implemented budget neutrally.
We proposed this policy budget neutrally because we believe implementing this budget neutral change is appropriate because the ESRD PPS base rate includes certain training
(
printed page 68811)
costs, similar to the budget neutral training add-on in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77856
). We included a detailed history of the training add-on changes, including the choices to implement certain changes budget neutrally, in response to comments in the CY 2017 ESRD PPS final rule (
81 FR 77853
through
77854
). In that rule we characterized the $95.60 add-on training amount as a temporary measure stated that we would collect and review cost report and claims data to eventually reevaluate the training add-on amount. As noted previously we have since reviewed the available cost report data and believe those data support our longstanding methodology based on 2.66 hours of RN time as an appropriate proxy for the labor costs associated with home dialysis training.
We do not believe it is appropriate at this time to increase overall expenditures under the ESRD PPS as home dialysis training is also accounted for in the base rate. We view this increase to the training add-on as moving dollars to effectively target this modality based on its relative resource use. We recognize that the training add-on was originally implemented non-budget neutrally and that if it had been added to the base rate it would have been increased by the annual ESRDB market basket update. In the CY 2011 ESRD PPS final rule, we acknowledged that there were dollars in the base rate for home dialysis training (
75 FR 49062
through
49064
) and we established a policy to implement the additional payment for training through an add-on payment, rather than a base rate increase. Regardless of how the training add-on was originally implemented, we are making this change to better allocate the money that is currently in the ESRD PPS, so budget neutrality is most appropriate at this time.
We acknowledge that this is a single budget neutrality factor reflective of changes since CY 2017 and is larger than if it only reflected typical changes in a single year. The budget neutrality factor is based on the estimated payments under the updated factor, the increase to which was based on the most recently available wage data. As noted previously, we will consider more routine updates to the training add-on in potential future rulemaking.
We disagree with the commenters who stated that a budget neutrality decrease would be contrary to our goal of supporting home dialysis uptake. Although a budget neutrality adjustment would decrease the ESRD PPS base rate, it would not decrease total ESRD PPS payments.
As noted previously, we are finalizing this proposal with a slight modification to decrease the onset adjustment factor based on the estimated training add-on spending during the onset period. This change will maintain budget neutrality for the expansion of the training add-on to the onset period, which reduces the impact of the budget neutrality factor for the base rate.
Final rule Action:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposals to increase the home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment amount and to allow the training add-on during the onset period. The final home dialysis training amount is $138.00 (2.66 × $51.88 = $138.00), based on an updated hourly RN wage of 51.88, which reflects an updated estimate of the change in labor compensation of the ESRDB market basket from CY 2025 to CY 2027. Additionally, we are finalizing a reduction to the onset add-on amount by a factor to account for the estimated training add-on spending during the onset period, reducing the factor from 1.327 to 1.311. These changes are being finalized budget neutrally with a budget neutrality factor of 0.99964, driven by the payment impact of increasing the training add-on amount. We note that the change in policy to reduce the onset factor has a lessening impact on the budget neutrality factor, which was proposed as 0.99884.
11. Modification to TDAPA and Post-TDAPA Add-On Payment Adjustment Average Sales Price (ASP) Policy
In the CY 2020 ESRD PPS final rule, we finalized a conditional policy for TDAPA payment based on the availability of ASP data (
84 FR 60679
). In that final rule, we explained that if drug manufacturers were to stop submitting full quarters of ASP data for products that are eligible for the TDAPA, and we had to revert to basing the TDAPA on the wholesale acquisition cost (WAC) or invoice pricing, we believed we would be overpaying for the TDAPA for those products. We stated that we would no longer apply the TDAPA for a new renal dialysis drug or biological product if CMS does not receive a full calendar quarter of ASP data within 30 days after the last day of the 3rd calendar quarter after the TDAPA is initiated for the product, or if CMS stops receiving the latest full calendar quarter of ASP data during the applicable TDAPA period specified in § 413.234(c)(1) or (2). We explained that once we determine that the latest full calendar quarter of ASP is not available, we would stop applying the TDAPA for the new renal dialysis drug or biological product within the next 2-calendar quarters. We adopted this conditional policy to avoid overpaying for the TDAPA on an ongoing basis and to ensure that TDAPA payment is based on the most appropriate data, that is, ASP.
In the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule we finalized the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment (
88 FR 76388
through
76397
). When we finalized this payment adjustment, we also finalized a similar conditional ASP policy where if CMS stopped receiving ASP data for a particular drug or biological product, we would no longer apply a post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment for that drug or biological product.
The CY 2024 ESRD PPS proposed rule (
88 FR 42472
) discussed that our regulation at § 413.234(c) did not address the application of the TDAPA conditional policy in situations where the manufacturer of the new renal dialysis drug or biological product submitted zero or negative sales ASP data to CMS. Zero or negative sales may occur for a variety of reasons, including no sales, recalls of a product, or repurchases of sold products. In the CY 2012 Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule (
76 FR 73296
), CMS clarified that zero or negative values are valid for ASP, ASP units, and WAC. Therefore, when such a scenario occurs for separately payable Medicare Part B drugs, we consider the submission of zero or negative sales to fulfill the reporting requirements of manufacturer ASP data to CMS as set forth in sections 1927(b)(3)(A)(iii) and 1847A(f) of the Act.
In the CY 2024 ESRD PPS final rule (
88 FR 76410
) we clarified that for purposes of the TDAPA conditional policy, in circumstances where a manufacturer submitted zero or negative sales ASP data during the TDAPA period, we consider CMS to have received the latest full calendar quarter of ASP data, and we will not discontinue TDAPA payment under the conditional policy in § 413.234(c). We further indicated that, consistent with the pricing methodologies for separately payable Medicare Part B drugs, in such circumstances, we will set the TDAPA payment amount based on WAC or, if WAC is not available, invoice pricing, for the quarter in which zero or negative sales were reported. Likewise, we finalized that we would also consider ASP reflecting zero or negative sales during the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment period as CMS having received the latest full calendar quarter of ASP data and would not discontinue the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment. We finalized that we would
(
printed page 68812)
use WAC or, if WAC is not available, invoice pricing, for the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment calculation (
88 FR 76396
).
In the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 97981
through
97982
), we specified that for the purposes of calculating a payment limit for Part B drugs, we will consider positive manufacturer's ASP data “available” and negative or zero manufacturer's ASP data “not available.” We further specified that the use of the most recent positive ASP data available for a billing and payment code for a drug is most consistent with the payment limit calculations described in section 1847A(b) and (c) of the Act, including section 1847A(c)(5)(B) of the Act. In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49737
) we noted that the published payment limit for a drug with negative or zero ASP data reported after January 1, 2025, could be based on a positive amount that is carried forward from a previous quarter in accordance with § 414.904(i).
In the CY 2027 ESRD PPS proposed rule, we proposed modifications to align the TDAPA and post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodologies with pricing methodologies applicable to separately payable Medicare Part B drugs under section 1847A of the Act, including the use of the most recent available positive ASP data (
91 FR 38834
). This proposed modification would not change the TDAPA payment for a new renal dialysis drug or biological product that is in the first three quarters of the TDAPA payment period for which ASP data has not been reported. Specifically, for any such product, TDAPA payment would continue to be based on 100 percent of WAC and, if WAC is not available, based on the drug manufacturer's invoice price. Consistent with our policy, if CMS does not receive a full calendar quarter of ASP data within 30 days of the last day of the 3rd calendar quarter following the initiation of the TDAPA, CMS will discontinue the TDAPA for that product beginning no later than 2-calendar quarters after CMS determines that such ASP data is not available. We note that, for purposes of this policy, the submission of zero or negative sales ASP data satisfies the manufacturer's ASP reporting requirement under sections 1927(b)(3)(A)(iii) and 1847A(f) of the Act.
Under this proposal, when ASP data are reported as negative or zero for a renal dialysis drug or biological product and CMS has received positive ASP data for the product in a prior calendar quarter, we would no longer base the TDAPA payment amount on WAC or, if WAC is not available, invoice pricing for that quarter. Instead, consistent with the approach adopted for separately payable Part B drugs in § 414.904(i), we would base the TDAPA payment amount on the most recent prior calendar quarter, with positive ASP data, which we consider the most recent available ASP for purposes of section 1847A of the Act. We proposed to apply a similar modification to the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment methodology. Specifically, when the most recent full calendar quarter of ASP data reflects negative or zero sales, and CMS has received positive ASP data for the product in a prior calendar quarter, we would not base the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment on WAC, or invoice pricing. Instead, we would base the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment on the most recent prior calendar quarter with positive ASP data.
We explained that, as under current policy, in circumstances where a manufacturer submits ASP data reflecting zero or negative sales, CMS considers the manufacturer to have satisfied its ASP reporting obligation, and such submissions do not trigger the discontinuation of the TDAPA under § 413.234(c). However, if a manufacturer ceases submitting ASP data, and CMS determines that the latest full calendar quarter of ASP data is not available, CMS will discontinue the TDAPA for the product within 2 calendar quarters, consistent with § 413.234(c). For purposes of the TDAPA and post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment, zero or negative ASP data are treated as not usable for purposes of determining the payment amount but are treated as submitted for purposes of the ASP reporting requirement.
We stated that we believe the proposed approach is consistent with section 1847A of the Act because it relies on the most recent available positive ASP data when current quarter ASP data is not usable for purposes of determining a payment amount. We further believe the proposed policy would improve payment accuracy and consistency across Medicare payment systems by avoiding reliance on WAC or invoice pricing when more representative ASP data are available. This is appropriate for the ESRD PPS as it aligns payment with resource use and promotes efficiency, consistent with the principles of the ESRD PPS.
We proposed modifications to § 413.234(c) and (g)(1) to effectuate this change by amending language to state that when the most recently available quarter of ASP data is not usable because it is zero or negative, we would instead use the most recently available quarter of positive ASP data, and that we would only resort to WAC or invoice pricing if a prior quarter of positive ASP data is not available.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter supported the proposed technical modifications to ASP pricing. Another commenter supported the technical modifications provided CMS confirms their understanding that the policy would apply for products that have previously reported usable ASP data and have a subsequent quarter where ASP is reported as zero or negative, and in this circumstance, CMS would use the most recently available usable quarter of ASP data as the basis for the adjustments. They requested we differentiate between a product that has previously reported ASP and subsequently reports an unusable ASP and a product which has not yet established ASP.
Response:
We appreciate the support for the proposed technical modifications to the ASP pricing policy. The commenter's interpretation is correct. This policy only applies if there is a prior quarter for which the drug has a reported ASP data which could be used for the calculation. If a drug has not yet reported ASP data, for example if it is in its first two quarters of the TDAPA period, we would still base payment on WAC, or invoice pricing if WAC is not available. The intent of this policy is to ensure that the TDAPA and post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment are based on the best available pricing data, which we believe is ASP, unless ASP reflects zero or negative sales. The intent of this policy is not to make any changes to payment before ASP is established or modify the conditional ASP policy in a way that changes what renal dialysis drugs or biological products would be available for an adjustment in a given quarter. We appreciate the commenter's support for this technical pricing change.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our policy to use older ASP data, when available, rather than WAC or invoice pricing when the most recent quarter of ASP data is not usable due to zero or negative ASP.

We received comments from a small regional dialysis chain, an LDO, and an advocacy group regarding the proposed revisions to payment for renal dialysis services furnished to Medicare beneficiaries with AKI. Commenters generally agreed that increasing the payment rate for renal dialysis services furnished to individuals with AKI to $299.55 and extending the home dialysis and self-dialysis training (the training add-on) payment adjustments to beneficiaries with AKI is appropriate. Commenters did not oppose the proposed changes to the payment for AKI but did request clarification of some points. We summarize these comments and provide our responses in the following section.
Comment:
Several comments supported the application of the proposed ESRD PPS base rate of $299.55 to payment for renal dialysis services furnished to beneficiaries with AKI. A commenter specifically noted the vulnerability of the AKI patient population and highlighted the importance of adequate payment for renal dialysis services for beneficiaries with AKI.
Response:
We appreciate the support for our longstanding policy to apply the ESRD PPS base rate for payments for renal dialysis services furnished to beneficiaries with AKI, which represents a payment increase for CY 2027. We agree that adequate payment for AKI dialysis is important and believe that the final AKI dialysis payment rate for CY 2027 will help continue to support high-quality care for beneficiaries with AKI. We note that the final ESRD PPS base rate is $297.52.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS to clarify how the phosphate binders and other bundled renal dialysis drugs should be provided and paid for in AKI patient care. The commenter stated that since the AKI dialysis payment rate is tied to the ESRD PPS rate, ESRD facilities need guidance on their responsibilities regarding bundled renal dialysis drugs and services and whether the payment method covers associated costs. Specifically, the commenter requested that CMS confirm in the final rule that ESRD facilities must provide phosphate binders to outpatient dialysis patients with AKI starting CY 2027. Further, the commenter stated that guidance should clarify that this responsibility applies only during outpatient renal dialysis services and not to AKI patients who are hospitalized, have not started outpatient dialysis, or have discontinued dialysis. The commenter noted that these distinctions will help define ESRD facility responsibilities for clinically complex AKI patients. Additionally, this commenter asked CMS to review the outpatient AKI benefit to ensure payment supports proper dialysis care and focuses on kidney recovery.
Response:
The AKI dialysis payment rate applies to all renal dialysis services, and ESRD facilities are responsible for furnishing all medically necessary renal dialysis services to beneficiaries with AKI who are receiving renal dialysis services as specified at § 413.374(a). While oral-only renal dialysis drugs and biological products have always met the definition of renal dialysis services, the statutory delays implemented in our regulations at § 413.174(f)(6) postponed their inclusion in the ESRD PPS bundled payment until January 1, 2025. During the TDAPA payment period for phosphate binders, the TDAPA did not apply to renal dialysis services furnished to beneficiaries with AKI and ESRD facilities were not yet responsible for furnishing them for beneficiaries with AKI (
89 FR 89172
). This is because phosphate binders were not originally included in the ESRD PPS base rate, and therefore were not reflected in the AKI dialysis payment rate that is based on the ESRD PPS base rate. As a result, during the TDAPA period, the AKI dialysis payment rate did not include any amount for phosphate binders, so ESRD facilities had no payment mechanism through which to furnish them to beneficiaries with AKI. Once the payment amount for phosphate binders is established and incorporated directly into the ESRD PPS base rate, that payment is applied for beneficiaries with AKI. Accordingly, the policies finalized in this rule to incorporate the costs of phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate mean that ESRD facilities must furnish phosphate binders to beneficiaries with AKI. The requirement that ESRD facilities furnish all renal dialysis services to beneficiaries with AKI has not changed.
Starting in CY 2027, ESRD facilities must provide medically necessary phosphate binders to beneficiaries with AKI receiving renal dialysis services. Section 1834(r) of the Act only addresses renal dialysis services (as defined in subparagraph (B) of section 1881(b)(14) of the Act) furnished to a beneficiary with AKI by a renal dialysis facility or provider of services. We do not believe that a renal dialysis facility or provider of services would provide renal dialysis services for AKI patients who are hospitalized, have not started outpatient renal dialysis, or have discontinued renal dialysis services including phosphate binders.
In the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule we included a discussion clarifying how the inclusion of oral-only drugs into the ESRD PPS bundled payment impacted MA plans (
89 FR 89152
). Now that payment is available under part B for furnishing phosphate binders for beneficiaries with AKI, we believe a similar clarification may be helpful to readers. With respect to MA, per section 1852(a)(1) of the Act and its implementation regulations (
42 CFR 422.100
and
422.101(a)
), Medicare Advantage organizations (MAOs) must cover items and services, including drugs, for which benefits are available under Parts A and B in the Original Medicare program, subject to limited exclusions. We note that phosphate binders are not subject to the limited exclusions at section 1852(a)(1) of the Act and, therefore, must be covered by MAOs. Specifically, in accordance with section 1852(a)(1) if the Act and
42 CFR 422.100
and
422.101(a)
, MAOs must provide coverage of, by furnishing, arranging for, or making payment for, generally all services that are covered by Part A and Part B of Medicare and that are available to beneficiaries residing in the plan's service area. Services may be provided outside of the service area of the plan if the services are accessible and available to enrollees. In addition, with respect to coverage of Original Medicare benefits such as Part B drugs, MAOs must comply with applicable Medicare statutes, regulations, national coverage determinations (NCDs) and local coverage determinations (LCDs) of Medicare contractors with jurisdiction for claims in the geographic area in which services are covered under the MA plan (
42 CFR 422.101(b)
). In general, an MA plan that offers Part D benefits (MA-PD) must determine whether payment for the drug is allocated under Parts B or D, consistent with Original Medicare and Part D program drug coverage policies (see Appendix C, Attachment II, Question 5 of Chapter 6
[
43
]
Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Manual for additional detail). Concerning how Part D sponsors will determine whether a drug is covered under Part B, in most cases Part B drug coverage should not impact payment decisions by Part D sponsors since Part B coverage is generally in a provider setting or physician's office rather than for drugs dispensed at a pharmacy. A Part D sponsor cannot deny payment for a particular drug on
(
printed page 68815)
the basis that it is covered under Part B in some instances and Part D in others unless there is Part B coverage as the drug is prescribed and dispensed or administered in that particular instance. The fact that a claim is received for a drug that is sometimes covered by Part B is not a basis for denial since the Part D sponsor would have to determine whether the drug is being prescribed and dispensed or administered on the basis under which Part B coverage is available. This will generally involve interaction between the Part D sponsor and the Medicare Part B contractor with jurisdiction in that geographic area for that drug. Regarding new drugs, as decisions are made nationally or by individual A/B MAC contractors, this information will be available on the CMS and contractor websites. MA-PD coordinated care plans must coordinate all benefits administered by the plan with respect to drugs for which payment as so prescribed and dispensed or administered to an individual may be available under Part A or Part B, or under Part D (
42 CFR 422.112(b)(7)
). As a result of the rules and regulations described here, MAOs must cover oral-only ESRD drugs, including phosphate binders, under their plans for beneficiaries with AKI receiving outpatient renal dialysis services, as these are drugs under Part B and are not subject to the limited exclusions under section 1852(a)(1) of the Act.
Regarding the commenter's suggestion on renal function recovery monitoring, because the ESRD facility Conditions for Coverage (CfCs) apply uniformly across the certified facility's patient population, the same monitoring expectations apply to AKI patients. In addition, any individualized needs specific to a patient's AKI status should be identified through the required patient assessment and reflected in that patient's individualized plan of care, consistent with existing CfC requirements. Facilities should also address these AKI-specific considerations in their facility policies and procedures to ensure staff consistently apply appropriate safeguards for this patient population in accordance with national standards of care.
We will continue to consider comments on dialysis adequacy and kidney recovery and may potentially address these concerns in future rulemaking.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS ensure AKI patients using home dialysis receive the same safety protections as ESRD beneficiaries, including comprehensive training and access to in-center back-up care. The commenter stated that sending patients to the hospital or requiring them to find another provider is not acceptable as back-up.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations regarding patient safety protections for individuals with AKI receiving dialysis in the home. We agree that appropriate patient training, access to necessary support, and monitoring for renal function recovery are important components of furnishing renal dialysis services to patients with AKI. We also agree that sending an AKI home dialysis patient to the hospital or emergency room or discharging the patient and requiring them to find a new ESRD facility or health care provider, does not satisfy the facility's obligation to provide back-up renal dialysis support services. The ESRD Facility CfCs at
42 CFR part 494
apply equally to all patients treated in a Medicare-certified ESRD facility, regardless of whether the patient's underlying diagnosis is ESRD or AKI. Because AKI patients receiving renal dialysis in a Medicare-certified facility are treated under that same facility's conditions for coverage, the existing home dialysis requirements, including comprehensive training on the home modality, and access to back-up renal dialysis support services already apply equally to AKI patients using home modalities. The CfCs do not distinguish between ESRD and AKI patients with respect to these protections; a Medicare certified facility must furnish the same standard of care, training, and support structures to any patient it treats, including AKI patients dialyzing at home.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of public comments, CMS is finalizing the CY 2027 AKI dialysis payment rate of $297.52, which is equal to the CY 2027 ESRD PPS base rate.

Under section 1834(r)(1) of the Act and regulations at § 413.372, the amount of payment for AKI dialysis services is the base rate for renal dialysis services determined for a year under section 1881(b)(14) of the Act (updated by the ESRDB market basket percentage increase and reduced by the productivity adjustment), as adjusted by any applicable geographic adjustment factor applied under section 1881(b)(14)(D)(iv)(II) of the Act. through
89167

b. Adoption of the Hyperphosphatemia Clinical Measure
(1) Measure Overview
The Hyperphosphatemia clinical measure is an outcome measure developed by CMS to assess long-term phosphorus control across the dialysis population by measuring the percentage of adult dialysis patients with a 6-month rolling average serum phosphorus value greater than or equal to 6.5 mg/dL.
[
56
]
The cohort for the Hyperphosphatemia clinical measure will consist of adult patients, aged 18 years and older, with ESRD who are receiving in-center hemodialysis, home hemodialysis, hemodiafiltration, or peritoneal dialysis and have been under the care of the same dialysis facility for the entire reporting month. Eligible patients must have had ESRD for more than 90 days and sufficient laboratory data to calculate a 6-month rolling average serum phosphorus level.
[
57
]
For more information about the testing, feasibility, scientific acceptability, meaningfulness, and validity of the Hyperphosphatemia clinical measure, we refer readers to
https://p4qm.org/​prmr-measures/​muc2025-064
.
(
printed page 68819)
(2) Measure Calculation
The numerator of this measure includes patient reporting months with a 6-month rolling average phosphorus value of 6.5 mg/dL or greater. The number of patient reporting months with a phosphorus average of 6.5 mg/dL or greater will then be divided by the total number of eligible patient reporting months for the facility and multiplied by 100 to calculate the percentage of patient reporting months with hyperphosphatemia. Patient reporting months will be excluded if the patient had a 6-month rolling average albumin level of less than 3.5 g/dL or a body mass index (BMI) of less than 18.5. The measure will be calculated only for facilities with more than 10 eligible patients during the reporting period.

3. Update to the National Healthcare Safety Network Bloodstream Infection in Hemodialysis Patients Clinical Measure
In the CY 2014 ESRD PPS final rule, we adopted the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Bloodstream Infection (BSI) in Hemodialysis Patients (hereafter referred to as the NHSN BSI) clinical measure into the ESRD QIP to assess BSIs among patients receiving hemodialysis at outpatient hemodialysis centers (
78 FR 72204
through
72207
). The NHSN BSI clinical measure is based on infection surveillance data reported by facilities to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) through the NHSN Dialysis Event surveillance system.
[
78
]
The current measure uses a standardized infection ratio (SIR), which compares the number of observed BSIs to the number of predicted BSIs among facilities. The predicted number of BSIs represents the number expected if a facility had a BSI rate equal to the national rate derived from 2014 NHSN surveillance data. The predicted number is estimated using pooled national BSI rates by patient access type, which are multiplied by facility-level patient-months for each access type.
[
79
]
We proposed to update the baseline and risk adjustment used to calculate the SIR for the NHSN BSI clinical measure beginning with PY 2029 to ensure that national benchmarks better reflect current healthcare practices, surveillance protocols, and infection prevention efforts. To estimate the expected number of BSIs, we proposed to update the national baseline from 2014 data to 2023 data and revise the risk adjustment model to incorporate additional patient and facility-level characteristics, including vascular access type, facility hospital affiliation, and number of dialysis stations, which were identified as significant predictors of BSI risk among the data reported to NHSN.
[
80
]
Additionally, these factors may reflect differences that are not fully within a facility's direct control. The predicted number of BSIs will be estimated using a regression model developed from the 2023 national baseline data. This model uses parameter estimates associated with the identified risk factors to calculate predicted BSIs for each facility-access type combination and then multiplies these estimates by facility patient-months to determine the predicted number of BSIs. Additionally, this updated risk adjustment model will better account for differences in facility characteristics associated with BSI risk. The proposed 2023 national baseline updates will not change the underlying SIR calculation formula but will instead be used to calculate revised denominators for the SIR by estimating the number of predicted BSIs for a given facility based on the 2023 national baseline data.
[
81
]
The proposed 2023 national baseline updates will allow facilities to compare their performance to more recent national data, improve the accuracy of benchmark comparisons, and serve as a new national reference point for measuring progress in BSI prevention. Because the updated 2023 national baseline reflects more recent national data, facilities may observe changes in their SIR values compared to their SIR values calculated using the 2014 national baseline. These changes may reflect differences in national baseline rates rather than changes in facility performance. The number of predicted infections may increase or decrease depending on multiple factors, including vascular access type, location, and number of stations in a facility. 4. Removal of Two Measures From the ESRD QIP Measure Set
We have undertaken efforts to review the existing ESRD QIP measure set to ensure continued clinical impact and effectiveness of the measures on facility performance. Based on that analysis and our evaluation of the ESRD QIP measure set, we proposed to remove the Medication Reconciliation reporting measure and the COVID-19 Vaccination Coverage Among Healthcare Personnel reporting measure, beginning with PY 2029.
a. Removal of the Medication Reconciliation Reporting Measure
To ensure continued impact and effectiveness of our measure set on facility performance, we proposed to remove the Medication Reconciliation (MedRec) reporting measure beginning with PY 2029. When we first adopted the MedRec reporting measure in the CY 2019 ESRD PPS final rule (
83 FR 57008
through
57010
), we stated that inclusion of the measure in the ESRD QIP measure set would align with national goals for patient safety and the reduction of harm caused by care delivery. The MedRec reporting measure assesses whether a facility has appropriately evaluated a patient's medications, an important safety concern for the ESRD patient population because those patients typically see multiple providers and may require numerous medications.
Our proposal to remove the MedRec reporting measure is consistent with evolving the ESRD QIP to focus on a measure set of high-value, impactful measures that have been developed to drive care improvements for a broader set of ESRD patients. As such, we proposed to remove this measure from the ESRD QIP measure set under measure removal factor 8, the costs associated with the measure outweigh the benefit of its continued use in the program (§ 413.178(c)(5)(i)(H)).
Although recent annual measure analyses have indicated that the MedRec reporting measure may not be fully topped out based on the statistical criteria that we adopted in the CY 2015 ESRD PPS final rule (
79 FR 66171
through
66174
), available data show consistently high performance and limited variation across facilities. For example, the mean MedRec reporting measure performance in CY 2024 was 97.3 percent and the median MedRec reporting measure score was 10 points, which indicates more than 50 percent of providers achieved perfect scores for the measure. These results suggest that the programmatic benefit of retaining the measure is limited.
One of the goals of the ESRD QIP is to advance the program in the least burdensome manner possible, while maintaining a parsimonious set of the most meaningful quality measures and continuing to incentivize improvement in the quality of care provided to patients. Our priority is a continued focus on measurable clinical outcomes to incentivize the improvement of dialysis care quality and health outcomes for all patients through measurement and transparency. In light of consistently high performance on the MedRec reporting measure, leaving limited opportunity for further distinctions or improvements in facility performance, and the burden facilities incur in collecting, documenting, and reporting data for the measure, the costs associated with the measure outweigh the benefit of its continued use in the ESRD QIP. Our proposal to remove the MedRec reporting measure from the ESRD QIP is consistent with these priorities.
