I. Executive Summary
The Secretary of Education recognizes accrediting agencies under existing regulations at
34 CFR part 602
to ensure that agencies are reliable authorities regarding the quality of education or training offered by the institutions or programs they accredit for the purposes of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended (HEA), or for other Federal purposes. Recognized institutional accrediting agencies serve as key gatekeepers in determining which institutions may participate in the Federal student aid programs, which currently provide more than $100 billion in Pell Grants and Federal student loans annually. To ensure that the Department only recognizes those accrediting agencies focused on high-quality, valuable education for students, we are realigning the regulations for recognition of accrediting agencies to have a greater focus on student achievement and ensure programs provide a high-quality, high-value education.
The final rule removes unnecessary requirements on agencies and the institutions or programs they accredit. These regulations eliminate requirements not required by statute, including the “two-year rule” for initial recognition of agencies, prescriptive site visit mandates, unnecessary documentation requirements, and rigid, overly long processing and procedural timelines.
These commonsense regulations also address the barriers that limit institutions from adopting practices that advance credential and degree completion and spur new models of education. They also remove existing regulatory barriers impeding institutions' ability to change accrediting agencies or work with more than one accrediting agency, while agencies will have more flexibility to apply certain standards that meet the needs of their accredited institutions and programs.
The final rule also introduces a new review framework for better oversight of key institutional accrediting agencies that serve as the primary gatekeepers for the Federal student aid programs, and whose potential failures pose the greatest risk to taxpayers.
Additionally, to reduce administrative costs that are negatively impacting college affordability, the final rule requires recognized accrediting agencies to apply their standards in ways that minimize institutional administrative burden, avoid duplicative reporting, and support the implementation of lower-cost, higher-value educational models. These changes also will shift the focus of institutions toward more cost-effective practices for staffing, facilities, student services, and program design.
The final rule promotes greater integrity in decision making by recognized accrediting agencies and eliminates previous regulatory exceptions that pose potential conflicts of interest. The final rule also eliminates geographic-scope distinctions for institutional accrediting agencies and makes other anticompetitive behavior a negative factor in consideration of agency recognition.
The final rule reinforces the existing legal, constitutional, civil rights, and consumer protection obligations already required of recognized accrediting agencies and the institutions and programs that they accredit. For example, under the final rule, accrediting agencies recognized by the Secretary must ensure that the institutions and programs they accredit have and apply policies consistent with all Federal and State laws and respond appropriately to findings of noncompliance by competent authorities. The final rule also prevents recognized accrediting agencies from applying standards that direct accredited institutions and programs to violate such laws. New student outcome and program-level performance expectations for the applications of agency standards will focus both accrediting agencies and institutions on important objective measures of student and institution performance such as course completion, licensure pass rates, and economic returns.
Further, the final rule addresses the persistent and costly issues with transfer of credit policies that have burdened students. These regulations reduce the likelihood that students will be required to undertake duplicative coursework and incur additional tuition charges that are not necessary. Although institutions will continue to have latitude to deny transfer of credit based on the credit failing to meet the receiving institutions' standards, institutions will have to explain those standards and provide written reasoning to the student for such denial. These regulations also require greater transparency before a student decides to transfer to another institution, so he or
(
printed page 68627)
she can have a full understanding of the scope and cost of transferring to that institution.
Taken together, this student-oriented final rule realigns the Secretary's recognition of accrediting agencies with a high-quality, high-value education that is free from unlawful discrimination and other violations of Federal law.
1. Summary of Major Provisions
These final regulations:
Amend § 600.11 to make it less burdensome for institutions that are changing accrediting agencies or wish to utilize more than one accrediting agency.
Amend § 602.2 to require the Department to provide public notice on its accreditation website if the Secretary denies continued recognition to a previously recognized agency, or if the Secretary limits, suspends, or terminates the agency's recognition before the end of its recognition period.
Amend § 602.3 to define and use the term “institution” in these regulations instead of “institution of higher education” which is defined in the HEA, and elsewhere in the Department's regulations, referring to a narrower subset of institutions, and to add a definition for “related, associated, or affiliated trade association.”
Amend § 602.10 to clarify that the Secretary's recognition extends only to those accrediting agencies whose institutions or programs actively participate in a Federal program.
Amend § 602.11 to require accrediting agencies to clearly describe the scope of their accrediting activities and remove geographic restrictions that restrict institutions and programs from choosing an accrediting agency.
Amend § 602.12 to remove references to geographic areas and geographic constraints and require review of contractions of scope. Additionally, amend the regulations to clarify the policies and capacity an accrediting agency must have to seek initial recognition, and eliminates the “two-year rule” for initial recognition.
Unreserve and amend § 602.13 to specify that an accrediting agency's recognition by the Department does not provide any immunity from antitrust laws.
Amend § 602.14 to strengthen the fiscal and administrative criteria an accrediting agency must meet to prove it is fully separate and independent from any related, associated, or affiliated trade or membership organization.
Amend § 602.15 to require accrediting agencies to administer their standards, policies, and procedures in a manner that minimizes unnecessary compliance costs and administrative burdens on accredited institutions, as well as require agencies to maintain appropriate conflict of interest controls and policies.
Amend § 602.16 to codify that an agency may establish additional lawful accreditation standards that are consistent with ensuring institutional or programmatic quality and integrity as it deems appropriate.
Amend § 602.17 to clarify expectations for reviewing student achievement and faculty related policies, including academic freedom and intellectual diversity. Additionally, add new requirements regarding institutional cost-benefit analyses, institutional flexibility and mission, program length review, and safeguards against misrepresentation.
Amend § 602.18 to require that accrediting agency decisions be neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology, except for agencies with a religious mission.
Amend § 602.20 to provide guidance to accrediting agencies on how to structure their arbitration procedures and remove overly prescriptive requirements.
Amend § 602.21 to remove overly prescriptive review requirements.
Amend § 602.22 to refine the list of changes requiring agency approval, add prison education programs as a defined substantive change, and remove outdated and overly prescriptive requirements.
Amend § 602.23 to require accrediting agencies to ensure institutions comply with all applicable Federal and State laws and remove overly prescriptive requirements.
Amend § 602.24 to strengthen accrediting agencies' oversight of institutional changes, expand requirements for teach-out planning, including transcript access, and increase transparency and support for students when institutions face disruptions.
Amend § 602.24 to establish clearer, fairer rules for credit transfer by defining consistent criteria, prohibiting discriminatory denials, requiring acceptance of comparable credits, and providing students with an appeals process.
Amend § 602.25 to remove overly prescriptive requirements for demonstrating due process.
Amend § 602.26 to update and modernize the required content of agency notices and better align these requirements with contemporary methods of disclosure and allow temporary continuation of eligibility for title IV, HEA funds for institutions to exhaust all due process options.
Amend § 602.27 to require agencies to update the Department's website on a regular, timely basis to display the current accreditation status of all institutions and programs.
Amend § 602.28 to broaden the circumstances under which an accrediting agency must re-evaluate an institution or program following negative actions by other authorities.
Amend § 602.30 to modernize how accrediting agencies submit applications and reports to the Department.
Amend § 602.32 and split into two sections: § 602.31 and § 602.32.
Amend § 602.31 to modernize and streamline the procedures accrediting agencies must follow when submitting applications for initial or renewed recognition.
Amend § 602.32 to modernize and clarify the processes used to review an accrediting agency's expansion or contraction of scope, compliance report, and increase in headcount enrollment.
Amend § 602.33 to modernize and streamline the procedures for review of agencies during the period of recognition, including the review of monitoring reports.
Amend § 602.34 to require the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI or Advisory Committee) to review applications for contractions of scope, and for accrediting agencies to post public notice of upcoming NACIQI reviews.
Amend §§ 602.35, 602.36, and 602.37 to update cross references.
Amend § 668.43 to require transfer of credit disclosures and direct applicable written notices to students.
2. Summary of Costs and Benefits
As further detailed in the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA), the final rule includes numerous provisions that may impact students, institutions, accrediting agencies, and the Federal government. Specifically, the final rule includes provisions related to transfer of credit policies, which may benefit students by making it easier for students to transfer credits to continue their postsecondary enrollment at a new institution. Students will likely benefit from these changes by spending less time and money retaking courses that failed to transfer, whereas institutions may experience costs due to the suspected foregone tuition revenue from transfer students.
The final rule also encourages accrediting agencies to include new criteria that evaluate program and institutional outcomes. This may
(
printed page 68628)
impose new costs on accrediting agencies, which may need to develop such criteria, and on institutions, which may need to implement changes to meet such criteria. Furthermore, the final rule will remove several barriers for new accrediting agencies to emerge and obtain Department recognition, which may ultimately benefit accrediting agencies through the reduction in administrative burden to gain initial recognition and maintain recognition. Additionally, the final rule would also require accrediting agencies to adopt several new policies and procedures that aim to increase college affordability and innovation, while also putting downward pressure on credential inflation. Students may benefit from these provisions if the changes result in more affordable and flexible educational opportunities.
As noted in the RIA, the Department does not estimate a significant net budget impact on the title IV, HEA Federal student aid programs from the final rule. In prior regulations
[
1
]
the Department estimated the accreditation reform would result in an increased number of applications for recognition due to easier recognition of new accrediting agencies. Increased petitions are also expected given an expanded scope to new credential levels, and the option for alternative standards to allow for faster introduction of innovative programs. In 2019, we did not estimate a significant change in repayment performance as institutions with less favorable program outcomes could find more lenient accrediting agencies. Institutions with strong programs can take advantage of the flexibility allowed by the substantive change policy revisions to expand their program offerings. At the time we noted the uncertainty of the extent to which increasing accreditation options and encouraging program innovation would shift Federal loan and grant volumes among more options for students versus generating new volume, and that uncertainty remains. Additionally, greater acceptance of transfer credits may increase Federal grant and loan volumes by encouraging some students to complete degrees but also may reduce volumes by credits being recognized by the institutions receiving transfers. In retrospect, we know the number of institutions that changed agencies was fairly low and it is difficult to attribute particular changes in volume to accreditation reforms given other economic, demographic, and programmatic developments during the same period.
II. Purpose of This Regulatory Action
In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14279, this regulatory action realigns the Secretary's criteria for recognition of accrediting agencies to promote high-quality, high value, and affordable education for students that—
Promotes such academic programs and activities at higher education institutions that are focused on student outcomes and are free from unlawful discrimination and other violations of Federal law;
Reduces barriers that limit competition, innovation, and new education models that advance credential and degree completion;
Holds institutions accountable for discrimination and other unlawful acts; and
Advances academic freedom, intellectual inquiry, and student learning by ensuring that accreditation requires that institutions support and prioritize intellectual diversity among faculty.
III. Background
Section 496 of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended (HEA), requires the Secretary of Education (Secretary) to establish criteria for determining whether an accrediting agency is a reliable authority, for purposes of participation in programs authorized under the HEA and other Federal programs, on the quality of education or training offered by the institutions and programs that they accredit. Such criteria are required to include appropriate measures of student achievement.
Consistent with the statute, the Secretary has established regulations for recognition of accrediting agencies at
34 CFR part 602
and has revised these regulations periodically.
E.O. 14279
, titled “Reforming Accreditation to Strengthen Higher Education,” issued on April 23, 2025, by President Trump, directs the Secretary to take several actions related to the recognition of accrediting agencies or associations by the Department. Some of these actions require changes to existing regulations.
These regulatory changes realign the Secretary's criteria for recognition of accrediting agencies to promote high-quality, high value, and affordable education for students that—
Promotes such academic programs and activities at higher education institutions that are focused on student outcomes and are free from unlawful discrimination and other violations of Federal law;
Reduces barriers that limit competition, innovation, and new education models that advance credential and degree completion;
Holds institutions accountable for discrimination and other unlawful acts; and
Advances academic freedom, intellectual inquiry, and student learning by ensuring that accrediting agencies review institutional policies in these areas.
Specifically, the Executive Order directs the Secretary to—
Resume recognition of new accrediting agencies to foster competition and expand institutional options; and
Mandate that accrediting agencies require member institutions to use data on program-level student outcomes to improve such outcomes, without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex.
The Department undertook this rulemaking in part to address the goals contained within the Executive Order, but also to propose substantive changes that would reform the static and outdated higher education accountability system. The final rule is intended to increase competition among accrediting agencies by reducing barriers to entry, facilitating institutional mobility among recognized agencies, and reducing regulatory requirements that may unnecessarily discourage the formation of innovative accrediting organizations and other related practices. Increased competition is expected to improve institutional responsiveness, reduce accreditation costs over time, and encourage greater innovation in the market for quality assurance validation.
Increasing competition among recognized accrediting agencies is likely to improve the quality, responsiveness, and effectiveness of accreditation. Accreditation has historically seen very little competition because it evolved from voluntary membership peer review groups to set uniform academic standards within those groups. Institutional accrediting agencies rarely engage in head-to-head competition; institutions face difficulty in changing accrediting agencies due to high switching costs and potential risks in maintaining eligibility for Federal student aid for their students; and there are regulatory barriers to the recognition of new agencies. During negotiated rulemaking, the Department explained
(
printed page 68629)
that competition among accrediting agencies is expected to generally improve quality and expand choices for institutions.
Competition creates incentives for agencies to innovate, respond to workforce changes, expand choices for institutions among agencies engaged in various types of innovative activities, and to develop new measures for assessing student success by institutions.
As explained by a Department economist during negotiated rulemaking, there is a high concentration of institutions that are accredited by a handful of institutional accrediting agencies. The Department recognizes that empirical evidence measuring the causal effect of institutions changing accrediting agencies is limited. Because institutions have historically rarely switched agencies, and those that do may differ systematically from those that do not, it is difficult to isolate the independent effect of changing agencies on institutional outcomes. Moreover, previous regulatory barriers have resulted in too few agency switches to permit rigorous statistical analysis. The absence of such evidence, however, does not undermine the broader economic evidence concerning the benefits of competition in quality assurance markets.
Economic research has consistently found that competition encourages innovation and improved performance. Joseph Schumpeter argued that competition produces “creative destruction” that drives innovation by creating new markets that render older ones obsolete, and more recent empirical work has found that introducing competition into concentrated markets substantially increases innovation. The Department believes these findings are relevant because higher education accreditation has historically exhibited many characteristics of an uncompetitive market.
Competition is also expected to improve the informational value of accreditation. During negotiated rulemaking, the Department explained that institutions seek credible signals of educational quality, and that in a competitive accreditation market, agencies would compete to provide those signals. Rather than offering only a binary “approved/not approved” determination, competing accrediting agencies may distinguish themselves by offering scaled ratings for institutional quality. On April 14, 2026, during opening remarks for negotiated rulemaking, the Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education stated:
“Competition will include competition for relevance and universities will signal their quality level through accreditation . . . Current accrediting agencies give universities and colleges pass-fail grades which provide very little useful information.”
[
2
]
This concern was further underscored in a recent decision letter from the Senior Department Official (SDO) to an accrediting agency, which cautioned that accreditation can devolve into a bureaucratic, “check-the-box” exercise in which meaningful, substantive feedback is replaced by a binary determination of compliance.
[
3
]
The official emphasized that accreditation should serve as a process that not only assesses compliance with minimum standards but also identifies opportunities for institutions and programs to strengthen their operations and improve educational quality.
This reasoning is consistent with the economic literature on certification intermediaries. In “Information Revelation and Certification Intermediaries”, Alessandro Lizzeri
[
4
]
demonstrates that monopolistic certifiers have incentives to reveal only limited information, whereas competition among certifiers results in more informative quality signals. Similarly, in “The Effect of Information on Product Quality: Evidence from Restaurant Hygiene Grade Cards” Giner Zhe Jin and Phillip Leslie
[4]
found that more detailed quality information improves quality outcomes.
A recent paper provides additional support for the Department's efforts to promote competition among accrediting agencies. Hatfield and Lowery
[
5
]
develop a theoretical model of certification markets, with particular attention to higher education accreditation. They find that monopoly accrediting agencies have incentives to establish inefficiently low-quality standards and impose institutional requirements unrelated to educational quality. Competition can raise quality standards and reduce such requirements. The authors further demonstrate that entry by an accrediting agency with preferences different from those of incumbent agencies can produce substantially greater improvements in quality and reductions in bias than entry by an otherwise similar agency.
These findings support the Department's efforts to reduce barriers to entry, facilitate institutions' ability to change accrediting agencies, and encourage competition among agencies with different approaches to evaluating educational quality. Although the study is theoretical, it provides an economic basis for concluding that greater competition can improve accreditation's effectiveness in protecting students and taxpayers while preserving institutional autonomy and encouraging innovation.
[
6
]
Competition can also strengthen, rather than weaken, quality of institutions and programs. During negotiated rulemaking, the Department explained that in instances where only one recognized accrediting agency effectively serves a sector, the withdrawal of recognition may significantly disrupt institutions and students, making it more difficult to impose such a penalty. By contrast, when multiple recognized agencies are available, institutions have viable alternatives, reducing barriers to enforcement. As the Department stated during negotiated rulemaking:
“With regional and programmatic monopolies, withdrawal of recognition can throw industries into chaos . . .” If the accreditation market is competitive, institutions can more easily switch accrediting agencies, which reduces incentives to continue the recognition of an agency out of fear of potential adverse fallout in the market.” While some hesitation to withdraw recognition may always be present, the Department believes that the more alternative accrediting agencies are available, the less hesitant the Department will be to derecognize agencies out of worry over market disruption.
[
7
]
The Department believes competition will increase accountability both for institutions and for accrediting agencies themselves.
Finally, competition will encourage innovation in accreditation. Accrediting agencies that face meaningful competition will have stronger
(
printed page 68630)
incentives to develop new approaches to quality assurance, reduce unnecessary costs, respond to institutional diversity, and improve services to institutions and students. As explained in the Department's written responses during negotiated rulemaking, barriers to switching generally reduce competition and increase market power through a lock-in effect. Eliminating or reducing those barriers promotes innovation and responsiveness.
For these reasons, the Department finds that reducing unnecessary barriers to competition among qualified accrediting agencies is likely to improve accreditation over time while preserving the Department's responsibility to establish minimum standards for Federal recognition. The Department does not believe competition will cause a “race to the bottom” but rather, the opposite will likely occur. Recognized accrediting agencies must continue to satisfy all statutory and regulatory recognition requirements, while competing to provide higher quality services, with more informative and innovative quality assurance services. As the Assistant Secretary stated during negotiated rulemaking, “We shouldn't fear healthy competition. It is the basis of a free market economy, and we need more of it in the coddled, protected business of higher education.”
[

IV. Implementation Date of These Regulations
Generally, the regulations included in this document are effective on July 1, 2027. Section 482(c) of the HEA requires that the Department publish final regulations affecting programs under title IV of the HEA in final form by November 1 to be effective for the next award year (July 1 of the calendar year following November 1).
However, the process for recognition of accrediting agencies is multi-year and the implementation of the changes to these regulations in the recognition process will require planning and coordination between Department staff and agencies who are seeking initial recognition or renewal of existing recognition prior to the July 1, 2027, effective date.
The Department is providing the following additional clarification of the implementation timeline:
For recognized agencies that submitted their applications for renewal of recognition prior to July 1, 2026, Department staff have been reviewing the applications under the regulations that were in place prior to the promulgation of these regulations. The agencies will have an opportunity to respond to the draft staff report when completed. After receiving a response from the agency on the draft staff report, the Department will present its final staff report on each application to the Advisory Committee at the 2027 meetings and proposed first meeting of 2028, which will be based on compliance with the regulations that were in effect prior to the promulgation of these regulations.
For agencies seeking initial recognition that submitted their application for recognition after July 1, 2026, those agencies must submit applications for review based on adherence to the requirements in these revised regulations.
Additionally, Section 482(c)(2) permits the Secretary to designate any regulatory provision as one that an entity subject to the regulations may choose to implement earlier and the conditions for early implementation. To facilitate the implementation of these final regulations, the Secretary is designating all sections of this regulation for early implementation beginning on January 1, 2027, provided that accrediting agencies that decide to adopt any new provisions prior to July 1, 2027, do not impose new requirements on institutions or programs resulting from that early implementation that would take effect prior to July 1, 2027.
Because compliance with these regulations may require accrediting agencies to make substantive revisions to their policies and procedures, which may necessitate stakeholder notice and comment periods and formal adoption by an authorized decision-making body, as well as training for agency staff and peer reviewers responsible for implementing the new requirements, accrediting agencies are strongly encouraged to initiate the necessary revisions and training promptly to ensure compliance with the new requirements by the applicable effective dates set forth herein.
V. Authority for the Regulatory Action
The authority for this rulemaking is Section 496 of the HEA. Section 496(a) of the HEA provides criteria that an accrediting agency must meet for the Secretary to recognize it as a reliable authority as to the quality of education or training offered. The same section states that the Secretary shall, after notice and opportunity for a hearing, establish criteria for such determinations.
Section 496(o) of the HEA directs the Secretary to establish, through regulation, procedures governing the recognition of accrediting agencies and the appeal of recognition decisions. At the same time, Congress provided that the Secretary shall not promulgate regulations with respect to the standards of an accrediting agency described in Section 496(a)(5). The Department interprets these provisions together to mean that the Secretary may establish recognition criteria governing whether an accrediting agency functions as a reliable authority under Section 496, while leaving accrediting agencies the responsibility for developing and applying their own substantive accreditation standards. Accordingly, these regulations establish the criteria the Secretary will use in determining whether an accrediting agency qualifies for Federal recognition. Except where expressly required by statute, the regulations do not prescribe the substantive content of accreditation standards, but instead establish minimum expectations regarding the processes, consistency, transparency, and lawful administration of those standards.
The Department has also reviewed existing regulations considering Section 496(o). Where current regulations prescribe requirements that extend beyond recognition procedures and instead direct the content or administration of accrediting standards without a clear statutory basis, the Department removes or simplifies those requirements to better align the regulations with Congressional direction and remove administrative burden.

§ 602.15—Administrative and Fiscal Responsibilities
The Department sought feedback about the extent to which the “conflict of interest” requirements impact accrediting agencies in relation to 401K plans, health insurance, and other areas. We understood that there may be some agencies who utilize the same resources as their related, associated, or affiliated trade association in these certain areas, and that there may be some consideration to the amount of time and resources it would take to unwind the sharing of resources in such instances.

Some of these agencies believed that these changes would result in costs that agencies would pass on to institutions through higher accreditation fees to programs. Discussion:
The Department disagrees with the recommendations. The Department's phase-in of the final rule for applications for initial and renewed recognition that were submitted during the transition period of the final rule will provide agencies approximately 20 months, through July 1, 2028, to make the necessary changes to comply with the regulations. If an agency is unable to comply by that date due to existing lease obligations, it may contact the Department to provide specific details regarding its circumstances. The Department may consider an agency's demonstrated, substantive progress toward achieving full compliance within a reasonable timeframe when determining whether to maintain its recognition status. Such progress must be supported by objective, verifiable evidence of concrete actions taken and measurable progress toward compliance, rather than statements of intent or unsupported assurances. The Department may require the agency to submit periodic reports and supporting documentation to assess its progress and determine whether the agency is on track to achieve full compliance within the applicable timeframe.

Regulatory Impact Analysis—Data Constraints
The Department recognizes that there is limited data available to estimate the proposed regulation's potential impact on accrediting agencies, institutions, programs, and students. Discussion:
The Department disagrees with commenters' assertion that its solicitation of public feedback to strengthen the RIA demonstrates a lack of empirical data to support the proposed changes. This assertion misconstrues the purpose of the Department's request for feedback, which is intended to ensure that its analysis is informed by the best available information and evidence. Seeking public input is a means of strengthening the analytical basis for informed policymaking, not an indication that the analysis lacks an adequate evidentiary foundation. In response to some commenters' feedback, the Department has supplemented the RIA with additional information to further support the proposed changes. This includes additional estimates for changes in title IV student aid disbursements that result from credit transfer policies and an increase in innovative and flexible educational models.

The Solution: The proposed rule holds institutions accountable by enforcing state and Federal laws, setting minimum student performance standards, and measuring real-world outcomes. This reform is critical to fixing a broken system and restoring accountability to American higher education.”
“. . . despite their immense power over institutions of higher education, accreditation agencies fail to ensure academic quality, operate like a monopoly, lack transparency, and stifle new and innovative educational models.”
Discussion:
The Department thanks commenters for their support. We agree that the final rule will reduce burden on agencies and their accredited institutions and programs by eliminating requirements not required by statute, focus on educational quality with increased accountability on agencies, and ensure that the standards and policies of agencies do not violate Federal or State law.
Changes:
None.
General Opposition to the Regulations
Comments:
Some commenters opposed the proposed rule and urged the Department to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule. Commenters were concerned that these regulations will shift academic and financial judgments from institutions and accrediting agencies to the Federal
(
printed page 68636)
government and argue that educational quality, affordability, and accountability will suffer as a result. Commenters argued that the final rule would allow the Department to indirectly withhold Federal student financial assistance, either by requiring accrediting agencies to end accreditation or by ending recognition for the institution's accrediting agency, when institutions are under investigation for a variety of issues such as interpretations of civil rights laws or political and ideological disputes.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with these perspectives and notes that the final rule does not replace institutional or agency discretion or judgment nor does it politicize the recognition process for accrediting agencies. Rather, in issuing this final rule, the Department is strengthening transparency of agencies and the institutions and programs they accredit and improving consistency and student protections across institutions and programs. The final rule preserves the core role of accrediting agencies in setting standards for and evaluating academic quality. Nothing in the final rule authorizes the Department to impose Federal viewpoints on agency or institutional decision-making. The final rule properly sets certain baseline expectations for recognition of agencies by the Department as reliable authorities on educational quality, such as protections for students during disruptions of educational services and consistent treatment of transfer credits when students change institutions or advance to higher levels, which are essential to safeguarding the integrity of the Federal student aid programs and ensuring accountability to taxpayers.
Changes:
None.
Comments:
A few commenters expressed concerns for programs serving students in prison education programs. The commenters stressed the proposed rules could lead to politically motivated State action against a prison education or post-incarceration reentry program and could trigger a fast-tracked accreditation review, giving State actors a new lever to pressure programs they find objectionable.
Discussion:
The Department maintains that all students, including those who are incarcerated, deserve increased accrediting agency oversight and will benefit from reinforcement of the existing legal, constitutional, civil rights, and consumer protection obligations already required of recognized accrediting agencies and the institutions and programs that they accredit.

None
Legal Authority
Comments:
Some commenters did not believe the Department has the statutory authority to regulate in several areas of this final rule, including the amendments under § 602.13 that add regulations on antitrust law; § 602.14 and § 602.15 that amend requirements on conflicts of interest; § 602.17 that amends the application of standards in reaching accreditation decisions, including student achievement standards and agency requirements on the application of civil rights law; § 602.23 that amends regulations on operating procedures all agencies must have; and § 602.24 that amends requirements for credit transfers.
Commenters often cited several statutory provisions to support their claims. Commenters stated Section 496(a)(5) of the HEA prescribes the specific standards for accreditation. Some commenters believe that the Department has added new standards that do not currently exist in statute. Commenters also cited Section 496(g) of the HEA as Congressional intent on the limitation of the Department's authority to establish additional standards: “Nothing in this Act shall be construed to permit the Secretary to establish criteria for accrediting agencies or associations that are not required by this section. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to prohibit or limit any accrediting agency or association from adopting additional standards not provided for in this section. Nothing in this section shall be construed to permit the Secretary to establish any criteria that specifies, defines, or prescribes the standards that accrediting agencies or associations shall use to assess any institution's success with respect to student achievement”. Commenters cited Section 496(o) that states the Secretary “shall not promulgate any regulation with respect to the standards of an accrediting agency or association described in subsection (a)(5)”.
Finally, commenters cited Section 103 of the Department of Education Organization Act as evidence of Congressional intent on the limits of the Department's authority: “No provision of a program administered by the Secretary or by any other officer of the Department shall be construed to authorize the Secretary or any such officer to exercise any direction, supervision, or control over the curriculum, program of instruction, administration, or personnel of any educational institution, school, or school system, over any accrediting agency or association, or over the selection or content of library resources, textbooks, or other instructional materials by any educational institution or school system, except to the extent authorized by law”.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with these commenters. The Secretary has express authority to “by regulation provide procedures for the recognition of accrediting agencies or associations and for the appeal of the Secretary's decisions,”
20 U.S.C. 1099b(o)
, and to “establish criteria” through notice-and-comment rulemaking to determine whether an agency is a “reliable authority as to the quality of education or training,”
20 U.S.C. 1099b(a)
. Thus, Congress expressly directed the Secretary to establish criteria for determining whether an agency is a reliable authority of the quality of education and training of the institutions and programs that it accredits. Congress narrowly limited the Secretary's authority in this area is prohibiting “promulgat[ing] any regulation with respect to the standards of an accreditation agency or association described in subsection (a)(5).”
20 U.S.C. 1099b(o)
.
The limitation in this section only means that the Department cannot add to the standards enumerated in subsection (a)(5). However, the Secretary is not prohibited from establishing the criteria used by the Department to determine whether an agency's standards, including those described in subsection (a)(5), comply with the statute and regulations.
The Department is not requiring any agency to adopt any requirements as standards. Instead, these regulations inform how the Department will assess whether the standards an agency has adopted are adequate to show that the agency is a reliable authority on institutional quality.
Changes:
None.
Comments:
Some commenters questioned the Department's authority to make many of the changes proposed to § 602.17. These commenters believe that the Department added new requirements to § 602.17 in contravention of express statutory prohibitions. Specifically, the commenters pointed to Section 496(g) of the HEA (
20 U.S.C. 1099b(g)
),
20 U.S.C. 1099b(o)
, and Section 103 of the Department of Education Organization Act . While many of the commenters were skeptical of the Department's authority to add any of the new requirements in § 602.17, many focused especially on the inclusion of student achievement, academic freedom, and cost-benefit analysis.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with these commenters. The Secretary
(
printed page 68637)
has express authority to “by regulation provide procedures for the recognition of accrediting agencies or associations and for the appeal of the Secretary's decisions,”
20 U.S.C. 1099b(o)
, and to “establish criteria” through notice-and-comment rulemaking to determine whether an agency is a “reliable authority as to the quality of education or training,”
20 U.S.C. 1099b(a)
. Thereby, Congress has commanded the Secretary to establish criteria by which the Secretary will determine whether an agency is a reliable authority of institutional quality. Congress limited the Secretary's authority in this area by prohibiting the Secretary from “promulgat[ing] any regulation with respect to the standards of an accreditation agency or association described in subsection (a)(5).”
20 U.S.C. 1099b(o)
.
The Department believes the best reading of this section is that the Department cannot add to the standards listed in subsection (a)(5). But, given the express command to establish criteria by which the Secretary will determine whether an agency is a reliable authority of institutional quality, the Secretary is not prohibited from explaining the criteria that the Secretary will use to determine whether an agency's subsection (a)(5) standards are effectively applied and enforced.
This is what the Department has done in Section 602.17. Section 602.17 does not add to the standards an agency must consider when assessing an institution's faculty, for example. Rather, these are the criteria the Department will use to determine whether an agency has effective subsection (a)(5) standards.
This interpretation is further supported by Section 496(a)(4)(A) of the HEA, which expressly requires accrediting agencies to consistently apply and enforce their standards, and section 496(n), which requires the Secretary to conduct a comprehensive and independent evaluation of accrediting agencies. These provisions authorize the Department to evaluate not only whether agencies have adopted standards, but also how those standards are applied and enforced. The requirements in § 602.17 implement these statutory responsibilities without prescribing the substantive content of accreditation standards. This distinction rests on the substance of the requirements, not merely their placement in the regulations.
To the extent the commenters believe that the Department is adding standards to Section 602.16, they are mistaken. While the Department's initial discussion draft prior to negotiated rulemaking included proposed changes to 602.16, the Department heard from several negotiators that the changes being sought were focused on the application of standards rather than changing the content of the standards themselves. Instead, these amendments inform how the Department will assess whether the standards an agency has adopted are adequate to show that the agency is a reliable authority on institutional quality. The negotiated rulemaking committee extensively discussed and ultimately reached consensus on changes to Section 602.17 to address how the Department determines whether agencies have effective mechanisms for evaluating compliance with its standards. The changes that were agreed upon by the negotiated rulemaking committee were proposed by the Department in the NPRM. These changes make only clarifying and technical changes to the requirements for standards in 602.16 and amend the evaluative criteria in 602.17 for the agency's application of standards in reaching accreditation decisions, which are designed for the Department to determine whether an agency is a reliable authority of educational quality for purposes of the HEA and other Federal purposes.
Changes:
None.
Comments:
Other commenters stated that the Department lacks authority to promulgate Section 602.14. In particular, the commenters argued that the Department could not apply the separate and independent requirement to programmatic accrediting agencies who do not serve as title IV gatekeepers. One commenter stated that the HEA was amended more than 30 years ago (Public Law 103-208) to make clear that “separation was not required for accrediting bodies with no title IV purpose.” The commenter stated that contemporaneous legislative history reinforces this point, because a US Representative, in introducing the Higher Education Technical Amendments of 1993, stated that: “. . . membership organizations requested clarification of the requirement for accrediting bodies to be separate and independent from their accrediting associations. Statements made on the House floor during consideration of the Higher Education Amendments of 1992 clarified that this separation was not required for accrediting bodies with no title IV purpose. However, the Department of Education informed us that a technical amendment is necessary to achieve congressional intent. Without this clarification these organizations will be required to undergo costly restructuring to meet the separate and independent requirements.”
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with the commenters. We first note that accrediting agencies will be required to demonstrate a Federal link in order to be recognized by the Department. Programmatic agencies who do not demonstrate such a link will not be considered for recognition and therefore need not comply with the separate and independent requirements. In any case, purely programmatic accrediting agencies recognized under 602.14(a)(3) are not required to comply with the separate and independent requirements in 602.14(b).
All accrediting agencies, including programmatic ones, are required to comply with 602.15, including by demonstrating clear and effective controls to avoid or resolve conflicts of interest. The commenters do not dispute the Department's authority to regulate under this section. To the extent commenters argue that the Department is effectively imposing the separate and independent requirements through 602.15(e), they are mistaken. Section 602.14(b) requires structural separation, meaning an agency must be independent of any related, associated, or affiliated trade association in its governance, budget, and personnel. In contrast, Section 602.15(e) does not require that separation. It requires only that the agencies identify and disclose relationships with trade associations and maintain clear and effective controls to prevent those relationships from improperly influencing accreditation decisions. An agency may maintain such relationships and comply with 602.15(e), so long as appropriate safeguards are in place.
The Department discussed at length its concerns with the influence that related, associated, or affiliated trade associations exert over accrediting agencies, leading the agencies to adopt standards and practices that do not always advance students' interests. The commenters fail to explain why the Department is incorrect to call this influence a conflict of interest or why the Department should not take steps to rein it in. The longstanding nature of the relationship between an accrediting agency and a related, associated, or affiliated trade association does not negate the existence of a conflict of interest, nor does it justify permitting such a conflict to persist.
Finally, the Department takes note of the legislative history cited in a comment but also notes that legislative history cannot change the plain language of the statute.
See State Farm Fire and Cas. Co.
v.
U.S ex rel. Rigsby,
580 U.S. 26, 36-37 (2016).
(
printed page 68638)
Here, the relevant statutes grant the Secretary authority to promulgate regulations and do not limit the Secretary's authority to specify what is considered a conflict of interest.

None.
§ 600.11 Special Rules Regarding Institutional Accreditation or Preaccreditation
Comments:
Some commenters strongly supported the amendments to § 600.11. They believed that competition among accrediting agencies will strengthen accountability, provide quality assurance, encourage innovation, and make accrediting agencies more responsive. Other commenters stated that the proposed regulations would lower barriers to entry while retaining statutory quality controls for agency recognition. Commenters stated that agencies should have incentives to demonstrate their value through effective quality assurance, reasonable processes, responsive service, appropriate standards, and efficient oversight. These commenters believed that allowing institutions to more easily change accrediting agencies creates those incentives and reduces the risk that accreditation relationships become permanent regardless of an agency's performance.
Discussion:
We agree and thank the commenters for their support. The final rule reduces regulatory burden on agencies in several areas but enhance accountability and direct focus on agencies' application of their standards and policies during the Department's recognition process.

None.
Comments:
Some commenters stated that loosening requirements for institutions to change accrediting agencies will result in institutions seeking out agencies with the lowest standards. Common themes in the comments opposing the amendments were (1) the regulations would weaken accreditation and result in a “race to the bottom” in terms of academic quality, (2) relaxed requirements for changing agencies and fewer barriers to Federal recognition would result in institutions shopping for the agencies with the weakest standards, (3) institutions would be able to easily evade accountability, (4) the rule ignores the negative consequences of policies that create competition for competition's sake, and (5) this change, combined with changes under § 602.11 and § 602.12, will drastically lower the requirements of accrediting agencies to be more easily recognized by the Department, with the probability of predatory institutions gaining accreditation increasing.
Discussion:
The Department has not reduced statutorily required oversight of accrediting agencies nor encouraged them to have lower standards. The commenters will note that all the statutorily required standards under Section 496(a)(5) remain unchanged. The Department has also added additional safeguards in the form of application of the required standards under § 602.17 to ensure agencies are accounting in their policies for things like post-completion and graduation outcomes, the educational and economic returns of programs, academic freedom protections, cost-benefit analysis of institutional activities, and optimization of students' time to credential to reduce the amount of borrowing for students.
The regulations will not result in a race to the bottom. In fact, the Department has raised the bar for outcomes of students receiving title IV, HEA assistance at eligible institutions. An agency will still apply to the Department for recognition and be evaluated by both Department staff and NACIQI, receive approval from the senior Department official, and continue to be re-recognized by the Secretary through Departmental periodic review of the agency's compliance with the rigorous standards contained in the regulations.

Comments:

Discussion:
While there may be an outlier, the Department does not envision a circumstance in which an institution voluntarily chooses to switch accrediting agencies and causes a gap in title IV funds access. § 602.3 What definitions apply to this part?
Accrediting Agency or Agency
Comments:
A few commenters supported the amended definition. One commenter stated that the revisions are an important shift from process-based compliance toward substantive quality assurance. The commenter stated that peer review should remain available, but the Federal government should not dictate unnecessary details for those processes. The commenter believed that reducing Federal micromanagement can allow accrediting agencies to devote more attention to student achievement, institutional performance, educational quality, and meaningful improvement while simultaneously reducing unnecessary administrative costs for institutions. Another commenter who supported the rule stated that accrediting agencies may wish to include professionals and experts on site visit teams who do not directly fit within the strictest meanings implied by “peer” or “peer reviewers.”
Discussion:
We agree and thank the commenters for their support.
Changes:
None.
Comments:
Some commenters opposed the Department's definition of accrediting agency or agency. Commenters opposed the removal of the requirement that an agency conduct activities through peer review. Commenters urged the Department to maintain the requirement for peer review for the following reasons:
Peer review is central to credibility independence and essential to the evaluation process, and peers are the most competent individuals capable of assessing quality of instruction.
Experts such as engineers, doctors, writers, physicists, and veterinarians know their subjects but have no understanding of education, teaching, or students.
The peer review process avoids the injection of political ideologies, political appointees, and overreach of outside Federal agencies into the accreditation process.
With no guardrails, agencies may contract individual reviewers with little to no expertise in the areas they are reviewing.
Current regulations already require agencies to include practitioners and employers as a part of their evaluation teams.
The Department itself encourages peer review in the preamble explanation to changes to site visits under § 602.24(b).
Discussion:
The regulatory requirement that an agency conduct activities through peer review is not prescribed in statute under the HEA. Where current regulations prescribe requirements that extend beyond recognition procedures and instead direct the content or administration of accrediting standards without a clear statutory basis, the Department removes or simplifies those requirements to better align the regulations with Congressional direction.
The regulations allow for an accrediting agency to continue utilizing the peer review model. There is no prohibition on peer review if that is the best option for the agency; however, the regulations do acknowledge that peer review is not the only appropriate model for the review of an institution or program. For example, an agency may determine that a practicing veterinarian or group of practicing veterinarians may be better suited for the review of a program than a professor(s) of veterinary sciences.
Under § 602.15(a)(2), any agency must have competent and knowledgeable individuals, qualified by education or experience as appropriate for their roles. This provision continues to include the agency's decision-making body and site reviewers. With this final rule the Department declines to apply a “one size fits all” approach to how an agency reviews its accredited institutions and programs; however, we still maintain high standards under § 602.16 and application of those standards under § 602.17 for the reviews.
Note that the preamble language for § 602.24 states “peer” or “independent” review: “For example, having a peer or independent reviewer alongside accrediting agency staff would help the evaluation reflect professional expertise and perspectives that extend beyond accrediting agency staff alone. Peer reviewers bring field specific knowledge that allows them to assess academic standards, administrative capacity, and institutional practices with appropriate depth. Independent reviewers, likewise, help the accreditation process not be unduly influenced by an agency's internal perspectives or by longstanding relationships with institutions.”

The commenters believe that agencies that accredit “professional programs” should be regulated by the Secretary to ensure quality. The commenter recommended that the Federal link should include a designated “professional program,” and those agencies should be required to seek Department recognition. Another commenter stated that agencies that oversee law, medical, dental, veterinary, pharmacy, and nursing schools should be required to be recognized by the Department due to their role in the U.S. social system.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with the recommendation. Section 496(a) requires a link to Federal programs in order for the Secretary to grant recognition. Institutional accrediting agencies primarily act as title IV gatekeepers for an institution to be eligible to participate in the title IV student financial aid programs. State licensure of professions does not establish a Federal link and law, medical, dental, veterinary, pharmacy, or nursing schools fall within an institutional accrediting agency's grant of accreditation to the institution. For programmatic accrediting agencies, the Federal link is usually through a non-HEA Federal program, and the Department will continue to recognize or review for recognition any agency with a non-HEA Federal link actively utilized by its accredited programs as well.
The Department will not recognize any agency that does not have a direct Federal link with either the Department or another Federal agency. As noted earlier, the Federal link is a statutory requirement for the Department's recognition and it is not intended to be a signal to State governments or licensure agencies to rely on those agencies for licensure or other State requirements.

None.

Discussion:
As stated in the final rule in 2019 when added, this provision is designed to decrease barriers to entry and enable new agencies to more easily enter the marketplace. Until a new agency is recognized, it is highly unlikely that an accredited institution would relinquish its current accreditation that enables it to meet title IV institutional eligibility requirements to attain accreditation from that new agency, even though the new agency may be better suited to the institution's mission. Therefore, we decline the commenter's suggestion to remove the provision.

If an agency has no institutions that participate in the title IV programs, then there would be no reason for a teach-out or notice period because no entity associated with the agency would be disbursing title IV aid to students. The two-year window is to ensure only accrediting agencies that have institutions and programs that utilize Federal programs are seeking recognition to avoid wasting Department and taxpayer resources.

Comments:
Some commenters opposed removing the two-year rule under current § 602.12(a)(2). They stated that accreditation exists to protect students and taxpayers by ensuring that a reliable, experienced authority is vouching for institutional and program quality, and a faster path to recognition should not come at the expense of that assurance. Several commenters stated that such a change would allow organizations with no record of responsible conduct to be created at will, which removes the value of accreditation entirely. Other commenters believed that the amendments of § 602.12 enable the creation of accrediting agencies with arbitrary standards and will increase accreditation of predatory institutions that saddle students with debt.
One commenter stated that the Department did not provide sufficient data to support the rescission of the two-year rule, and instead the Department merely speculates that its lower bar will entice new agencies to seek recognition and further speculates that developing the accrediting agency market will lead to competition and better educational outcomes. 20 U.S.C. 1099b(n)
. In addition, the commenter stated that the proposal is contrary to law as the Secretary can “only recognize” accrediting agencies which “accredit” (present tense) institutions or programs for the purpose of enabling participation in Federal funding, per

Additionally, all agencies are reviewed for compliance with the Secretary's Criteria for Recognition and are subject to the recognition process, which ensures a comprehensive evaluation.
The Department disagrees with the commenter's argument that the Secretary can “only recognize” accreditors which “accredit” (present tense) institutions or programs. Section 496(m) describes the purpose of recognition, not a requirement that an agency already have accredited institutions or programs. This interpretation is consistent with Section 496(a)(2)(A), which defines qualifying agencies by their principal purpose of accreditation. The Secretary must still conduct a comprehensive review and determine that an applicant satisfies all applicable statutory requirements, including demonstrated ability and experience, but the statute does not require two years of prior operations.

§ 602.13 Effect of Recognition
Comments:
A few commenters offered general support for the provision stating that the Secretary's recognition of an agency confers no antitrust immunity. One commenter stated that some agencies have operated like anticompetitive gatekeepers. Another commenter stated that the regulations make clear that accreditation should not be used to impose unnecessary educational requirements that restrict entry into a profession.

We thank these commenters for their support.

None.
Comments:
One commenter stated that the regulations repeat requirements that already exist in Federal law and are enforced through the Department of Justice. The commenter stated that inclusion of § 602.13 in the regulations suggests that the Department seeks to enforce provisions within the purview of other Federal agencies. The commenter recommended eliminating § 602.13.
Discussion:
The Department noted in the NPRM—and repeats here—that it is not the enforcer of antitrust law, but accrediting agencies are expected to comply with Federal law, including avoiding anti-competitive practices. The purpose of this provision is to make it clear that agencies cannot affirmatively claim that they enjoy any antitrust immunity flowing from their recognition. “Repeals of the antitrust laws by implication from a regulatory statute are strongly disfavored.”
Norfolk & W. Ry. Co.
v.
Am. Train Dispatchers Ass'n,
499 U.S. 117, 129 (1991) (quoting
United States
v.
Phila. Nat. Bank,
374 U.S. 321, 350 (1963). There is nothing in this regulation or the HEA that suggests that the antitrust laws are displaced explicitly or implicitly, and the amendments in § 602.13 make that explicitly clear.
Furthermore, the Department would not enforce the antitrust laws under § 602.32(3) either. When enforcing § 602.32(3), the Department would rely on, as evidence of an antitrust violation, a final judgment in state of Federal court, an admission by an accrediting agency, or a settlement where the agency admitted to have engaged in anticompetitive conduct. Only in these circumstances would the Department view the conduct as a negative factor when reviewing for compliance under § 602.32(3). Mere allegations of anticompetitive conduct would not be a sufficient basis for the Department to view that conduct as a negative factor when adjudicating an agency's recognition.

None
Comments:
A commenter stated that there is no specific exemption for accrediting agencies in the antitrust laws, and case law has long supported the view that accrediting agencies are subject to such laws, but at the same time § 602.17(a)(1)(ii)(E) requires accrediting agencies, in setting and applying student achievement standards, to assess the reasonableness of institutional and programmatic earnings relative to cost of attendance.
The commenter also stated that the Department seeks to have accrediting agencies conduct a “cost-benefit” analysis under proposed § 602.17(a)(3) of an institution's “budget, resource utilization, and allocation.” The commenter believes that these provisions are fundamentally irreconcilable with the statement that accrediting agencies are subject to antitrust laws.
The commenter further expressed that by compelling accrediting agencies to engage in cost-based assessments while simultaneously denying them any antitrust protection for doing so, the proposed rule creates a trap: an agency that complies with the Department's mandate exposes itself to an antitrust claim or enforcement action, while an
(
printed page 68645)
agency that declines to comply in order to mitigate antitrust risk faces loss of recognition. The commenter stated that the Department cannot lawfully impose regulatory obligations that force accrediting agencies to violate antitrust laws while simultaneously stating that such agencies are not immune from those laws.
Discussion:
The Department does not believe the regulations are irreconcilable with antitrust laws. Nothing in the regulation requires an agency to set tuition and fees, assess an institution's tuition and fees with respect to other institutions, otherwise pressure or compel institutions to set tuition and fees at a certain level, or act against an institution because of the institution's tuition and fees. The standard requires an agency to assess whether the institution has done a reasonable analysis to determine whether its own tuition and fees are reasonable in light of its own costs. Beyond that, agencies and institutions may wish to consult with counsel to effectively implement these regulations within Federal antitrust law. This does not, contrary to the commenter's suggestion, require any institution to engage in concerted action with other institutions. In particular, institutions can make their own decisions about how to conduct the cost-benefit analysis, which requires institutions to engage in reasoned decision making and to avoid arbitrary requirements, including those that may be unduly costly. The Department certainly does not want accrediting agencies to engage in any conduct that would violate the antitrust laws, which may include accrediting agencies developing uniform standards for making decisions in institutions' cost benefit analysis that could, directly or indirectly, fix prices. To the degree that an accrediting agency has a good faith belief that a specific action would violate the antitrust laws and abstains from taking that action on those grounds, the Department will credit those concerns when evaluating the compliance with the recognition criteria.
The commenter is also mistaken with regard to the regulation requiring agencies to perform cost/benefit analysis. Agencies are only required to review cost/benefit analysis performed by institutions.

Discussion:
We believe we have struck a fair and nuanced balance under the regulations in § 602.14 and § 602.15 to reduce conflicts of interest between recognized agencies and their stakeholders. The Department recognizes that professional associations, testing organizations, certification bodies, and other organizations can provide valuable expertise, information, and services that contribute to effective accreditation. Such cooperation can improve the development of accreditation standards, facilitate the evaluation of educational quality, and reduce unnecessary duplication of effort.
At the same time, these organizations may have interests that differ from those of students and the public. The Department's regulations are intended to prevent relationships that create conflicts of interest or give outside organizations inappropriate influence over accreditation standards or other decisions, without unnecessarily restricting legitimate collaboration or the exchange of expertise. The Department believes this approach preserves the benefits of cooperation while ensuring that accrediting agencies remain accountable for independently carrying out their responsibilities to protect educational quality and the public interest.

The Department would not publish a form that violated antitrust laws. In addition, we do not enforce the antitrust laws, so it would not be appropriate to create an exhaustive list of regulatory provisions that do not violate antitrust laws.

Discussion:
The commenters concerns are unfounded because these regulations are fully within the Department's authority and are simply common-sense steps to prevent conflicts of interest by individuals who set an agency's standards. The regulations prevent such individuals from setting standards that directly benefit their institution or program(s). The provision continues to allow anyone the agency chooses to be a member of the standards-setting body, which may include members of the agency's decision-making body. However, the members of the standards-setting body cannot vote to adopt or revise standards or policies if they are an officer, director, or employee of an accredited institution or program because of the conflict of interest that this poses.
There is nothing to restrict an agency from including in its decision-making body employers, students, practitioners, administrators, academics, and/or educators from institutions or programs not accredited by the agency. This provision also does not limit members regarding other responsibilities of the decision-making body, which can include fiduciary, accreditation decisions, procedures for implementing standards and policies, and other administrative procedures.

Comments:
Some commenters opposed the requirements for operational separation from related, associated, or affiliated trade association or professional organization under § 602.15(e)(4). The commenters stated that the provisions will substantially increase the cost of accreditation while also limiting the clinical, surgical, and educational expertise available to inform standards that directly affect the preparation of future podiatric physicians and surgeons. Several commenters were concerned that the requirements would go significantly beyond ensuring independent accreditation decision-making by prohibiting the sharing of personnel, services, facilities, equipment, information technology infrastructure, and office space with an affiliated professional organization. One commenter requested that the Department allow specialized and professional accrediting agencies to demonstrate independence through effective, enforceable safeguards rather than requiring complete physical and operational separation in all circumstances.
Discussion:
Similar to responses under § 602.10 and § 602.14, the Department strongly believes that the shared use of resources, personnel, services, equipment, facilities, information technology, and office space, has led to the outsized and direct influence of related, associated, or affiliated trade association over accreditation standards and decisions.
These arrangements can give trade associations influence over the selection, supervision, and compensation of personnel, control over budgets and access to essential services, and access to confidential accreditation information. Even in the absence of direct interference in individual accreditation decisions, an accrediting agency's dependence on a trade association for essential operational resources can compromise its ability to establish standards, conduct evaluations, and make accreditation decisions independently, particularly when those decisions conflict with the interests of the trade association or its members.
Such influence can harm students and the public in several ways. A trade association may have an interest in protecting its members from adverse accreditation decisions, even when those decisions are necessary to protect students. It may also seek to weaken standards that impose costs on its members or, conversely, support unnecessarily restrictive standards that protect established institutions from competition and innovation. These conflicts of interest can result in students receiving an inadequate education, incurring debt for credentials of limited value, or being denied access to lower-cost or innovative educational opportunities. They can also expose taxpayers to losses when institutions that fail to provide adequate educational quality continue to participate in the Federal student aid programs.

Discussion:
We disagree with the commenters' statements. Sections 496(g), (o), and (p) limit the Secretary's authority to prescribe the substantive content of accreditation standards, particularly student achievement standards. They do not prohibit the Secretary from regulating how recognized agencies apply and enforce their standards. Section 496(a)(4)(A) expressly requires the Secretary to determine that an agency “consistently applies and enforces standards,” and Sections 496(a)(6) and (c) establish requirements governing accreditation review and general operating procedures, respectively.
The Department therefore interprets Section 496 as distinguishing between prescribing the substance of an accrediting standard and establishing recognition criteria governing the consistent and lawful application of an agency's own standards. The Department maintains that the substance of this section is related to the Department's evaluation of how an agency applies its standards, and does not prescribe the content of the standards themselves.

section of this final rule. The Department is not providing exceptions to requirements in the regulations because the statute does not support the positions advocated by the commenters. Discussion:
See prior discussion under Legal Authority and § 602.17(a)(1) of this final rule. Academic freedom and intellectual diversity are important considerations in evaluating the quality of higher education. The new regulations require accrediting agencies, when applying their standards, to consider institutional policies and practices relating to academic freedom and intellectual diversity. Contrary to the hyperbole exercised by several commenters, the new regulations also do not prescribe the content of policies relating to academic freedom and diversity, do not require institutions to adopt particular policies, and do not require accrediting agencies to establish separate substantive standards in these areas.
An institution's decision not to adopt a formal policy on academic freedom or intellectual diversity does not, by itself, constitute noncompliance. Rather, an accrediting agency must consider relevant institutional policies and practices in the context of its existing standards and the institution's mission. Where an agency has adopted standards addressing these matters, it must apply and enforce those standards consistently.
These provisions govern the process by which accrediting agencies evaluate institutions, rather than prescribing particular accreditation standards.

Discussion:
The Department disagrees with the commenters. The Department provides more than $100 billion annually in Pell Grants and Federal student loans, a substantial portion of which supports institutional revenue through tuition, fees, and other charges. Many institutions depend on these Federal student aid programs to sustain their operations. Accordingly, the Department has a responsibility to ensure that institutions receiving Federal funds exercise sound fiscal stewardship, including by conducting meaningful cost-benefit analyses and evaluating how institutional spending decisions affect costs borne by students.
Section 602.16(a)(1)(iv) currently requires that an “agency's accreditation standards must establish requirements for the institutions or programs it accredits” in the area of “Facilities, equipment, and supplies.” Because cost/benefit analysis is an integral part of responsible capital investment planning, the Department is requiring agencies to review whether institutions have conducted cost/benefit analysis and for agencies to review them if they are performed by an institution.
We disagree that this provision infringes on institutional governance because it only requires agencies to review analysis that is performed; there is no requirement for any institution to do or enact anything.
Cost-benefit analysis decreases costs and increases educational quality for students by ensuring that capital expenditures are properly scrutinized and justified.
