Comments:
Some commenters had concerns with § 602.23(j). The main concern from commenters was that these provisions could limit the ability of accrediting bodies to respond when State action interferes with academic freedom, institutional governance, curriculum, or established professional and educational standards. One commenter stated that an accrediting agency cannot simultaneously be instructed to verify an institution's constitutional compliance and be barred from reviewing the governance decisions through which that compliance is or is not maintained.
One commenter stated that it is unclear in § 602.23(j) what is included within the scope of “aspects of institutional governance of public institutions that are established by State law,” beyond the issue of “appointment of institutional directors or officers by elected or appointed State officials.”
Another commenter stated that under proposed § 602.23(j), the politically motivated appointment of regents established by State law would be outside the accrediting agency's review. This is a threat to independent accreditation, making it effectively a rubber stamp of whatever States decide to do—whether or not those actions materially weaken the quality of education for students at institutions within those States. The commenter asserted that the provision strips the ability of accrediting agencies to effectively enforce their standards in any meaningful way.
One commenter recommended revising § 602.23(j) to preserve accrediting agencies' ability to evaluate governance matters relevant to institutional quality, even where particular governance structures are established by State law. Another commenter recommended revising § 602.23(j) to read: “The agency shall not penalize or place on probation any public or private nonprofit institution for actions taken by its governing board that fall within the board's statutory, charter, or legal authority” or “The agency must only review aspects of institutional governance of public institutions to ensure their compliance with State and Federal laws, including the appointment of institutional directors or officers by elected or appointed State officials.”
Another commenter stated that the Department should clarify the terminology in § 602.23(j) to expressly reference typical public institution governance bodies such as “boards of trustees,” as it does in the preamble language. The commenter indicated that the regulations should also make clear whether the provision protects only governance structures and appointments of institution or program leaders prescribed by State law, or whether it also protects decisions for which State law assigns decision-making authority to a public institution's governing board. The commenter requested that the final text not prevent an agency from reviewing a State law governance decision when the review concerns compliance with Federal law, the institution's own policies, or valid academic and institutional quality standards. The commenter also argued that the regulations should not authorize an agency to direct the outcome of a governance decision that State law reserves to the State or its governing bodies.
Discussion:
We disagree with the commenters' assertions. The Department's intent is to ensure that an agency's standards do not supersede State law. For example, if a State passes a law that grants the Governor authority to appoint an administrator to an institution, then the agency may not review any subsequent decision by the Governor to make an appointment of the specific administrator. The Department intends this requirement to remain broad. We decline to prescribe an exhaustive list in regulation of the scope of § 602.23(j). As issues arise, the Department will work with agencies and States to clarify guidance and resolve issues.
We decline to add a reference to a “board of trustees” or specify that the regulations prevent accrediting agencies from reviewing decisions for which State law assigns decision-making authority to an institution's governing board because the list in regulation is not exhaustive. The regulation states that the agency must refrain from reviewing aspects of institutional governance of public institutions that are established by State law, “including” any appointment to institutional governance established by State law; the Department does not intend for that to be the only item that cannot be reviewed.
The regulations under § 602.23(j) do not prevent an accrediting agency from reviewing concerns with an institution's compliance with Federal law or valid academic and institutional quality standards that are clearly under the direct purview of the agency under the law and regulations, even if those standards might be impacted by the policies of a State governance board. The requirements under § 602.23(j) are specifically intended to prevent accrediting agencies from intervening in governance matters that are under the clear and rightful purview of the State. Where there are governance matters that could affect academic quality but remain under the purview of the State, the accrediting agency may act as an advisor but not as the arbiter of the institution's policies.
Finally, we believe that § 602.23(h) already addresses the requested amendment related to State law compliance with Federal law.

§ 602.24 Additional Procedures Certain Institutional Agencies Must Have
Teach-Out Plans and Agreements, and Closed Institutions
Comments:
Several commenters argued that if an institution is on provisional certification, that does not imply that they are at risk of closure. Commenters believed that institutions that undergo routine change-in-ownership reviews, operational or compliance issues, or are placed on provisional certification during Heightened Cash Monitoring do not indicate any real risk of closure and should be exempted from the teach-out requirements in § 602.24(c). Commenters urged the Department to only require teach-out plans when appropriate and that such requirements be tied directly to demonstrated institutional risk rather than being automatically triggered by broad status classifications like provisional certification. Commenters believed linking teach-out obligations to financial or operational risk would ensure that the requirement serves its intended purpose—protecting students from abrupt closures. One commenter noted that the changes in § 602.24(c)(1)(iii) will require large public institutions to identify teach-out partners across numerous programs, and the mandated student communications will create confusion by implying closure risks that do not exist. The commenter recommended maintaining the current language in § 602.24(c)(1)(iii), which requires a teach-out plan for a defined subset of institutions on provisional certification, rather than for every institution on provisional certification.
Another commenter suggested revising § 602.24(c)(1)(iii) to read: “The Secretary changes an institution's participation in the title IV, HEA programs from full certification to provisional certification based on circumstances that present a material risk to the institution's continued operation or its ability to provide instruction to enrolled students.” A different commenter raised concerns about financial protection requirements, such as letters of credit, when an institution cannot secure a teach-out agreement. The commenter warned that these requirements will inadvertently create or worsen financial distress because letters of credit can be costly and can significantly constrain an institution's liquidity.
Discussion:
The Department appreciates commenters' suggestions to maintain the current language in § 602.24(c)(1)(iii) or revise the language, but we will not be adopting the suggestions. Provisional certification is, by definition, a status associated with elevated oversight and potential risk, whether financial, administrative, or related to consumer protection. The Department is strengthening early warning systems to ensure that students are protected when institutions encounter operational or financial challenges that may impair their ability to continue offering educational programs. In many cases, indicators that lead to provisional certification come before more significant problems. Requiring institutions in provisional status to develop a teach-out plan ensures that, if circumstances worsen, students will not face abrupt disruption or loss of educational continuity. The Department also emphasizes that a teach-out plan is a planning tool, not a presumption of closure, and an overall best practice to mitigate lost educational opportunities when unforeseen events or circumstances occur. Teach-out plans can be scaled appropriately to the institution's structure and circumstances, and institutions retain discretion to design plans that reflect their program offerings, size, and stability.
With respect to financial protection requirements such as letters of credit, the Department acknowledges the commenter's concern that these measures can be costly. Nonetheless, financial protection plays a critical role when an institution cannot secure a teach-out agreement, particularly in situations where operational or financial deterioration creates heightened student risk. These safeguards help ensure that resources will be available to support students if closure occurs. Moreover, institutions unable to secure a teach-out agreement must document the reasons for this difficulty, and the Department may require financial protection only when necessary to secure student continuity in the event of institutional disruption.
The Department agrees that regulatory obligations must be carefully calibrated to risk, and the final rule incorporates several mechanisms to strengthen early warning systems and align requirements with the conditions institutions face. At the same time, the Department declines to limit teach-out or financial protection requirements solely to instances of demonstrated closure risk because doing so could delay safeguards until risks become acute which may compromise student protections.

Several commenters are concerned about the 30-day requirement for institutions to submit teach-out plans or teach-out agreements under §§ 602.24(c)(1) and (c)(3). One commenter suggested extending the 30-day timeline for submission of a teach-out plan and/or teach-out agreement(s) to at least 60 days. Another commenter argued that large, multi-campus institutions cannot produce comprehensive, high-quality teach-out plans within 30 days, especially when those plans must account for every educational program and site. The commenter cautioned that requiring rushed plans risks poor quality submissions that fail to adequately protect students and recommended applying the same flexibility currently afforded under § 602.24(c)(3) to § 602.24(c)(1). In addition, the commenter recommended the Department be required to notify accrediting agencies immediately when it places an institution on provisional certification or takes other teach-out triggering actions listed in §§ 602.24(c)(1) and (c)(2). A different commenter requested that the Department clarify that the 30-day timeline proposed in § 602.24(c)(1) can be shortened when circumstances warrant quicker action.
Discussion:
The Department acknowledges the commenters' concern regarding the 30-day requirement for institutions to submit teach-out plans or teach-out agreements under §§ 602.24(c)(1) and (c)(3), but we will maintain the proposed language. The 30-day timeline reflects the Department's commitment to early and proactive intervention when institutions encounter circumstances such as a change from full to provisional certification. As stated before, provisional certification signals heightened oversight, and institutions will retain discretion to tailor the plan to their size, academic structure, and operations. Nothing in the regulation precludes an accrediting agency from requiring a teach-out plan at regular intervals, such as at each renewal of accreditation review, or at other points, which would relieve the 30-day timeline obligation, and agencies retain the discretion to do so.
Regarding the commenter's recommendation that the Department notify accrediting agencies right away when an institution gets provisional certification or faces other teach-out actions, the Department is committed to improving communication with accrediting agencies. However, we will not add new rules requiring immediate notification. In addition, the Department agrees with the commenter's statement that there may be instances where a more expedited response is necessary to protect students or to ensure the integrity of the accreditation and oversight processes. The 30-day period in § 602.24(c)(1) represents the maximum time allotted for agencies to take the required action. Nothing in the regulation precludes an accrediting agency from acting sooner when circumstances justify a shorter timeframe, and agencies retain the discretion to do so.

None.

One commenter suggested adding the following to § 602.24(c): “A teach-out plan must identify a teach-out opportunity in a program reasonably similar in content, structure, and scheduling to the program in which the student is enrolled, and may not rely solely on an additional location or branch campus of the closing institution.”
Discussion:
Although the Department appreciates the commenter's suggested additions, the Department believes the final regulatory text strikes an appropriate balance by enhancing protections for students, improving transparency, and strengthening continuity measures without imposing unnecessary rigidity. The Department emphasizes that the final rule requires accrediting agencies to ensure institutions include record-retention plans, maintain transcript access, and identify comparable program pathways in teach-out plans and agreements.

Comments:

One commenter stated that once the institution is no longer a member of the agency, the responsibilities envisioned in § 602.24(d)(i), securing teach-out options after closure, and § 602.24(d)(ii), establishing transfer options with institutions named in a teach-out plan, are not feasible. Commenters argued that an institution that closes without a teach-out plan would not have pre-identified teach-out institutions, making the provision impossible to carry out and recommended narrowing § 602.24(d) to include only paragraphs (iii) and (iv).
Discussion:
The Department appreciates the commenters' perspective on the scope of § 602.24(d), but the Department will not adopt the recommendation to limit the provision to paragraphs (iii) and (iv). As described in the NPRM, § 602.24(d) is designed to ensure that, when an institution closes without a teach-out plan, accrediting agencies, States, and the Department act promptly and cohesively to help students identify reasonable opportunities to complete their education without additional charges. § 602.24(d) does not require accrediting agencies to act on behalf of a closed institution; rather, it requires them to work, to the extent feasible, with the Department and appropriate State agencies to help students secure reasonable opportunities for educational continuation. Therefore, these provisions serve as expectations for coordinated student protection rather than as prescriptive requirements mandating specific teach-out arrangements.

Transfer of Credit Policies
Comments:
Several commenters support the proposed transfer of credit protections, emphasizing that students should not be denied credit simply because their coursework was completed at an institution accredited by a different accrediting agency. While supporting greater transparency and fairness in transfer of credit decisions, commenters stressed the need to preserve institutional authority to determine academic comparability, program coherence, sequencing, and specialized accreditation requirements.
Discussion:
The Department appreciates the significant support for the proposed transfer of credit protections, and we recognize the concerns regarding the importance of preserving institutional authority over academic determinations. The Department clarifies that decisions related to comparability, program sequencing, coherence, and specialized accreditation requirements rest with institutions and their faculty, as they are responsible for maintaining academic quality and the integrity of degree pathways. The final rule does not require institutions to accept transfer credit that is not comparable or that would compromise program quality; rather, they require institutions to apply their criteria transparently, consistently, and not reject credit solely due to differences in the recognized accrediting agency.
Changes:
None.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that the Department clarify that the transfer of credit provisions do not create a presumption that credit from another accredited institution must be accepted, and that institutions retain meaningful academic discretion to determine whether prior coursework is comparable and applicable to their curricula, particularly at institutions with a religious mission. The commenters stated that these institutions must retain the ability to decline credit from institutions that do not share their theological commitments and should not be required to conduct individualized case-by-case reviews. Commenters requested explicit recognition of institutional mission, worldview, curricular coherence, program sequencing, residency requirements, professional accreditation and licensure standards, and similar academic considerations as valid bases for denying transfer credit.
One commenter stated that transfer of credits in STEM disciplines carries unique academic risks, such as courses with identical numbers and similar curricula varying significantly depending on the faculty member, instructional approach, and rigor. Because of these variations, the commenter argued that automatic or presumed acceptance of STEM credit is inappropriate and potentially harmful. The commenter recommended that the Department require every transfer student have a conversation with a faculty member for each STEM course to ensure the student is adequately prepared and placed appropriately.
Another commenter asked for clarification on the permissible types of academic criteria preserved by 602.24(e)(4)'s “academic standards or curricular requirements” qualifier for limiting transfer credit. A different commenter argued that § 602.24(e)(3-5) endangers the integrity of undergraduate courses and recommended that those paragraphs be removed. The commenter stated that it does students no favors to assume that all courses are equivalent, and that institutions should continue to carefully negotiate transfer credit criteria.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with the assertions that § 602.24(e)(3-5) presumes that all courses are equivalent or undermines academic quality. Likewise, the Department also disagrees
(
printed page 68666)
with the claim that the transfer of credit provisions in § 602.24(e) eliminate institutional discretion or prevents institutions from considering mission-based factors when determining whether coursework is comparable and applicable. The regulations under § 602.24(e) do not require institutions to accept coursework that does not meet their academic standards, curricular requirements, or program specific expectations. Instead, the regulations require institutions to apply published criteria consistently and prohibit the denial of credit solely based on the institution or its recognized accrediting agency. The Department recognizes that institutions retain discretion to establish and apply academic criteria when evaluating transfer credit. Such criteria may include, for example, determining whether prior coursework is sufficiently comparable in content, learning outcomes, level, prerequisites, accreditation-related program requirements, or degree-specific curricular expectations. These examples are illustrative rather than exhaustive and are intended to reflect institutions' authority to make individualized academic determinations consistent with their educational mission and program requirements.
Further, the Department recognizes the concerns stated by the commenter while noting that all credits are not created equal. The Department believes this rule establishes appropriate checks and balances to ensure that institutions accept those credits that are equal through careful evaluation, and ensuring that students are provided the appropriate, additional education where it deems, with a reasoned explanation, that these credits are not equal. These requirements do not override institutional judgment regarding comparability or academic fit; therefore, the Department declines to add new regulatory language enumerating all possible academic bases for denying credit.
The Department appreciates the commenter's concerns regarding the unique challenges when evaluating transfer credit in STEM fields; however, these requirements do not require institutions to provide “blind” acceptance of STEM credit as the commenter asserted, nor do they interfere with faculty judgment regarding whether a student is adequately prepared for advanced coursework. Institutions may, and should, continue to engage faculty in evaluating demanding STEM courses and determining appropriate placement or support to protect student success. At the same time, the Department maintains that students deserve clear explanations when credit is not accepted and timely information about how their prior coursework will count before committing financially to enrollment at the transfer institution. This transparency supports informed decision-making and reduces the likelihood of students repeating coursework unnecessarily. The Department believes the final rule appropriately balances institutional discretion with the need for fair, transparent, and consistently applied transfer credit practices, and ensures that students receive clear explanations for credit determinations while institutions maintain full authority over academic requirements.
Changes:
None.
Comment:
A few commenters requested a process to evaluate several categories of coursework, including Registered Apprenticeship-related instruction, pre-apprenticeship and noncredit occupational training, industry-recognized credentials, dual enrollment, military training and service-related learning, documented employment-based learning, pre-pharmacy coursework, direct-entry pathways, integrated undergraduate-professional curricula, and competency assessments. One commenter emphasized that the regional accrediting agency affiliation remains important for evaluating transfer credit, especially across States, as standards and coursework may not align with local licensure expectations. Another commenter asked whether institutions may maintain differentiated transfer policies based on enrollment status, modality, or instructional setting.
Discussion:
The Department recognizes that institutions and accrediting agencies play a central role in determining whether coursework aligns with local programmatic or licensure expectations. The final rule does not alter institutions' ability to assess comparability of content, rigor, and learning outcomes, including State-specific requirements in fields such as teacher education or health programs. Institutions may continue to apply differentiated transfer policies where distinctions reflect legitimate academic considerations and are applied transparently and consistently. As a reminder, the Department no longer recognizes “regional” accreditation as a separate Federal category; all recognized institutional accrediting agencies are held to the same standards and therefore no longer held to an arbitrary geographic distinction. Therefore, the commenter's concerns here are not applicable, and the Department declines to make such changes.

Comments:
Several commenters urged flexibility in establishing transcript submission and review timelines, using business days rather than calendar days for appeals, and allowing institutions at least 30 business days for appeals requiring additional faculty review. One commenter warned that the 15-day appeal window requirement is significantly more restrictive than existing State frameworks, which may lead to rushed and error prone evaluations. Another commenter suggested § 602.24(e)(5) to read: “Provide the student an opportunity to appeal the decision or request a competency-based or direct assessment evaluation of the student's knowledge of the subject-matter within 15 calendar days of receipt of the institution's written notification if an institution declines to award transfer credit under paragraph (4).” A different commenter asserted their belief that the Federal appeals process was unnecessary, as institutions already publish transfer credit policies and maintain procedures for addressing student concerns. According to the commenter, imposing a mandatory Federal process would add administrative burden and costs without improving educational quality.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees that 30 business days are needed to carry out the appeal requirements in the regulations. Timely and transparent communication to students is essential, including the resolution of credit transfer appeals within a predictable and consistent timeframe. Therefore, the Department will not adopt the recommendations to replace calendar-day deadlines with business-day deadlines or provide 30 business days for appeals requiring additional faculty review. The Department believes a clear and accessible appeal opportunity is an important safeguard for students, particularly to those who may otherwise be required to retake coursework unnecessarily or who may not understand the basis for denial. Although institutions may already have internal complaint or appeals processes, those processes differ widely. A minimum Federal requirement helps ensure that students' rights are protected consistently across institutions, as well as provide necessary information timely to students so they can make informed decisions about their education. The Department encourages institutions to adopt efficient transcript review systems, standardized explanation templates tied to academic criteria, and
(
printed page 68667)
collaborative transfer pathway agreements that support student mobility.

The commenter argued that using the date the institution sends the notification would create a clear, administratively feasible standard, reduce burdens on students to prove receipt of an email, and avoid ambiguity that could undermine the fairness of the appeal process.
Discussion:
The Department acknowledges there could be some practical challenges, as described by the commenter, regarding verification of receipt and administrative tracking. However, the Department notes that the purpose of the regulatory language is to ensure that students receive the full benefit of the appeal period and are not disadvantaged by delays in communication systems or institutional processes outside their control. Aligning the appeal timeline to the date the institution issues the notification could, in some cases, unintentionally shorten the time available to students, particularly those experiencing delays in email access, inconsistent connectivity, or other barriers.

The commenters urged the Department to clarify that any policy conditioning transfer of credit on the old “regional” group or on a subset of recognized accrediting agencies constitutes a decision that is prohibited under the criteria, as it is based on “solely” on an accrediting agency.
Discussion:
The Department acknowledges the concerns of institutional practices relying on the former “regional” accreditation construct. The final rule ensures that institutions do not deny credit transfer based solely on the identity of the institution's recognized accrediting agency, and that credit transfer determinations focus on the comparability of coursework, rather than outdated accreditation categories. The Department clarifies that conditioning transfer credit on accreditation by specific agencies or on any subset of recognized accrediting agencies is a form of denial based “solely” on accrediting agency and is prohibited under § 602.24(e)(3). Institutions must evaluate transfer credit using transparent, academically grounded criteria that are unrelated to the branding or historical categorization of accrediting agencies.

Graduate and professional programs are not included within the scope of these transfer of credit requirements. Institutions retain full discretion, consistent with their published policies, to evaluate graduate-level prior learning using appropriate criteria for specialized, advanced, or professionally regulated programs.

Comment:
One commenter recommended extending these protections to graduate programs, noting that accrediting agency-based discrimination similarly affects graduate admissions and graduate transfer credit. The commenter proposed adding a new § 602.24(g) that would bar graduate programs from denying admission or transfer credit solely because of the accrediting agency of the applicant's prior institution. The commenter proposed the following: “Graduate admission and graduate transfer of credit policies. For agencies that accredit institutions offering graduate or professional programs, the accrediting agency must confirm, as part of its review for initial accreditation or preaccreditation, or renewal of accreditation, that the institution does not deny admission to a graduate or professional program, or deny the award of graduate transfer credit, solely on the basis of the accreditation status of the agency that accredited the applicant's or student's prior degree-granting institution, provided that institution was accredited by an agency recognized by the Secretary under this part at the time the degree was awarded.”
Another commenter argued that universities apply inconsistent credit transfer standards between American and international students. According to the commenter, institutions often deny American students' transfer credits without explanation, forcing them to retake courses unnecessarily. In contrast, the commenter claimed that universities accept full credits from international institutions, such as those in India, without comparable scrutiny, which results in more international students entering taxpayer-funded graduate programs. The commenter further asserted that, because many American colleges now offer fully online undergraduate programs, international students also earn regionally accredited degrees which eliminates any justification for treating their credits differently. The commenter suggested that transfer of credit compliance be enforced equally, regardless of national origin.
Discussion:
The Department appreciates the concern that accrediting agency-based discrimination also affects graduate students; however, the Department declines to add proposed § 602.24(g). The transfer of credit framework in § 602.24(e) is intentionally scoped to undergraduate coursework, reflecting both the predominant volume of student mobility at the undergraduate level and the need to maintain institutional discretion for programmatic and discipline-specific graduate admission standards. Regarding the inconsistency of international credit transfer, the Department agrees that institutions should apply their transfer of credit policies consistently and transparently. The final rule does not prescribe specific academic standards for accepting or rejecting transfer credit, nor do they require institutions to evaluate coursework from different States or countries in any specific manner. However, what the regulations do require is that an institution apply the standards it determines appropriate to its mission, programs, students, and content consistently, across all students, regardless of international status. Institutions retain responsibility for establishing and applying their transfer of credit policies consistent with applicable law and accrediting agency requirements.

Comment:
One commenter asked whether accrediting agency recognition in 602.24(e)(3) is measured at course completion or at evaluation. The commenter also asked the Department to address transcript delays beyond the students' and receiving institution's control.
The commenter requested confirmation that late transcripts would not reopen prior evaluations or appeal periods. On the other hand, another commenter request clarification that a school cannot reject a timely, well-supported appeal solely due to circumstances beyond the student's control that caused them to miss the standard deadline.
Discussion:
Recognition is determined based on the accrediting agency's status at the time the student completed the course or program. One of the purposes of the Database of Accredited Postsecondary Institutions and Programs (DAPIP) is to provide students, employers, licensing bodies, and other stakeholders with a historical record that can be used to verify whether an institution or program was accredited at the time a student attended or completed the program. Maintaining recognition determinations based on the accrediting agency's status during the period of attendance promotes transparency, consistency, and the reliability of accreditation records. DAPIP serves as an important resource for validating the accreditation status applicable to a student's course of study or credential at the time it was earned.
We understand the commenters' concerns regarding transcript delays that are outside the control of the student or the receiving institution. Timelines for transcript review may vary widely across institutions, and delays can arise from staffing limitations, prior institutions' processing schedules, or mail delivery issues. The Department acknowledges these practical concerns and clarifies that late-arriving transcripts do not re-open prior evaluations or restart appeal periods, provided the institution made its determination based on the information available at the time and in accordance with its established criteria. The Department agrees that appeals processes must offer meaningful student protection and confirms that institutions may not dismiss an otherwise valid appeal purely because external circumstances impeded a student's ability to meet an administrative timeline. This principle is reflected in Departmental due process expectations, which require agencies and institutions to afford students reasonable opportunities to respond or supply supporting evidence before adverse determinations are finalized.

The commenter argued that such clarification would not expand institutional obligations or interfere with accrediting agency authority, but that it would instead prevent an overly narrow interpretation.
Discussion:
§ 602.24(e) is focused on ensuring that students receive clear, academically grounded explanations of credit transfer determinations, particularly involving coursework completed at institutions accredited by title IV gatekeeper agencies. The Department notes that this requirement does not limit institutions or accrediting agencies from applying similar evaluative principles to other forms of learning, including standardized examination credit, credit for prior learning, or other competencies, provided such practices remain within accrediting agency standards and institutional authority. The Department agrees that applying these principles consistently across credit-evaluation contexts can promote student understanding and institutional fairness. The final rule establishes baseline expectations for transfer credit determinations while preserving institutional and accrediting agency flexibility to adopt broader frameworks where appropriate. This is consistent with the Department's intention to ensure clarity for students while allowing accrediting agencies and institutions to accommodate variation in academic structures and evaluation practices.

The commenter asserted that the phrase shifts focus away from learning outcomes and could encourage institutions to invoke extraneous criteria, such as course modality or accrediting agency of the sending institution. The commenter believed that credit should be awarded if there is 70 percent or more alignment in learning outcomes. Discussion:
The purpose of § 602.24(e) is to ensure that students receive clear, academically grounded explanations when transfer credit is denied, not to prescribe a uniform evaluative methodology across institutions or mandate specific thresholds. The Department recognizes that institutions
(
printed page 68669)
increasingly rely on learning outcome-based evaluation models and affirms that accrediting agencies and institutions may rely primarily on learning outcomes when determining equivalency. Nothing in § 602.24(e) prohibits or discourages such practices.
However, the Department does not believe that removing the phrase “comparable in content” or establishing a Federally mandated percentage threshold would be appropriate or consistent with statutory limits on the Secretary's authority. Accrediting agencies and institutions must retain discretion to determine appropriate academic criteria based on institutional mission, program structure, content, learning outcomes, sequencing, licensure requirements, or other academically relevant factors. For some disciplines, content comparability remains an essential component of academic quality, even when learning outcomes are also evaluated. Accordingly, the Department declines to revise the regulation to remove the phrase “comparable in content” or to substitute a fixed percentage standard.

The commenters asserted that the HEA does not authorize the Secretary to require policies, procedures, or practices by institutions of higher education with respect to transfer of credit. The Department's final rule is grounded in its long-standing authority to establish criteria for accrediting agency recognition, and to ensure that accrediting agencies apply standards consistently and transparently. The transfer of credit provisions in § 602.24(e) do not mandate how institutions must award credit, nor do they dictate academic judgments. Rather, they require accrediting agencies to confirm that institutions publicly disclose their transfer of credit policies and apply their stated criteria consistently and without arbitrary discrimination. These provisions fall squarely within the Department's statutory authority to oversee accrediting agency recognition and to protect students through transparent, fair, and predictable institutional processes. The Department agrees that institutions must retain academic discretion to evaluate comparability and applicability of coursework, and confirms that the final rule continues to allow consideration of content, outcomes, and other academically relevant factors as part of an institution's decision-making framework.

The Department declines to remove § 602.24(e). § 602.25 Due Process
Comments:
One commenter stated that the proposed changes to § 602.25 should be reconsidered because they are unnecessary and risk weakening meaningful due process. The commenter stated that the Department should preserve the current due process framework, which sufficiently protects institutions without recreating the burdens of litigation inside the accreditation process.
Discussion:
We decline the commenter's recommendation. The Department believes the changes satisfy due process while also reducing prescriptive requirements on accrediting agencies that are not required by statute. The changes to § 602.25 are limited to the administration of the appeals process by an agency and do not weaken or fail to satisfy due process.

None.
Comments:
One commenter asserted that institutions face informal expectations from accrediting agencies that are unwritten and only verbally communicated through evaluators, staff, guidance, or prior decisions. The commenter stated that institutions face pressure to comply with these verbal directives and requested that the rule clearly state that adverse actions must be provided in writing and based on a written identified accreditation standard and accurate information, not an unwritten expectation.
Discussion:
The regulations in this section currently require written notification and specification regarding adverse action. If an institution receives an informal adverse action based on an unwritten expectation from an agency, then the institution should submit a formal complaint against the agency to the Department.

§ 602.26 Notification of Accrediting Decisions
Comments: Most commenters broadly disagreed with the revised § 602.26. Commenters stated the following as rationale for opposition to the provisions:
The final rule would weaken the consumer information role and effectiveness of accrediting agencies;
The final rule would weaken safeguards surrounding institutions that change accrediting agencies;
The Federal government would be weaponizing title IV, HEA funding eligibility;
The Department could keep an institution's title IV eligibility active for an unreasonable or unlimited period while an adverse accreditation action is under appeal;
The standard or discretion is unclear for keeping an institution's title IV eligibility active while an adverse accreditation action is under appeal;
The final rule would constrain accrediting agencies and reduce the standing of the U.S. globally;
The final rule should require fair and specific procedures before an accrediting agency takes adverse action;
The Department could second-guess accrediting agency decisions; and
Rapid disclosure of agency actions may affect enrollment decisions, transfer activity, employee recruitment, philanthropy, etc., before an underlying dispute is resolved.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with these comments. Our intention in amending this regulation, and our expectations for institutions and accrediting agencies after this rule is promulgated, is that this rule will establish a uniform disclosure framework of accreditation actions, enhance transparency, and strengthen consumer protection. Regarding new § 602.26(h), we feel the stated timeframe allows appropriate latitude when needed, and provides limits regarding the length of time an institution's eligibility may be extended. We do not expect this provision to be employed as frequently as some commenters expressed. The Department may provide additional guidance in the future regarding the process for an institution to request a continuation of eligibility for title IV, HEA program funds when it is challenging an agency's decision to end its accreditation.
Regarding the concern of rapid disclosure of agency actions adversely affecting enrollment decisions, the Department reasserts its desire to enhance transparency and strengthen consumer protections. Finally, the Department disagrees that a new review framework overseeing recognized accrediting agencies that serve as the primary gatekeepers for the Federal student aid programs equates to weaponizing the title IV, HEA programs. Rather, these revisions ensure that students are protected from misuse of these funds, and that their continuing education is protected. The review framework ensures that all institutions that receive title IV, HEA program funds are worthy, and also allows institutions that believe they were wrongly judged to continue educating their students while legal actions proceed. The final rule is needed to improve educational quality, protect students and taxpayers, and promote a higher education accreditation system that supports innovation, accountability, and legal compliance. We do not see any reason to believe that these changes will undermine the world standing of the United States, nor did the commenter provide a persuasive argument that this would occur.

§ 668.43 Institutional and Programmatic Information; Reporting and Disclosure of Information
Comments:
Several commenters expressed concern about the administrative burden associated with course-specific determinations and written explanations that would be required by the regulations prior to enrollment or financial commitment. Commenters emphasized these concerns were specifically formulated based on smaller or newer institutions without extensive articulation databases or dedicated transfer evaluation staff. Several commenters suggested permitting standardized, criteria-based explanations tied to published academic policies instead of individualized narratives for each course, technology and data sharing infrastructure for resource constrained institutions, and Statewide articulation agreements and transfer partnerships between community colleges and HBCUs. A few commenters also asked if institutions were permitted to use categorical rules for groups of courses—including Bible and theology courses, core curriculum, upper-level major requirements, clinical courses, laboratories, and capstone experiences—rather than being required to apply individualized determinations for each course.
Discussion:
The Department recognizes commenters' concerns about administrative burden, but we emphasize the importance of students receiving prompt decisions that support their informed enrollment planning and reduce uncertainty that may affect program progression. Institutions may establish reasonable timelines for transcript review and course material evaluation, provided they supply prospective students with clear and timely information about credit transfer policies. Institutions may also use structured or standardized templates tied to academic criteria when explaining course specific denials, so long as the reasoning remains specific enough for students to understand the academic basis for determination. This flexibility supports clarity for students while accommodating variations in institutional size and staffing. The Department also supports efforts by States, systems, and institutions, including HBCUs and community colleges, to build articulation frameworks that facilitate smoother transfer and reduce barriers for students.
Changes:
None.
Comments:
A few commenters asked the Department to establish a specific timeframe for when an institution must receive a student's transcript to ensure a timely review, while other commenters urged the Department to remove the pre-enrollment disclosure entirely. These commenters believed it would lead to rushed, error-prone evaluations, especially when an official transcript has not been received. Some commenters were concerned that without a defined deadline, students would not know when they need to submit their transcripts to allow sufficient processing time. One commenter suggested that, similar to the explicit timeframe for filing an appeal under § 602.24(e)(5) “within 15 calendar days of receipt,” § 668.43 should likewise include a clearly defined period to provide consistency and clarity for students.
Discussion:
The Department declines to remove the pre-enrollment disclosure requirement, and we decline to add a specific timeframe for transcripts to be received. The Department believes the pre-enrollment disclosure requirement is an essential element in promoting clarity and avoids situations in which students enroll without necessary information about how their earned credit will apply. Institutions have the flexibility in designing their transcript review systems, including assigning review responsibilities to academic units in a timely manner, using structured templates tied to academic criteria, and adopting technology solutions and articulation agreements. Institutions are required to disclose the date by which a student must submit transcripts for review in their transfer of credit policies. This approach provides transparency while maintaining flexibility for institutions to account for differences in program offerings, enrollment cycles, and administrative processes. While § 602.24(e)(5) includes an explicit timeframe for appealing a transfer of credit denial, “within 15 calendar days of receipt,” that provision addresses the appeals process rather than the initial submission of transcripts. The Department does not believe that applying a uniform Federal deadline to transcript submission would appropriately reflect the diversity of institutional practices or support the efficient administration of credit evaluations across institutions.

One commenter believes this distinction will help clarify the confusing use of “awarded for courses” in § 668.43. A few commenters pointed out that a credit that transfers as an unassigned elective does not necessarily shorten a student's path to a degree and that students need to know whether accepted credits satisfy elective, general education, or major requirements. One commenter also urged the Department to extend disclosures to include learning earned through registered apprenticeships. The commenter recommended that § 668.43(c)(3)(i) read: “Inform the student of the credit that will be awarded for courses on that transcript, inclusive of related technical instruction as appropriate, and how that credit will apply toward the student's intended program of study, including whether it satisfies elective, general education, or major requirements.”
Discussion:
The Department agrees that transferability and applicability have distinct meanings and that clarity between awarding credit and applying credit is important to help students make informed decisions about their educational pathways. § 668.43 ensures that students receive clear information about both which credits may be accepted and how those credits will apply to the program they intend to pursue. The regulation does not prohibit institutions from distinguishing transferability from applicability in their policies and the Department encourages institutions to do so.
The Department acknowledges that institutions may maintain different applicability standards across categories (
e.g.,
major requirements, general education, electives), as commenters noted. While the Department supports expanded transparency regarding credit for prior learning, including apprenticeship-related learning, the Department must also ensure that any additional disclosure requirements remain aligned with statutory authority and are administratively feasible. Therefore, the Department declines to revise the regulatory text to incorporate additional prescriptive applicability requirements or to mandate specific
(
printed page 68675)
disclosure language related to apprenticeships in § 668.43, as these additions exceed the scope and purpose of this rule.

Comments:
One commenter noted a potential contradiction between § 668.43(a)(11)(i), which requires institutions to disclose any criteria used for evaluating transfer credit, including identifying types of institutions or sources from which they will not accept credit, and the Department's proposed prohibition in § 602.24(e)(3) against denying credit based on the sending institution. The commenter argued that § 668.43(a)(11)(i) implies that institutions may legitimately refuse credit from certain sources and asked for clarification on how both provisions would function together.
Discussion:
The Department does not view these provisions as contradictory. The disclosure requirements in § 668.43(a)(11)(i) are intended to promote transparency by ensuring that students understand the criteria an institution uses when evaluating transfer credit. § 602.24(e)(3), by contrast, addresses the substance of transfer credit determinations that states that institutions may not deny transfer credit solely based on the sending institution or its recognized accrediting agency. Institutions remain free to evaluate transfer credit using academically relevant factors, including course content, learning outcomes, level, applicability to program requirements, prerequisites, sequencing, or other legitimate academic considerations. However, institutions may not rely exclusively on the identity of the sending institution or its recognized accrediting agency as the basis for denying credit. Accordingly, the disclosure requirements in § 668.43(a)(11)(i) and the requirements in § 602.24(e)(3) serve complementary purposes. The former promotes transparency regarding institutional policies, while the latter establishes limits on the criteria that institutions and accrediting agencies may use in credit transfer decisions. Institutions must disclose their transfer of credit policies, but those policies must remain consistent with the requirements of § 602.24(e)(3).

Comments:

Commenters stressed the strain institutions may face by preparing credit transfer determinations for prospective students who ultimately may not enroll.
Discussion:
The Department recognizes that credit transfer evaluations can involve complex academic judgments and that institutions may require time to obtain and review official transcripts, course descriptions, and other supporting documentation. The Department does not intend to compel institutions to make credit transfer determinations based on incomplete information or to sacrifice academic rigor in favor of speed. As noted elsewhere in the preamble, institutions may establish reasonable processes and timelines for transcript review and course evaluation, provided they furnish students with clear and timely information regarding credit transfer policies and determinations. At the same time, the Department remains committed to students receiving meaningful credit transfer information before making financial commitments that could expose them to unexpected costs or extended time to completion. The timing requirement will improve transparency and enable students to make informed enrollment decisions, particularly where transferability of prior coursework may affect educational affordability and degree progress. Nothing in the regulation requires institutions to disregard legitimate academic review processes or to reach final determinations in the absence of information necessary for an accurate evaluation. Further, the Department expects institutions to communicate clearly to students when a determination remains pending because additional documentation or faculty review is required. The Department continues to believe that students should receive credit transfer information before enrollment, registration, or other significant financial commitments whenever reasonably possible while preserving institutional discretion to conduct appropriate academic reviews.

Regulatory Impact Analysis
a. Need for Regulatory Action
The Department proposes this regulatory action to align the Secretary of Education's (Secretary) criteria for recognition of accrediting agencies to promote high-quality, high-value, and affordable education for students as outlined in
E.O. 14279
, titled “Reforming Accreditation to Strengthen Higher Education,” issued on April 23, 2025, by President Trump.
[
13
]
E.O. 14279
directs the Secretary to take several actions related to the Department's recognition of accrediting agencies or associations to ensure agency standards and enforcement actions are focused on student outcomes and free from unlawful discrimination and other potential violations of Federal and State law.
The Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended (HEA), requires the Secretary to establish criteria for determining whether an accrediting agency is a reliable authority, for purposes of the HEA and for other Federal purposes, on the quality of education or training offered by the institutions or programs that they accredit. Consistent with the statute, the Secretary has established regulations for recognition of accrediting agencies and has revised these regulations periodically.
The final reduces barriers that limit competition among accrediting agencies and recognition of new accrediting agencies. Similarly, via changes to accrediting agency requirements, the final rule will likely increase educational innovation and foster new education models that advance credential and degree completion. To improve student outcomes on student loan repayment, graduate earnings, and financial value and affordability, the final rule requires that recognized accrediting agencies assess member institutions on program-level student outcomes, without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex.

c. Discussion of Cost, Benefits, and Transfers
The final rule will likely affect students, institutions of higher education, accrediting agencies, and the Federal government. The Department expects students and the Federal government to benefit from the final rule. The final rule is likely to impose new costs on institutions and accrediting agencies.
This analysis focuses on four major policy areas within the final rule that are likely to have the most significant costs and benefits:
(1) changes to accrediting agencies' transfer of credit policies;
(2) a new requirement that agencies adopt policies that assess program-level student outcomes;
(3) regulatory changes that will allow for greater competition among existing and newly recognized accrediting agencies; and
(4) reforms that align accreditation standards with efforts to reduce college costs and credential inflation.
We discuss the costs and benefits associated with each of these areas below. The Department notes that there is little critical data available on which to base estimates of the proposed regulation's effect on the accrediting agency marketplace and responses by institutions and students. For this regulatory impact analysis, the Department has relied primarily on the publicly available Database of Accredited Postsecondary Institutions and Programs (DAPIP) and its own administrative data on title IV, HEA student aid recipients in the National Student Loan Data System (NSLDS) and the Common Origination and Disbursement (COD) System.
Transfer of Credit
The final regulation would make it easier for students to transfer credits to continue their postsecondary enrollment at a new institution. Under Section 602.24(e)(3), accrediting agencies would be required to ensure member institutions adopt several policies regarding transfer of credit that should increase the number of credits students are able to retain when transferring to a new institution. For example, the final rule would require that accrediting agencies prohibit an institution from denying transfer of credit based on the recognition of the institution, or type of institution, at which the student completed the coursework, so long as the agency accrediting that institution is recognized by the Secretary. Accrediting agencies must also require an institution to award transfer credit for undergraduate programs for coursework that has been successfully completed at another institution, is accredited by an agency recognized by the Secretary, and is comparable in content and learning outcomes to the institution's own course offerings, unless the institution provides a written basis for denial.
Students could benefit from these changes because they may spend less time and money retaking courses that failed to transfer. A 2017 study by the U.S. Government Accountability Office using Department of Education data found that transfer students typically lose 43 percent of their credits when they transfer.
[
14
]
Under the proposed rule, it is more likely that students will retain more of their credits earned at prior institutions, allowing them to complete their postsecondary education faster.
It is difficult to estimate the precise effect this policy may have on enrollment and title IV, HEA student aid disbursements, and the Department acknowledges a variety of outcomes could occur. First, the policy may induce more students to enroll in higher education because students will have more flexibility to switch programs without losing a substantial amount of credit earned at prior institutions. The policy may also reduce the dropout rate as students are able to maintain more of their prior credits when transferring, thereby reducing the total cost and enrollment duration of their program which should facilitate credential completion. It may also make transfer more desirable, allowing students to better match themselves to different programs and enhancing their ability to continue their education. If this occurs, the policy may ultimately increase enrollment and title IV, HEA student aid disbursements, imposing new costs on taxpayers and the Federal government. Additionally, higher education institutions may benefit, as they would likely receive additional revenues due to higher enrollment levels.
Alternatively, the policy may result in a reduction in title IV, HEA disbursements, providing a benefit to the Federal government and taxpayers and a new cost for higher education institutions. This would occur if higher education enrollment remains constant and if the proposed provision allows students to finish their credentials faster, resulting in fewer title IV, HEA disbursements. If this occurs, institutions may experience costs because their transfer students will likely spend less time enrolled (because they will not need to retake the credits that the institution previously did not accept in the transfer).
To better understand the potential impact of the transfer of credit policies for accrediting agencies in this rule, the Department is providing information from the National Student Loan Data System on the number of undergraduate students who transferred institutions between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 award years and the title IV, HEA student aid they received. This information is presented in Tables 3.1 and 3.2. Specifically, Table 3.1 shows that, between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 award year, a total of 1.8 million title IV, HEA students transferred institutions, and among those students, roughly 60 percent received title IV, HEA student aid in the award year they transferred (2024-25). Table 3.2 shows that these title IV, HEA recipients received a total of $8.8 billion in title IV, HEA funds at their new institution in 2024-25, or an average of approximately $8,300 per transfer student.
While the Department lacks readily available data to determine how much title IV, HEA disbursements could change due to the transfer of credit provisions, these data help establish a method to gauge the potential impact for both students and taxpayers. Standards for Program-Level Student Outcomes
Under the final regulation, accrediting agencies are required to review the use of additional student outcome metrics in their standards for institutions. Under Section 602.17, accrediting agencies must review their criteria for assessing whether an institution is successful in achieving its stated objectives at both the institutional and program levels, including minimum expectations regarding student outcomes such as graduation rates, post-completion employment and educational and economic returns using earnings data for former students relative to the total cost of attendance.
Requiring accrediting agencies to review their standards and criteria may impose new costs on both accrediting agencies and institutions. Some accrediting agencies may review their usage of student outcome criteria and ultimately make no adjustments to the standards they use because they have found, in their evaluation, that their standards are sufficiently rigorous and properly evaluate student success. In these cases, the cost to accrediting agencies and institutions is likely to be small.
In other cases, accrediting agencies may review and then adopt new standards related to student outcomes for the institutions they accredit. Agencies that choose this action may experience costs from several factors. First, for agencies that do not have a mechanism in place to assess the student success metrics of the institutions or programs they accredit, they will need to develop these new standards and apply them routinely in the accreditation process. Second, accrediting agencies may also need to develop systems and processes that allow them to collect new data from institutions, and to invest in new analytical capacity to assess the extent that institutions meet minimum requirements related to student outcomes.
Institutions accredited by agencies who review and adopt new standards may also incur new costs as those institutions work to comply with the new standards and requirements from their accrediting agency. This is likely to include new reporting costs between institutions and accrediting agencies. Institutions are also likely to incur costs as they work to change and improve any programs that fail to achieve compliance with any new standards related to student achievement imposed by an accrediting agency. Some institutions may ultimately decide to close noncompliant programs, which will also cause institutions to incur new costs, both in operational costs to shutter a program, and in reduced enrollment and revenue associated with those closed programs.

Accrediting Agency Competition and New Agencies
The final rule will remove barriers for new accrediting agencies to emerge and obtain Department recognition. Specifically, the rule simplifies and streamlines the Department's regulations for recognition and review of accrediting agencies, including eliminating superfluous requirements for recognition of new accrediting agencies that reduce competition and institutional choices when selecting an accrediting agency. The final rule also simplifies procedures for institutions to change accrediting agencies so that institutions are not forced to comply with standards that are antithetical to their values and missions. For example, the rule would remove the Department's current requirement that an accrediting agency grant or deny accreditation or preaccreditation to an institution for at least two years prior to seeking recognition by the Department. This two-year requirement is not statutory and represents an unnecessary burden for new accrediting agencies. Similarly, the final rule streamlines the process for institutions to change accrediting agencies by clarifying that the Secretary may not delay, condition, or otherwise adversely affect an institution's participation in the title IV, HEA programs solely because the institution seeks accreditation from, or changes accreditation to, another agency recognized by the Secretary. Under Section 602.13, the final regulation also specifies that recognition by the Department does not confer immunity from antitrust laws, which may further stimulate competition among accrediting agencies.
Reducing barriers to entry may also facilitate innovation by making it easier for new accrediting agencies to emerge and for institutions offering new educational models to obtain appropriate accreditation. To the extent such models attract students who receive Pell Grants or Federal student loans, the rule could affect Federal student aid outlays. The Department has provided estimates for the potential increases in enrollment and title IV, HEA student aid disbursements that could arise from new models and innovations. These estimates, which are based on historical growth rates among short-term certificate programs and exclusively online programs, are discussed later in this Regulatory Impact Analysis and are shown in Tables 3.6 and 3.7.
The Department also believes that reducing barriers to entry may improve accreditation by increasing contestability in the market for accrediting services. Contestability refers to the extent to which potential
(
printed page 68692)
competitors can realistically enter a market and existing customers can switch providers, even if relatively few firms currently compete or customers actually switch. Economic theory suggests that incumbent organizations respond not only to actual competition but also to the credible possibility of new entry or customer mobility. Baumol's theory of contestable markets predicts that reducing barriers to entry encourages incumbent firms to improve quality, reduce unnecessary costs, and become more responsive to consumers, while Demsetz emphasized that competition for a market can discipline incumbent firms even in concentrated industries. See William J. Baumol, “Contestable Markets: An Uprising in the Theory of Industry Structure,” 72 American Economic Review 1 (1982); Harold Demsetz, “Why Regulate Utilities?,” 11 Journal of Law and Economics 55 (1968). The Department believes that reducing unnecessary barriers to the recognition of new accrediting agencies and facilitating institutional mobility among recognized agencies is therefore likely to improve accrediting agency performance even if relatively few institutions ultimately change accrediting agencies. Accordingly, to the extent that these changes increase the credible possibility of new accrediting agency entry or institutional mobility, economic theory suggests they may improve accrediting agency performance even if relatively few institutions ultimately change accrediting agencies.
Although the Department lacks sufficient data to estimate how these changes will affect the accreditation marketplace, the changes will likely increase the number of institutional accrediting agencies recognized by the Department and may increase the number of institutions seeking to change agencies. To provide context regarding the potential impact of the changes, the Department used information from DAPIP to examine the growth and contraction in the number of institutional accrediting agencies and the rate and number of institutions that switch agencies over time. This analysis adds evidence to the Department's view that both new accrediting agency recognition and changes in agency by institutions are rare. For example, Figure 3.4 and Table 3.4 show that there has been little change in the number of institutional accrediting agencies over the past 30 years, and that in recent decades the number of recognized agencies has actually declined, despite the large increases in higher education enrollment over this time. Additionally, Table 3.5 shows that since 2020, only 10 institutions have voluntarily switched from one of the agencies formerly known as a regional accrediting agency, and that fewer than 50 have ever voluntarily switched away from these accrediting agencies.
One of the key goals of the final rule is that, through reforms to reduce burden and enhance competition among accrediting agencies, more institutional agencies will choose to be recognized and greater numbers of institutions will decide to change institutional accrediting agencies, thereby enhancing competition. While prior regulatory reforms may not have resulted in a descriptive change in the number of accrediting agencies and amount of accrediting agency switching that takes place (see Figure 3.4 and Table 3.5), the final rule includes additional provisions aimed at spurring competition, which may ultimately enhance the ability for accrediting agencies to enter and institutions to switch. Specifically, the reduction in time from initial petition to review for recognition by the senior Department official is likely to ultimately result in additional accrediting agencies applying for recognition, providing more options for institutions. These proposed changes also coincide with regulatory efforts by some States that require the State's institutions to switch accrediting bodies. Ultimately, accrediting agencies may benefit from the final rule because they will likely experience less burden to gain initial recognition and maintain recognition. Institutions, similarly, could benefit from these regulations if they value the ability to choose from a greater number of potential agencies, or if the new agencies that may emerge are better aligned with the institution's mission.

Affordability and Innovation
The Department's final rule would require accrediting agencies to adopt several new policies and procedures that aim to increase college affordability. Specifically, under Section 602.17 (Application of standards in reaching accreditation decisions), the final rule would require accrediting agencies to consider efficiency in their review of institutions and to conduct cost-benefit analyses to ensure institutions' activities justify the associated financial, administrative and opportunity costs, and the impact of capital expenditures on future operating expenses. Such analyses could put downward pressure on institutional costs and, by extension, tuition prices. If some institutions prove to be incapable of conducting credible cost/benefit analyses, the number of accredited institutions could fall, but this is unlikely.
Similarly, the final rule could put downward pressure on student costs by helping to reduce excessive program length by requiring that accrediting agencies apply standards that ensure program length is appropriate to the objectives of the program and credential awarded at the institution. The final rule also aims to reduce credential inflation and prevent agencies from restricting institutions from offering short-term programs, which may help reduce costs for students because they will be able to pursue fewer or shorter credentials to work in a given occupation. This may ultimately increase enrollment and title IV, HEA student aid disbursements if more students pursue postsecondary education as a result of the improved affordability and reduced time to completion.
The final rule would also specify in Section 602.17 that accrediting agencies' standards related to student achievement may include credit for prior learning. Granting credits for prior learning should reduce costs for students because it allows them to earn credit from skills obtained outside the institution, such as service in the armed forces, employment, or other demonstrated competency.
While these provisions would likely provide benefits to students through lower prices and less time enrolled, they could also reduce revenues for institutions and transfers of Federal title IV, HEA funds to institutions. Institutions may therefore bear additional costs as they adjust their programs and policies to align with new accreditation standards. Accrediting agencies will bear new costs as they work to incorporate these proposed

The final rule includes several provisions that ensure accrediting agencies do not unnecessarily constrain innovations that could further reduce costs to students and institutions, and may also increase program quality. For example, Section 602.15 (Administrative and fiscal responsibilities) would be amended to require that accrediting agencies provide training to all agency representatives and staff that includes topics related to best practices in various educational delivery methods, models, and modalities; innovative or lower-cost educational delivery models that may provide high-quality education to students; and avoiding unnecessary costs to institutions in the accreditation process. Department Administrative Costs
The Department expects the final rule to impose only modest incremental administrative costs on the Federal government. Most provisions modify the criteria and procedures the Department uses when recognizing accrediting agencies rather than establishing new Federal programs or recurring operational responsibilities.
Implementation will primarily require Department staff to review new, or additional, accrediting agency recognition applications and petitions under the revised standards. These reviews are already part of the Department's regular recognition process, and the final rule generally changes the substance of those reviews rather than creating new review processes. As a result, the Department expects most implementation activities to be absorbed within existing recognition cycles and staffing levels.
Some additional staff time may be required during the initial implementation period to review revised accrediting agency policies and procedures addressing issues such as conflicts of interest, independence from affiliated organizations, antitrust compliance, student outcomes, academic freedom, intellectual diversity, research integrity, and other revised recognition criteria. The Department also anticipates limited one-time costs associated with updating guidance documents, internal training materials, and information systems necessary to administer the revised regulations.
To the extent the final rule encourages the recognition of additional accrediting agencies or increases the number of institutions seeking to change agencies, the Department could experience a modest increase in recognition-related workload. However, these activities are expected to occur gradually over multiple recognition cycles and to remain manageable within existing administrative structures.
The Department also anticipates offsetting administrative savings. Since the Department announced its accreditation reform efforts, three accrediting agencies have voluntarily withdrawn from Department recognition.
