As additional agencies determine that they no longer wish to maintain Federal recognition under the revised regulatory framework, the Department expects the number of Federally recognized accrediting agencies requiring recognition reviews, interim monitoring, compliance reporting, and other oversight activities to decline. A smaller number of recognized agencies would reduce the Department's workload associated with recognition petitions, staff reviews, National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI) proceedings, monitoring, and related administrative actions, thereby partially offsetting the implementation costs associated with the final rule.
The final rule may also generate longer-term administrative efficiencies by establishing clearer recognition standards and focusing Department oversight on areas presenting the greatest risk to students and taxpayers. To the extent these reforms improve the efficiency of the recognition process, they could reduce both Federal administrative costs and private-sector compliance burdens over time.
Accordingly, the Department does not anticipate that implementation of the final rule will require significant additional Federal resources. Over time, the Department expects that the offsetting of administrative savings and efficiencies described above may reduce the overall Federal administrative burden associated with oversight of Federally recognized accrediting agencies.
4. Additional Benefits
The Department expects the final rule to produce several important benefits that cannot be reliably quantified but that are nevertheless relevant in evaluating the overall effects of the rule.
First, the final rule is expected to increase competition among recognized accrediting agencies. The Department anticipates that reducing unnecessary barriers to the recognition of new accrediting agencies, simplifying the process by which institutions may change accrediting agencies, and eliminating unnecessary geographic distinctions will increase institutional choice and create stronger incentives for accrediting agencies to innovate, improve responsiveness to institutions, and reduce unnecessary costs. While the Department cannot reliably estimate the magnitude of these effects, economic theory and experience in other quality-assurance markets suggest that increased competition is likely to improve quality and efficiency over time.
Second, the final rule is expected to improve transparency and accountability. The new requirements regarding transfer-of credit policies, public disclosure of accrediting actions, institutional representations, and research integrity will provide students, taxpayers, employers, and policymakers with more complete and reliable information regarding institutional quality and performance. Greater transparency improves decision making by prospective students and encourages institutions to maintain high standards. Although these benefits cannot readily be expressed in monetary terms, the Department expects them to improve the functioning of the higher education marketplace.
Third, the final rule is expected to strengthen academic freedom, intellectual inquiry, and the free exchange of ideas. The Department believes that institutions providing an environment in which lawful viewpoints may be expressed and examined, faculty are evaluated without regard to viewpoint or ideology, and students are exposed to a range of scholarly perspectives are better positioned to fulfill the educational purposes recognized by the Higher
(
printed page 68698)
Education Act. While these educational benefits cannot be quantified, the Department considers them an important component of institutional quality and student learning.
Fourth, the final rule is expected to reduce regulatory uncertainty by more clearly distinguishing the Department's recognition criteria from accrediting agencies' own substantive accreditation standards. The Department expects that clearer recognition standards, streamlined procedures, and more transparent expectations will reduce unnecessary disputes, improve the efficiency of the recognition process, and allow both accrediting agencies and institutions to devote greater resources to educational quality rather than regulatory compliance. Although these benefits cannot be quantified, they are expected to improve the administration of the Federal recognition process over time.
Finally, the final rule will likely strengthen public confidence in the accreditation system. By emphasizing educational quality, lawful administration of accreditation standards, research integrity, objective measures of student outcomes, transparency, and institutional accountability, the Department expects the final rule to reinforce public confidence that accreditation serves students and taxpayers while respecting institutional diversity, including intellectual diversity, and mission. Although these effects are inherently difficult to quantify, they are central objectives of the proposed rule.

Application of Standards in Reaching Accreditation Decisions (§ 602.17(a)(1) and (2))
During negotiated rulemaking and the public comment period the Department received extensive feedback on the application of accreditation and preaccreditation standards related to student achievement and faculty. An accrediting agency must consider relevant institutional policies and practices in the context of its existing standards and the institution's mission. Where an agency has adopted standards addressing these matters, it must apply and enforce those standards consistently.

2. Regulatory Flexibility Act
This section considers the effects that the final rule may have on small entities in the Educational Sector as required by the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA, 5 U.S.C.
et seq.,
Pub. L. 96-354) as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (SBREFA). The purpose of the RFA is to establish as a principle of regulation that agencies should tailor regulatory and informational requirements to the size of entities, consistent with the objectives of a particular regulation and applicable statutes.
The RFA generally requires an agency to prepare a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) or any other statute unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a “significant impact on a substantial number of small entities.”
This final rule implements regulatory changes to realign the Secretary's criteria for recognition of accrediting agencies.
Congress has prohibited the Department from intervening in the curricular decisions of an institution or attempting to exert control over its faculty, administration, or academic programs. Instead, under the HEA, accrediting agencies oversee the quality and academic sufficiency of instructional programs at institutions participating in the title IV, HEA programs. Accrediting agencies are independent, membership-based organizations that review member institutions or programs to ensure they meet certain standards for academic quality and rigor.
The HEA requires the Secretary to establish criteria for determining whether an accrediting agency is a reliable authority, for purposes of the HEA and for other Federal purposes, on the quality of education or training offered by the institutions or programs that they accredit. Such criteria are required to include appropriate measures of student achievement. Consistent with statute, the Secretary has established regulations for recognition of accrediting agencies at
34 CFR part 602
and has revised these regulations periodically.
E.O. 14279
directed the Secretary to take several actions related to the recognition of accrediting agencies or associations by the Department. Some of these actions require changes to existing regulations. The goal of these regulatory changes is to realign the Secretary's criteria for recognition of accrediting agencies to promote high-quality, high value, and affordable education for students.
The Department estimates that the final rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of institutional accrediting agencies that meet the definition of small entities. However, the Department believes that the final rule will only indirectly impact institutions of higher education.
Description of, and, Where Feasible, an Estimate of the Number of Small Entities to Which the Regulations Will Apply
The Department believes that institutions of higher education are not directly regulated by the final rule and could only be indirectly impacted by actions accrediting agencies take in response to the final rule. For this reason, the Department does not examine the possible impact of the final rule on small entities that are institutions of higher education. The Department also notes that it is difficult to estimate the impact of the final rule on institutions of higher education that are small entities because accrediting agencies have wide discretion in how they implement the final changes, and
(
printed page 68704)
data on the impact of accreditation regulations on institutions are not available. Moreover, as explained in Section 5 of this RIA (“Net Budget Impact”), several of the final regulatory changes are likely to have offsetting revenue effects for institutions, including on institutions of higher education that are small entities. For example, institutions will be subject to new student outcome standards for recognition purposes, which could force some institutions to reform or close programs, negatively affecting their revenues. Policies aimed at increasing credit transfers for students could have similar negative revenue effects on small entities. On the other hand, the final rule includes several provisions meant to prevent accrediting agencies from unnecessarily restricting innovation in educational models, which should allow institutions—including small entities—greater operational flexibility, which could increase their revenue. The final reforms to increase new entrants and agency switching should also promote greater operational flexibility by creating a more favorable environment for institutions looking to innovate.
The group directly affected by the final rule is accrediting agencies. Most accrediting agencies are organized as nonprofit entities that are defined as “small entities” if they are independently owned and operated and not dominant in their field of operation. While dominance in accreditation is hard to determine for institutional accrediting agencies, as it currently stands, the Department believes programmatic accrediting agencies—that is, recognized agencies that accredit specific programs within an institution—very often have dominance in their field. This is because there are usually, at most only one or two, and in rare cases multiple, programmatic agencies that provide recognition for a given field or occupation, that is used not only for Federal programs, but also as for educational requirements related to professional licensure.
[20]
Therefore, we do not consider programmatic accrediting agencies to be small entities for the purposes of this analysis. This determination is consistent with the Department's past position on accrediting agency size standards.
The Department believes that institutional accrediting agencies, which function as gatekeepers to title IV, HEA program funds and are subject to many of the policy changes in the final rule, meet the standard for small entities. The Department considers these agencies to be “professional organizations” as classified under the North America Industry Classification System (813920). The SBA defines small professional organizations as businesses having less than $24 million in total annual revenue. Each accrediting agency recognized by the Department as institutional accrediting agencies report annual revenue below this threshold (Table 6.1).
To determine whether the final rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of institutional accrediting agencies, the Department uses information on the burden the final rule would impose on institutional accrediting agencies included in the Paperwork Reduction Act section of this final rule. The final rule is estimated to require 352 hours of labor per institutional accrediting agency to comply with the final regulations because institutional accrediting agencies will need to update their processes, data collection efforts, and reporting activities.
Using the median hourly wage for Education Administrators, Postsecondary (11-9033) from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics ($50.29 in 2025) and then doubling that figure to account for overhead costs and employee benefits, results in an average annual burden imposed on an institutional accrediting agency of $35,404.

Alternatives Considered (Small Entities)
It is the Department's general policy to minimize compliance costs and regulatory burden for all regulated entities, especially small entities, and to develop regulations that are consistent with statutory requirements. The Department considered other options and changes to the proposed rule intended to reduce compliance costs and administrative burden for small entities such as whether institutional accrediting agencies who meet the definition of small entities could have fewer reporting requirements, or exemptions from certain aspects of the regulation. Discussion
The purpose of the regulations at
34 CFR part 602
is to ensure that accrediting agencies are, for purposes of the HEA and other Federal purposes, reliable authorities regarding the quality of education or training offered by the institutions or programs that they accredit. Accreditation in the United States has generally involved non-governmental entities that develop quality criteria and conduct evaluations, primarily through peer review, to determine whether or not those criteria are met. Reliance on the recognized accrediting agencies' quality assurance function is one of the three main elements of oversight for the HEA's Federal student aid programs. In order for students to receive Federal student aid from the Department for postsecondary study, the institution must be accredited by an accrediting agency (or, for certain vocational institutions, approved by a State approval agency) recognized under these regulations, be authorized by the State in which the institution is located, and receive approval from the Department through a program participation agreement.
As of October 1, 2026, the Secretary recognized 50 accrediting agencies that
(
printed page 68706)
are independent, membership-based organizations designed to ensure students have access to qualified faculty, appropriate curriculum, and other support services. Of these 50 accrediting agencies recognized by the Secretary, 34 are institutional for title IV HEA purposes and 16 are solely programmatic. Institutional accrediting agencies accredit entire institutions of higher education, while programmatic accrediting agencies accredit specific educational programs within institutions that prepare students for entry into a profession, occupation, or vocation. The Paperwork Reduction Act section will use these figures in assessing burden. Additionally, we use the number of title IV eligible institutions noted in the Regulatory Impact Analysis as the basis for assessing institutional burden in the Paperwork Reduction Act section.
General Comments
Some commenters believed that the burden estimates provided in the NPRM did not properly account for one-time and recurring costs for institutions and accrediting agencies. Some examples cited were: revising standards, developing processes, collecting and analyzing information, training personnel and reviewers, conducting additional reviews, reporting, and maintaining new requirements. Some commenters made suggestions that the Department assess the full institutional cost of the proposed regulation.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees. The President's Executive Order specifically directed the Secretary of Education to take appropriate steps to reduce barriers that limit institutions in adopting practices that advance degree completion and new education models, as well as increasing the consistency, efficiency, and effectiveness of the accrediting agency recognition process, and streamlining the process for institutions to change accrediting agencies. Moreover, in doing this review directed by the Executive Order, the Department considered and reviewed the existing burden on accrediting agencies and institutions in the current regulations before considering additional changes to the existing requirements.
The final rule achieves the goals set forth in the Executive Order and further eliminates requirements that the Department identified as unnecessarily burdensome. These changes were proposed in negotiated rulemaking and included in the draft regulations that the negotiated rulemaking committee achieved consensus on.
This Paperwork Reduction Act analysis estimates the burden of both one-time implementation actions and any recurring requirements from new regulatory changes in the final rule.
Comments:
Some commenters suggested that the burden estimates in the NPRM rested on unstated assumptions about future institutional academic records and to what extent such records are provided as structured documents. (In considering this comment, the Department assumed that in referring to “structured documents,” the commenters were referring to electronic or physical documents that organize information using a predefined template, strict hierarchy, or markup or data schemas so that every piece of content appears in a predictable location and form.)
Discussion:
The burden hour estimates for this final rule are based on a review of past estimates for requirements in each section, currently approved information collections, and the degree to which the final rule adds to or changes existing requirements. Additionally, while the Department did consider that certain records, such as institutional records, would generally be in electronic form, it did not assume that all documents, such as academic transcripts, were structured documents in uniform formats across varying institutions. The discussion in this section and in the description of the changes in the preamble clearly identify the basis for the Department's estimates, and no assumptions have been left unstated.
Comments:
Several commenters noted that institutions are likely to already demonstrate compliance with some of the proposed regulations. They supported the new requirements in the recognition regulations and believed them to be best practices currently demonstrated by agencies or institutions. Other commenters suggested that the Department rely on institutions using their current practices rather than changing regulatory requirements for all.
Discussion:
The Department appreciates these comments and the support for the regulations. However, the Department declines to rely solely on an institution's current practices and has included in the recognition criteria in the final rule accrediting agency best practices that promote transparency and consistency across recognized accrediting agencies and the institutions and programs that they accredit.
Comments:
Several large institutions submitted comments stating their belief that the Department underestimated the burden on institutions of the new regulations on credit transfers and the costs of implementing the regulations, such as the cost of changes to institutional policies and student information systems that will be needed. One commenter stated that applying the same 300-hour estimate to institutions regardless of the scale and complexity of their transfer operations significantly understated the burden on many institutions and does not adequately reflect the resources necessary for implementation. Commenters asked the Department to re-assess burden estimates to include all aspects of implementation and consider the complexity of the size and operations of the school.
Discussion:
The Department disagrees with the commenters' statements that burden estimates did not consider changes to institutional policies and student information. As part of the NPRM, the Department published supplemental information documenting the burden analysis for transfer credits described in the Paperwork Reduction Act section.
The Department also declines to adjust the 300-hour burden estimate. We also note that 300 hours is an estimate, and we expect some institutions will incur more or less burden. The estimate is consistent with the Paperwork Reduction Act, which requires an estimate of burden based on the estimated number of responses multiplied by the estimated average hourly burden per respondent.
This action contains the following new information collection requirements and amendments to existing collections:
§ 600.11 Special Rules Regarding Institutional Accreditation or Preaccreditation.
Requirements
The final rule in § 600.11 will reduce burdensome requirements on institutions seeking to add or change recognized accrediting agencies. Currently, institutions are required to submit materials to the Department demonstrating a reasonable cause for changing accrediting agencies, and then wait for the Department's approval of the change in accrediting agency. The current regulations include several criteria for which the Secretary will not determine such change to be reasonable cause. Section 600.11 removes the approval step and the latter criteria unless the Secretary determines that the change is being sought to evade or circumvent a requirement of Federal law or regulation; avoid or delay enforcement or oversight by the
(
printed page 68707)
Department or an accrediting agency; obtain eligibility for title IV, HEA programs through misrepresentation or other unlawful means; or otherwise undermine the integrity of the title IV, HEA programs.
Institutions seeking accreditation from multiple recognized accrediting agencies will only be required to submit a brief, reasonable explanation to the Department for this request.
Additionally, the institution will be required to use all reasonable efforts to notify current students and recent graduates of any change of accrediting agency within 10 days.
Comments:
We received two comments disagreeing with the proposed changes to § 600.11 citing increased burden and documentation on institutions when seeking to change accrediting agencies.
Discussion:
The changes to § 600.11 in the final rule will not introduce new burden on institutions. Prior to the final rule the regulations in this section already required institutions to provide documentation to the Department when seeking to change accrediting agencies. The changes in the final rule will decrease the amount of documentation and justification that institutions will be required to submit to the Department and will eliminate the requirement to wait for the Department's approval before seeking to change recognized accrediting agencies.
Burden Calculation
In the Paperwork Reduction Act section of the NPRM, the Department noted that institutions will be required to submit a form with required information on switching accrediting agencies and that burden for this requirement will be assessed under a new OMB control number and will be made available for public comment prior to the rule becoming effective.
However, the Department has re-evaluated this position in the final rule and will not be requiring a new form for institutions changing accrediting agencies. Since this notification is currently required under prior regulations no burden calculation has been made for this change.
§ 602.3 What definitions apply to this part?
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.3 revises some key definitions and adds new definitions used in these regulations.
Burden Calculation
Accrediting agencies and institutions will be required to review the new definitions and update internal policies and procedures to ensure they are compliant with the new regulations. The Department estimates that it will take recognized accrediting agencies 20 hours and institutions 5 hours to review, update, and make any relevant changes not otherwise referenced in this section to be required to be in compliance with the regulations. The Department anticipates this will be a one-time burden.
§ 602.12 Accrediting Experience
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.12(a) requires that an agency seeking initial recognition demonstrate that it has sufficient accreditation experience prior to submitting an application for recognition.
Burden Calculation
Burden for the regulation is assessed elsewhere throughout the changes and in the burden estimates for requirements for recognition.
§ 602.14 Purpose and Organization
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.14 strengthens the fiscal and administrative requirements that a recognized agency must meet in order for an agency to demonstrate that it is “separate and independent” from any related, associated, or affiliated trade association or membership organization. Section 496(a)(3) of the HEA requires an accrediting agency to operate “separate and independent” of any related, associated, or affiliated trade association or membership organization unless that agency is categorized as having a voluntary membership of institutions or programs that utilize the agency's accreditation to access other Department or Federal programs. Section 496(b) of the HEA defines the term “separate and independent”.
Under the final rule, agencies subject to the “separate and independent” requirements are prohibited from any joint use of personnel, services, equipment, or facilities with a related, associated, or affiliated trade association or professional organization. In addition, such recognized agencies must establish and implement conflict of interest controls for each member of their decision-making body.
The final rule in § 602.14 will also require as part of the initial and renewal
(
printed page 68708)
of agency recognition process, an authorized representative of the agency to submit a signed statement certifying that it has met the requirements for being separate and independent. This certification must also include information regarding any complaints received during the current recognition period.
Burden Calculation
The change under § 602.14(b)(6) will require an authorized representative of the agency to submit a signed statement certifying that it has met the requirements to be “separate and independent.” The Department estimates that this change will take an agency five hours to complete the statement and obtain the necessary signature annually.
34 Institutional Accrediting Agencies × 5 Hours = 170 Burden Hours
§ 602.15 Administrative and Fiscal Responsibilities
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.15 will clarify that conflict of interest controls are an integral part of the administrative and fiscal capability criteria the Department uses for determining recognized accrediting agencies. Prior to this final rule, conflict of interest controls were not included in the administrative and fiscal responsibilities regulations. With this final rule, agencies will now be required to have conflict of interest controls.
Additionally, the final rule in § 602.15 will require training to be provided to agency representatives and staff, focusing on best practices and avoiding unnecessary costs. The final rule will also require an agency to cooperate with other agencies and the Department to develop common accreditation templates.
Burden Calculation
The Department estimates that it will take each accrediting agency 30 hours to create, review and update conflict of interest controls.
50 Accrediting Agencies × 30 Hours = 1,500 Burden Hours
Developing and conducting training for representatives and staff would create burden on accrediting agencies. We estimate it would take 18 hours for an agency to create or research appropriate training for their staff. The Department anticipates this will be an ongoing burden.
50 Accrediting Agencies × 18 Hours = 900 Burden Hours
§ 602.17 Application of Standards in Reaching Accreditation Decisions
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.17 will clarify expectations for agency review of student achievement and faculty-related standards and policies, including those addressing academic freedom and intellectual diversity. They will also encompass agency review of institutional cost/benefit analyses, educational objectives, student success, faculty performance and evaluation, facilities, academic freedom, and intellectual diversity.
The final rule is consistent with Section 496(a)(6)(A) of the HEA which states that no accrediting agency may be determined by the Secretary to be a reliable authority as to the quality of education or training offered or for other Federal purposes, unless the agency meets criteria established by the Secretary. The statute states that such criteria shall include appropriate measures of student achievement and require that an agency establish and apply review procedures throughout the accrediting process, including evaluation and withdrawal proceedings, which comply with due process procedures.
Comments
Some comments submitted by institutions mentioned the burden estimate for the cost/benefit analysis in § 602.17, which the Department estimated in the NPRM to be 750,150 burden hours across Title IV-participating institutions. Some commenters disagreed with the estimate, asserting it was severely underestimated while others expressed concern it was too high. Other comments stated the burden of the cost/benefit analysis could not be estimated due to lack of instruction on specific requirements of such analysis. One comment stated the Department omitted burden on institutions for § 602.17 entirely and only considered it for accrediting agencies.
Discussion
None of the comments received from institutions included suggestions to improve the accuracy of the estimates of the administrative burden that were proposed to this section. However, the Department re-evaluated the burden estimate for institutions under this section in response to the comments. The Department has revised its analysis of reporting burden for the changes in Section 602.17 of the final rule. The changes in this section address how accrediting agencies seeking recognition by the Department apply their standards and do not impose new requirements on institutions or programs, and the Department has removed calculation of institutional burden from the burden calculation below.
Burden Calculation
The regulations in § 602.17 that have already been in effect prior to the final rule require a recognized agency to have effective mechanisms for evaluating an institution's or a program's compliance with the agency's standards before reaching a decision to accredit or preaccredit the institution or program. Additionally, many agencies already have policies and procedures in place that are consistent with many of the requirements in this section of the final rule.
To comply with § 602.17, the Department estimates that all agencies will be required to review the final rule and assess whether or not their application of its current policies and procedures comply with the new requirements. As a result of this review, some agencies are likely to be required to make some changes to their policies and procedures, which will vary agency by agency. Based on the comments, we assume that most agencies currently do not review institutional cost/benefit analyses in the areas identified by the regulations. Thus, the estimate is an average amount of time across all agencies, with some agencies incurring more burden and some incurring less.
We estimate this would take an agency approximately 20 hours to review initial compliance with § 602.17.
50 Recognized agencies × 20 Hours = 1,000 Burden Hours
We estimate the change to existing policies and procedures would take an average of 40 hours; however, we do not estimate that the changes in this section would increase the overall time for an agency to review an institution or program. Thus, the estimate is an average amount of time to take steps to change policies across all agencies, with some agencies incurring more burden and some incurring less.
50 Accrediting agencies × 40 Hours = 2,000 Burden Hours

on non-binding arbitration language has been in effect since December 5, 2023; therefore, we do not estimate this change to create additional burden.
§ 602.21 Review of Standards
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.21 will streamline the prescriptive requirements in the prior regulations for an accrediting agency to maintain a comprehensive systematic program of review. Specifically, the final rule removes the requirements in paragraphs (b), (c), and (d) of § 602.21 that are not based on statute. Removing these paragraphs eliminates burdensome and complex regulations that are difficult for accrediting agencies to implement and difficult to enforce effectively and consistently. The final rule continues to retain the statutory requirement for accrediting agencies to regularly review their standards which, in totality, affords them the flexibility to innovate but also maintain essential requirements for a regular review process.
Burden Calculation
The Department estimates the changes to § 602.21 in the final rule will reduce annual burden on recognized accrediting agencies. The last time burden was assessed for this regulation under OMB Control Number 1840-0788 the Department estimated that reviewing standards would take approximately 12 hours to complete each year. In the NPRM, we estimated a reduction of 4 hours per agency. However, after reviewing the requirements in response to comments, we now estimate that the requirement will take 6 hours per agency to complete, a 50 percent reduction in annual burden compared to the prior requirements. The Department is adjusting the annual burden hours under OMB Control Number 1840-0788 accordingly.
§ 602.22 Substantive Changes and Other Reporting Requirements
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.22 will clarify, streamline, and reduce the types of situations that are defined in the agency's definition of substantive change.
Burden Calculation
The Department estimates that the changes to § 602.22 in the final rule will reduce burden on recognized institutional accrediting agencies. Under the final rule, the definition of substantive change will include a more precise set of situations, achieve a better balance of which changes require additional oversight, and provide deference to recognized accrediting agencies to make the decisions on the specific types of substantive changes they review and approve.
We estimate there will be a reduction of 16 burden hours per institutional agency annually.
34 Institutional Accrediting Agencies × 16 Hours = 544 less annual Burden Hours
§ 602.23 Operating Procedures All Agencies Must Have
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.23(c)(1) will include preaccredited institutions. Prior to the final rule, the regulations only required that recognized accrediting agencies review complaints received for accredited institutions.
The final rule in § 602.23(c)(3) will require agencies to also review conflicts of interest and require agencies to document actions when complaints about institutions are reviewed.
The final rule in § 602.23(d) will require that a recognized accrediting agency have operating procedures that ensure that institutions or programs it accredits will publicly disclose any action by the agency that triggers the enforcement timeline provision in § 602.20(a) or (b).
The final rule in § 602.23 will prevent recognized agencies from having policies that would require institutions or programs to act in violation of any Federal or State law. The agency will also be required to have internal controls to ensure compliance with antitrust laws.
The final rule in § 602.23(k) will require recognized agencies to have a timely procedure to accelerate the comprehensive accreditation process for an institution or program seeking initial accreditation.
Lastly, the final rule in § 602.23(l) will require recognized agencies to establish and maintain at least one structured mechanism through which currently enrolled students, employed staff, and employed faculty of accredited or preaccredited institutions or programs may communicate directly with the agency.
Burden Calculation
In 2019, the Department estimated that it would take 2 hours annually for each accrediting agency to comply with § 602.23. We now estimate that by adding these additional consumer protection provisions in the final rule, it would take each agency an additional two hours annually to comply.
50 Accrediting Agencies × 2 Hours = 100 Burden Hours
§ 602.24 Additional Procedures Certain Institutional Agencies Must Have
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.24 would codify the current practice of most agencies that a peer or independent site visitor accompany accrediting agency staff during on-site reviews, clarify when institutions must submit teach-out plans and agreements, and establish clear timelines and documentation expectations.
The final rule in § 602.24 will also enhance transparency and student support by requiring accrediting agencies to coordinate teach-outs, ensure transcript access and transfer pathways, and notify other agencies when cross-agency agreements are approved. Additionally, institutions will be required to update and publicly disclose comprehensive transfer of credit policies, adopt consistent criteria for evaluating comparable credits, prohibit discriminatory denials, and provide students with an appeals process.
(
printed page 68710)
Prior to this final rule, the regulations did not distinguish between the circumstances requiring institutions to provide teach-out plans versus teach-out agreements. Under the final rule, institutions will be required to submit a teach-out plan within 30 days when specified events occur, such as when an institution's certification status changes from full to provisional. On the other hand, teach-out agreements will be required within the same 30-day window when institutions experience triggering events that signal heightened operational risk, including financial concerns or adverse actions. To ensure institutions act promptly when they are unable to secure a teach-out agreement, the Department adds a new requirement mandating that institutions provide their accrediting agency and the State with documentation explaining why a teach-out agreement could not be secured within 30 days. In addition, institutions in this situation will be required to notify the Department, which may then require the institution to provide proof of financial protection to safeguard students in the event of closure.
Prior to the final rule, the regulations required institutional accrediting agencies to evaluate teach-out agreements based on elements that went beyond what the HEA requires, and provided insufficient contingency measures for institutions that closed. Under the final rule, accrediting agencies will be required to coordinate with institutions to secure teach-out agreements, review teach-out plans and agreements and confirm that students retain access to transcripts and transfer pathways. In addition, if a teach-out agreement includes a program or institution that is accredited by another recognized agency, the accrediting agency must notify the other accrediting agency of its approval.
Burden Calculation
The final rule will remove several overly prescriptive requirements that are not supported in the statutory framework. The removal of these requirements will decrease unnecessary burdens on institutional accrediting agencies and institutions. However, several other consumer protection provisions in § 602.24 will add burden on institutional accrediting agencies.
Requiring a peer or independent site visitor to accompany accrediting agency staff during on-site reviews will require some accrediting agencies to assign additional peer or independent site visitors to be present during site visits. As noted above, most agencies already have such a site visitor present during on-site reviews, and the Department estimates that codifying this practice in the regulations as a quality assurance criterion for all recognized agencies will only impact several agencies. Recognized accrediting agencies will also be required to request and review documents from institutions and maintain communication with institutions and State agencies, another common practice.
In the NPRM, the Department estimated that this new requirement would take approximately 470 hours for each agency and each institution to initially implement this provision of the final rule. However, the Department found that its analysis in the NPRM was incorrect because it mistakenly included burden for all institutions when the provisions in the final rule will only apply to recognized agencies. The Department also reassessed its estimates in the NPRM for the one-time burden on institutional agencies to implement this provision of the final rule.
To implement these new regulations, institutional accrediting agencies will be required to review and identify the scope of the new regulations (20 hours), amend policies and procedures (40 hours), train volunteers and staff (100 hours). The Department estimates that this will take approximately 160 hours per institutional accrediting agency.
§ 602.26 Notification of Accrediting Decisions
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.26 will make minor modifications to the requirements for accrediting agencies to report accrediting decisions to the Secretary. Recognized accrediting agencies will now be required to maintain a record of all actions taken against institutions or programs accredited by the agency on its website for a period of at least five years.
Burden Calculation
Prior to the final rule, Section 602.26 required recognized agencies to maintain on their website a clear record of all actions taken for each institution or program it accredits or preaccredits for a period of at least five years. The final rule provides additional transparency and consumer protections which adds burden to accrediting agencies. This additional burden includes requiring agencies to expand their monitoring and reporting processes. Agencies will need to review the new requirements and create a process to ensure their website is compliant with this proposed rule. Agencies may also have to update their systems or train staff to keep their website up to date with actions taken for each institution or program. We estimate this will add 100 burden hours per year.
100 Burden Hours × 50 Accrediting Agencies = 5,000 Burden Hours
§ 602.27 Other Information an Agency Must Provide the Department
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.27 will require more frequent updates of an agency's accredited and preaccredited institutions and programs to the Department's website directory. The proposed reporting requirements would require agencies to submit regular and timely updates throughout the year rather than an annual list.
Burden Calculation
Complying with these requirements in the final rule will require recognized accrediting agencies to expand their reporting processes to allow for more frequent reporting submissions to the Department. Agencies are already accustomed to reporting actions taken.
In 2023, the Department estimated that each website update would take an agency 20 minutes to complete. Under the final rule, we estimate that this will take an average of 2 hours per update. More frequent updates will also increase burden for this regulation. Before this final rule, accrediting agencies were required to submit an update to the Department's website directory once per year. Under the final regulation, agencies are required to submit regular and timely updates throughout the year.
If an agency updates the Department's website directory four times per year, this increases burden to 8 additional burden hours per agency per year.
50 Accrediting Agencies × 8 Hours = 400 Burden Hours
§ 602.28 Regard for Decisions of States and Other Accrediting Agencies
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.28 requires accrediting agencies to expand the function of reviewing the accreditation or preaccreditation of certain institutions and allow agencies to place institutions on a show cause or equivalent status. This change allows agencies to more precisely specify that programs, not just institutions, are subject to review by an agency when another recognized agency has initiated an adverse action or placed a program on probation or an equivalent status. The final rule will also expand the term “other recognized agencies” to include State and Federal oversight agencies to
(
printed page 68711)
provide increased accountability for institutions or programs subject to negative or adverse actions by those entities.
Burden Calculation
Complying with these new regulations will require agencies to expand their institutional review processes. We estimate this would require 30 additional burden hours per year.
50 Accrediting Agencies × 30 Hours = 1,500 Burden Hours
§ 602.30 Agency Applications and Reports To Be Submitted to the Department
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.30 will modernize how accrediting agencies submit applications and reports to the Department. The submission timeline and concurrent submission requirements are removed, and there is a new requirement for an accrediting agency to submit a written application to the Secretary if it seeks a contraction of scope. The final rule will also prohibit an accrediting agency from prematurely redacting business and other non-Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in its applications and reports submitted to the Department.
Burden Calculation
Section 602.30 will impose only a nominal amount of burden on recognized accrediting agencies. Prior to this final rule, there has been no requirement for an agency to apply for a contraction of scope. Based on historical trends, we estimate that fewer than 1 accrediting agency per year will apply for a contraction of scope.
In 2019, the Department estimated it would take 20 hours per expansion of scope application. However, since the requirements for contraction of scope are simply a notification and require less explanation and documentation than expansion, we estimate it would take only 1 hour to complete a contraction of scope application. If only 1 agency submits a contraction of scope application every 2 years this adds .5 burden hours per year.
.5 Accrediting Agencies × 1 Hour = .5 Total Burden Hours
§ 602.31 Procedures for Submitting Applications for Recognition and Renewal of Recognition
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.31 will change the application process for recognition or renewal of recognition to provide specific instructions and requirements based on scope of agency activities.
Specifically, under the change in the final rule, if institutions accredited by an agency receive a substantial portion of all Title IV, HEA program funds, institutional accrediting agencies seeking initial or renewed recognition will be required to submit a comprehensive application for recognition. When not designated for review, the institutional accrediting agency would submit an application demonstrating its adherence to the regulatory requirements. When submitting information to the Department, agencies are no longer required to redact certain information prior to submission.
Burden Calculation
The changes in the final rule to § 602.31 will reduce burden on accrediting agencies. In 2019, the Department estimated that accrediting agencies would require 285 additional hours of burden or 5.37 hours per agency. The Department estimates that removing these requirements eliminates 268.5 burden hours (5.37 hours * 50 agencies).
§ 602.32 Procedures for Review of an Expansion of Scope, a Contraction of Scope, Compliance Reports, or Increases in Headcount Enrollment
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.32 will revise procedures for expansions and contractions of scope, compliance reports, and increases in headcount. Specifically, under § 602.32(a)(1) and (2) of the final rule, the Department will consider applications for an expansion or contraction of an accrediting agency's scope only when submitted together with an application for recognition, unless Department staff, at their discretion, elect to review such a request independently.
For compliance reports, Department staff will complete their evaluation and a draft analysis. The draft, along with any materials received by the Department, will be sent to the agency identifying any potential areas of noncompliance. The agency will be invited to submit a written response within at least 45 days.
Under § 602.32(c), reports related to increases in headcount enrollment submitted pursuant to § 602.30(d) will be processed by the Department using the same procedures applicable to compliance reports.
Burden Calculation
The Department estimates there will be 12 agencies invited to respond to a written compliance report per year. We estimate this response would take an agency 15 hours to outline, draft, complete, and transmit it to the Department.
12 Accrediting Agencies × 15 Hours = 180 Burden Hours
§ 602.34 Advisory Committee Meetings
Requirements
The final rule in § 602.34 will require the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI) to review applications for contractions of scope. The Department also now requires that accrediting agencies post public notice of upcoming NACIQI reviews.
Burden Calculation
Under the final rule, agencies will be required to post notices of upcoming reviews to be completed by NACIQI. The Department estimates this will take 2 hours per agency per year to determine if notification is necessary and publish any relevant information.
50 Accrediting Agencies × 2 Hours = 100 Burden Hours
§ 668.43 Institutional and Programmatic Information
Requirements
The final rule in § 668.43(a)(11) will add an additional requirement to the information that institutions participating in the Federal student aid programs are required to provide to enrolled and prospective students. Specifically, the final rule will add an additional student consumer disclosure that requires institutions to inform students and prospective students of the timeline by which a transcript must be submitted for timely review for transfer of credit. This timeline must conclude prior to the student's enrollment, registration, or making a nonrefundable financial commitment, so that a prospective student will know how many credits that they have earned at other institutions will transfer to a new institution before he or she incurs cost and time at that institution.
Before the final rule, institutions were only required under this section to provide a description of the transfer of credit policies established by the institution, including a statement of the institution's current transfer of credit policies that included: any established criteria the institution uses regarding the transfer of credit earned at another institution and any types of institutions or sources from which the institution will not accept credits; a list of institutions with which the institution has established an articulation
(
printed page 68712)
agreement; and written criteria used to evaluate and award credit for prior learning experience including, but not limited to, service in the armed forces, paid or unpaid employment, or other demonstrated competency or learning.
The final rule in § 668.43(c) will also require that if an institution declines to award credit under its transfer of credit policy, the institution must provide a written rationale to the student as to why the transfer credit was not accepted and provide information on each course that did not result in transfer credit.
Burden Calculation
The final rule in § 668.43(a)(11) will require institutions to update their transfer of credit disclosure to include a timeline for submission of transcripts that meets the requirements of the new regulations. The Department notes that all institutions already have policies and procedures for submission of transcripts under their current transfer of credit policy. However, while this is not a new requirement, the Department acknowledges that some institutions may need to revise their timelines to comply with the new requirements. In calculating administrative burden with the new requirements, the Department assumes institutions will continue their current practices to receive transcripts and send their required disclosures and communications to students electronically.
In the NPRM, the Department estimated that this new requirement would take approximately 470 hours per institution to initially implement. After reviewing its prior analysis in response to the comments, the Department found that its analysis in the NPRM included burden associated with complying with existing requirements in addition to the new requirements in the final rule. The Department has revised its estimates, as explained below.
Institutions will be required to review the requirements and scope of the new regulations (5 hours), identify the scope of the new requirements (10 hours), and amend policies and procedures (25 hours). The Department estimates that this will take approximately 40 hours per institution one time.
The Department also reassessed its estimates for student reporting burden from its estimate in the NPRM. The analysis in the NPRM improperly identified the regulation as a new reporting requirement. Students seeking transfer of credits already submit transcripts from other institutions to new institutions and the new regulations do not change this practice or impose a new requirement on students. In fact, the new regulations will likely benefit students by ensuring that they do not unwittingly enroll at a new institution under the false presumption that the credits they earned at other institutions will be accepted toward a certificate or degree at that institution.

Special rules regarding institutional accreditation or preaccreditation.

Change of accrediting agencies.

Accreditation
means the status of public recognition that an accrediting agency grants to an institution or program that meets the agency's standards and requirements.
Accrediting agency or agency

Act

Adverse accrediting action or adverse action
means the denial, withdrawal, suspension, revocation, or termination of accreditation or preaccreditation, or any comparable accrediting action an agency may take against an institution or program.
Advisory Committee
means the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity.
Compliance report
means a written report that the Department requires an agency to file when the agency is found to be out of compliance to demonstrate that the agency has corrected deficiencies specified in the decision letter from the senior Department official or the Secretary. eligible institution
found in
34 CFR 600.2
.
Institutional accrediting agency

means a report that an agency is required to submit to Department staff when it is found to be substantially compliant. The report contains documentation to demonstrate that—
(i) The agency is implementing its current or corrected policies; or
(ii) The agency, which is compliant in practice, has updated its policies to align with those compliant practices.
Program
means a postsecondary educational program offered by an institution that leads to an academic or professional degree, certificate, or other recognized educational credential.
Programmatic accrediting agency
means an agency that accredits specific educational programs, including those that prepare students in specific academic disciplines or for entry into a profession, occupation, or vocation.
Recognition
means an unappealed determination by the senior Department official under § 602.36, or a determination by the Secretary on appeal under § 602.37, that an accrediting agency complies with the criteria for recognition listed in subpart B of this part and that the agency is effective in its application of those criteria. Related, associated, or affiliated trade association
means an organization that:

§ 602.20
Enforcement of standards.
(a) If the agency's review of an institution or program under any standard indicates that the institution or program is not in compliance with that standard, the agency must—
(1) Follow its written policy for notifying the institution or program of the finding of noncompliance;
(2) Provide the institution or program with a written timeline for coming into compliance that is reasonable, as determined by the agency's decision-making body, based on the nature of the finding, the stated mission, and educational objectives of the institution or program. The timeline may include intermediate checkpoints on the way to full compliance and must not exceed the lesser of four years or 150 percent of the—
(i) Length of the program in the case of a programmatic accrediting agency; or
(ii) Length of the longest program at the institution in the case of an institutional accrediting agency;
(3) Follow its written policies and procedures for granting a good cause extension that may exceed the standard timeframe described in paragraph (a)(2) of this section when such an extension is determined by the agency to be warranted; and
(4) Have a written policy to evaluate an institution's or program's progress in resolving the finding of noncompliance.
(b) Notwithstanding paragraph (a) of this section, the agency must have a policy for taking an immediate adverse action, and take such action, when the agency has determined that such action is warranted.
(c) If the institution or program does not bring itself into compliance within the period specified in paragraph (a) of this section, the agency must take adverse action against the institution or program, but may maintain the institution's or program's accreditation or preaccreditation until the institution or program has had reasonable time to complete the activities in its teach-out plan or to fulfill the obligations of any teach-out agreement to assist students in transferring or completing their programs.

20 U.S.C. 1099b(e)
. Any agency arbitration standard or policy must be nonbinding, except that both parties may agree to binding arbitration after a dispute arises on a case-by-case basis. If an agency has an arbitration policy or standard, it must:

(2) Ensure that the arbitration process is fair and impartial; and

34 CFR 668.14
,
668.15
,
668.16
,
668.41
, or
668.46
, but if, in the course of an agency's work, it identifies instances or potential instances of noncompliance with any of these requirements, it must notify the Department.

(h) The agency must have a policy for restoring accreditation (including retroactive restoration) in circumstances that the agency determines are appropriate, including if required by an applicable judicial decision.

Transfer of credit policies.

§ 602.25
Due process.
The agency must demonstrate that the procedures it uses throughout the accrediting process satisfy due process. The agency meets this requirement if the agency does the following:
(a) Provides adequate written specification of its requirements, including clear standards, for an institution or program to be accredited or preaccredited.
(b) Uses procedures that afford an institution or program a reasonable period of time to comply with the agency's requests for information and documents.
(c) Provides written specification of any deficiencies identified at the institution or program examined.
(d) Provides sufficient opportunity for a written response by an institution or program regarding any deficiencies identified by the agency, to be considered by the agency within a timeframe determined by the agency, and before any adverse action is taken.
(e) Notifies the institution or program in writing of any adverse accrediting action or an action to place the institution or program on probation or show cause. The notice describes the basis for the action.
(f) Provides an opportunity, upon written request of an institution or program, for the institution or program to appeal any adverse action prior to the action becoming final.
(1) The appeal must take place at a hearing before an appeals panel that—
(i) May not include current members of the agency's decision-making body that took the initial adverse action; and
(ii) Is subject to a conflict of interest policy.
(2) The agency must recognize the right of the institution or program to employ counsel to represent the institution or program during its appeal, including to make any presentation that the agency permits the institution or program to make on its own during the appeal.
(g) The agency notifies the institution or program in writing of the result of its appeal and the basis for that result.
(h)(1) The agency must provide for a process, in accordance with written procedures, through which an institution or program may, before the agency reaches a final adverse action decision, seek review of new financial information if all of the following conditions are met:
(i) The financial information was unavailable to the institution or program until after the decision subject to appeal was made.
(ii) The financial information is significant and bears materially on the financial deficiencies identified by the agency. The criteria of significance and materiality are determined by the agency.
(iii) The only remaining deficiency cited by the agency in support of a final adverse action decision is the institution's or program's failure to meet an agency standard pertaining to finances.
(2) An institution or program may seek the review of new financial information described in paragraph (h)(1) of this section only once and any determination by the agency made with respect to that review does not provide a basis for an appeal.

§ 602.30
Agency applications and reports to be submitted to the Department.
(a)
Applications for recognition or renewal of recognition.
An accrediting agency seeking initial or continued recognition must submit a written application to the Secretary. Each accrediting agency must submit an application for continued recognition at least once every five years, or within a shorter time period specified in the final recognition decision. The application must consist of—
(1) A statement of the agency's requested scope of recognition;
(2) Documentation that the agency complies with the criteria for recognition listed in subpart B of this part, including a copy of its policies and procedures manual and its accreditation standards; and
(3) Documentation of how an agency that includes or seeks to include distance education, correspondence courses, or direct assessment education in its scope of recognition applies its standards in evaluating programs and institutions it accredits that offer distance education or correspondence courses.
(b)
Applications for expansions or contractions of scope.
An agency seeking an expansion or contraction of scope by application must submit a written application to the Secretary. The application must—
(1) Specify the scope requested;
(2) Provide copies of any relevant standards, policies, or procedures developed and applied by the agency for its use in accrediting activities conducted within an expansion of scope proposed and documentation of the application of these standards, policies, or procedures; and
(3) Provide the materials required by § 602.32(a).
(c)
Compliance or monitoring reports.
If an agency is required to submit a compliance or monitoring report, it must do so within 30 days following the end of the period for achieving compliance as specified in the decision of the senior Department official or Secretary, as applicable.
(d)
Review following an increase in headcount enrollment.
If an agency that has notified the Secretary in writing of its change in scope to include distance education or correspondence courses in accordance with § 602.27(a)(4) reports an increase in headcount enrollment in accordance with § 602.19(e) for an institution it accredits, or if the Department notifies the agency of such an increase at one of the agency's accredited institutions, the agency must, within 45 days of reporting the increase or receiving notice of the increase from the Department, as applicable, submit a report explaining—
(1) How the agency evaluates the capacity of the institutions or programs it accredits to accommodate significant growth in enrollment and to maintain education quality;
(2) The specific circumstances regarding the growth at the institution or program that triggered the review and the results of any evaluation conducted by the agency; and
(3) Any other information that the agency deems appropriate to demonstrate the effective application of the criteria for recognition or that the Department may require.
(e)
Consent to sharing of information.
By submitting an application for recognition, the agency authorizes Department staff throughout the application process and during any period of recognition—
(1) To observe its site visits to one or more of the institutions or programs it accredits or preaccredits, on an announced or unannounced basis;
(2) To visit locations where agency activities such as training, review and evaluation panel meetings, and decision meetings take place, on an announced or unannounced basis;
(3) To obtain copies of all documents the staff deems necessary to complete its review of the agency; and
(4) To gain access to agency records, personnel, and facilities.
(f)
Public availability of agency records obtained by the Department.
(1) The Secretary's processing and decision-making on requests for public disclosure of agency materials reviewed under this part are governed by the Freedom of Information Act,
5 U.S.C. 552
; the Trade Secrets Act,
18 U.S.C. 1905
; the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended,
5 U.S.C. 552a
;
5 U.S.C. chapter 10
(Federal Advisory Committees); and all other applicable laws. In recognition proceedings, agencies must, before submission to the Department—
(i) Redact the names and any other personally identifiable information about individual students and any other individuals who are not agents of the agency or of an institution or program the agency is reviewing;
(ii) Redact the personal addresses, personal telephone numbers, personal email addresses, Social Security numbers, and any other personally identifiable information regarding individuals who are acting as agents of the agency or of an institution or program under review;
(iii) Designate, but not redact, all business information within agency submissions that the agency believes would be exempt from disclosure under exemption 4 of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA),
5 U.S.C. 552(b)(4)
. A blanket designation of all information contained within a submission, or of a category of documents, as meeting this exemption will not be considered a good faith effort and will be disregarded; and
(

(3) The Secretary processes FOIA requests in accordance with
34 CFR part 5
and makes all documents provided to the Advisory Committee available to the public.

Length of submissions.

§ 602.31
Procedures for submitting applications for recognition and renewal of recognition.
(a) An agency must submit an application for initial or renewal of recognition and meet the submission deadline set by the Department. The type of application that must be submitted and the scope and priority of the Department's review are determined by the Department as follows:
(1) If the total title IV, HEA program funds received by the institutions accredited by an accrediting agency constitute a substantial portion, as determined by the Secretary, of the total funds awarded for the title IV, HEA programs, the agency must submit a comprehensive application that addresses the agency's compliance with all criteria in subpart B of this part.
(2) If an institutional accrediting agency is not identified for review under paragraph (a)(1) of this section, the agency must submit an application that addresses the agency's compliance with §§ 602.15, 602.16, 602.17, 602.19, and 602.20 and any other criteria as directed by Department staff. (3) If the Secretary determines that an agency or its officers or directors have been the subject of legal actions, complaints, or other compliance issues that individually or in the aggregate raise substantial concerns regarding the agency's compliance with this part, the agency must submit a comprehensive application that addresses the agency's compliance with all criteria in subpart B of this part.
(4) If an agency is exclusively a programmatic accrediting agency and is not identified for review under paragraph (a)(3) of this section, the agency must submit an application that addresses the agency's compliance with the criteria in §§ 602.10, 602.16, 602.17, 602.19, and 602.20 and any other criteria as directed by Department staff. (5) An agency described in paragraph (a)(2) or (4) of this section must submit a comprehensive application that addresses the agency's compliance with all criteria in subpart B of this part at least once every third cycle of review.
(6) The Department may also consider factors that include but are not limited to—
(i) Whether any of its accredited institutions closed without an approved teach-out agreement in place when such an agreement was required in accordance with § 602.24(c);

(iii) Whether the agency has significantly increased the number of institutions or programs it accredits; and
(iv) The number and severity of noncompliant findings identified in the senior Department official's or Secretary's decision letter for the agency's application for renewal of recognition.
(7) An agency submitting an application for initial recognition must submit a comprehensive application that addresses the agency's compliance with all criteria in subpart B of this part.
(b)(1) After receipt of an agency's application for initial or renewal of recognition, Department staff publishes a notice in the
Federal Register
stating that the agency submitted an application and inviting the public to provide information concerning the performance of the agency to assist the Department in determining whether the agency meets the criteria for recognition and establishing a deadline for receipt of information from the public.
(2) Within 10 business days after publication of the notice described in paragraph (b)(1) of this section, the agency must publish the request for information on the agency's website to include instructions on how the public can submit information in response to the request.

(1) A site visit, which may be conducted as an in-person visit at the agency, including an on-site file review of agency documents, or through a virtual file review of agency documents. (3) Review of complaints or legal actions involving the agency; and

Senior Department official's decision.

To calculate growth rates in exclusively online programs, we used IPEDS data on distance enrollment from 2012-13 to 2024-25. We then computed the annual percent change in the share of students in exclusively online programs for each year from 2013-14 to 2024-25. We acknowledge that between 2019 and 2020, the distance enrollment IPEDS file changed from Fall Enrollment to 12-Month FTE enrollment; however, the change in definition does not influence our estimates because we compute annual percent changes, and we exclude this year due to its overlap with the Covid-19 pandemic. To calculate growth rates in short-term programs, we used IPEDS data on student charges for vocational programs from 2014-15 to 2023-24, the most recent year of data available at the time when this analysis was conducted. We defined short term programs as programs that were at least 600 clock hours in length but shorter than 12 months. After identifying this set of programs, we then merged this IPEDS data to Department data on title IV enrollments using common OPEID6, credential level, and 6-digit CIP codes.
