ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Putnam Museum and Science Center intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of unassociated funerary objects and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Hailey Lorenzen,
(
printed page 68545)
Putnam Museum and Science Center, 1717 W 12th Street, Davenport, IA 52804, email
hlorenzen@putnam.org
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the Putnam Museum and Science Center and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 28 cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 28 unassociated funerary objects are ceramics, beads, a spear point, and shell cups and digging tools. This number includes 11 unassociated funerary objects that are missing, including one ceramic, one lot of shell beads, and nine shell cups.
In 1926, Warren K. Moorehead removed one shell cup and two ceramics from burial contexts in the Etowah Mound group in Bartow County, GA, and donated them to the Museum the same year.
In 1904, Clarence B. Moore removed one lot of shell beads, two shell cups, and one spear point from burials in a mound on the north end of Creighton Island, McIntosh County, GA, and one lot of shell beads, and 20 shell cups and digging tools from burial contexts in Bourbon Field, Sapelo Island, in McIntosh County, GA and donated them to the Museum the same year.
The Putnam Museum and Science Center has no evidence of potentially hazardous substances being used to treat any of the unassociated funerary objects.
Determinations
The Putnam Museum and Science Center has determined that:
The 28 unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and The Muscogee (Creek) Nation.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 30, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the Putnam Museum and Science Center must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The Putnam Museum and Science Center is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.
Authority:
Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,
25 U.S.C. 3004
and the implementing regulations,
43 CFR 10.9
.

Human remains representing, at least, two individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present with them. The remains were donated to the historical society's collection prior to 1990 by an unknown individual and were likely collected in Kankakee county or the surrounding area. Records indicate no known hazardous substances were used on these items.

The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the University of Rhode Island, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Unaffiliated “Box 1,” “Box 2,” “Box 3”
Human remains representing, at least, six individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The University of Rhode Island presently holds no documentation within its archives indicating geographic origin, archaeological context, or acquisition history for the remains housed in “Box 1,” “Box 2,” and “Box 3.” Based on a 2022 osteological inventory, human remains representing, at least, seven individuals were present. At the request of consulting parties, non-invasive analysis of the skeletal remains was conducted on campus in 2026 to confirm Native American ancestry, at which time the remains of one individual determined not to be of Native American ancestry were removed, bringing the minimum number of individuals to six.
Consultation
Invitations to consult were sent to the Mashantucket Pequot Indian Tribe (2026); Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe (2026); Mohegan Tribe of Indians of Connecticut (2026); Narragansett Indian Tribe (2026); and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) (2026).
An invitation to consult was also sent to the Assonet Band of the Wampanoag Nation (2024), a non-federally recognized Indian group.
The Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe; Mohegan Tribe of Indians of Connecticut; Narragansett Indian Tribe; and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) responded to the invitation and participated in consultation.
Cultural Affiliation
The following types of information about the cultural affiliation of the human remains in this notice are available: biological, expert opinion, Native American traditional knowledge. The information, including the results of consultation, identified:
1. No earlier group connected to the human remains.
2. No Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization connected to the human remains.
3. No relationship of shared group identity between the earlier group and the Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization that can be reasonably traced through time.
Determinations
The University of Rhode Island has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of six individuals of Native American ancestry.
No known lineal descendant who can trace ancestry to the human remains in this notice has been identified.
No Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation to the human remains described in this notice has been clearly or reasonably identified.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Upon request, repatriation of the human remains described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 30, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the University of Rhode Island must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains are considered a single request and not competing requests. The University of Rhode Island is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.

Abstract of Information Available
Barrington Case
Human remains representing, at least, one individual has been identified. The three associated funerary objects are glass vials containing soil samples. This individual was transferred by local law enforcement to the Rhode Island State Crime Laboratory at the University of Rhode Island sometime between 1958 and 1969 for evaluation. Once determined not to be of forensic concern, the Ancestor was transferred to the University's Department of Sociology & Anthropology. The only surviving documentation is a note by Dr. Harold C. Harrison, Director of the Crime Lab reading: “Bones from Medical Examiner's Office—Barrington case—age, sex, and as much as possible including time (approx. since death).” Efforts to obtain additional information through the Barrington Police Department, the Rhode Island Medical Examiner's Office, and the Crime Lab archives have yielded no results. During osteological and cultural assessments in the 1980s, URI faculty determined that the individual was of Native American descent, and that brass staining on the
(
printed page 68548)
remains suggests a post-contact context. Three small glass vials containing soil, presumed to have been collected from the burial context, are included with the individual and recorded as associated funerary objects.

Abstract of Information Available
Dartmouth Case
Human remains representing, at least, three individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The only original documentation associated with this case is a handwritten label on the original storage box reading “Dartmouth Material.” Based on the box label and research practices of the 1980s, when we believe these Ancestors arrived at the University, the remains are reasonably determined to have originated from Dartmouth, Massachusetts, though this cannot be confirmed. At the request of consulting parties, non-invasive analysis of the skeletal remains was conducted on campus in 2026 to confirm Native American ancestry, at which time the individuals were deemed to be very likely of Native American descent.
Luce Collection (Ridge Hill Site, Main Street Site, Kenoza Camp Site):
Human remains representing, at least, three individuals have been identified. The one associated funerary object is animal bone. The Luce Collection originates from archaeological work conducted by Fred and Thera Luce and was originally curated at the Buttonwoods Museum in Haverhill, Massachusetts. In the mid-1980s, several Ancestors were loaned to the University of Rhode Island for osteological study, as documented in a 1986 report by Thomas Mahlstedt of the Massachusetts Historical Commission. Some Ancestors were returned to Buttonwoods, while others remained at URI. In 2022, URI staff confirmed that Buttonwoods retained two Ancestors whose remains were intermingled with those held by the University. In consultation with the Museum, it was agreed that the Ancestors from the Ridge Hill, Main Street, and Kenoza Camp sites would be reunited under URI's legal control. The Buttonwoods Museum retains all original documentation, including notebooks and photographs, from the Luce Collection.
Ridge Hill Site (19-ES-41; Luce #4907):
On June 16, 1932, an eroding cairn burial containing one individual was recorded in Groveland, Massachusetts, near the Merrimack River. Fred Luce and assistants documented the burial and removed approximately sixty cobblestones to expose the remains, which were later examined by the local Medical Examiner and identified as Native American. Luce retained the remains and they entered into the Luce Collection.
Main Street Site (19-ES-559; Luce #3292):
On June 12, 1915, workmen excavating a water line trench in Groveland uncovered a burial. The remains were recovered by a local resident and documented by Thera Luce in her register of excavations, thus becoming part of the Luce Collection.
Kenoza Camp Site (19-ES-27; Luce #2398):
In August 1913, during road construction near Kenoza Lake and Winnekenni Park in Haverhill, workmen encountered a burial later attributed to site 19-ES-27. Fred Luce purchased these skeletal remains from the workmen and they subsequently
(
printed page 68552)
became part of the Luce Collection. Cultural materials were found in the area, but documentation indicates this burial contained no associated funerary objects.

Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.

The University of Rhode Island has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of six individuals of Native American ancestry.
The one object described in this notice is reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah).

2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 30, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the University of Rhode Island must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. The University of Rhode Island is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation, Division of Archaeology (TDEC-DOA) has completed an inventory of human remains from an unknown site in Polk County, TN, and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains in this notice may occur on or after November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice to Phillip R. Hodge, Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation, Division of Archaeology (TDEC-DOA), 1216 Foster Avenue, Cole Building #3, Nashville, TN 37243, email
Phil.Hodge@tn.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the TDEC-DOA, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing, at least, two individuals were donated to TDEC-DOA in 2026 by a private citizen. The donor reported that her father removed the remains from an unknown site location along the Hiwassee River in Polk County during the early 20th century. There is glue present on the jaw of one of the individuals. During consultation, it was determined that the glue would remain to prevent further damage to the remains. There are no other known exposures to hazardous substances or treatments.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains described in this notice.
Determinations
The TCED-DOA has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of, at least, two individuals of Native American ancestry.
There is a connection between the human remains described in this notice and the Cherokee Nation; Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians; The Muscogee (Creek) Nation; and the United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians in Oklahoma.
(
printed page 68546)
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 30, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the TDEC-DOA must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains are considered a single request and not competing requests. The TDEC-DOA is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.

In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Birmingham Museum of Art (BMA) intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of unassociated funerary objects, sacred objects, and/or objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:

ADDRESSES:

.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the BMA, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of information Available
A total of five cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is a miniature totem pole carved of walrus ivory. The one object of cultural patrimony is a spoon. The three sacred objects/objects of cultural patrimony are one harpoon head, one harpoon point,
(
printed page 68550)
and one spear point. The items were collected on unknown dates from unknown locations, possibly in the Arctic and Subarctic. The miniature totem pole was collected by Thyrza Hamilton Orr of Birmingham, Alabama on an unknown date before 1971. Orr gifted the item to the BMA in 1971. The miniature totem pole is documented in museum records as Inupiat or Tlingit or Haida. The spoon was collected by Dr. Noble Ashworth Endicott, Jr. and Dr. Wilma Jean Gunter Endicott sometime prior to 1991. The Endicotts donated the item to the BMA in 1991. The spoon is documented in museum records as Inupiat. The harpoon head, harpoon point, and spear point were collected by Axel Rasmussen, who served as superintendent of schools in Wrangell, Alaska from 1926 to 1938, and in Skagway from 1938 until his death in 1945. In 1948 the Portland Museum of Art purchased the entire Rasmussen Collection. BMA purchased the items in 1956. The three items are documented in museum records as Inupiat.
BMA has no knowledge of any potentially hazardous substances used to treat the cultural items. However, no testing has occurred.
Determinations
The BMA has determined that:
The one unassociated funerary object described in this notice is reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary object has been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
The one object of cultural patrimony described in this notice has ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision), according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
The three sacred objects/objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice are, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization, specific ceremonial objects needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, and have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision).
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Native Village of Barrow Inupiat Traditional Government.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 30, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the BMA must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The BMA is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.

Abstract of Information Available
Based on the information available, human remains representing, at least, two individuals have been reasonably identified. The one adult (likely female) and one subadult (likely male) arrived at UM prior to 1991 and were assigned University of Montana Forensic Collection (UMFC) accession number UMFC 50. The 18 associated funerary objects are two unmodified copper wire bracelets, one copper wire bracelet with linear marks, and 15 machine twisted copper wire bracelets (two of which are double strand). The adult individual was reported as wearing these 18 bracelets on the forearm at the time of discovery. It is unknown whether or how the two individuals were connected. To date, their geographic place of origin and history of how they came to be at UM remains unknown and to the best of UM's knowledge there is no recorded use of hazardous substances to treat the human remains or associated funerary objects.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
UM has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of two individuals of Native American ancestry.
The 18 objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation, Montana.

Abstract of Information Available
A total of nine cultural items, identified as Honoko'a Gulch items “Lots 1-9,” have been requested for repatriation by the Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice. The nine unassociated funerary objects include carved ki'i (stick images), 'ipu 'aina (refuse bowls), nae (feather cape fragment), ki'i wahine (carved female figure), hair helmet/wig, and a boar tusk bracelet. These items were collected by David Forbes, Friedrich Haenisch, and William Wagner in 1905 from the Honoko'a Gulch Cave Complex, in an area known as Forbes Cave, in Kawaihae, Hawai'i Island, and received by BPBM in 1907.
Determinations
The BPBM has determined that:
The nine unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed with or near human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Mary Kawena Pukui Cultural Preservation Society; the 'Ohana Diamond; the 'Ohana Kekumano; the 'Ohana Keohokālole; the 'Ohana Olds; and the Temple of Lono (collectively, the Pukui Society Group) and Aloha 'Āina o Hawai'i, Inc.
The Mary Kawena Pukui Cultural Preservation Society; the 'Ohana Diamond; the 'Ohana Kekumano; the 'Ohana Keohokālole; the 'Ohana Olds; and the Temple of Lono (collectively, the Pukui Society Group) have the closest cultural affiliation and are the most appropriate requestors for these unassociated funerary objects.

Abstract of Information Available
A total of one cultural item have been requested for repatriation. The one sacred object is a shield. This shield was collected ty Finlay Ross (1847-1933) and donated to the WSCHM in 1939 by his widow, Ella Fuller Ross. This shield is associated with the Anadarko Affair, also known as the Battle of the Wichita
(
printed page 68556)
Agency, a conflict between the Comanche and Kiowa tribes against the Agency. A 1930 article published in the “Wichita Beacon” newspaper mentioning both the shield and battle stated, “The battle at the Wichita agency is commemorated by a beautiful round shield. . . belonging to Mr. Finlay Ross.” The article further states that Ross “took it from the Comanche village after it was captured by the calvary . . . .” This provenance is further supported by the WSCHM accession ledger, stating, “Shield captured at battle . . . Anadarko Indian Territory between US Troops, Civilians, and Comanche Indians August 22, 1874.” The WSCHM records indicate no known hazardous substances used to treat the item.

The WSCHM has determined that:
The one sacred object described in this notice is a specific ceremonial object needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe.

DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:

kent.johnson@cortland.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the SUNY Cortland Sociology/Anthropology Department, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing, at least, six individuals have been identified. The, at least, 94 bags (of various sizes) of associated funerary objects include seeds, shell fragments, rock fragments, charred wood fragments, soil, non-human animal bone fragments, and plant fragments. At minimum, six individuals and their belongings were brought to SUNY Cortland by Dr. Ellie McDowell-Loudan in around the year 2010. The individuals and their belongings had been in the possession of the widow of an avocational archaeologist, thought to be Stephen J. Petrovsky. After his passing, his widow brought the individuals and their belongings to Dr. McDowell-Loudan at
(
printed page 68543)
SUNY Cortland. It is unknown when and from where the individuals were removed, but Mr. Petrovsky lived in and primarily excavated in and around Susquehannock lands in the 1970s, so it is believed the individuals were removed from a location in Susquehanna County, PA or Broome or Tioga County, NY. The individuals and their belongings were discovered in the archaeology lab at SUNY Cortland several years after Dr. McDowell-Loudan's retirement, at which time they were moved to a secure location within the SUNY Cortland Sociology/Anthropology Department.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
The SUNY Cortland Sociology/Anthropology Department has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of, at least, six individuals of Native American ancestry.
The, at least, 94 bags of objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Onondaga Nation.

ADDRESSES

Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 30, 2026. A. Overview of Information Collection
Title of Information Collection:
Financial Documentation for the HUGS Recipient Portal.
OMB Approval Number:
2535-New.
Type of Request:
New.
Form Number:
N/A.
Description of the need for the information and proposed use:
HUD is implementing the HUGS Recipient Portal to strengthen its oversight and stewardship of Federal grant funds and improve visibility into the use of those funds. The proposed information collection would require recipients of covered HUD grant awards to submit financial and supporting documentation associated with grant expenditures through the Recipient Portal. This may include: invoices and vendor billings; proof of payment and disbursement records; payroll or cost allocation documentation; subrecipient cost documentation; invoices for vendor and subcontractor spending made by the recipient and the subrecipient and other supporting documentation identified by HUD and described in the regulations. HUD will use the information to substantiate expenditures, support monitoring and oversight activities, assess financial and compliance risks, and identify transactions or patterns that may warrant additional review. HUD will publish forthcoming implementation guidance that will provide additional details regarding the submission of financial documentation through the HUGS Recipient Portal, including details on scope and applicability, the Recipient Portal, submission frequency, required financial and supporting documentation, privacy safeguards, and additional resources.
This information collection aligns with cross-government priorities to strengthen stewardship of Federal funds and better identify and address potential fraud, waste, and abuse in a timely manner. The information collection is also supported by several key provisions of
Part 200 of Title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(
2 CFR 200
):
2 CFR 200.208
(Specific conditions) authorizes Federal agencies to impose additional requirements, including requiring additional or more detailed record production and financial reports, when appropriate.
2 CFR 200.302
(Financial management) requires recipients to maintain records identifying the amount, source, and expenditure of Federal funds and to support records with source documentation.
2 CFR 200.328
(Financial reporting) requires Federal agencies and pass-through entities to collect financial reports no less than annually and no more than quarterly unless a specific condition has been implemented in accordance with
2 CFR 200.208
.
2 CFR 200.334
(Record retention requirements) requires recipients and subrecipients to retain Federal award records, including financial records and supporting documentation, generally for three years following submission of the final financial report; and
2 CFR 200.337
(Access to records) provides Federal agencies and their authorized representatives the right of access to any records of the recipient or subrecipient that are pertinent to a Federal award for audits, site visits, or any other official use.
The Recipient Portal is not a reaction to an individual incident of fraud, waste, abuse, or noncompliance, though there are well-reported incidents across HUD programs. However, HUD usually does not find these issues until well after the fact, so there is a need for proactive monitoring that this information collection will allow. HUD also clarifies that this information collection will not impact existing
(
printed page 68541)
reimbursement or draw-down processes; required financial and supporting documentation will be submitted on a quarterly basis, not prior to the disbursement or voucher payment.
HUD has considered feedback, including concerns that HUGS duplicates existing oversight requirements and recommendations that it be limited only to certain grantees through a risk-based approach. However, while HUD already has important controls, including payment systems, program reporting, audits, and monitoring, these mechanisms were developed for different purposes and do not provide a consistent Department-wide view of supporting transactions and documentation. The proposed collection supports expenditure substantiation, monitoring, risk assessment, and stewardship of Federal funds by providing a more complete understanding of how award funds are spent. Over time, HUD anticipates that this collection and its broader grants modernization efforts may allow existing financial monitoring collections or processes to be consolidated or replaced where appropriate.
HUD also received feedback on the burden estimate and has updated the calculation accordingly. Recipients are already required to maintain financial records and supporting source documentation associated with their Federal awards as established in
2 CFR 200
. The proposed collection generally requires submission of applicable records recipients maintain in the ordinary course of administering those awards; it does not require recipients to create a new financial analysis, recalculate expenditures, or manipulate the underlying financial information into a new format solely for submission to HUD. HUD recognizes, however, that identifying, organizing, digitizing where necessary, and submitting applicable documentation through the Recipient Portal requires administrative effort and that this effort may vary by recipient and program. Therefore, clear, proactive communication is essential. HUD is preparing for full engagement with grantees and industry and has engaged a technical assistance provider to guide grantees through the transition with hands-on support and training. After consideration, HUD has determined that the documents that HUD seeks through HUGS are authorized by existing law as described above.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106744; File No. SR-CboeBYX-2026-039]
October 27, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 15, 2026, Cboe BYX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “BYX”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Exchange filed the proposal as a “non-controversial” proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
3
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
4
]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe BYX Exchange, Inc. (“BYX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to amend Rule 11.1(a) to adopt a Start Time order instruction, based on the Start Time instruction adopted by its affiliated exchange, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“EDGX”). The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​byx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 11.1(a) to adopt a “Start Time” order instruction that would permit a User to designate, in thirty-minute increments prior to the commencement of Regular Trading Hours,
[
5
]
the time at which an order entered prior to Regular Trading Hours becomes eligible for execution. The proposed rule change is based on EDGX Rule 11.1(a)(2),
[
6
]
but the Exchange is proposing to adopt only the Start Time instruction and related provisions. The Exchange intends to implement the proposed rule change on December 7, 2026, in coordination with the implementation of the Start Time instruction on EDGX, so that Members have access to consistent order handling functionality across the Cboe-affiliated equities exchanges.
Current Rule
Under current Rule 11.1(a), Users may enter orders into the System from 6:00 a.m. until 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time (“ET”).
[
7
]
Orders entered between 6:00 a.m. and 7:00 a.m. are not eligible for execution until the start of the Early Trading Session,
[
8
]
Pre-Opening Session,
[
9
]
or Regular Trading Hours, depending on the Time in Force
[
10
]
selected by the User. At the commencement of the Early Trading Session, orders entered between 6:00 a.m. and 7:00 a.m. are handled in time sequence, beginning with the order with the oldest time stamp, and are placed on the BYX Book, routed, cancelled, or executed in accordance with the terms of the order. The current rule therefore provides a single, fixed point (the commencement of the Early Trading Session at 7:00 a.m.) at which orders entered prior to the Early Trading Session become eligible for execution, and does not permit a User to designate a later point prior to Regular Trading Hours at which an order becomes eligible.
Current Rule 11.1(a) also provides that the Exchange will not accept the following orders prior to 7:00 a.m.: BYX Post Only Orders,
[
11
]
ISOs,
[
12
]
BYX Market Orders
[
13
]
other than those with a Time in Force of Regular Hours Only or Stop Orders,
[
14
]
Minimum Quantity Orders
[
15
]
that also include a Time in Force of Regular Hours Only, RPI Orders,
[
16
]
and all orders with a Time in Force of IOC
[
17
]
or FOK.
[
18
]
Proposed Start Time Instruction
The Exchange proposes to amend the time-sequencing provision so that it is no longer limited to orders entered between 6:00 a.m. and 7:00 a.m., and to adopt a flexible Start Time instruction. As proposed, in addition to the Time in Force, a User may also designate a start time for an order (“Start Time”). Start Times may be designated in thirty-minute increments and must be set to a time prior to the commencement of Regular Trading Hours; Start Times may not be designated during Regular Trading Hours. This language is substantively identical to the Start Time language in EDGX Rule 11.1(a)(2), which replaced EDGX's 4:00 a.m. Start and 7:00 a.m. Start designations with the same flexible and uniform framework. Because orders on the Exchange are not eligible for execution prior to the commencement of the Early Trading Session at 7:00 a.m., the earliest
(
printed page 68572)
Start Time that will have practical effect is 7:00 a.m., and the latest permissible Start Time is 9:00 a.m.
The Exchange also proposes to provide that, at the commencement of the Early Trading Session and at each Start Time, orders will be handled in time sequence, beginning with the order with the oldest time stamp, and will be placed on the BYX Book, routed, cancelled, or executed in accordance with the terms of the order. This provision is consistent with the sequencing provision adopted by EDGX, which provides that, at each Start Time, orders will be handled in time sequence beginning with the oldest time stamp.
[
19
]
The Exchange proposes to retain the reference to the commencement of the Early Trading Session so that orders that are entered prior to the Early Trading Session without a Start Time designation continue to become eligible for execution, in time sequence, at the commencement of the Early Trading Session, as they do today.
For example, a User may enter an order at 6:15 a.m. with a Start Time of 8:00 a.m. That order would be accepted but would not be eligible for execution until 8:00 a.m., at which time it would be handled in time sequence with all other orders designated with an 8:00 a.m. Start Time, beginning with the order with the oldest time stamp, and would be placed on the BYX Book, routed, cancelled, or executed in accordance with its terms.
Order Acceptance Restrictions
The Exchange proposes to amend the order acceptance restrictions in Rule 11.1(a) so that they apply prior to 7:00 a.m. or, if later, prior to the order's designated Start Time. The Exchange is not proposing any change to the categories of orders subject to these restrictions, which will continue to be: BYX Post Only Orders, ISOs, BYX Market Orders other than those with a Time in Force of Regular Hours Only or Stop Orders, Minimum Quantity Orders that also include a Time in Force of Regular Hours Only, RPI Orders, and all orders with a Time in Force of IOC or FOK. The Exchange is also retaining the existing 7:00 a.m. threshold. Under the proposal, an order in one of these categories designated with a Start Time later than 7:00 a.m. will not be accepted prior to its Start Time. Today, the Exchange does not accept these orders before 7:00 a.m., when orders first become eligible for execution. Tying the restrictions to an order's designated Start Time applies the same approach to the more flexible Start Time framework, so that these orders are not accepted before the point at which the order may execute. EDGX similarly ties its order acceptance restrictions to the period before orders become eligible for execution, which on EDGX is the Order Acceptance Queueing Time.
[
20
]
The Exchange is not proposing to change its order entry window, which will continue to begin at 6:00 a.m., or the Time in Force instructions available to Users. Orders entered prior to the Early Trading Session without a Start Time designation will continue to become eligible for execution at the start of the Early Trading Session, Pre-Opening Session, or Regular Trading Hours, depending on the Time in Force selected by the User. Use of the Start Time instruction is optional.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
21
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
22
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5) requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes the proposed Start Time instruction removes impediments to and perfects the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system because it replaces the single fixed point at which orders entered prior to the Early Trading Session become eligible for execution with a flexible and uniform framework. Under that framework, Members may control the time at which their orders become eligible for execution prior to Regular Trading Hours. The Commission approved the same Start Time framework for EDGX, which replaced EDGX's 4:00 a.m. Start and 7:00 a.m. Start construct.
[
23
]
The Start Time instruction provides Members with additional flexibility to manage the timing of their order flow in the period before Regular Trading Hours. This includes aligning order eligibility with anticipated market conditions or with their own trading strategies, without requiring Members to manually enter orders at a particular time.
The Exchange believes the proposed time-sequencing provision promotes just and equitable principles of trade and protects investors because orders that become eligible at the commencement of the Early Trading Session or at a given Start Time will be handled in a transparent and objective manner, in time sequence beginning with the order with the oldest time stamp. This is the same manner in which orders are handled today at the commencement of the Early Trading Session, and it is consistent with the sequencing provision approved for EDGX.
The Exchange believes that tying the existing order acceptance restrictions to the later of 7:00 a.m. or the order's designated Start Time protects investors and the public interest. The proposal preserves the existing categories of restricted orders and the existing 7:00 a.m. threshold. It applies those restrictions consistently to orders that will not be eligible for execution until a later Start Time, ensuring that order types that are not suitable for queueing are not accepted before the order may execute. The proposed rule change does not loosen any existing restriction.
The proposed rule change also promotes consistency across the Cboe-affiliated equities exchanges, which reduces complexity for Members that access multiple Cboe-affiliated exchanges and fosters cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities. The proposed rule change does not permit unfair discrimination because the Start Time instruction will be available to all Members on the same terms, and its use is optional.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance
(
printed page 68573)
of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange does not believe the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intramarket competition because the Start Time instruction will be available to all Members on an equal and non-discriminatory basis, and its use is optional. The Exchange does not believe the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intermarket competition because it is based on a rule that the Commission approved for EDGX, and it is designed to provide Members with consistent order handling functionality across the Cboe-affiliated equities exchanges rather than to address any competitive issue. Other exchanges are free to adopt similar functionality.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not:
A. significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest;
B. impose any significant burden on competition; and
C. become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
24
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
25
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-CboeBYX-2026-039 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeBYX-2026-039. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeBYX-2026-039 and should be submitted on or before November 20, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
26
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106743; File No. SR-NYSEAMER-2026-96]
October 27, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 21, 2026, NYSE American LLC (“NYSE American” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to modify Rule 900ByRDs (Applicability; Definitions), Rule 910ByRDs (Determination of the Settlement Price), Rule 915ByRDs (Criteria for Underlying Securities), Rule 916ByRDs (Withdrawal of Approval of Underlying Securities), Rule 958ByRDs (Maximum Bid-Ask Differentials), Rule 980ByRDs (Automatic Exercise of Binary Return Derivatives) and Rule 928.1NYP (Price Reasonability Checks—Orders and Quotes) with respect to the trading of Binary Return Derivatives (“ByRDs”) on the Exchange. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to modify Rule 900ByRDs (Applicability; Definitions), Rule 910ByRDs (Determination of the Settlement Price), Rule 915ByRDs (Criteria for Underlying Securities), Rule 916ByRDs (Withdrawal of Approval of Underlying Securities), Rule 958ByRDs (Maximum Bid-Ask Differentials), Rule 980ByRDs (Automatic Exercise of Binary Return Derivatives) and Rule 928.1NYP (Price Reasonability Checks—Orders and Quotes) with respect to trading of ByRDs on the Exchange. More specifically, the Exchange proposes to use the closing price of the security underlying a ByRD options contract as reported by the primary listing market (“Closing Price”) in place of using the “composite price” volume weighted average price (“VWAP”) to determine the settlement price of the ByRD options contract on the date of expiration and adopt a new initial and continued listing criteria for ByRDs whose underlying security is an individual stock. The Exchange also proposes to eliminate settlement price rounding practices, instead redefining Finish High ByRDs to return the settlement amount if the underlying security closes at or above the strike price.
(
printed page 68564)
Overview of ByRDs
[
3
]
ByRDs
[
4
]
are European-style option contracts on individual stocks, exchange-traded funds (“ETFs”) and Index-Linked Securities that have a fixed return in cash based on a set strike price; satisfy specified listing criteria;
[
5
]
and are auto-exercised at expiration pursuant to the Rules of the Options Clearing Corporation (the “OCC”).
[
6
]
ByRDs are binary options and, as such, differ from traditional options traded on U.S. options exchanges by providing a discontinuous or non-linear payout. The payout of a ByRD options contract is an amount contingent upon the occurrence of the option being in- or at-the-money at expiration rather than the degree to which the option is in-the-money.
[
7
]
An in-the-money ByRD options contract will pay a fixed sum at expiration regardless of the magnitude of the difference between the option's strike price and the settlement price.
[
8
]
A “Finish High” ByRD (equivalent to a call option) returns $100 per contract if the settlement price of the underlying security is above the strike price at expiration, and a “Finish Low” ByRD (equivalent to a put option) returns $100 per contract if the settlement price of the underlying security is below the strike price at expiration.
[
9
]
Currently, Rule 910ByRDs(a) provides that the Exchange will use the “composite price” VWAP during regular trading hours for the entire business day of their expiration, or, in the case of an option contract expiring on a day that is not a business day, the entire business day immediately preceding the expiration date. The rule further provides that to calculate the VWAP, the Exchange would use composite prices during regular trading hours as reported by industry price vendors.
[
10
]
If the security underlying a ByRDs option contract does not trade or is unavailable during regular trading hours at expiration, the settlement price may be fixed pursuant to the OCC's rules on a basis that the OCC believes is appropriate under the circumstances, including using the last sale price during regular trading hours on the most recent trading day for which a last sale price is available.
[
11
]
Exchange rules also currently provide that the settlement price is calculated such that it will always round up $.01 in those instances when the settlement price exactly equals an expiring strike price.
[
12
]
For example, if the calculated settlement price is $20.00, and there are expiring ByRDs Finish High and Finish Low contracts with a strike price of $20.00, the settlement price is rounded up to $20.01 so that the Finish High options will pay off. The effect of rounding is to have long $20.00 strike Finish High holders receiving $100.00 and long $20.00 strike Finish Low holders receiving $0. Absent this rounding, a participant may potentially have a position that appears to guarantee a pay-off of $100 at expiration but would instead receive $0. For example, if an investor holds both a $20.00 strike Finish High contract and a $20.00 strike Finish Low contract, the investor will receive $0 if the settlement price was calculated to exactly equal the $20.00 strike price. Although the risk of the settlement price equaling the strike price is small, the Exchange believes that this could cause problems both for hedging and explaining to investors what would happen in the unusual circumstance where the settlement price matched the strike price of an expiring ByRDs option contract exactly. This rounding method ensures that either the Finish High or the Finish Low ByRDs option contracts will always pay off at expiration. The Exchange believes this results in less opportunity for investor confusion and less uncertainty for participants as a whole.
Proposed Rule Change
The purpose of the proposed rule change is to determine the settlement price of a ByRDs options contract by using the underlying security's Closing Price, in place of using the security's composite price VWAP on the day of expiration. In connection with the proposed rule change, the Exchange proposes the following changes to certain of the rules that permit the listing and trading of ByRDs.

In connection with this change, the Exchange also proposes to delete Rule 900ByRDs(b)(4) in its entirety and renumber current Rule 900ByRDs(b)(5) and current Rule 900ByRDs(b)(6) (while also implementing minor language changes to current Rule 900ByRDs(b)(6) to further specify that the ByRDs settlement amount is a fixed amount in cash equal to $100) as Rule 900ByRDs(b)(4) and Rule 900ByRDs(b)(5), respectively.

As proposed, the revised sentence would be as follows: “The Exchange will use the closing price of the security underlying the Binary Return Derivative as reported by the primary listing market on the business day of their expiration, or, in the case of an option contract expiring on a day that is not a business day, the business day immediately preceding the expiration date as reported by industry price vendors.”

The Exchange believes not requiring Market Makers to continuously enter quotations in their appointed ByRDs class is appropriate because Market Maker appointments apply at the underlying security level, and a Market Maker appointed in an underlying security is therefore automatically appointed in that security's corresponding ByRDs option contract as well, regardless of whether the Market Maker has chosen to participate in that product. At expiration, they pay a completely flat, fixed return of exactly $100.00 per contract if they finish in-the-money or at-the-money, regardless of whether the stock clears the strike price by one penny or one hundred dollars; If they finish out-of-the-money, they pay $0.00. The Exchange believes adopting the Closing Price to determine the settlement price of an expiring ByRDs option contract has several benefits and is appropriate for four reasons. First, the Closing Price is considered the most carefully determined price of the day. The Closing Price is determined by a call auction process run by the underlying security's primary listing exchange, which allows market participants to participate in real-time price discovery. It represents the consensus value after a full day of price discovery, with maximum participation from all market participants. Second, auctions are the among the most transparent parts of the market. Primary listings markets disseminate auction information frequently during a prescribed period of time, providing transparency to all market participants. This real-time flow of data—including indicative prices, imbalances, and matched volumes—gives all participants equal visibility in where the market is heading before the price is set. Third, Closing Prices (especially in highly-liquid securities such as those that qualify for ByRDs listings) are stable and not susceptible to manipulation. Because the Closing Price is set through a structured, transparent, rules-based auction aggregating broad order flow, it is far less susceptible to end-of-day price manipulation than other point-in-time benchmarks. Closing auction mechanisms are designed to make Closing Prices more reliable and less vulnerable to manipulation, providing a more robust and manipulation-resistant closing price discovery mechanism that reflects true supply and demand. Fourth, there is a concentration of liquidity to determine the Closing Price. Closing auctions within U.S. equity markets have grown significantly—in 2026, they have matched just over $100 billion per day and accounted for 9.4% of total notional value traded.

When ByRDs were designed, the Exchange noted that by using a VWAP a trader may “smooth” the average price paid or realized for a large position. Specifically, the VWAP for a given underlying security means the sum of the dollar value of trades reported to the Consolidated Tape (price multiplied by number of shares traded) divided by the total number of shares traded during the entire last day of trading on the business day of their expiration. The concern at the time was that a single closing price could be more susceptible to manipulation, and that smoothing over a full day of trading would produce a more representative settlement value. The Exchange believes that rationale has been substantially overtaken by market structure developments over the last 2 decades, and that the Closing Price is now a superior alternative. For one, a VWAP settlement requires aggregating all trades reported to the Consolidated Tape across the entire trading day. This creates several practical problems: it depends on data vendor accuracy and timeliness, it requires handling of out-of-sequence and late reported trades (which can distort the calculation), and it is not a number any participant can observe in real time. By contrast, the closing price from the primary listing market is a single, publicly observable, instantaneous value produced by a supervised exchange auction process, available immediately and unambiguously at 4:00 p.m. Second, a full-day VWAP creates hedging complexity and mismatch. Because ByRDs currently settle on the full-day VWAP, a holder trying to hedge a ByRDs position on expiration day cannot do so cleanly—their hedge would need to track the cumulative weighted average of all trades from open to close, which shifts continuously throughout the day in ways that are difficult to replicate. A closing-price settlement, by contrast, would allow hedgers to concentrate their activity in the closing auction, which is exactly what participants in standard listed equity options already do. This alignment with standard options hedging practice would reduce friction and basis risk. The Exchange acknowledges that for cash-settled options generally, settlement based on the Closing Price may concentrate the unwinding of hedge positions in the
(
printed page 68567)
closing auction, which adds a layer of mechanical flow that can amplify volatility. The Exchange believes, however, that this consideration does not raise significant concerns with respect to ByRDs, for the following reasons. First, ByRDs are subject to comparatively low position limits. Pursuant to Rule 904ByRDs, Binary Return Derivatives on each underlying security are subject to a position limit of 25,000 contracts on the same side of the market. This is the lowest position limit applicable to any options product under Rule 904, Commentary .07(e). The Exchange believes that this limit constrains the size of any hedge position that a market participant could be required to unwind at expiration. Second, the need to unwind positions in the underlying security at or near expiration is not a new risk introduced by closing-price settlement. Such activity was equally present under the VWAP settlement methodology when ByRDs were initially approved. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the proposal does not introduce a new category of hedging activity. Third, the universe of eligible underlying securities is highly liquid. As set forth in Rule 915ByRDs, Commentary .01, an underlying security must satisfy heightened eligibility requirements, including a minimum market capitalization of $290 billion and a minimum average daily trading value of $10 million in the primary listing market's closing auction. In light of these requirements, the Exchange believes that any hedge unwinding at the close can be absorbed by the market without undue price impact. Lastly, VWAP is more susceptible to intraday manipulation than a supervised closing auction. This is somewhat counterintuitive given the original rationale for VWAP, but it is well-supported. “Marking the close”—where participants deliberately transact in the final period to move the VWAP toward a favorable settlement—is classified as market manipulation. Because VWAP is computed from all Consolidated Tape prints throughout the day, large coordinated order flow at any point during the session can shift the VWAP in ways that are difficult to detect in real time. A closing auction, by contrast, is a supervised, transparent, single-price process with published imbalance information that regulators and surveillance systems can monitor closely.

Specifically, as noted above, the Exchange proposes to amend Rule 915ByRDs, Commentary .01, to add a new eligibility requirement for the initial listing of a ByRDs option contract on an underlying stock. Proposed Rule 915ByRDs, Commentary .01(vi) would provide that to be eligible for an initial listing, individual stocks “maintain an average daily trading value in the primary listing exchange's closing auction of at least $10 million over the prior six months.”

The proposed new eligibility requirement would apply to the initial and continued listing of ETFs and Section 107 Securities also as the current rule provides that to be eligible for an initial listing of a ByRDs option contract, an ETF or Section 107 Security must meet the criteria for individual stocks set forth in Rule 915ByRDs, Commentary .01. Additionally, the proposed increase to the minimum market capitalization requirement, from $40 billion to $290 billion, would limit the number of underlying securities that would be eligible for an initial listing of a ByRDs option contract.
[

]
Applying both the amended ByRDs listing liquidity thresholds and the newly-proposed auction liquidity threshold to eligible listed securities yields 100 eligible ByRDs underliers, as opposed to the 305 eligible ByRDs underliers without the newly proposed criteria. The median closing auction value traded across these 100 eligible securities is $92.5 million per day, based on a recent review conducted by the Exchange.
The Exchange believes the proposed new eligibility requirement makes using Closing Price to determine the settlement price less susceptible to manipulation. Because the Closing Price is set through a single, centralized auction that consolidates the full day's residual buying and selling interest into one print, influencing that price requires trading against the entire pool of auction liquidity rather than a thin, point-in-time quote. At the liquidity levels required by proposed new Rule 915ByRDs, Commentary .01(vi), a participant seeking to move the close by any meaningful amount would have to commit substantial capital against prevailing order flow and absorb the offsetting interest of other participants, all within a brief and closely observed window. The closing auction's transparency compounds that burden: with indicative prices, imbalances, and matched volumes disseminated in real time, a distortive order becomes visible to the market and tends to draw offsetting liquidity that both counters it and further stabilizes the Closing Price. The economic cost and ready detectability of such conduct, together with the deep and growing liquidity of U.S. closing auctions described above, make the closing auction a robust and manipulation-resistant basis for determining ByRDs settlement prices.
Similarly, the Exchange believes eliminating the settlement price rounding convention is reasonable and appropriate because it removes an unnecessary and artificial adjustment to price data that is no longer needed to achieve its intended purpose. Under the current rules, the Settlement Price is rounded up $0.01 whenever it would otherwise exactly match the strike price of an expiring ByRDs option contract, solely to ensure that a Finish High contract pays off rather than leaving both the Finish High and Finish Low contracts unexercised. However, because Finish High ByRDs as proposed would be defined to pay off whenever the underlying security closes at or above the strike price—a category that already includes an exact match—this outcome is achieved automatically by the definition itself, without requiring any adjustment of the reported price.
The Exchange believes that removing the rounding convention has several benefits. First, it allows the Settlement Price to reflect the underlying security's actual, unadjusted Closing Price, rather than an artificial value that may not correspond to any price at which the security actually traded or was reported. This promotes transparency and consistency between the Settlement Price used for ByRDs and the Closing Price used elsewhere for the same underlying security. Second, it would simplify the rule structure by resolving the at-the-money scenario through the proposed payout definitions of a Finish High ByRD and a Finish Low ByRD, rather than through a separate, purpose-built rounding mechanism layered on top of such rules. Lastly, it would eliminate any potential investor
(
printed page 68568)
confusion that could arise from a reported Settlement Price that differs by $0.01 from the security's actual closing price for no economic reason other than avoiding a tie. For these reasons, the Exchange believes the proposed change is consistent with accurately and transparently determining ByRDs settlement outcomes and does not disadvantage either side of an expiring Finish High or Finish Low ByRDs option contract.

Specifically, the Exchange believes that adopting the Closing Price to determine the settlement price of an expiring ByRDs option contract would increase participation among investors to trade in binary options given the importance of the closing auction on primary listing markets and, as discussed above, would reduce the hedging friction and basis risk associated with the current full-day VWAP methodology by aligning ByRDs settlement with the closing-auction hedging practices already standard among listed options market participants, a benefit that also furthers the protection of investors by reducing the difficulty of explaining and managing settlement risk for ByRDs holders. The NYSE closing auction remains the largest liquidity event in the U.S. equity market. The closing price produced by these auctions reflects a deep concentration of institutional and retail order flow precisely calibrated to produce a single, authoritative reference price, and thereby remove any impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market.
The Exchange believes the proposal to adopt the Closing Price to determine the settlement price of an expiring ByRDs option contract would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market for several reasons. First, the Closing Price is considered the most carefully determined price of the day as it is determined by a call auction process run by the underlying security's primary listing exchange, which allows market participants to participate in real-time price discovery. Second, primary listing markets disseminate auction information frequently during a prescribed period of time, providing transparency to all market participants. This real-time flow of data gives all participants equal visibility in where the market is heading before the price is set. Third, closing prices (especially in highly-liquid securities such as those that qualify for ByRDs listings) are stable and not susceptible to manipulation. Because the Closing Price is set through a structured, transparent, rules-based auction aggregating broad order flow, it is far less susceptible to end-of-day price manipulation than other point-in-time benchmarks consistent with the Section 6(b)(5) requirement that exchange rules be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices. By contrast, because VWAP is computed by aggregating trades reported to the Consolidated Tape across the entire trading day, it can be moved by coordinated trading at any point during the session in ways that are difficult to detect in real time, a vulnerability the proposed change eliminates by settling ByRDs against a single, supervised auction print instead. Closing auction mechanisms are designed to make Closing Prices more reliable and less vulnerable to manipulation, providing a more robust and manipulation-resistant closing price discovery mechanism that reflects true supply and demand. Lastly, closing auctions within U.S. equity markets have grown significantly. This concentration of liquidity makes closing auctions an especially efficient execution point, as large orders can be filled with minimal price impact.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system because it would determine the settlement price of a ByRDs option contract using the Closing Price of the underlying security at expiration, while also reinforcing the resistance of that settlement price to manipulation. The Closing Price is a carefully designed, rules-based reference anchored to a closing auction process: transparent, liquidity-rich, resistant to manipulation, and widely trusted. Using it to settle an expiring ByRDs option contract further perfects the mechanism of a free and open market because it would yield a settlement price that reflects the most recent and reliable market information available. The proposed rule change also furthers the Act's objective of fostering cooperation and coordination among persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities by relying directly on the auction process conducted by the underlying security's primary listing market rather than requiring the Exchange to independently construct a settlement value. The Exchange does not believe that using Closing Price to determine the settlement price of a ByRDs option contract at expiration would render the marketplace for such options more susceptible to manipulative practices. The Exchange notes that, as discussed above, the Commission has recognized the robustness of closing auction liquidity in an analogous context, granting the Chicago Mercantile Exchange conditional exemptive relief to use a closing, rather than opening, price to settle certain cash-settled single-stock futures based in part on the growth of closing auction volumes and the use of official closing prices in other products, which the Exchange believes further supports the reliability of the Closing Price as a settlement benchmark for ByRDs.
